artigo.texto: This year's Congressional Black Caucus Annual Legislative Conference, which wraps Sunday, has taken on a different feel than its usual college homecoming vibe. The event, which has drawn thousands of attendees to Washington, took on a more serious tone with briefings and conversations focused on artificial intelligence opportunities and regulation amid escalating concern about threats posed by the technology. "I stand 100%, and so does the CBC on regulation," CBC Vice Chair Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., told CNBC. "I think we need guardrails, I think we need transparency, I think we need to prepare and protect the community from the potential ills that come with it." Carter said at least 60 of the 62 members of the CBC would vote for a bill to regulate artificial intelligence, creating guardrails and placing guidelines on human safety. He added that competition with China should not be a factor in any legislation. "I'm not going to run and race with China, they're not doing it the right way. They are not protecting communities," he said. "Our race should be enhanced innovation, advanced technology, while we simultaneously protect the rights of the American people." The CBC is an influential group whose members include 29% of Democrats in the U.S. House. As Democrats aim to take control of the House in November's midterm election, the caucus's standing could rise. The CBC's tackling of AI came amid the backdrop of Open AI becoming the latest company to report an incident where AI agents conducted what they call 'concerning model behavior,' It's one of a growing number of so called 'jailbreaks,' the slang term for when models bypass guidelines and perform unauthorized actions. "The message they wanted me to bring is how we can do this in a way that protects our communities but do not put us in a position to lose in a national security race," said X. Eyee, an AI expert and Army veteran, who spoke with CBC members about striking a balance between putting boundaries on the technology without inhibiting innovation. "To do that, it does require addressing some of these areas where algorithms are being used with little boundaries around them." Carter said he is talking with voters about how important the upcoming midterm elections are for AI regulation. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., this month asked that the House stay in session to find a way to legislate AI safeguards. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., after President Donald Trump called AI-safety concerns a "hoax," countered that "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people." "They're not bringing it to the floor because I'm not sure that they want the regulation that we want," Carter said of Republican House leadership. "I've heard them say pump the breaks. I've heard them say let's let innovation handle it on its own, but we can't afford to do that." With AI skepticism high in the caucus, the AI and tech industries also showed up for the CBC's Washington gathering. Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick touted the economic benefits of data centers and the AI buildout they power. Meta is building the Hyperion data center project in Louisiana, and its hyperscaler rivals, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, are all also in the data center expansion race. "Technology and AI are the economic revolution of our generation," Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., a former CBC chair who now leads its technology committee, told CNBC. "That means that as Black Americans, we cannot allow this innovation to pass us by." Horsford spoke about the importance of helping shape the energy-intensive AI buildout on a panel with Exelon CEO Calvin Butler. Exelon provides power and grid services for the Philadelphia, Chicago, Baltimore, and Washington areas, and Butler said he is having continuing conversations with lawmakers about the potential impact on energy prices and residents' quality of life. "AI is a real conversation because people are trying to figure out where they fit in and can have a voice," Butler told CNBC. "What they are saying is we can't sit on the sidelines and let our constituents be impacted, and you as energy companies have a role in helping us solve this problem." Data centers, the CBC and redistricting The debate over AI regulation and data centers took on greater urgency because congressional redistricting could affect CBC members. The Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais will make creating "minority-majority" districts difficult and have major ramifications for the 2028 election and 2030 census, according to the Harvard Kennedy School. CBC Chair Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., estimated earlier this year that as many as 19 seats held by CBC members are at risk due to redistricting. Carter said that while that number is lower now after court challenges to redistricting plans, the impact on the Black community remains. "This is not just about congressmen," he said. "This is about school boards. This is about legislative seats." Horsford echoed concerns about threats to minority representation in Congress. "This has never been about protecting any one district, and it is absolutely not about protecting one party or another," he said. "It's about protecting the voters' right to pick their representatives, and not the representatives being able to pick which voters they serve. And as long as we keep that at the center of the work, then we're honoring what our democracy is supposed to be about."

artigo.texto:
Por que a China está menos preocupada com alertas sobre IA? Entenda
Pesquisa da Morgan Stanley mostra que 80% dos chineses usam IA semanalmente, contra 54% nos EUA, refletindo visões opostas sobre a tecnologia
Ao contrário do que ocorre nos Estados Unidos, ninguém na China parece estar abertamente preocupado com a perspectiva de a humanidade ser destruída pela inteligência artificial em breve.
Lá, os cidadãos acessam serviços do governo local por meio de funcionários digitais movidos por IA; estudantes recebem feedback instantâneo sobre tarefas escritas ao enviar uma foto; e hóspedes de hotéis retiram encomendas entregues à sua porta por robôs.
A ampla adoção da IA na China atual ressalta o quanto o país abraçou a nova tecnologia. Uma pesquisa da Morgan Stanley divulgada na segunda-feira revelou que 80% dos entrevistados chineses usavam IA pelo menos semanalmente, superando em muito os 54% registrados nos EUA.
Mesmo enquanto executivos de tecnologia e pesquisadores americanos pedem uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento da IA citando sua ameaça existencial à humanidade, o público chinês permaneceu comparativamente impassível.
"Esta tecnologia foi criada para servir à humanidade", disse Xu Jingyuan, 22 anos, estudante de administração de Pequim. "Não devemos vê-la como algo a temer, mas como algo que traz mais comodidades às nossas vidas."
Ele disse que o governo é "absolutamente capaz" de gerenciar seus riscos.
Os comentários de Xu ecoaram os de várias pessoas com quem a CNN conversou nesta semana, refletindo uma divisão nas atitudes em relação à IA na sociedade chinesa e americana, bem como diferentes níveis de confiança na capacidade dos respectivos governos de lidar com as ameaças potenciais representadas pela tecnologia.
"Nos EUA, há uma percepção geral do público de que, sem denúncias, grandes corporações poderiam escapar da responsabilização ou do escrutínio devido à fraca supervisão governamental", disse Lian Jye Su, analista-chefe da empresa de pesquisa tecnológica Omdia.
"Já na China, acredito que existe uma confiança muito forte por parte do público de que, se qualquer m*erda acontecer, o governo vai intervir."
Analistas também apontam diferenças na exposição à IA, no discurso público em torno da tecnologia e no contexto cultural e histórico mais amplo como possíveis explicações para essa divisão.
Em uma pesquisa da empresa de pesquisa de marketing Ipsos realizada no início deste ano, 83% dos entrevistados chineses consideraram produtos ou serviços baseados em IA empolgantes, enquanto apenas 33% dos entrevistados nos EUA sentiram o mesmo.
Enquanto isso, outra pesquisa da consultoria de marketing Edelman mostrou que 86% dos entrevistados na China afirmaram confiar em seu próprio governo para fazer o que é certo, em comparação com apenas 39% nos EUA.
Uma diferença marcante entre as duas nações é o sistema político.

artigo.texto: Data centers: Brasil precisa resolver o gargalo da infraestrutura elétrica Em artigo à CNN Infra, João Carlos de Oliveira Mello alerta que, se conexão à rede demorar, investimentos podem procurar outros destinos A inteligência artificial colocou os data centers no centro de uma disputa global por investimentos. Países capazes de oferecer energia competitiva, segurança de suprimento, conectividade e regras previsíveis terão vantagem na economia digital. O Brasil reúne atributos importantes nessa corrida, em especial uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável. Porém, hoje há um descompasso entre a velocidade dos investimentos digitais e a expansão da infraestrutura necessária para atendê-los. Um data center pode entrar em operação em cerca de dois anos. Os reforços na estrutura do sistema de transmissão podem exigir de cinco a sete anos. Para projetos que disputam capital em escala global, essa diferença é decisiva. Se a conexão à rede demora, o investimento procura outro destino. O problema não está na falta de energia. O Brasil dispõe de grande potencial de geração renovável, mas enfrenta restrições na rede, tanto para escoar a produção quanto para conectar novas cargas. A chegada de empreendimentos que demandam centenas de megawatts e alta confiabilidade exige que o planejamento elétrico incorpore uma realidade que muda rapidamente. O país passou a adotar regras mais rigorosas para o acesso ao sistema de transmissão. O objetivo é legítimo: impedir que agentes sem projetos consistentes reservem uma capacidade escassa para fins especulativos. A questão é encontrar o equilíbrio. Garantias financeiras elevadas, exigidas quando ainda existem definições importantes sobre o empreendimento, podem afastar também investidores com projetos sólidos. A regulação precisa ser capaz de distinguir essas complexidades e diferenças. Critérios como maturidade do projeto, capacidade financeira, experiência de investidores e consistência técnica podem contribuir para a seleção de empreendimentos com condições reais de implantação sem impor a todos o mesmo nível de exigência. A tributação é outra questão que pode se tornar outro obstáculo. Equipamentos representam parcela relevante do investimento em um data center, e a diferença de custos em relação a outros mercados reduz a competitividade brasileira. Medidas tributárias capazes de corrigir essa desvantagem são importantes, mas precisam fazer parte de uma estratégia mais ampla e holística. A agenda digital deve estar alinhada ao planejamento do setor elétrico, à política tributária e às regras para infraestrutura tecnológica e tratamento de dados. O país não pode tratar cada uma dessas questões de forma isolada. A conexão entre elas é crucial. Também é necessário aproximar os horizontes de planejamento. O setor elétrico trabalha com obras de longa maturação por razões técnicas, ambientais e regulatórias. A economia digital opera em ciclos muito mais curtos. Essa diferença não desaparecerá, entretanto, a adoção de processos mais eficientes, planejamento antecipado e soluções de transição podem reduzir seus efeitos. Data centers são parte da infraestrutura que sustentará computação em nuvem, serviços digitais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Os países que atraírem esses investimentos ampliarão sua capacidade de processamento e sua inserção nas cadeias tecnológicas globais. O Brasil ainda pode ocupar uma posição relevante nesse mercado. Para isso, precisa oferecer um caminho previsível entre a decisão de investir e a conexão à rede. Regras devem afastar a especulação sem transformar a falta de infraestrutura em uma barreira adicional. A corrida global por capacidade computacional já começou. Se a rede elétrica brasileira não acompanhar a velocidade dessa transformação, o investimento encontrará outro destino. * João Carlos de Oliveira Mello é CEO e fundador da Thymos Energia

artigo.texto: Rejeição a data centers vira aposta de democratas em eleições nos EUA Em Ohio, comunidade coleta assinaturas para proposta de emenda constitucional e aprova moratória contra grandes instalações de tecnologia Nenhuma empresa anunciou planos para um centro de dados em Defiance, uma cidade de 17 mil habitantes cercada por plantações de soja no noroeste de Ohio, nos Estados Unidos. Mas os moradores dessa comunidade não estão dispostos a correr riscos. Após descobrirem que o grupo de desenvolvimento econômico do condado havia recebido consultas de empresas de tecnologia, os residentes passaram meses coletando assinaturas para uma proposta de emenda constitucional, que será votada em 3 de novembro, com o objetivo de proibir todos os centros de dados, exceto os menores. Autoridades municipais anunciaram uma moratória de seis meses para a aprovação de novos projetos. A luta em Defiance faz parte de uma reação política mais ampla em Ohio — e em todo o país — onde a crescente preocupação pública com a IA e a infraestrutura de computação em nuvem transformou a construção de centros de dados, antes uma história de sucesso econômico, em uma questão controversa nas eleições de meio de mandato. Muitos na cidade já estavam preocupados com os impactos do desenvolvimento da IA nas terras agrícolas, na demanda por eletricidade e no consumo de água. As preocupações aumentaram neste verão após a divulgação de registros fiscais estaduais que mostraram que Ohio deixou de arrecadar mais de US$ 2 bilhões (cerca de R$ 10,2 bilhões) em receita de impostos sobre vendas devido a incentivos para data centers em 2024 e 2025, beneficiando empresas como Amazon e Meta. Cerca de 71% dos habitantes de Ohio agora apoiariam uma proibição temporária da construção de novos data centers, de acordo com uma pesquisa de 31 de agosto da Bowling Green State University. "A maioria das pessoas se sente explorada pelas grandes empresas", disse Becca Rupp, fundadora da Citizens for Responsible Development - efiance. A crescente onda de protestos contra data centers durante o período eleitoral abriu uma nova oportunidade para os candidatos democratas no Meio-Oeste rural dos EUA, onde eles têm enfrentado dificuldades para competir durante a presidência de Donald Trump. Ohio é um dos poucos estados com disputas acirradas que devem decidir o controle do Congresso. O governador republicano de Ohio, Mike DeWine, suspendeu novos pedidos de isenção fiscal para centros de dados enquanto aguarda reformas legislativas, mas os parlamentares estaduais não tomaram nenhuma providência antes do recesso de verão, deixando o futuro do desenvolvimento de IA em Ohio incerto — e propício a ataques políticos. Conflito sobre incentivos fiscais A deputada democrata Marcy Kaptur enfrenta uma das disputas de reeleição mais difíceis de sua carreira de quatro décadas no Congresso, em um distrito recém-redesenhado que inclui Defiance e outras áreas rurais conservadoras. Ela tem apostado fortemente em uma estratégia de comunicação focada na questão dos centros de dados, veiculando anúncios de televisão que acusam seu oponente republicano, Derek Merrin, de apoiar incentivos fiscais impopulares. Em um comunicado, Kaptur associou os centros de dados ao aumento dos custos de serviços públicos e a preocupações mais amplas sobre a influência corporativa. "Políticos estão permitindo que essas empresas repassem os custos de suas enormes demandas de energia e serviços públicos aos consumidores de Ohio e, em seguida, concedem-lhes bilhões em isenções fiscais para tornar o negócio mais atraente", disse ela. As contas de eletricidade residencial em Defiance subiram entre 10% e 15% em junho em relação ao ano anterior, segundo a concessionária FirstEnergy. Merrin não respondeu aos pedidos de comentário. Em uma publicação no Facebook na semana passada, ele afirmou que Kaptur estava "me culpando por uma isenção fiscal para centros de dados que foi aprovada ANTES mesmo de eu ser eleito para a legislatura de Ohio". A questão também ganhou destaque na disputa pelo Senado dos EUA no estado — uma corrida muito acompanhada — que coloca frente a frente o republicano Jon Husted e o senador democrata Sherrod Brown (que busca a reeleição). Com pesquisas recentes mostrando Brown à frente, grupos republicanos investiram US$ 14 milhões em publicidade em Ohio apenas na última semana, na esperança de aumentar as chances de Husted. Brown tem criticado repetidamente seu oponente por promover o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de IA e incentivos fiscais, descrevendo-o como o "melhor amigo dos centros de dados". "Os habitantes de Ohio, e não Jon Husted e seus amigos bilionários, devem decidir se centros de dados serão construídos em suas comunidades", afirmou a campanha de Brown em um comunicado. A campanha de Husted rejeitou as críticas, ressaltando que ele patrocinou uma legislação que exigiria que as operadoras de centros de dados arcassem com os custos de construção de novas capacidades de geração e transmissão de eletricidade. "Sherrod Brown teve três décadas no Congresso para liderar essa questão", disse a porta-voz da campanha, Amy Natoce, em um comunicado. "Em vez disso, ele não fez nada e, de repente, finge se importar em pleno ano eleitoral." Divulgação de subsídio fiscal mobiliza ativistas Lyn Cox, líder da organização de defesa local Conserve Ohio, afirmou que a divulgação da dimensão dos subsídios fiscais transformou o que antes era uma série de disputas isoladas sobre zoneamento em uma questão política de âmbito estadual. "Acho que foi um grande ponto de virada", disse Cox, que mora na área rural de Waterville Township, a cerca de 64 km de Defiance. Ela relatou que candidatos de ambos os partidos foram forçados a dialogar com ativistas e a elaborar políticas formais sobre o desenvolvimento de centros de dados. artigo.texto: Voto latino, inflação e data centers aumentam chance de democratas no Texas Fatores econômicos, reação nacional às operações anti-imigração e ao crescimento da inteligência artificial testam o Partido Republicano, que controla o estado há 20 anos “E agora?”, perguntou Gina Hinojosa, olhando para a casa inacabada do outro lado do terreno, onde a equipe não havia aparecido naquela manhã. Os trabalhadores haviam sido parados? Eles voltariam amanhã? Estavam apenas atrasados? “Seu palpite é tão bom quanto o meu”, disse Ronnie Cavazos, presidente da South Texas Builders Alliance, enquanto conduzia a candidata democrata ao governo do estado por um breve passeio por um bairro que vinha sendo procurado por novos trabalhadores da SpaceX, empresa de Elon Musk. Cavazos tem uma longa lista de problemas enfrentados por seu setor. As tarifas elevaram o preço da madeira e de outros materiais. As operações de fiscalização migratória em locais de trabalho provocaram um impacto muito maior sobre uma força de trabalho preocupada com a possibilidade de ser detida indefinidamente caso saísse de casa. A inflação elevou todos os custos, assim como as taxas de juros mais altas sobre terrenos que permaneceram inacabados por muito mais tempo. E há ainda o aumento histórico do preço do diesel. Em pé sobre uma fundação que não recebia obras desde que o concreto foi despejado, 60 dias antes, Cavazos disse que não votou pessoalmente no presidente Donald Trump, mas conhece muitas pessoas que votaram nele dois anos atrás, especialmente nessas cidades ao longo da fronteira dos EUA com o México, onde os latinos mudaram fortemente seu apoio em favor do presidente, em um movimento que muitos viram na época como um sinal de que a comunidade estava perdida para os democratas. O Partido Republicano controla todos os cargos estaduais do Texas há quase duas décadas. Mas uma combinação de fatores econômicos, da reação nacional às operações de fiscalização migratória e do crescimento da inteligência artificial, além da indicação, pelo Partido Republicano, de candidatos com uma série de controvérsias que poderiam ofender eleitores moderados, faz com que este outono talvez represente a maior oportunidade para os democratas romperem o domínio de um único partido no segundo estado mais populoso dos Estados Unidos. “A diferença é que, no passado, achávamos que poderíamos vencer apenas com base no quanto o outro lado era ruim e no carisma do nosso lado. E isso não é suficiente”, disse Hinojosa mais tarde naquela tarde, sentada no pequeno café de uma livraria independente em Brownsville. “Recebemos presentes nesta campanha, em uma tempestade perfeita de coisas acontecendo ao mesmo tempo. Temos um esforço coordenado forte de uma maneira que não tivemos na história moderna, com todos trabalhando juntos perfeitamente para garantir que levemos os eleitores às urnas no estado.” Essa coordenação significa que Hinojosa ocasionalmente aparece ao lado de seu colega na Câmara dos Deputados do Texas, o candidato democrata ao Senado James Talarico, que disputa uma acirrada corrida pelo Senado contra o procurador-geral estadual Ken Paxton, envolvido em uma série de escândalos. Mas, na maior parte do tempo, os dois se dividem para cobrir mais terreno no enorme estado. É a primeira vez no século 21 que há mais de um democrata forte concorrendo em âmbito estadual. Barack Obama já fez uma aparição conjunta surpresa no Taco Joint, em Austin, com os dois, e eles, por sua vez, têm levado candidatos à Assembleia estadual e a outros cargos locais a seus próprios eventos. Talarico está direcionando US$ 600 mil da enorme arrecadação nacional que vem obtendo para campanhas locais. Pela primeira vez desde pelo menos 1972 — período ao qual remontam os registros do Partido Democrata do Texas —, os democratas apresentam candidatos para todas as cadeiras da Assembleia estadual, muitos recrutados em parte pelo grupo Powered by People, de Beto O’Rourke, que também já reuniu quase 100 mil números de celulares ao registrar e organizar eleitores, principalmente em campi universitários. “É loucura que isso esteja acontecendo no Texas”, disse O’Rourke à CNN enquanto dirigia entre compromissos. “Mas está acontecendo por uma razão.” Então, na semana passada, o candidato republicano ao cargo de comissário estadual de ferrovias publicou uma foto de estudantes de pele parda em um jogo de futebol americano da Universidade do Texas e disse que a substituição de americanos por estrangeiros está “em toda parte e é muito pior do que qualquer um de nós poderia imaginar”. A publicação foi considerada racista, inclusive por muitos republicanos. Até o famoso estrategista republicano Karl Rove declarou, em um artigo de opinião: “Neste novembro, votarei em apenas um segundo democrata na minha vida.” (O primeiro foi o ex-vice-governador Bob Bullock, o último democrata a vencer uma eleição estadual.) Mas até os democratas mais entusiasmados que trabalham no estado admitem que a enorme conta de campanha do governador republicano Greg Abbott, combinada com os grandes gastos de grupos aliados a Trump e Musk, tornará difícil uma mudança. Toda conversa sobre os liberais alimentando esperanças é assombrada pelas lembranças de quando essas esperanças foram frustradas, de Wendy Davis a O’Rourke e Colin Allred. Mas eles também acreditam que, neste ano, podem ter finalmente encontrado uma maneira de fazer isso acontecer. O voto latino muda novamente No ano passado, Abbott apoiou as exigências de Trump para redesenhar os distritos da Câmara dos Representantes dos EUA, em parte com base no Vale do Rio Grande, região mais ao sul do estado. Os republicanos apostaram que os latinos que ajudaram a garantir grandes vitórias para o presidente nos quatro condados da região eram eleitores com os quais poderiam contar quando ele não estivesse na cédula. artigo.texto: Anitta é coroada rainha de bateria da Grande Rio; veja Artista ocupa o posto antes ocupado pela influenciadora Virginia Fonseca; a cantora também assina um dos samba-enredos que competem na grande final deste domingo (20) A cantora Anitta, 33, foi coroada Rainha da Bateria da escola de samba Acadêmicos do Grande Rio no início da noite deste domingo (20). A coroação acontece durante a grande final de samba-enredo da agremiação em Duque de Caxias, na Baixada Fluminense. A artista recebeu a coroa diretamente de Eloína dos Leopardos, travesti pioneira e considerada a primeira rainha de bateria da história do Carnaval brasileiro. Veja galeria de fotos acima. Com a coroação, Anitta assume o posto antes ocupado pela influenciadora Virginia Fonseca, 28. Anunciada como a nova rainha em setembro, Anitta afirma que o enredo da escola se conecta com o momento atual de sua carreira musical. Neste ano, Anitta lançou o álbum "Equilibrium", que retrata sua conexão com a ancestralidade e espiritualidade por meio de sua religião, o candomblé. Em 2027, a escola vai levar para a Marquês de Sapucaí o enredo "Sankofa Tabon - Os Retornados da Costa do Ouro e a Estrela Negra da Liberdade", para contar a trajetória de africanos escravizados que, após a liberdade, retornaram ao continente africano. A cantora, inclusive, assina uma composição de samba-enredo ao lado de Arlindinho, Igor Leal, Fred Camacho, Fabian Juarez e Diego Nicolau. Veja o momento da coroação a seguir: HISTÓRICO! Anitta sendo coroada por Eloína dos Leopardos, travesti pioneira e considerada a primeira rainha de bateria da história do carnaval brasileiro. pic.twitter.com/0xI3YRB6V2 — Anitta Press (@AnittaPress) September 20, 2026 🚨 ANITTA SAMBANDO pic.twitter.com/BBKm10Hlh8 — Anitta Press (@AnittaPress) September 20, 2026 Chegada de Anitta na Grande Rio Após uma série de especulações, Anitta foi oficialmente anunciada como rainha de bateria no dia 6 de setembro. Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, a artista disse que o enredo escolhido pela Grande Rio para falar sobre fé e ancestralidade teve uma conexão imediata com o seu momento de vida e carreira. "Sabendo a importância do carnaval na vida de tantas milhares de pessoas, e para a história de um povo lutador que há décadas faz dos desfiles um ato político e revolucionário. E por isso nada na minha presença pode ser maior do que a escola, o desfile, a comunidade e os profissionais que trabalham nesse espetáculo", afirmou ela. Substituindo o reinado da influenciadora Virginia Fonseca, 27, a cantora garantiu ainda que, como tudo o que faz, se esforçará para dar o seu melhor, mesmo com a agenda cheia e a rotina agitada. *Com informações de Carolina Ferreira, da CNN Brasil

Oracle e Alura oferecem curso gratuito de IA para além dos profissionais de Tecnologia
Ideia é estender a formação - que no primeiro semestre mobilizou mais de 7 mil inscrito - para quem quiser aprender a usar a tecnologia. Imersão será de 21 a 28 de setembro. Inscrições estão abertas.
O Oracle Next Education (ONE), programa gratuito de capacitação tecnológica e inclusão social da Oracle, amplia sua formação em Inteligência Artificial (IA) no Brasil com uma nova jornada voltada a profissionais de áreas de negócios. Em parceria com a Alura, escola online de tecnologia do país, a imersão do ONE AI for Business acontecerá de 21 a 28 de setembro, com inscrições abertas até a data inicial da ação, para pessoas de todos os municípios brasileiros, com conhecimento prévio ou não em tecnologia.
Com formação 100% online, a nova edição amplia a proposta do programa ao oferecer caminhos distintos para quem desenvolve tecnologia e para quem busca aplicar IA no dia a dia dos negócios e preparar-se para as novas demandas do mercado, em áreas como Marketing, Vendas, Finanças e RH.
Desenhada junto a especialistas da Alun Business, unidade B2B do Grupo Alun que contempla Alura, FIAP, PM3 e StartSe, o curso é uma introdução à jornada de formação de aproximadamente dez semanas ligada a fundamentos de IA generativa e automação. A iniciativa, também 100% online e gratuita, oferece certificado Oracle e Alura, desenvolvimento de projetos e acesso à Alumni ONE, comunidade de profissionais que já passaram pelo curso.
No primeiro semestre, o programa realizou o ONE AI for Tech, voltado a profissionais e estudantes da área de tecnologia interessados na criação e arquitetura de soluções de IA. A formação registrou 7 mil inscritos. Agora, ao estender o programa a áreas distintas, o ONE AI for Business irá explorar a utilização de Inteligência Artificial no apoio a tarefas, aumento de produtividade e otimização de processos.
“A atualização da nossa grade reflete o compromisso de preparar talentos em um mercado em evolução. Ao oferecermos caminhos distintos para quem constrói a tecnologia e para quem a aplica nos negócios, garantimos que a Inteligência Artificial seja uma ferramenta de produtividade ao alcance dos perfis profissionais”, explica Amanda Gelumbauskas, head do Oracle Next Education.
Para a Alura, a Inteligência Artificial já ultrapassa as barreiras técnicas, e o seu próprio portfólio é uma resposta a esse movimento. Oferecendo mais de 125 cursos voltados à IA, a empresa já observa o crescimento de profissionais de diferentes setores e níveis em suas formações e, cada vez mais, o público entende que essas ferramentas passaram a ser hard skills essenciais a inúmeras carreiras, e não um conhecimento restrito às áreas de tecnologia.
Desde sua criação, o ONE já impactou mais de 116 mil pessoas e contribuiu para o ingresso de 19 mil participantes no mercado de trabalho. O programa também registra impacto indireto estimado de US$ 167 milhões por ano em salários gerados pe

Disparada dos preços de componentes provoca colapso global nos smartphones abaixo de US$ 100
GSMA adverte que essa alta dos preços, impulsionada pela demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, tende ampliar a exclusão digital no mundo.
O aumento dos custos de componentes de smartphones, impulsionado pela demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, ameaça ampliar a exclusão digital e tornar a internet móvel menos acessível financeiramente em países de baixa e média renda (LMICs). A advertência foi feita pela GSMA, no relatório State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2026 (Estado da Conectividade à Internet Móvel 2026).
Dados da Counterpoint Research mostraram que os preços de memórias mais do que dobraram entre o terceiro trimestre de 2025 e o primeiro trimestre de 2026, antes de registrarem um aumento adicional de 80% a 90% no segundo trimestre de 2026. Essa disparada de preços está impactando os valores dos smartphones de entrada; a associação do setor alerta que custos mais elevados podem desacelerar o progresso na redução da lacuna de uso da internet móvel.
O relatório da GSMA constatou que, embora 4,8 bilhões de pessoas já utilizem a internet móvel em seus próprios dispositivos, o ritmo de crescimento desacelerou: foram cerca de 160 milhões de novos usuários em 2025, ante 190 milhões em 2024. Além disso, 38% da população mundial — aproximadamente 3,1 bilhões de pessoas — vivem em áreas com cobertura de banda larga móvel, mas não a utilizam; desse contingente que não utiliza o serviço, 70% não possuem um dispositivo próprio. Outras 650 milhões de pessoas acessam a internet móvel exclusivamente por meio de dispositivos emprestados ou compartilhados.
Segundo a GSMA, prevê-se que as remessas globais de smartphones sofram a “maior queda anual já registrada”, impulsionadas por um colapso no segmento de aparelhos com preço inferior a US$ 100. A expectativa é que os mercados emergentes sejam os mais afetados.
A acessibilidade financeira dos aparelhos foi apontada como a maior barreira para a adoção da internet móvel nos países de baixa e média renda, seguida por questões de alfabetização e habilidades digitais. No final de 2025, um aparelho de entrada com acesso à internet custava, para os 20% mais pobres desses países, o equivalente a 44% de sua renda mensal média — índice que chegava a 76% na África Subsaariana.
Patamares de preço
O estudo revelou que, até um ano atrás, reduzir os preços dos smartphones de entrada para US$ 30 poderia ter tornado os dispositivos acessíveis a quase 1,6 bilhão de pessoas. Um patamar de preço de US$ 20 poderia ter alcançado cerca de 2,2 bilhões de pessoas residentes em áreas com cobertura de banda larga móvel. No entanto, a alta nos custos de memória tornou esses preços inacessíveis. Como resultado, a GSMA conclamou fabricantes de chipsets e memórias a aumentar a disponibilidade de componentes acessíveis e instou formuladores de políticas, operadoras e fabricantes de dispositivos a apoiarem medidas

artigo.texto: O candidato à reeleição, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, disse, durante ato de campanha em Santa Catarina, que o programa de incentivo ao desenvolvimento de data centers, o Redata, deve atrair investimentos da ordem de R$ 500 bilhões. Segundo ele, o País tem tudo para ser um grande polo desse setor por ser abundante em energia renovável. Mas ele ressaltou que, pelo projeto, as empresas que vierem para o Brasil terão que construir as suas usinas para abastecer os seus centros. "Não vamos deixar que a energia produzida vá somente para o data center, quem quiser vir pra cá terá que investir na construção em energia renovável", disse o presidente. Lula também exaltou a sanção da Lei de Minerais Críticos e terras raras e disse que o Brasil conhece apenas 30% de seu território e mesmo assim é a segunda maior reserva de terras raras do mundo, perdendo apenas para a China. Em pronunciamento, Lula criticou a ingerência externa e exaltou as riquezas naturais do Brasil. "Mas não temos tecnologia para explorar, por isso, temos que ter cursos em nossas universidades, para ter mais capacidade do que o chinês", afirmou. "Queremos vender chip, bateria, queremos exportar inteligência, conhecimento. Por isso temos que ter informação e investimento em pesquisa". "Prometo a você e à minha consciência que em 10 anos esse País não estará devendo nada para formar um engenheiro ou cientista, não queremos ficar na guerra entre China e EUA, queremos formar os jovens", complementou. - - Lula sanciona projeto de lei do Redata, regime de desoneração do setor de data centers - - Agência nuclear da ONU estima que energia atômica pode triplicar até 2060 com IA Lula também falou das políticas que seu governo fez para o agronegócio e disse que abriu 693 mercados para o setor, dentre eles, para a produção de proteína animal. O Senado aprovou um projeto para atrair um "boom" de data centers no Brasil, visando o potencial energético do País. Santa Catarina é um dos Estados que mais produzem carnes suína e de frango. "Sabe quantos mercados eu abri para carne de aves e derivados? 34 novos mercados de exportação. Para carnes suínas e derivados, 25 mercados para vender os nossos produtos, bovinos e derivados, 37, pescados, 22 novos mercados", detalhou. "Somando as 4 proteínas aqui em Santa Catarina, foram 118 mercados que o Lulinha, que eles não gostam, abriu para venderem os seus produtos. O problema com agronegócio é porque eu sou nordestino, não por dinheiro. Porque nunca houve tanto crédito para o agro como agora", argumentou Lula. Segundo ele, a escolha do candidato Gelson Merísio ao governo estadual pelo PSB foi feita para dialogar com o agronegócio. artigo.texto: The threat of a data center being built in Beacon Falls has proven so unpopular with residents that they’re objecting even before any formal proposal comes forward. Homeowners are organizing lawn sign displays and a social media campaign, while three separate online petitions got under way this summer urging town leaders to kill the idea immediately. “We should say ‘no’ to this. We have a beautiful, peaceful town. We want to keep it like that,” longtime resident Brian Hourigan said Wednesday. “What would it do the water supply? What about the environmental impact — and the noise? They run 24/7.” The response is a dramatic turnaround from four years ago, when the town appeared eager to get a smaller data center on the same property. It was never built. Now, following the lead set by data center opponents in West Haven, Groton, Morris and other communities, a group of Beacon Falls residents is calling on their town to pass a moratorium. Officials of the 6,000-population town in the Naugatuck Valley convened a public information meeting in August to emphasize that there’s no formal application pending. But residents countered that recent commercial real estate ads are promoting the property with the phrase “Largest data center in Connecticut.” The listings speak of a “100MW green-powered data center” and a 294,000-square-foot building, and include computer renderings of a massive structure marked “Beacon Falls Technology Center.” An online listing by The Agency, a California-based real estate brokerage, states “Beacon Falls presents a rare, clean slate opportunity to develop a purpose built digital infrastructure campus across 49 acres with up to 100MW of utility power in place – one of the most compelling and supply constrained sites available in the Northeast. “For equity partners and co-developers, the asset offers significant long term appreciation potential in a sector where institutional appetite continues to substantially outpace available product.” The listing also states the project would ultimately have 33 fuel cells on site. Torrington-based O&G Industries, among New England’s most powerful construction and paving companies, is listed as the developer of the project. O&G owns 49 acres of woods and former gravel pits off Lopus Road. “We are presently marketing 1 Lopus Road as a data center,” company President David Oneglia wrote in an email Thursday. The controversy illustrates just how deeply public opinion has switched against data centers. Across the country, many communities were trying to lure data center projects, drawn largely by the prospect of major new revenue from taxes and fees. In Beacon Falls, for instance, residents at a town meeting in 2022 unanimously authorized selectmen to sign a contract for a 32MW data center on the same parcel off Lopus Road. The agreement would have given the town $6 million over the first three years, and more than $2.5 million a year after that. But that project never went forward. The mood was vastly different when selectmen met Monday night: Several residents spoke against allowing any data center in town, and at least two asked about imposing a moratorium against them. Nobody spoke to support a data center or raised the issue of revenue. When the Economic Development Commission hosted a public meeting Aug. 24, the message was about the same: Nearly a dozen people spoke opposing data centers in town, while none endorsed the idea. Selectmen have repeatedly said that nobody has applied to build a data center in town, and that they have to avoid premature decisions. In a July 31 social media post, Selectman Peter Betkoski urged the public to be patient and rejected complaints that town leaders have been secretive. “What I find most concerning are the accusations that there have been ‘backroom deals’ or that elected officials have somehow hidden information from the public. Those are serious allegations. They don’t just question opinions — they accuse public officials of improper or even illegal conduct,” he wrote. On Thursday, Betkoski told The Courant that it’s too early to offer opinions. “It’s simple: there is no application. When there’s an application we can talk about the pros and cons and make a fair decision. I can’t now because the decision would become prejudiced,” Betkoski said. “So there’s really no comment.” First Selectman Gerard Smith was away this week; a message referred callers to Selectman Michael Krenesky. Krenesky did not return two calls this week. Online petitions signed by more than 3,000 people are pushing for more transparency about what’s happening — and a hard line against data centers. “In our tranquil community of Beacon Falls, a storm is brewing. Plans for a colossal data center — slated to become the largest in our state — threaten to overshadow our town’s serene landscape and delicate ecosystem,” reads one. “Our elected officials owe us transparency and action,” says another petition on the topic. “As residents, it’s our duty to stand up for the environment we cherish and the financial well-being of our community. We must demand comprehensive evaluations and clear communication before any irreversible steps are taken.”

artigo.texto: The Evolution of Data Center Design: Meeting the Demands of AI AI acceleration is redefining first principles AI training and inference have raised the stakes for how fast we can build and how reliably we can operate. The result is a step‑change in expectations for thermal performance, electrical architectures, deployment velocity, and resiliency. Our industry’s response will shape the next wave of capacity and the sustainability and community impact of facilities located near where people live and work. At ebm‑papst, we see three themes converging: hybrid cooling as the operating norm, HVDC readiness in new builds, and resilient, local‑for‑local supply chains that keep projects on schedule despite global volatility. No matter the theme, the mandate is the same: upfront design for efficiency, acoustics, interoperability, and redundancy. Hybrid cooling is here to stay Rack-level liquid cooling is becoming unavoidable for modern chip thermal loads; air alone cannot remove that heat density. Yet liquid does not eliminate the need for air movement in the data center. Airflow management around enclosures, corridors, and supporting systems remains critical to equipment reliability and serviceability. Facilities maintain cool temperatures inside the data center by rejecting heat outdoors, commonly through air cooled chillers, cooling towers, or dry coolers. What that means for design teams: - Plan for coexistence: Expect rack-level liquid cooling and air throughout the room, coordinated by controls that understand both domains. - Engineer for acoustics: As campuses move closer to communities, noise abatement for outdoor equipment will become a siting and permitting issue. - Target every watt: Efficiency is capacity. Watts saved in cooling translate into watts available for computing, especially in power‑constrained markets. Power density keeps rising without bigger footprints Computing density continues to rise, while real estate and retrofit constraints remain tight. Operators are asking for more airflow and higher static pressure in the same mechanical footprint. That challenges the entire system, from fan and motor selection to controls and mechanical integration. The winning designs will deliver higher power density without sacrificing efficiency or acoustics. Practical implications: - Specify equipment that can scale output within fixed geometry while maintaining high wire‑to‑air efficiency. - Use model‑based design and digital twins to simulate thermal interactions across the room and on the roof line before steel is cut. - Treat controls as a first‑order lever: smarter modulation beats brute force. Aligning electrical and thermal strategies for HVDC While retrofits to high‑voltage DC (HVDC) are often impractical for existing sites, new builds increasingly evaluate HVDC‑ready architectures (frequently discussed around ~800 VDC). Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, which can reduce copper in bus bars and conductors and lower the cost. HVDC distribution can also simplify power quality, reducing harmonic mitigation hardware on sensitive circuits. For thermal systems, this shift is more than an electrical detail. It affects drive selection, controls, and EMI/EMC considerations across fans, pumps, and outdoor equipment. Designing cooling assets to be compatible with HVDC ecosystems helps future‑proof facilities as the powertrain evolves. Interoperability first: BMS and protocol pluralism No two owners standardize their operational technology stacks in the same way. To stay deployable, cooling equipment should be BMS‑agnostic, supporting a wide set of protocols, including Modbus, BACnet, PROFINET, and others. This “interoperability-by-default” mindset reduces integration friction and shortens commissioning timelines, especially on fast‑tracked AI builds. Couple that with on‑premises digital twins that mirror plant behavior, and operators can test control strategies in software, apply AI‑guided optimization, and roll successful tactics into production with confidence. We’ve consistently seen strong alignment between simulated and realized efficiency gains when these models are calibrated and maintained. Supply‑chain resilience is a design decision Localization is more than a procurement strategy; it’s a project‑schedule strategy. A local‑for‑local manufacturing model (Americas, Europe, Asia) lowers tariff exposure, reduces transit time, and provides redundant regional capacity when disruptions strike. In a market where schedules are measured in weeks, not quarters, the difference between six weeks of ocean freight and a domestic lead time can define a project’s critical path. The most effective operators share multi‑year demand signals. Two‑to‑three‑year forecast corridors, supplemented by longer‑range directional views, enable upstream suppliers to secure critical components and expand capacity ahead of demand. That collaboration is how the industry turns macro uncertainty into dependable delivery. The grid constraint is a catalyst for better designs Many U.S. metros face power availability constraints that will shape site selection, phasing, and even micro‑siting. Some operators are assessing on‑site generation (including low‑ or zero‑carbon options) while advocating for utility‑led capacity expansions. Regardless of which path wins in each market, the mechanical plant must be ultra‑efficient, acoustically responsible, and ready to ramp in step with staged electrical availability. What we’re working toward as an industry - Hybrid cooling that’s quiet, efficient, and serviceable at scale. - HVDC‑ready cooling assets that integrate cleanly into evolving powertrains. - Interoperable controls that plug into any owner’s BMS ecosystem. - Digital‑twin‑driven operations that turn models into measurable savings. - Local‑for‑local resiliency with redundant regional manufacturing and long‑range planning. - Community‑minded design that respects neighbors while unlocking compute growth.

artigo.texto: Grid Constraints Steer Dutch Data Centers Beyond Amsterdam Amsterdam remains a top European data center hub, but power constraints are shifting new capacity to Rotterdam and other regional Dutch markets with available grid connections. Amsterdam’s data center market continues to grow, but the very infrastructure that made it a European hub increasingly determines where new capacity can be built. As of Q1 2026, the city was Europe’s fourth-largest data center market, with inventory up 11% year over year, or 64.3 MW, according to CBRE’s 2026 market review. Its vacancy rate tightened to 9.4%, evidence that customers continue to absorb capacity even as power constraints and planning restrictions limit development. JLL’s latest EMEA report shows that in H1 2026, Amsterdam delivered 16.3 MW, while Paris added 72.5 MW over the same period. Amsterdam still offers the connectivity, customers, and operators of a top-tier hub, but faster growth is shifting toward locations that can provide large power blocks on reliable schedules. The Dutch market is therefore set to become more geographically dispersed. Amsterdam remains the commercial and network center, while Rotterdam, Groningen, Eindhoven, and other regional markets compete for projects the capital cannot accommodate. Amsterdam’s Network Advantage Holds Amsterdam’s status within the FLAP-D group – Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin – rests on an interconnection ecosystem built over decades. In 2025, the Amsterdam Internet Exchange (AMS-IX) handled 35.66 exabytes of traffic, four times its 2015 volume, and ended 2025 with 902 connected parties. That density keeps carriers, cloud providers, content companies, and enterprises close to the networks they need, conferring an advantage on established colocation operators that newer markets cannot quickly replicate. “Amsterdam is characterized by the availability of skilled labor and an established infrastructure by large colocation service providers such as Equinix and Digital Realty,” said Luis Fernandes, senior research manager for cloud, data centers, and enterprise infrastructure at IDC, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. He also noted the large number of subsea cables landing in the Netherlands from multiple regions. Geography reinforces this position. Amsterdam offers low-latency access to major European business centers, a mature enterprise customer base, and an energy market where operators can pursue renewable power purchase agreements (PPAs). “Add to this a favorable energy mix with a large component of offshore wind farms, as well as a prime market for sustainable PPAs,” Alex Mariage, head of regional operations at global data center consultancy BCS, told Data Center Knowledge. “This continues to make Amsterdam a very attractive and traditional opportunity for global investments.” These advantages support demand, but they do not guarantee a grid connection. The challenge is to preserve Amsterdam’s network ecosystem while placing workloads where power is actually available. The Equinix AM3 data center tower in Amsterdam. (Image: Getty Images) Deliverable Power Dictates the Next Build Deliverable power now outweighs land prices, incentives, and even fiber in site selection. Developers need to know when a connection will arrive, how much capacity it will provide, and whether equipment can be procured in time to use it. “Site selection in 2026 is driven primarily by deliverable power,” Assad Noori, executive director and EMEA head of data centers at JLL, told Data Center Knowledge. “If developers cannot secure megawatts on a predictable timeline, incentives, land costs, and fiber connectivity become secondary.” “If developers cannot secure megawatts on a predictable timeline, incentives, land costs, and fiber connectivity become secondary.” – Assad Noori, executive director and EMEA head of data centers at JLL AI has amplified the volume of requests reaching utilities and developers. Noori noted that single-site requirements, once in the 30-60 MW range, can now reach 300 MW, while transformer lead times can extend up to three years. Power commitments and long-lead equipment orders must therefore precede construction by years. “Cost and delivery timeline are now co-equal with availability in site decisions,” he said. Behind-the-meter generation can help when grid queues become too long. Noori advises developers to establish their queue position, connection cohort, offtake and export rights, backup service terms, exit rights, and penalties before committing to a site. Amsterdam’s limited land has encouraged taller data centers, enabling more intensive site use but complicating planning and permitting. Flood risk is addressed through national and regional defenses, with some facilities adding perimeter floodgates. Mariage said the Dutch engineering response to land and water constraints is mature, but the electricity bottleneck is now slowing projects. “Grid congestion is the key challenge here,” he said. “Every investor will confirm that this aspect is the top constraint slowing down projects and investments at the moment.” Capacity Shifts to Rotterdam and Regional Hubs Amsterdam’s constraints do not suppress demand; they widen the search radius. National policy generally restricts hyperscale facilities to designated zones in Hollands Kroon (including Middenmeer) and Het Hogeland (home to Eemshaven). Meanwhile, colocation and other developments are testing a broader field of Dutch locations. Rotterdam stands out for certain workloads, combining port infrastructure, proximity to Amsterdam, an established business base, and experience in reclaiming former harbor land. The AMS-IX added a Rotterdam point of presence in April 2026, strengthening the city’s role on the national connectivity map. artigo.texto: Space Data Centers Inch Toward Reality, With Caveats At the AI Infra Summit, a panel of executives and a US government IT leader discussed the promise and challenges of building data centers in space. SANTA CLARA, Calif. – Orbital data centers are edging closer to reality, but significant technical and economic obstacles remain, according to industry and government leaders who discussed the future of computing in space at the AI Infra Summit, held Sept. 15-17. Thermal, Bandwidth, and Launch Hurdles Sumeet Singh, chief data and AI officer at Viasat, a satellite communications company, identified three primary challenges. The first is thermal management – the ability to keep orbital systems cool. In the vacuum of space, heat can only be shed through radiators, which must be large enough to dissipate substantial thermal loads. “With size comes weight. Weight is a huge currency when you think about orbital data centers,” he said during a panel discussion on Thursday, Sept. 17. Singh also pointed to limited downlink and uplink capacity – the ability to move data to and from orbit – and the cost of launching the data centers into low Earth orbit (LEO). He said today’s costs of $2,500 to $3,000 per kilogram would need to drop to roughly $200 to $500 per kilogram for orbital data centers to make financial sense. Joe Yaffe, COO and chief legal officer of Cowboy Space Corp., which is building orbital data centers and aims to launch them, agreed that those obstacles are real. He added that reliance on a single dominant satellite launch provider has become a bottleneck in its own right. Yaffe said Cowboy Space is tackling the bottleneck by developing its own launch vehicle and using the rocket’s second stage as the data center itself. To address bandwidth, the company plans to use optical links. “We’re believers that data transmission needs to take place optically, uplink and downlink, in order to move what will be increasingly larger amounts of data,” Yaffe said. Power is another constraint. Camille Bergin, chief marketing officer of Star Catcher, an in-space energy utility, said the company is working on laser-based power beaming to augment existing solar arrays, potentially delivering up to 10 times more power to orbiting systems. Customer Readiness and the Road to Scale From the customer standpoint, the US Air Force is not yet ready to adopt orbital compute at scale, said Deepak Sachdeva, CIO of the US Air Force. His priorities are operational effectiveness, real-time or almost real-time latency, resilience, and security. By those measures, he said, the technology still falls short. “From a consumer-to-consumer level, I think it’s ready. But from an operational need, which is global in its nature, I think there is still some work to be done,” he said. “The best approach, in my view, is to do some sort of proof of concept.” Singh, whose company, Viasat, wants to participate in the emerging orbital data center ecosystem, said the industry must prove itself incrementally – both technically and commercially. He cited StarCloud’s November 2025 launch of a satellite featuring an Nvidia H100 GPU as a promising sign, while noting a single-GPU demo is a far cry from megawatt- and gigawatt-class facilities. “We suddenly talk about megawatt- and gigawatt-class data centers. I think we need intermediate proof points … something in between where you have 100- to 500-kW-class compute,” he said. Other key milestones, Singh added, include ensuring sufficient launch capacity to get these systems into orbit and demonstrating that customers will actually buy compute in space. Bergin agreed on the need to “crawl, walk, run,” describing how her company first proved its technology on Earth before moving to space-based demonstrations. “There are a lot of people in this industry who have a tendency to just say, ‘This is the thing that we’re going to build, and it’ll just happen,’” she said. “I think from the orbital compute perspective, what are those incremental steps? How do we get from operating at 5% to 10% on a single H100 as a prototype to a megawatt-class, gigawatt-class data center? … We can’t just design something in space because we think it’s cool and it’s the next frontier. There has to be a real need and a real business model.” Bergin also argued that orbital data centers could address community pushback against terrestrial facilities. “All of us are super-familiar with the fact that people don’t like these data centers. They don’t want them in their communities. They are super-problematic. … So space [is] offering a solution if we can get there.” Despite the challenges, Singh remains confident. “This isn’t a question of if it would happen. I think this is more of a question of the step function. When would this happen?” he said.

artigo.texto: COMMERCE CITY, Colo. — Commerce City leaders are deciding Monday night if the city should hit pause on data center development. At their regularly scheduled meeting, city council will consider a six-month moratorium on approving data center development plans or zoning applications. See the full story from Alex Dowd in the video below Council communications say the city’s land development code doesn’t address some of the “unique characteristics of data center facilities.” The draft ordinance says data centers can have significant impacts on city infrastructure like power and water supply, neighborhood character and surrounding land use. With growing interest in building these large scale computer system warehouses, city council officials are deciding if they should take a step back and “establish a reasonable period of time during which permit applications, site development plans and amendments, and zoning applications for new or expanded data centers will not be processed or approved.” The ordinance says that during the six-month pause, officials and city staff will take the time to research and potentially develop amendments to existing regulations that specifically address data centers. A survey from Magellan Strategies shows that Colorado residents are overwhelmingly opposed to data centers in their neighborhoods with 86% of surveyed voters opposing a data center near their neighborhood. This isn’t the first time a Colorado city has considered this type of pause. In early August, Aurora City Council voted down a similar six-month moratorium. Instead, Aurora officials opted to create regulations to address community concerns heard during that meeting. Weeks later, the council voted unanimously to ban evaporative cooling systems for new developments. That’s an option for Commerce City officials. While the staff recommendation is to pass the six month ban as written, councilmembers have the option to accept, amend, revisit or reject this ordinance. If accepted, the city won’t be able to approve any data center development plans or applications until March 2027. That timeline can be extended with another council vote. artigo.texto: Democrats try to ride data center backlash to election victory in rural US Midwest Mounting public anxiety about AI, cloud-computing infrastructure has transformed data center construction into a contentious midterm elections issue No company has announced plans for a data center in Defiance, a city of 17,000 people surrounded by soybean fields in northwestern Ohio. But people in the aptly named community are not taking any chances. After learning the county’s economic development group had fielded inquiries from tech companies, residents spent months gathering signatures for a November 3 ballot measure to ban all but the smallest data centers. City officials announced a six-month moratorium on new project approvals. The fight in Defiance is part of a broader political backlash throughout Ohio — and across the nation — where mounting public anxiety about AI and cloud-computing infrastructure has transformed data center construction from an economic success story into a contentious midterm elections issue. Many in Defiance were already concerned about the impacts of AI development on farmland, electricity demand and water consumption. Their misgivings deepened this summer after the release of state tax records showing Ohio had foregone more than $2 billion in sales-tax revenue through data-center incentives in 2024 and 2025, benefiting companies such as Amazon and Meta. Some 71% of Ohioans would now support a temporary ban on new data center construction, according to an August 31 poll from Bowling Green State University. "Most people feel preyed upon by big business," said Becca Rupp, founder of Citizens for Responsible Development - efiance. The groundswell building against data centers during election season has given Democratic candidates a new opening in the rural US Midwest, where they have struggled to compete during Donald Trump's presidency. Ohio is one of a handful of states with competitive races expected to decide control of Congress. Ohio's Republican Governor Mike DeWine has suspended new applications for data center tax exemptions pending legislative reforms, but state lawmakers did not act before summer recess, leaving the future of AI development in Ohio uncertain — and ripe for political attack. Clash over tax incentives Democratic US Representative Marcy Kaptur faces one of the toughest reelection races of her four-decade congressional career, in a newly redrawn district that includes Defiance and other conservative rural areas. She has leaned heavily into data-center messaging, running television ads accusing her Republican opponent Derek Merrin of supporting the unpopular tax incentives. In a statement, Kaptur linked data centers to rising utility costs and wider concerns about corporate influence. "Politicians are letting these companies pass the costs of their enormous energy and utility demands onto Ohio ratepayers, then handing them billions in tax breaks to sweeten the deal," she said. Residential electricity bills in Defiance rose 10% to 15% in June from a year earlier, according to utility FirstEnergy. Merrin did not respond to requests for comment. In a Facebook post last week, he said Kaptur was “blaming me for a tax break for data centers that was enacted BEFORE I was even elected to the Ohio legislature.” The issue has also featured prominently in the state's closely watched US Senate race, pitting Republican incumbent Jon Husted against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who lost his old seat in 2024. With recent polls showing Brown leading, Republican groups have poured $14 million into advertising in Ohio in the past week alone, hoping to boost Husted's chances. Brown has repeatedly criticized his opponent for promoting AI infrastructure development and tax incentives, describing him as "data centers' best friend." “Ohioans, not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends, should get to decide if data centers are built in their community,” Brown’s campaign said in a statement. Husted's campaign rejected the criticism, noting he has sponsored legislation that would require data-center operators to cover the cost of building more electricity generation and transmission. “Sherrod Brown had three decades in Congress to lead on this issue,” campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce said in a statement. “Instead, he did nothing and is suddenly pretending to care in the middle of an election year.” Tax subsidy disclosure galvanizes activists Lyn Cox, a leader of the local advocacy organization Conserve Ohio, said disclosure about the scale of tax subsidies transformed what had been a series of scattered zoning disputes into a statewide political issue. "I think it was a huge turning point," said Cox, who lives in rural Waterville Township, about 40 miles (64 km) from Defiance. She said candidates from both parties have been forced to engage with activists and develop formal policies on data-center development. Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who previously voiced support for attracting tech investment, released an "Ohioans First" data-center proposal that would eliminate local property-tax abatements for data centers, direct revenue toward homeowner rebates and require projects to cover incremental residential electricity costs. His opponent, Democrat Amy Acton, has proposed restricting tax incentives, requiring developers to pay for their own power infrastructure and mandating union labor standards. Both candidates have also called for limiting construction on productive farmland. Cox remains skeptical of campaign promises from both parties. "They're just words," she said. "They both came up with a policy because they're starting to understand this is a sleeper issue." Conserve Ohio is pursuing a state constitutional amendment in 2027 that would ban the construction of data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power, while supporting similar local ballot initiatives across the state. artigo.texto: A new design direction has been presented to improve the performance of all-solid-state batteries, which have a lower risk of fire. The principle by which the rotation and arrangement of anions inside solid electrolytes facilitate the movement of lithium ions has been identified, and is expected to be used to develop solid electrolytes with high ionic conductivity. The Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) announced on the 21st that a research team led by Senior Researcher Youngju Lee of the Intelligent Secondary Battery Strategy Research Group has elucidated how anion rotation in next-generation solid electrolyte materials enhances battery performance. The research findings were published on June 26 in the international journal Small. An all-solid-state battery is a type of battery that uses a solid electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid electrolyte. While the risk of fire is lower, lithium ions find it more difficult to move freely within the solid electrolyte. To improve battery performance, it is crucial to increase the speed of ion transport. The research team focused on the anion "borohydride" contained in argyrodite-type solid electrolytes. Argyrodite-type materials are considered promising candidates for next-generation all-solid-state batteries due to their high ionic conductivity and good processability. Borohydride is an anion consisting of four hydrogen atoms bonded to a central boron atom. Within the crystal structure of the solid electrolyte, it can change orientation while rotating in place. Previous studies had shown that incorporating borohydride can increase the ionic conductivity of solid electrolytes, but the precise role of borohydride rotation in lithium-ion transport had not been clearly understood. Using solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, the team found that borohydride rotation and lithium-ion movement repeatedly interlock with each other. When the rotation of borohydride was restricted in the simulations, lithium-ion diffusivity dropped to nearly half. This confirmed that borohydride rotation assists the long-range migration of lithium ions. The position of borohydride also turned out to be important. When borohydride simultaneously occupies two distinct crystallographic sites inside the solid electrolyte, the space through which lithium ions move forms uniformly. As a result, the energy difference required for lithium ions to move between adjacent sites decreases, allowing them to travel smoothly over long distances. This study presents a new direction for all-solid-state battery design, suggesting that not only the composition of the solid electrolyte but also the arrangement and dynamics of internal species must be considered. The results are expected to help efficiently develop high-performance solid electrolytes in which lithium ions move rapidly, reduce trial and error in research, and accelerate the commercialization of all-solid-state batteries with superior safety and performance. Senior Researcher Youngju Lee said, "We have clarified how the rotation of surrounding anions within solid electrolytes facilitates lithium-ion transport," adding, "These findings can serve as a new design criterion for enhancing ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries." doi.org/10.1002/smll.73722

artigo.texto: In a move that challenges Orange Juicer and Buick Electra for the highly coveted Best Name in the EV Business title, a new venture between CATL and Octopus Energy called “Swaptopus” has been formed to build out a European battery swap network for commercial trucks. First announced at Octopus Energy’s Energy Tech Summit back in June, the Swaptopus concept got a bit of a boost at last week’s IAA Transportation event in the form of TECTRANS II, a next-generation commercial vehicle battery solution built specifically to serve as a modular, universal electric truck platform that promises to eliminate long charge times and battery life concerns that have remained key barriers to commercial fleet electrification. According to the original CATL press release for TECTRANS II, the new battery system improves fleet economics in three ways: - Higher energy density – boasting a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, around 13% above the industry average, the battery enables vehicles to carry approximately 0.6 tonnes of additional payload at the same battery capacity. - Longer Range, Faster Charging – its maximum configuration offers up to 1,000 km of range and 80% charging in 25 minutes with megawatt-level fast charging, minimizing downtime on long-haul routes. - Higher energy efficiency – the world’s first full-tab low-impedance design enables 96% system round-trip efficiency (RTE), reducing charging losses and delivering more usable energy for daily operations. “Commercial vehicle electrification will unfold over more than a decade,” said Zhu Lingbo, CTO of CATL Global Business Unit. “With our deep technological expertise and long-term commitment, CATL is ready to be the most reliable partner for customers worldwide and for the global electrification of freight transport.” Once in full swing, CATL and Octopus claim their proposed network could support 300,000+ electric trucks and unlock more than £30 billion in private investment while creating jobs and reducing Europe’s dependence on imported oil by replacing fossil fuels with sustainably produced electricity. It takes a village Along with Octopus, CATL announced that it’s signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with global shipping giants DHL Group that aims to accelerate the electrification and decarbonization of road freight transportation across Europe by engaging a broad coalition of industry stakeholders that includes Xiaomi-backed mobile power plant specialists Quibo Energy and FleetBoost, who provide mobile charging and battery energy storage systems (BESS), including the “FleetBooster” trailer (shown, above) which integrates CATL battery technology. This level of collaboration points to an industry united in a single goal: avoiding high fuel prices decarbonization. Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business, emphasized that sort of “holistic” approach to fleet decarbonization, saying, “by combining real logistics demand with vehicles, charging, energy storage, battery swapping and lifecycle services, CATL plans to work with DHL and other ecosystem partners to create practical and scalable solutions for zero-emission freight.” For DHL Group, the partnership is a critical next-step toward its corporate goal of achieving net-zero logistics-related emissions by 2050, following other steps we’ve covered in these pages here and here. artigo.texto: Leapmotor has unveiled two major technologies that will underpin its next generation of electric vehicles, beginning with models scheduled to launch from 2027. The Chinese EV manufacturer introduced the LEAP 5.0 New Mobile Space Architecture and its latest Cell-to-Chassis (CTC) 3.0 High-Low Fusion Battery at the 2026 Leapmotor Tech Day, held at the company’s Hu Zhou Battery facility in Hangzhou on September 16. Both technologies are designed to fundamentally change how Leapmotor vehicles use interior space and manage electrical power. The company describes the development as a major shift comparable to the transition from traditional feature phones to smartphones. LEAP 5.0 Architecture Focuses on Interior Space The LEAP 5.0 New Mobile Space Architecture has been developed specifically for Leapmotor’s next-generation vehicles, with the first models using the platform expected to be revealed in 2027. According to Leapmotor, the architecture achieves 100% space efficiency compared with its previous vehicle architectures while integrating vehicle control systems into a centralized configuration designed to support modern electric and increasingly automated vehicles. One of the biggest changes comes from combining the air-conditioning system with a rear-mounted powertrain. Previously separate components are integrated into a more compact arrangement, increasing available cabin length by 19%. The design also reduces the number of components by 18% and cuts the amount of required piping by 30%. The front suspension layout has also been redesigned. A new vertical shock absorber arrangement with an aluminum tower reduces the amount of hardware intruding into the passenger compartment while increasing front-row lateral legroom by 37.5%. A Taller, More Open EV Interior Leapmotor is also using the architecture to rethink the traditional EV cabin. A new skateboard-style platform allows the company to combine a higher roof with a completely flat floor. Leapmotor says this increases interior height by 63.7%, creating a more open, loft-style cabin with enough space for full standing height. The approach could give future Leapmotor EVs significantly more usable interior space without requiring a corresponding increase in the vehicle’s exterior dimensions. The LEAP 5.0 architecture is intended to serve as the foundation for the company’s next generation of vehicles, with the first production models arriving from 2027. Leapmotor CTC 3.0 Battery Eliminates the Traditional 12-Volt Battery The second major technology unveiled at Tech Day is the Cell-to-Chassis 3.0 High-Low Fusion Battery. It represents the latest development of Leapmotor’s package-less battery and power supply technology, integrating battery components directly into the vehicle chassis. More significantly, CTC 3.0 can supply both high- and low-voltage electrical functions. Leapmotor says the system has achieved a seven-fold increase in low-voltage capacity and functionality compared with its previous generation. That capability allows future vehicles using the technology to eliminate the conventional 12-volt lead-acid auxiliary battery. The 12-volt battery has traditionally supplied power to many of a vehicle’s electrical systems, including lighting, windshield wipers, infotainment, HVAC controls, security systems and other functions. In conventional vehicles, it has remained a separate part of the electrical architecture even as high-voltage battery systems have become increasingly sophisticated. Leapmotor’s CTC 3.0 technology instead integrates these functions into a unified battery and power distribution system. High- and Low-Voltage Systems Share the Same Battery Hardware The CTC 3.0 system removes the need for separate battery modules by integrating the cells and modules directly into the chassis. High- and low-voltage functions use the same battery cells and modules, while also sharing thermal management and energy distribution systems. This creates a more integrated electrical architecture and reduces the number of separate components required. Leapmotor says the technology can deliver the equivalent low-voltage power traditionally supplied by a 12-volt battery while removing the auxiliary battery itself. The company claims that its next-generation vehicles will therefore be the first road-going vehicles in more than 70 years to operate without a conventional lead-acid auxiliary battery. Potential Environmental and Ownership Benefits Removing the traditional 12-volt battery could have benefits beyond vehicle packaging. Lead-acid batteries require periodic replacement during the lifetime of many vehicles. Leapmotor says its CTC 3.0 system is designed for lifetime maintenance-free operation, potentially eliminating the need for owners to replace an auxiliary battery every few years. At large scale, Leapmotor believes the technology could also reduce the number of lead-acid batteries entering the waste stream. The company estimates that widespread adoption could eventually eliminate the need for tens of millions of such batteries each year. The technology also demonstrates how EV manufacturers are increasingly looking beyond range and charging speed to improve the underlying architecture of electric vehicles. Leapmotor’s Next Generation Starts in 2027 The LEAP 5.0 architecture and CTC 3.0 High-Low Fusion Battery are designed to work together as the foundation for Leapmotor’s next-generation EVs. Rather than simply increasing battery capacity or adding new software features, the technologies target the physical architecture of the vehicle itself. More compact components, greater interior space and a simplified electrical system could allow Leapmotor to develop EVs with different packaging possibilities from today’s conventional designs. The first production vehicles based on the new architecture are expected to be unveiled in 2027, marking the next major stage in Leapmotor’s EV development.
