artigo.texto: Georgia Power leaders recently joined state and local officials and leaders from Robins Air Force Base to celebrate the commercial operation of the Robins Battery Facility, a 128-megawatt (MW) battery energy storage system (BESS) located near Warner Robins, GA. The facility can deliver stored energy to the grid for up to four hours, enhancing grid reliability and flexibility. Paired with the nearby Robins Solar Facility, the battery system strengthens energy resilience and helps support Georgia's continued growth. Robins Air Force Base Col. Johari Hemphill, Sen. Larry Walker, Sen. David Lucas, Sen. Steven McNeel, Rep. Anissa Jones, Central Georgia Joint Development Authority Chairman James Vaughn, Macon-Bibb County Mayor Lester Miller and other community leaders joined Georgia Power executives to celebrate the commercial operation of the Robins Battery Facility. The event reflected the strong partnerships that helped bring the project to life and highlighted its role in strengthening Georgia's energy infrastructure while supporting economic growth and investment in Macon-Bibb County. “Seeing the Robins Battery Facility enter commercial operation is an important milestone for Georgia Power and for the future of energy in our state,” said Rick Anderson, senior vice president and senior production officer for Georgia Power. “By pairing battery storage with solar generation, we’re creating a more flexible and resilient grid that can respond to customer needs during periods of peak demand while supporting Georgia’s continued growth. Projects like this demonstrate how we are thoughtfully investing in innovative technologies and working alongside strong community and industry partners to deliver reliable, affordable energy for decades to come.” At the 128 MW Robins Solar and Battery Facility, battery energy storage captures renewable energy during periods of lower customer demand and stores it for use when demand is higher, such as on cold winter mornings or during peak energy use. By pairing solar generation with battery storage, the facility provides greater flexibility and reliability while supporting Georgia's growing energy needs. The project is part of Georgia Power's broader strategy to add cost-effective energy resources through the Georgia Public Service Commission's (PSC) Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) process. Burns & McDonnell served as the engineering, procurement and construction contractor for the Robins Battery Facility and delivered the project on schedule. Expanding Battery Storage Across Georgia The Robins Battery Facility is one of four battery energy storage projects approved in the 2023 IRP Update. Georgia Power has completed battery storage facilities in Cherokee and Lowndes counties totaling 579.5 MW and is nearing completion of a 57.5 MW facility in Floyd County. The PSC has also approved nine additional BESS facilities across eight sites statewide, adding more than 3,000 MW of energy storage capacity. Sites were selected based on their ability to efficiently support grid operations, including proximity to existing infrastructure, substations and company-owned properties. Planned facilities include locations at Plants Bowen, Hammond, McIntosh, Wansley and Yates, as well as stand-alone sites in Hall and McDuffie counties. To help meet growing energy needs, Georgia Power has also received approval for two solar facilities paired with battery storage, providing a combined 350 MW of generating capacity. These projects are designed to maximize solar production while minimizing land impacts. The new solar-plus-storage facilities will be located in Laurens and Mitchell counties.

artigo.texto: Artificial intelligence has seemingly, overnight, integrated into our daily lives. From requesting a recipe to a Fortune 500 company automating tasks, we have come to rely on AI for its efficiency, convenience and productivity. With growing demand for AI technologies comes a stark question – where will the data centers that fuel AI be built, what are their potential impacts and how can those impacts be mitigated? Digital backbone Data centers power AI systems by providing the computing, storage and networking necessary to process vast amounts of data. These facilities accommodate thousands of servers that train AI models and generate responses. AI tools like ChatGPT rely on data centers to perform the calculations required to understand prompts, retrieve information and produce responses in real time. Demand has grown rapidly as businesses, governments and consumers increasingly adopt AI-powered tools. Community impacts As demand for data centers grows, so do public concerns about their potential impacts. Among the most commonly cited concerns: Electricity demand: Data centers require substantial electricity. A single ChatGPT response uses 10 times more electricity than a Google search; using generative AI in each Google search would consume the annual output of four to five nuclear reactors. Water usage: Data centers use significant quantities of water to cool their machines. A medium-sized data center can consume approximately 110 million gallons annually, while larger facilities can use up to 5 million gallons per day. Noise: Data centers produce persistent noise from cooling equipment and backup generator testing. Without adequate mitigation, data centers can disturb nearby residents who face elevated risks of annoyance and sleep disturbance. Pollution: Data centers connected to an electric grid increase emissions from fossil-fuel power plants, including fine particulate matter, nitric oxide and sulfur dioxide. Emissions from diesel backup generators include nitrogen oxide and particulate matter. Zoning controls Municipalities administer zoning laws that control where and how data centers can be built and operated, placing them at the forefront of weighing data center benefits against their potential impacts. The benefits of data centers should not be ignored — they generate substantial property tax revenue, garner private investment and create construction and permanent technical jobs. On a national scale, AI can bolster American business competitiveness and enhance U.S. military capabilities. Developers, municipalities and interested parties alike should be attuned to how data centers can and have been regulated. Municipalities that do not enact data center-specific regulatory standards risk forfeiting control over their development. For example, Stratos, a 40,000-acre data center project in Box Elder County, Utah — covering an area roughly the size of Manhattan — is moving forward with minimal local government oversight because the county had not established zoning regulations before the project was proposed. To plan for data centers, municipalities have certain land use controls at their disposal. One tool is a zoning moratorium, which temporarily suspends a particular type of development while local officials establish regulations governing that use. In May, for example, the town of Morris, Connecticut, enacted a one-year moratorium prohibiting data center development. Moratoria, however, must be limited in duration and scope, making them a short-term solution to a long-term planning need. Another tool is zoning regulations. The town of Groton has developed regulations that limit data center size and proximity to other data centers, restrict cooling infrastructure and fuel sources, and establish noise mitigation, fire suppression, utility agreement and buffer requirements to protect nearby residential districts. Other municipalities have imposed outright bans or restrictions. Mansfield, Massachusetts, for example, recently banned data centers requiring more than 10 megawatts of electricity. While data centers may be an emerging land use, developers should anticipate a regulatory process akin to other complex proposals, which can include layers of oversight from municipal, state and federal government agencies. Andrew R. Morin is an associate in the Real Estate group at law firm Hinckley Allen.

artigo.texto: No hyperscale data center has been formally proposed in Connecticut. None has come before a local land-use board, and none has signed an agreement to connect to the electric grid. But data center developers are interested in Connecticut and have been quietly exploring whether such large-scale projects could work here. In fact, they are paying Eversource Energy to examine potential sites and estimate how much it would cost to connect them to the grid, according to Jacob Lucas, the utility’s vice president of transmission system planning. Eversource defines a hyperscale data center as one that would connect directly to the high-voltage transmission system and use at least 100 megawatts. Until two years ago, the utility had not received a study request from a data center of that scale. Since then, Eversource has received more than 50, about half involving Connecticut sites, Lucas said. The potential electricity demand from hyperscale projects under study by Eversource across Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire has ranged from 1,000 to 5,000 megawatts, he said. At the high end, that would exceed twice the generating capacity of Connecticut’s Millstone nuclear plant. Projects currently under study would require just over 1,000 megawatts combined, Lucas said. If they operated continuously at that level, they would use roughly as much electricity as 1 million typical Connecticut homes. “We are absolutely seeing more interest in Connecticut than any of our other service territories,” Lucas said at a Hartford Business Journal energy conference Sept. 1 at the Society Room in Hartford. The interest comes despite the state’s increasingly skeptical stance toward the industry. Gov. Ned Lamont has said he does not want hyperscale data centers in Connecticut unless developers add enough electricity generation to serve them. State lawmakers also considered, but did not pass, a bill this year that would have eliminated the state’s data center tax incentives. Several municipalities are considering restrictions of their own. Still, developers are testing the market. Preliminary plans Paying for a study is only an early step in the development process. It does not mean a developer has committed to building a data center, Lucas said. Federal rules require Eversource to study any request to connect to the transmission system, and to tell the developer what the necessary upgrades would cost. “In no way, shape or form can we deny service,” Lucas said. “We are obligated to study whatever requests they give us, even if they’re bad.” A handful of the paid study requests have advanced to the next step, in which developers begin negotiating connection agreements with Eversource. That is the furthest any of the inquiries has progressed, Lucas said. Eversource determines what infrastructure would be needed to connect a project to the grid and how much the developer would have to pay. Large data centers generally need direct connections to high-voltage transmission lines, making sites near that infrastructure less expensive to connect. The utility does not determine whether a project ultimately makes financial sense. “Viability is something we often can’t prove,” Lucas said. The companies approaching Eversource are not household names. Data center developers typically build the facilities and sell computing capacity to technology companies such as Amazon, Google and Meta. Lucas said he was barred from identifying the developers or potential locations involved. He said he could only speculate about why developers are considering Connecticut. Established data center markets such as northern Virginia and Atlanta are becoming more constrained, pushing developers into regions they previously might have overlooked. Connecticut also sits along major fiber-optic routes that carry the bulk of the country’s internet traffic, another factor in site selection. Lucas said Eversource currently serves roughly 150 smaller data centers across Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire. Together, they account for about 400 megawatts of demand. Most use a few megawatts or less, and serve banks, hospitals, universities and military bases. The grid question None of the developers behind Eversource’s hyperscale inquiries have proposed generating their own electricity, Lucas said. That is notable because much of the public policy debate has focused on requiring large data centers to provide some of their own power or reduce demand during periods when electricity supplies are tight. That concern is becoming more urgent as electricity demand rises. ISO New England projects that the region’s reserve margin — the cushion between available electricity supply and peak demand — will fall from 15% in 2029 to 8% in 2034. Eversource requires data center developers to pay the full cost of any grid upgrades their projects trigger, Lucas said. His larger concern is the wholesale electricity market, where additional demand could force the region to rely more frequently on expensive and less efficient power plants, increasing costs for other customers. “I see no way, from an energy affordability or electric reliability perspective, that other customers would benefit from a hyperscale data center,” Lucas said. His concerns were echoed in May by Eversource CEO Joe Nolan, who told investors during an earnings call that he was “resisting data centers” in New England because they offered “no value” to customers and would drive energy costs higher. Eversource has no financial stake in whether a data center gets built. The utility earns regulated returns on the infrastructure it builds, not on the amount of electricity flowing through it. Policy pushback Concerns about costs and reliability have fueled data center pushback from policymakers in Connecticut and elsewhere. artigo.texto: Umicore Major supplier of premix anode slurries for EV batteries According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Anode Slurry Premix market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global anode slurry premix market is positioned for robust expansion over the 2026-2035 forecast period, with demand projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 6-9%. This growth is underpinned by the rapid scale-up of lithium-ion battery electrode production, particularly for electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. Anode slurry premix, a ready-to-coat blend of active anode material, conductive carbon, binder polymers, and solvent or water, has become a critical intermediate in battery manufacturing, enabling consistent viscosity, dispersion stability, and higher coating speeds. artigo.texto: Tesla Major cell & pack producer A US battery storage trial backed by technology company Google has shown that batteries are able to soak up excess renewable power and release it when fossil-fuel generation is more prevalent. The demonstration, unveiled on 17 September, produced what those involved call the first environmental revenue stream for battery energy storage system assets. Running for three months, the trial was executed by Quintrace, a unit of sustainable energy infrastructure investor Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners, together with developer esVolta and renewable energy procurement adviser LevelTen Energy. Hourly, time-stamped Granular Certificates were used to direct solar power to grid-connected battery storage and move it into hours when Google's energy use outstripped its renewable supply. esVolta supplied its 240MW/480MWh Anole project and 100MW/200MWh Burksol project for the trial. Quintrace furnished the software platform for verification, while LevelTen handled registry accounts to avoid double-counting and supplied the transaction framework for the storage-shift agreements. The companies said battery storage has historically been hard to capture in carbon accounting, since renewable matching has been assessed against yearly targets while storage value is hourly by nature. The Science Based Targets initiative, a corporate climate action body, is starting to mandate hourly reporting for large energy users, and the GHG Protocol is presently reviewing how to tackle the matter. The trial aimed to show both a commercial route that provides battery storage operators with a carbon-based revenue stream and a tracking route that properly accounts for and retires the hourly certificates underpinning it. Google agreed defined daily charging and discharging windows based on projected gaps in carbon-free energy generation, and operators dispatched their batteries according to those guidelines. The agreements featured a notable structure: Google contracted with battery operators to time-shift environmental attributes it already held, without tolling the batteries or taking on merchant or dispatch risk. That arrangement kept operators fully in charge of their assets, including pre-defined flexibility to chase energy price signals and react to grid emergencies. During the trial, the batteries charged with renewable energy in the defined mid-day charging window and discharged in the defined evening window, with Quintrace verifying each hour against the EnergyTag standard. Over the three months, the batteries charged and discharged a total of 9.2GWh within the respective windows. Quintrace's software tracks renewable energy from the point it charges a battery until it is returned to the grid. The company asserted that its dynamic loss calculations guarantee the clean energy claimed is only the clean energy actually delivered. The software can also use different accounting methods to suit each agreement structure between a battery operator and a buyer. Earlier in September, Google said alongside renewables developer-operator MN8 Energy and zinc hybrid cathode battery and storage system maker Eos Energy Enterprises that they would support the Mammoth Solar project in Kanawha County, West Virginia. The project pairs 86MW of solar with a 10MW/100MWh Eos Z3 zinc-based long-duration energy storage solution and a 70MW/280MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system. The newest announcement adds to a rising number of Google-backed trials and investments in battery energy storage and long-duration energy storage. Energy-Storage.news Premium recently interviewed esVolta chief executive Randolph Mann at the 2026 US Battery Asset Management Summit in Garden Grove, California, where he said storage assets are placed directly connected to the grid because that is where they can deliver the greatest benefit to the grid and to consumers, and that putting storage behind the meter for one customer sacrifices some of the asset's functionality. In separate news, San Diego-based home battery storage company NeoVolta said its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power, has signed a binding capacity reservation agreement with Infinite Grid Capital to supply battery energy storage equipment for Northern Ontario Edge artificial intelligence data centre projects during calendar year 2027. Announced on 17 September, the roughly US$53 million binding commitment is the first major commercial commitment under NeoVolta Power's previously announced utility-scale framework with Infinite Grid Capital, which envisages approximately 1.1GWh of potential battery storage deployments and approximately US$200 million of potential supply across multiple markets. The capacity reservation agreement is meant to support the Northern Ontario Edge AI data centre project and marks an initial commercial step in NeoVolta's wider relationship with Infinite Grid Capital. NeoVolta held a grand-opening ceremony for its NeoVolta Power facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, on 17 September. The 210,600-square-foot facility is a purpose-built domestic battery energy storage manufacturing platform intended to assemble commercial, industrial and utility-scale energy storage products. The company's initial Pendergrass production line is moving through commissioning and site acceptance testing, with the production ramp still on track for the fourth quarter of 2026. This comes after the 10 September news that NeoVolta secured a US$20 million senior credit facility from RoHo Capital Opportunity Fund, a joint venture between Horizon Technology Finance Corporation and CR Financial Holdings. artigo.texto: Dimensionamento de Armazenamento em Baterias: Usar Dados Operacionais Reais para Melhorar a Bancabilidade de BESS Segundo Ashutosh Vats, que lidera o desenvolvimento de negócios de BESS na 3E, as baterias já em operação oferecem pontos de referência valiosos para o trabalho essencial de dimensionar corretamente os sistemas de armazenamento e para outras escolhas significativas de projeto. Em um artigo para o Energy-Storage.news, Vats sustenta que os projetos de armazenamento podem começar a perder receita no momento em que entram em operação, e que a verdadeira tarefa está em extrair lições das operações reais e aplicá-las para afinar as premissas que sustentam os projetos subsequentes. O artigo explora por que as premissas sobre o dimensionamento de baterias podem influenciar a economia do projeto mais do que muitos desenvolvedores percebem, e como a combinação de dados operacionais ao vivo com modelagem financeira pode gerar casos de investimento mais críveis e confiáveis, redefinindo, em última análise, os critérios do que torna um projeto de bateria bancável. O armazenamento é atualmente a tecnologia de energia de crescimento mais rápido no mundo. A Agência Internacional de Energia estima a capacidade recém-implantada em 2025 em 108GW, um aumento de 40% em relação a 2024 e onze vezes a base instalada de apenas quatro anos antes. Modelos Financeiros Apoiados em Premissas que Mudam Quase todo projeto de BESS é sustentado por um modelo financeiro que contém um estudo de dimensionamento que define potência e duração, projeta receita e gera a taxa interna de retorno necessária para liberar capital. Vats destaca uma realidade incômoda para desenvolvedores e produtores independentes de energia que enfrentam seus primeiros empreendimentos de BESS: esse modelo se apoia em premissas, e cada uma delas começa a mudar no momento em que o ativo entra em operação. Veja como funciona um estudo padrão de dimensionamento de baterias. Para determinar a configuração ideal, o modelo simula a operação da bateria ao longo de vários anos, com base em projeções granulares de preços de energia e geração renovável. Na prática, ele presume previsão perfeita do futuro. Isso não é uma falha do método. O propósito é estabelecer um parâmetro teórico: o teto de receita que uma bateria poderia obter com informação completa e decisões consistentemente corretas. Se um modelo financeiro assume, por exemplo, 2% de queda de capacidade anual enquanto o campo entrega 4%, a receita será superestimada anualmente, acumulando-se ao longo do prazo da dívida. Essa discrepância pode determinar se um projeto consegue ou não cobrir suas obrigações de dívida. Ainda assim, a maioria dos modelos continua a depender de curvas de fabricantes, e a maior parte das plataformas operacionais apenas repassa o estado de saúde informado pelo sistema de gerenciamento de bateria no local, frequentemente fornecido pelo próprio OEM que concedeu a garantia. Consequentemente, as premissas que decidem se um projeto de BESS é financiável são frequentemente as mais difíceis de avaliar a partir de uma ficha técnica. As evidências mais fortes vêm de baterias que já operam comercialmente. Aqui o ciclo de retroalimentação importa. Ele deve se basear em medições independentes, orientadas pela física, e não em dados fornecidos por fornecedores de equipamentos. Gêmeos Digitais Independentes e Dados Operacionais ao Vivo Um gêmeo digital autônomo pode monitorar como as baterias conectadas realmente se comportam ao longo do tempo. Em vez de depender puramente de especificações, ele pode revelar o verdadeiro comportamento de mercado de uma bateria: como seu estado de saúde evolui, como diferentes mecanismos de degradação influenciam o desempenho, quanta receita ela garante e quão disponível permanece nos intervalos em que os preços de energia atingem o pico. Isso sustenta o SynaptiQ, a plataforma de desempenho de ativos da 3E: medir de forma independente como as baterias realmente se comportam em uma frota em operação e aplicar essa comprovação para refinar os modelos usados nos próximos projetos. Esses mesmos dados operacionais podem depois ser encaminhados de volta à ferramenta de dimensionamento de BESS da 3E. Como resultado, as premissas de degradação deixam de se apoiar exclusivamente em especificações de fabricantes. Elas podem se basear em como baterias de química idêntica se degradaram na prática sob condições operacionais, ciclos de trabalho e climas semelhantes. Durante o desenvolvimento, os investidores podem usar a ferramenta de dimensionamento para avaliar diferentes tamanhos de bateria e estratégias de mercado e medir seu comportamento em diferentes cenários. O processo de otimização integrado pode então identificar configurações que entregam o melhor equilíbrio entre desempenho técnico e retorno financeiro. Na Espanha, por exemplo, onde a instalação conjunta de usinas fotovoltaicas e/ou parques eólicos com armazenamento em baterias está florescendo, compreender como as distintas tecnologias produzirão eletricidade de modo a otimizar a acumulação de receitas por meio do tamanho correto do BESS exige uma ferramenta de otimização capaz de incorporar muitas variáveis, abordagens de entrada no mercado e simulação genuína de como os diversos ativos funcionarão ao longo do tempo. Nos últimos 2 anos, as simulações indicaram progressivamente a necessidade de baterias de 4 horas em vez de baterias de 2 horas para alcançar lucratividade e VPL ideais. Repensando a Bancabilidade Para investidores e credores, isso altera como a bancabilidade deve ser concebida. Um projeto invariavelmente dependerá de premissas sobre preços futuros, degradação, disponibilidade e receitas. No entanto, essas premissas se tornam mais sólidas quando continuamente validadas em relação ao desempenho de ativos em operação real. artigo.texto: Dois projetos australianos de armazenamento em baterias entram no Market Management System da AEMO Dois empreendimentos de armazenamento em baterias de escala utilitária na Austrália avançaram para uma fase decisiva de registro de mercado, conforme noticiado pelo GPE NEMLog, um rastreador de dados de projetos em todo o Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade. As instalações são o Tailem Bend BESS 3, da Vena Energy, na Austrália do Sul, e o Wooreen BESS, em Victoria, de copropriedade da EnergyAustralia e da Banpu Energy Australia. Em 15 de setembro de 2026, os dois sistemas foram admitidos no Market Management System do Operador do Mercado de Energia da Austrália sob os códigos TB3B1 e WOORB1, respectivamente. Geoff Eldridge, do GPE NEMLog, observou que ingressar no Market Management System é diferente de alcançar a plena operação comercial, mas permite que uma unidade avance para testes e comissionamento antes da participação padrão no mercado. Tailem Bend BESS 3 O Tailem Bend BESS 3 tem um máximo operacional registrado de 204MW, uma capacidade registrada de 263MW e 408MWh de armazenamento, o que corresponde a uma duração de duas horas e uma taxa de rampa de 82MW por minuto. Situado a cerca de 2,5km a sudeste do município de Tailem Bend e a aproximadamente 89km a leste-sudeste de Adelaide, o projeto se conecta ao Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade por meio da Subestação Tailem Bend adjacente, da ElectraNet. Ele fica ao lado de outros dois ativos da Vena Energy no mesmo local. A Vena Energy, divisão de desenvolvimento de renováveis do Vena Group, sediado em Singapura, iniciou a construção desse projeto autônomo em dezembro de 2025, com comissionamento previsto para 2027. Este é o terceiro projeto de baterias do desenvolvedor na Austrália, depois do Wandoan South BESS, de 100MW/150MWh, em Queensland. A iniciativa sucede a conclusão, pela Vena Energy, de uma bateria menor no mesmo local. Em janeiro de 2025, a empresa instalou uma bateria de 41,5MW ao lado de sua usina solar existente de 87MW em Tailem Bend, finalizando o que chama de Tailem Bend 2 Hybrid Project e elevando a produção combinada na rede de suas duas usinas solares co-localizadas de 182MW para 223,5MW. A Austrália do Sul obtém aproximadamente 75% de sua demanda anual de eletricidade de fontes eólicas e solares e pretende alcançar 100% de energia renovável líquida até o fim de 2027. Wooreen BESS O Wooreen BESS tem um máximo operacional registrado de 350MW, uma capacidade registrada de 491MW e 1.400MWh de armazenamento, resultando em uma duração de quatro horas e uma taxa de rampa de 140MW por minuto. Ele está em desenvolvimento em Hazelwood North, no Vale Latrobe, em Victoria, ao lado da existente Jeeralang Power Station, da EnergyAustralia, e a cerca de 138km a leste-sudeste de Melbourne, situado dentro de um aglomerado em expansão de armazenamento e infraestrutura de rede em toda a Gippsland. A EnergyAustralia, geradora e varejista de energia australiana, alcançou o fechamento financeiro do projeto em fevereiro de 2025 e iniciou a construção em poucos dias. O sistema de armazenamento em baterias deve entrar em operação antes da aposentadoria da usina termelétrica a carvão Yallourn, de 1.450MW, da EnergyAustralia, prevista para meados de 2028. Em julho de 2025, a EnergyAustralia alienou uma participação de 50% no projeto para a tailandesa Banpu Public Company, que opera na Austrália como Banpu Energy Australia, em uma transação avaliada em aproximadamente AU$700 milhões, ou US$490 milhões. O grupo finlandês de tecnologia marinha e de energia Wartsila foi contratado para fornecer o hardware das baterias, a engenharia, o comissionamento e um contrato de serviço de 15 anos, utilizando suas unidades Quantum High Energy e a GEMS Digital Energy Platform. A Wartsila concluiu a entrega e a instalação de todas as 1.038 unidades Quantum no local em julho de 2026. O sistema foi projetado para operar em modo grid-forming, a fim de fornecer inércia sintética à medida que a geração a carvão se retira da rede de Victoria. A Zenviron, joint venture do grupo de engenharia Monadelphous e da desenvolvedora de energia renovável ZEM Energy, recebeu o contrato de balance-of-plant do projeto em fevereiro de 2025, abrangendo projeto, construção, instalação e comissionamento. Tilt Renewables atua como desenvolvedora do projeto, e as operações comerciais do Wooreen têm como meta 2027. artigo.texto: A new aluminum coating could simplify how battery components are manufactured by protecting the metal during forming while adding properties needed inside electric vehicle and energy storage systems. Novelis is expanding its portfolio of coated aluminum solutions for battery applications, targeting components including battery enclosures, casings and electrical connectors known as bus bars. The approach combines automotive-grade aluminum sheet with surface treatments designed to improve corrosion resistance and formability. The company says the coated material can also be engineered to provide electrical insulation for specific battery applications. A key part of the technology is a water-based coating applied to aluminum coils before they are formed into components. The coating is designed to remain effective after stamping, potentially allowing manufacturers to remove some processing steps used with untreated aluminum. Coating simplifies battery production Battery components must withstand demanding manufacturing and operating conditions. Aluminum is attractive because it is lightweight, durable and recyclable, but components may require additional surface treatments to protect them from corrosion or provide electrical insulation. Novelis says its pre-applied coating can address some of those requirements before the aluminum reaches the forming stage. Because the coating is already on the coil, manufacturers may be able to reduce reliance on external lubrication and additional e-coating processes. “Leveraging decades of automotive expertise, we have developed aluminum solutions that combine advanced surface technologies with high-performance sheet products for demanding battery applications,” says Milan Felberbaum, Director R&D, Novelis Europe. “By integrating these capabilities, we help customers improve manufacturing efficiency while supporting battery performance and durability.” More from Energy See All The company says the coating has already been proven and is in use on its advanced coating line in Germany. Its ability to withstand stamping is important because battery components often need to be shaped into complex forms after the coating is applied. Aluminum targets tougher battery demands The coated aluminum can be used for battery enclosures and casings, where corrosion protection can help improve component durability. It can also be tailored for electrical insulation, a property that can be useful for components that need to prevent unwanted electrical contact. The technology is aimed at both electric mobility and stationary energy storage. That gives the material a role across different battery systems rather than limiting it to automotive applications. Novelis is also emphasizing the use of recycled aluminum. The company says high-recycled-content, low-carbon aluminum can support efforts to reduce the environmental impact of battery supply chains. Closed-loop recycling could allow aluminum recovered from products to be returned to the manufacturing cycle. The announcement is therefore focused less on changing battery chemistry and more on changing the material and manufacturing process around the battery. By combining aluminum’s low weight with a pre-applied coating, the company is targeting a way to make battery components easier to manufacture while meeting durability and insulation requirements. Fewer steps for battery makers The approach could also help manufacturers reduce manufacturing complexity if fewer coating and lubrication stages are required. However, the announcement does not provide quantified figures for cost savings, production-time reductions or improvements in battery performance. Novelis is positioning the expanded portfolio for the growing battery and energy storage markets, building on its experience supplying aluminum products to the automotive industry.

Financiamentos semelhantes, respaldados por locatários com grau de investimento, foram vendidos a rendimentos inferiores a 6% no início deste ano. Investidores apresentaram pedidos equivalentes, aproximadamente, a quatro vezes o tamanho total da emissão lançada na quinta-feira (17), disseram as pessoas, sob condição de anonimato, pois não estão autorizadas a falar publicamente. A captação ajudará a financiar a construção de um data center em Sandersville, no estado americano da Geórgia, segundo um documento regulatório. O Morgan Stanley lidera a emissão, disse outra pessoa. A instalação foi totalmente alugada pela Anviran, subsidiária da Meta, por meio de um contrato de US$ 6,6 bilhões com duração de 20 anos, de acordo com uma apresentação da CleanSpark. Data centers: fluxo de receitas A previsão é que o data center comece a operar no quarto trimestre de 2027, e a Meta garantirá o pagamento do aluguel e das despesas operacionais, informou a empresa. Trata-se da primeira emissão de junk bonds vinculada a data centers da Meta, segundo dados compilados pela Bloomberg. O compromisso da Meta com a CleanSpark oferece à empresa tomadora, classificada como de grau especulativo, um fluxo de receita previsível para sustentar o financiamento de um projeto caro. Desenvolvedores de data centers venderam cerca de US$ 39 bilhões em títulos classificados como high yield – de alto rendimento e risco elevado – até agora neste ano, a maioria respaldada por contratos de locação de longo prazo com empresas de computação em nuvem em hyperscalers, incluindo Oracle e Amazon, segundo dados compilados pela Bloomberg. A CleanSpark e o Morgan Stanley não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de comentário. A Meta se recusou a comentar. Sediada em Las Vegas, a CleanSpark está entre o número crescente de empresas abertas de mineração de bitcoin que estão se tornando operadoras de data centers para dar suporte a aplicações de inteligência artificial. A companhia tem valor de mercado de aproximadamente US$ 3,29 bilhões.

artigo.texto: Mais de 1 milhão de candidatos a emprego procuraram vagas em data centers no site de recrutamento Indeed neste ano. Em agosto, o volume de buscas era oito vezes maior que no início de 2022. Pesquisas do site de empregos constataram que, entre os trabalhadores horistas responsáveis por manutenção e instalação, os data centers oferecem salários cerca de 42% maiores do que funções semelhantes em outros tipos de empresa. Segundo o Indeed, um gerente de projetos em um data center ganha por volta de US$ 115 mil por ano — cerca de R$ 591 mil pela cotação de R$ 5,14 por dólar. A Digital Realty afirmou que engenheiros iniciantes em suas instalações podem ganhar aproximadamente US$ 66 mil por ano, ou cerca de R$ 339 mil, enquanto a remuneração média pode superar US$ 120 mil, o equivalente a cerca de R$ 617 mil, para profissionais mais experientes. Profissionais com conhecimento em sistemas elétricos, engenharia de redes e sistemas de refrigeração são muito procurados, disse Brandi Galvin Morandi, diretora de recursos humanos da operadora de data centers Equinix. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, entre elas a Meta Platforms, investiram na formação de mão de obra especializada para construir essas instalações. Na Virgínia, onde há uma grande concentração de data centers, o Northern Virginia Community College lançou, com a ajuda do setor privado, um programa de capacitação para o trabalho nessas unidades. “Essas são instalações essenciais, que operam 24 horas por dia, e isso exige uma combinação específica de formação técnica, disciplina de segurança e experiência prática — algo que está em falta diante da velocidade com que o setor cresce”, disse Cindy Fiedelman, diretora de recursos humanos da Digital Realty. A empresa opera mais de 300 data centers em seis continentes. Em unidades como a de Ashburn, a Digital Realty aluga espaço para grandes empresas de tecnologia que precisam de capacidade computacional. Entre seus clientes estão Oracle, Meta e IBM. A Digital Realty também enfrenta a reação pública cada vez mais intensa contra a construção de data centers. Em Atlanta, a companhia busca uma exceção a uma proibição local de data centers perto de terminais de transporte enquanto tenta construir na cidade uma unidade de US$ 500 milhões — cerca de R$ 2,57 bilhões. Moradores se opuseram ao projeto, que atualmente se encontra num impasse. Um porta-voz da Digital Realty afirmou que o projeto criaria empregos bem remunerados e que a empresa estava “comprometida em chegar lá da maneira correta”, em parceria com a comunidade. A unidade de Ashburn reúne trabalhadores administrativos e operacionais. Entre eles estão seguranças, técnicos que cuidam da estrutura de cabos dos clientes, profissionais da cadeia de suprimentos que buscam materiais e engenheiros que monitoram possíveis problemas. As funções são semelhantes em outros data centers pelo país. A parte mais importante do trabalho é manter os centros em funcionamento. A Digital Realty estima que seus data centers ficam operacionais durante 99,999% do tempo, mas agora busca alcançar 99,9999%. A diferença parece pequena, mas equivale a reduzir o tempo de interrupção de seis minutos para 30 segundos por ano. Don Atkinson trabalha na empresa há cerca de 14 anos, depois de passar 17 anos nas Forças Armadas e exercer uma função na manutenção de sistemas de energia de reserva. Hoje, aos 53 anos, ocupa um cargo de gestão e orienta engenheiros mais jovens. Assim como muitos trabalhadores do setor, Atkinson tenta lidar com a mudança repentina na opinião pública a respeito de um ambiente de trabalho no qual construiu uma carreira estável. “Nós amamos os Estados Unidos, amamos o país, amamos o setor, e é simplesmente estranho”, disse ele sobre a reação pública. Atkinson também observou que ele próprio não usa muita inteligência artificial. “É um momento estranho.” Outro funcionário, Malcolm Mosely, disse que sua família às vezes menciona as questões políticas envolvendo os data centers, mas ele tenta não se concentrar nisso: “Eu apenas venho aqui fazer meu trabalho”. Em uma quinta-feira recente, Mosely estava dentro de uma gaiola preta repleta de fios amarelos, verificando um cabo de interconexão que liga a operação de um cliente à de outro. Waddy, que trabalha na unidade de Ashburn há três anos, tem formação superior de curta duração em administração e anteriormente trabalhava com vendas em uma empresa de aquecimento, ventilação e ar-condicionado. Ele começou no turno da noite do data center, ajudando a manter máquinas de clientes espalhados pelo mundo. Desde então, subiu na hierarquia. Suas rondas diárias incluem a inspeção da galeria de tratamento de ar da unidade, onde enormes aparelhos de ar-condicionado bombeiam ar frio para o restante do data center. No andar de cima, o salão de dados parece um vestiário, com servidores empilhados em gabinetes ou gaiolas que as empresas podem alugar. Não há logotipos nem nomes de empresas, porém, porque concorrentes mantêm operações lado a lado. O uso de protetores auriculares é recomendado no local para evitar danos provocados pelo rugido dos servidores quando se chega perto deles. No telhado, Waddy verifica centenas de condensadores dispostos em fileiras organizadas para ajudar a resfriar a instalação. Ele procura defeitos ou estragos causados por pássaros que gostam de bicar os equipamentos. Do telhado, é possível ver ao longe um guindaste usado na construção do data center de um concorrente. “É agradável aqui em cima”, disse Waddy. “Adoro esta ronda.” Traduzido do inglês por InvestNews

artigo.texto: RWE builds one of the Netherlands' largest battery systems RWE has made the final investment decision to build one of the largest battery storage systems in the Netherlands. Published on September 21, 2026 Team IO+ selects and features the most important news stories on innovation and technology, carefully curated by our editors. RWE has made the final investment decision to build one of the largest battery storage systems in the Netherlands: a 400 MW/1,100 MWh battery at the power plant in Moerdijk. The system will consist of 208 containers with lithium-ion batteries and will be able to deliver its full capacity for nearly three hours. Construction will begin shortly, and commissioning is scheduled for the second quarter of 2028. Nikolaus Valerius, CEO of RWE Generation SE: “This battery represents an important milestone for a reliable power supply and for relieving the strain on the power grid in North Brabant. As one of the largest and most powerful battery systems in the Netherlands, it will be able to meet the peak evening demand of approximately 500,000 households for nearly three hours. At the same time, it can absorb excess electricity from the grid within seconds. Battery storage plays a crucial role in building a resilient energy system that accommodates a growing share of renewable energy sources.” Mark Lentjes, Regional Director of TenneT South Netherlands: “We are pleased that RWE in West Brabant intends to contribute to a more efficient use of the power grid with a large-scale battery that acts as a congestion reliever. RWE’s large-scale battery is located near the 150,000-volt Moerdijk-Noord high-voltage substation and helps alleviate the bottleneck there, which in turn reduces congestion throughout North Brabant.” Alleviating congestion on the power grid The new battery system will make optimal use of the existing infrastructure: it will be connected to the national power grid via the existing substation at the RWE power plant in Moerdijk. Through capacity management agreements with grid operator TenneT, the battery will be used to alleviate congestion in the North Brabant region. Thanks to this development, space will be created on the grid for parties on the waiting list who wish to purchase electricity. TenneT, together with the regional grid operator Enexis, will investigate what this means for whom and when in the coming period. The grid operator will incorporate this development, along with other developments in the region, into the reassessment of the congestion management study December 2026. The new battery system will be able to provide advanced grid services, such as immediate reserve (inertia). The Moerdijk site already hosts the first synthetic inertia battery connected to the continental European grid, with a capacity of 7.5 MW/11 MWh. Linking offshore wind energy to onshore flexibility The 795 MW offshore wind project by RWE and TotalEnergies off the Dutch coast is designed to combine offshore wind power generation with onshore flexibility solutions that help align renewable energy production with electricity demand. In Moerdijk, the battery projects play a key role in this by storing electricity when wind production is high and feeding it back into the grid when needed. This helps smooth out fluctuations and optimize the use of renewable energy. Together with technologies such as electrolysis, e-boilers, and EV charging, this supports OranjeWind’s ambition to integrate offshore wind energy more effectively into the Dutch energy system.

artigo.texto: Two dozen years ago, Gina and Darin Madsen bought a house in Monrovia, a small community in Morgan County, planning to stay there through retirement. But their peace and quiet has been disrupted by the construction of a massive data center virtually on their doorstep — something they didn’t want and didn’t even know about until it was too late. “We really didn’t have a lot of time to even react to it,” Gina Madsen said. “Even if we had reacted, which some people did ... voices were not heard.” Like other Monrovia residents, the Madsens received little notice about the 400-acre data center plans before the deal was signed and sealed. And it would be months before they discovered that the builder was Google, one of the wealthiest and most powerful companies in the world. That’s because of a non-disclosure agreement signed by the Morgan County Board of Commissioners, promising to keep the owner’s name private until the transaction was complete. Research by the Arnolt Center for Investigative Journalism and the Limestone Post found such agreements are not unusual. The Arnolt Center and the Limestone Post researched 46 AI data centers identified by the Indiana Citizens Action Coalition as existing, proposed, or withdrawn, and found seven projects where an NDA was used. The center then filed records requests with 26 communities either with active data sites or ones under development and found: - Officials in New Carlisle in northwest Indiana and in Morgan County signed NDAs - 12 communities denied having any responsive records - 12 communities never responded to records requests New proposals continue to proliferate across the state as Indiana’s business-friendly environment has made it a magnet for data centers. As of February 2026, the state has 38 operational data centers and 54 planned data centers, according to the Pew Research Center. Opposition to the centers spans the political spectrum, as residents worry about the environmental impact on their communities and the relatively small number of permanent jobs planned for such large-scale projects. Some communities, including Indianapolis, are weighing regulations to block data center projects. “Signing an agreement that prevents them from disclosing to the very public they serve [is] really important information, right? I find that hugely problematic,” said Pat Garofalo, director of state and local policy at the American Economic Liberties Project. “I think, in terms of just democracy and our understanding of how American democracy is supposed to function, it simply should not be allowed for a public official to sign away their right to communicate with their constituents, to a private corporation.” ‘Already set in stone’: Monrovia development moves forward The Madsens received a letter from the Morgan County Economic Development Corporation on January 24, 2025, informing them of a community meeting February 10 about a potential data center development in Morgan County. Gina Madsen said the meeting was informational and people could speak up and ask questions. At that meeting, the Morgan County Plan Commission announced plans for “Project Louie,” a large data center project on West Keller Hill Road in Monroe Township, close to Monrovia. The Morgan County Economic Development Corporation had made a rezoning request for the 391-acre site on behalf of an unnamed company. Despite opposition from community members, on February 18, the Morgan County Board of Commissioners unanimously approved a rezoning request for the site from agricultural to a planned unit development, laying the groundwork for the construction of the data center. “It was already set in stone. Man, went from day one, it’s a done deal,” Darin Madsen said. In October 2025, Google issued a written statement announcing it was the previously unnamed developer of the data center. That same month, the Morgan County Commissioners voted to approve the rezoning of an additional 158 acres, bringing the total for the site to 549 acres. As of April 2026, the town of Monrovia initiated proceedings to annex land to the east, including the entire site data center site, allowing the town to receive additional tax revenue. Emails leaked to the Morgan County Correspondent said that Google offered Monrovia $12 million in wastewater treatment plant upgrades if the Town Council dropped its bid to annex the land that includes the data center. The Morgan County Commissioners in June proposed a tax increment financing district that would include the Project Louie site. The Morgan County Redevelopment Commission voted unanimously in favor of the TIF at a July 15 meeting. The site of the Monrovia data center in mid-June, looking northeast. The Indianapolis skyline can be seen faintly on the horizon in the top right corner. The Madsens are devastated about the sudden disruption to their retirement plans. “We were looking out over a nice field and a nice sunset for 23 years,” Gina said. “We have a front porch we love to sit out on and have that view, and that’s gone, that will never be back.” NDAs keep key details, developers shielded Indiana is attracting a large number of data centers, according to the available data from the Data Center Map. Nationwide, Virginia and Texas lead with 685 and 466 data centers [operational or planned] respectively. Indiana State Representative Matt Pierce, a senior lecturer in The Media School at Indiana University, said it is difficult for the public to get information about data centers when public officials sign non-disclosure agreements. “The problem is when the public comes to the public hearing, or they’re discussing whether or not to approve the data center, the local officials can’t have a complete discussion,” he said. “They can’t really inform the public about all the impacts of data centers that they’ve signed a non-disclosure agreement that says they can’t tell the public about the information they have.” As the number of data centers grows, concerns about ND

artigo.texto: Ireland proposes deal to end spat over EU carbon market permits Ireland proposed a compromise plan to adjust the European Union’s carbon market supply controls, seeking to end a dispute between member states over surplus emission allowances. Ireland, which holds the EU rotating presidency until the end of this year, wants to introduce additional assurances a broader reform of the emission trading system should gradually tighten the limit on excessive carbon permits kept in a reserve for potential interventions Ireland's plan was on Monday shared with member states as part of talks on revising the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) regulation, according to people with knowledge of the issue. The design of the MSR, which absorbs surplus permits from the market and can release them in the case of price shocks, has divided EU member states as the bloc seeks to reconcile its ambitious climate policies with the need to protect its industry in the face of rising energy prices and tougher global competition. The revision of the reserve was originally put forward by the European Commission in April, after EU leaders called on the bloc’s executive to take steps to reduce energy costs that were already stubbornly high before the Iran war. The proposal was to make the MSR more flexible by scrapping invalidation of permits it absorbs from the market and keeping them usable for potential future interventions. The Irish presidency will seek agreement on the MSR on Wednesday, said a spokesperson for the presidency, adding the proposal was time-sensitive and European leaders had called for its urgent adoption. The goal was to reach a fast deal on the MSR adjustment to calm the market and then discuss potential further changes during a broader reform of the ETS, which the commission unveiled in July and member states discuss separately. The MSR became a key feature of the ETS in 2019, when it began absorbing surplus permits from the market once a certain threshold of allowances in circulation was reached. The legislation currently in force invalidates any allowances held in the reserve above a threshold of 400 million on January 1 each year. The commission sought to overturn that provision to build a bigger buffer of permits that could be used to stabilise the market. Earlier this month, Ireland proposed letting the excess allowances sit in the MSR until the end of 2030. From the start of 2031, the reserve could keep up to 800 million allowances, with the level to be potentially reduced during the post-2030 reform of the ETS. In a last-minute push to further tighten the regulation, Germany called for an annual 4% reduction of the threshold starting in 2028, in line with the declining emissions cap. The country also wants to maintain the rate at which the MSR absorbs allowances at 24%, and to reduce the level triggering the withdrawal of surplus permits from circulation. It should be set at 650 million compared with the current 833 million. The German proposal was opposed by a group of countries including Poland and the Czech Republic. In its new compromise, the Irish presidency is seeking to resolve the spat by embedding in the deal an additional commitment to include in the broader ETS reform an annual reduction of the limit on surplus permits in the reserve. The proposal will be discussed on Wednesday by ambassadors representing member states to the EU. If they reach a deal, it will become their stance for talks with the European Parliament on the final shape of the MSR regulation.

artigo.texto: O Nordeste reúne condições de energia renovável e conectividade internacional que podem ampliar sua participação na disputa por investimentos em data centers, segundo avaliação do ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. A declaração foi feita nesta terça-feira (15/09/2026), durante o evento Transição Energética: O Nordeste como hub digital do futuro, realizado em Fortaleza (CE). De acordo com o ministro, a combinação de energia, conectividade e segurança jurídica está entre os fatores considerados por empresas de tecnologia na escolha de locais para instalação de grandes estruturas de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Ele afirmou que a região já dispõe dos dois primeiros elementos e que o Governo Federal trabalha na criação de condições regulatórias para investimentos. A matriz elétrica brasileira possui 86,8% de fontes renováveis, enquanto o Nordeste concentra mais de 90% da geração eólica nacional e 52% dos projetos de geração solar fotovoltaica centralizada. Para o ministro, a proximidade entre fontes de energia e data centers pode ser relevante diante do peso da eletricidade nos custos operacionais dessas estruturas. Fortaleza concentra nove sistemas de cabos submarinos A posição geográfica também foi apresentada como um fator de competitividade para o Nordeste. O Brasil conta atualmente com 16 sistemas de cabos submarinos com presença no país, sendo que nove têm aterrissagem em Fortaleza. A infraestrutura faz da capital cearense um dos principais pontos de entrada e saída de dados internacionais do Brasil. Segundo os dados apresentados pelo ministro, cerca de 90% do tráfego internacional brasileiro passa por Fortaleza, conectando a infraestrutura nacional aos mercados dos Estados Unidos, Europa e África. Na avaliação apresentada durante o evento, a concentração de rotas de comunicação permite que estruturas instaladas em Fortaleza tenham baixa latência e alternativas de conexão internacional. O ministro relacionou essa característica à possibilidade de implantação de centros de processamento de dados voltados a serviços digitais, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. Outro aspecto mencionado foi o potencial de utilização de parte da energia renovável que deixa de ser gerada em determinados períodos devido a restrições de demanda ou de transmissão. Entre janeiro e abril de 2026, o Nordeste registrou 2.233 MW médios de curtailment, termo utilizado para indicar a redução ou interrupção de uma geração de energia que poderia ser produzida, mas não é aproveitada naquele momento. Data centers podem ampliar aproveitamento da geração renovável Segundo o ministro, a instalação de data centers próxima aos grandes centros de geração pode contribuir para elevar o aproveitamento da energia disponível. A proposta está relacionada à possibilidade de criar demanda adicional em locais onde existem períodos de restrição à geração. A segurança do fornecimento para os data centers, conforme a explicação apresentada, está relacionada à integração do sistema elétrico ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A estrutura permite combinar diferentes fontes de geração, enquanto baterias e tecnologias de armazenamento podem auxiliar no gerenciamento da demanda. O ministro também citou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) como instrumento para ampliar a previsibilidade dos investimentos. O regime prevê incentivos tributários para equipamentos e infraestrutura tecnológica e mecanismos destinados a estimular a instalação de data centers nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste. Redata busca ampliar investimentos fora do Sudeste A política também está associada à estratégia de descentralização da infraestrutura digital brasileira, com estímulo à implantação de novos polos fora do Sudeste. Para o ministro, a previsibilidade regulatória é um dos elementos considerados por investidores na definição dos projetos. O Ceará foi citado como exemplo dessa estratégia. Em janeiro de 2026, Fortaleza recebeu o primeiro financiamento do país com recursos do Fundo de Universalização dos Serviços de Telecomunicações (Fust) destinado a um data center. O financiamento, de R$ 233 milhões, será utilizado na expansão do empreendimento Mega Lobster. O projeto tem previsão de alcançar 20 MW de capacidade até 2029 e de gerar aproximadamente 400 empregos. O estado também abriga, no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, um dos projetos de data center em desenvolvimento na América Latina. Ceará é apontado como referência para o Nordeste A experiência do Ceará foi apresentada pelo ministro como possibilidade de referência para outros estados nordestinos. A estratégia federal prevê a combinação de energia renovável, conectividade internacional, financiamento, incentivos tributários e segurança jurídica para estimular novos projetos de infraestrutura digital. A expansão dos data centers também está relacionada ao crescimento da inteligência artificial, que demanda maior capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e transmissão de dados. Estudo da Fundação Getulio Vargas citado pelo ministro estima que um único data center destinado à inteligência artificial poderia mobilizar aproximadamente R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos. Segundo a estimativa apresentada, um empreendimento desse porte poderia gerar cerca de 12,5 mil empregos durante a implantação e aproximadamente 1.860 postos permanentes. Os efeitos econômicos também alcançariam segmentos como construção civil, energia, telecomunicações, serviços especializados e formação profissional. A estratégia defendida pelo Governo Federal considera a distribuição da infraestrutura digital de acordo com a disponibilidade de energia e a proximidade dos usuários dos serviços. artigo.texto: Evento no Acre adota metodologia para compensar pegada de carbono e reúne especialistas em painel A sustentabilidade e a transição para uma economia de baixo carbono deixaram de ser pautas do futuro para se tornarem compromissos do presente na Amazônia. Durante a realização do Inova Amazônia Summit, em Rio Branco, o evento não apenas debateu o assunto, mas aplicou na prática o conceito de neutralidade ao descarbonizar as suas atividades. A iniciativa é viabilizada em parceria com a climatetech de descarbonização Compensei, responsável por aplicar a metodologia MRC (Medir, Reduzir e Compensar) ao longo de toda a programação. “O Carbono Neutro é um evento onde a gente a Compensei consegue medir e reduzir as emissões e compensar o impacto ambiental e climático. É a metodologia MRC: medir e reduzir e compensar. Primeiro a gente mede o quanto de emissão o evento está gerando desde o pré-evento, da seleção de fornecedores, montagem e desmontagem, e durante o evento a gente faz algumas ações para redução dessas emissões”, explicou João Vitor, analista de Inteligência Comercial. As emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE) geradas pelo evento serão mapeadas e neutralizadas por meio de créditos. “O Sebrae está investindo em créditos de carbono dentro de um projeto da Amazônia, que é justamente esse que remove o carbono da atmosfera. O crédito de carbono equivale a uma tonelada de gás de efeito estufa removida da atmosfera. Para engajar os visitantes, o evento disponibilizou o “Carbonômetro”, uma ferramenta acessível via QR Code nos crachás, permitindo que cada participante calcule sua pegada de carbono individual. Além da medição, o evento estimulou atitudes sustentáveis como a gestão correta de resíduos, o uso de copos de papel e a substituição do plástico descartável por garrafas reutilizáveis. “Hoje a nossa missão é impactar o máximo de pessoas, máximo de empresas e o máximo de eventos pra que todo mundo consiga avançar cada vez mais na ação climática. Essa iniciativa do Sebrae representa um grande passo e uma grande visibilidade principalmente para nossa Amazônia e para tantos microempreendedores que estão aqui trazendo produtos sustentáveis e trazendo inovação”, explicou. Painel aborda oportunidades e integridade dos créditos verdes na Amazônia Conectado às ações práticas de descarbonização do evento, o painel “Mercado de carbono: oportunidades reais para a Amazônia, integridade e créditos verdes”reuniu especialistas para discutir os caminhos que transformam o potencial ambiental do bioma em resultados concretos para o território e para os pequenos negócios. A moderação do painel foi conduzida por Elaine Novetti, analista técnica do Sebrae Nacional, especialista em gestão de pequenos negócios administração marketing e gestão de pessoas. O debate reuniu referências na área ambiental e de inovação. Vilena Ribeiro, bióloga, doutora em Biodiversidade e CEO da Compensei, enfatizou o papel da ciência e o avanço institucional do Sebrae ao incorporar parâmetros de sustentabilidade nas diretrizes. “Nós somos uma startup que trabalha com inovação aplicada à sustentabilidade. Então nós temos três eixos grandes de atuação fornecendo esses serviços tanto para empresas quanto para eventos e hoje é uma grande felicidade da gente estar aqui junto ao Sebrae Nacional como uma empresa licitada, o que significa que o Sebrae incorporou em todas em toda a sua concepção de eventos”, disse. “Eu sempre falo que o impacto negativo, o que a gente tem que fazer é transformar em impacto positivo. Esse é o primeiro passo, já o segundo passo é reduzir as emissões a partir do momento que eu conheço da minha operação e do meu evento e o que eu posso fazer para reduzir ao máximo as emissões. Isso é muito importante, é mais um passo que está sendo dado para atendimento dessa agenda 2030”, continuou. Contexto histórico e o papel do Brasil Resgatando a trajetória global do mercado climáticos, Thiago Mendes lembrou que a estruturação desse mercado teve início com o Protocolo de Kyoto, em 1997. Mendes citou a participação brasileira em iniciativas históricas, como o projeto do Banco Mundial (Prototype Carbon Fund) no final dos anos 1990, que utilizou áreas degradadas e florestas plantadas para produção de carvão vegetal no setor siderúrgico. “O Brasil chegou a ser o maior produtor de créditos de carbono do mundo entre 2003 e 2004, antes de ser ultrapassado por China e Índia. No entanto, a nossa principal vantagem comparativa — a capacidade de remoção de carbono pelas florestas tropicais — ainda precisa ser plenamente contemplada e valorizada”, destacou Thiago. Tecnologia espacial e o monitoramento MRV O engenheiro aeroespacial, pesquisador com certificação NASA e CEO da DivTER Amazon SarTec, Renan Santos detalhou como a tecnologia aeroespacial resolve gargalos históricos de medição e verificação na Amazônia através de geotecnologias e inteligência artificial. “Trabalhamos com o radar de abertura sintética (SAR), capaz de mapear a biomassa e monitorar a floresta mesmo sob a cobertura de nuvens, que atinge até 70% do tempo na região. Desenvolvemos uma plataforma para viabilizar projetos de REDD+ com rapidez e transparência, cruzando dados de desmatamento, biomassa e riscos de incêndio”, explicou Renan.

artigo.texto: Moss Landing shelter-in-place and road closure lifted after battery storage fire Firefighters responded Friday morning to a fire at the Moss Landing battery storage facility operated by Vistra Energy, the same facility damaged in a major battery fire in January 2025. The North Monterey County Fire District was dispatched shortly after 6:15 a.m. Crews arrived to find smoke and flames coming from the facility’s north side. The fire involved 1,500 batteries that were still energized inside a structure damaged during the 2025 fire. Officials said Friday’s fire was not comparable to the January 2025 fire in scale or complexity. They anticipate it could burn itself out over the next 24 hours. Everyone working at the facility has been accounted for, and no injuries have been reported. The incident is being managed under a unified command that includes the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office. The county’s Emergency Operations Center has also been activated. The Sheriff’s Office lifted the shelter-in-place order for the area within one-third of a mile of 7301 Highway 1, known as Zone PAZ-1. The hard closure of Dolan Road between Highway 1 and Via Tanques Road has also been lifted. Highway 1 remains open. The EPA is monitoring air quality in the area. KSBW 8 contacted the EPA and Vistra Energy for additional information but had not received a response. The North Monterey County Unified School District said its shelter-in-place order had been lifted. Schools and activities will continue as scheduled, and air-quality readings were in the normal range. Assemblymember Dawn Addis said she was “frustrated and deeply concerned” about the fire. “I'm frustrated and deeply concerned by the repeat fire at Moss Landing. Early this morning I received initial briefings on the Moss Landing battery energy storage fire. Although initial cleanup and battery removal, under the supervision of the federal EPA, were completed two weeks ago, 1,500 hard-to-access batteries remain in the damaged area of the facility. This incident is ongoing, and we don't yet know all details. I strongly ask surrounding communities to follow all safety instructions from emergency services." Additional information will be provided as it becomes available.

Lombardo order forces data center developers to fund Nevada schools and protect water and grid resources
Friday, Sept. 18, 2026 | 8:30 a.m.
Editor's note: Este artículo está traducido al español.
Gov. Joe Lombardo signed an executive order imposing new requirements on data center developers in Nevada, mandating they pay the state’s Local School Support Tax in full, cover their own project-related costs and protect local water and electrical grid resources.
The order, dated Wednesday and announced by his office today, establishes what the governor’s office calls the “Nevada Standard for Responsible Data Center Development.”
It sets guardrails on tax abatement legislation the Nevada Legislature passed in 2015, which required the Governor’s Office of Economic Development (GOED) to grant abatements to data centers meeting employment, wage and investment thresholds. That law contained no protections for energy or water use and gave the GOED Board no flexibility to deny abatements.
In 2025, lawmakers expanded the board’s authority to deny applications, approve them for lesser amounts or attach conditions.
Under the order, data center applications seeking a partial tax abatement cannot go before the GOED board unless the developer agrees to pay the school support tax in full and signs a binding “Community Support Commitment.”
Developers must also meet local water standards, cover the cost of serving their facility without passing those costs to ratepayers, and avoid straining the electrical grid during emergencies. GOED’s executive director will develop the commitment framework in consultation with the state engineer, the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada, state agencies, local governments and school districts, Lombardo’s office said. The order directs GOED’s executive director to publish the standard form of the commitment on or before Nov. 6.
The order also directs the state to produce a “Responsible Speed to Power Plan” identifying facilities needed to serve anticipated large-load demand through 2036, while pledging that costs will not be passed on to ratepayers. Language in the order’s preamble states it is in Nevada’s interest to protect its water, grid reliability, school funding, local land-use authority and taxpayers.
“They must pay their share, protect our water resources, keep costs from being passed on to ratepayers, and protect the communities that host them,” Lombardo said in a statement.
The governor said the order would also restore funding to public schools, putting “money back into our schools that otherwise would have been lost under outdated state law.”

artigo.texto: A Wilson County data center zoning ordinance is one step closer to becoming the rule after the county’s data center committee worked out the final details and passed the resolution during its Sept. 15 meeting. The committee went through the initial resolution section by section, evaluating what information Wilson County Planning Services Director Christopher Lawless included in the ordinance. The committee members then made changes as they worked through the draft ordinance. Among the details they discussed were berm height and vegetation; noise and vibration from the data center; third-party plan review; parking spaces; size classifications and property line distance; distance from location where people assemble; eliminating possible interference of public electricity, gas, water, sewer and internet; and generators which the data centers could use in an emergency. Berm height would be determined at 40 percent of the height of the building and would have state-approved vegetation such as maple, oak or magnolia trees on it to help deter the noise affecting any other structures. The data centers would have to have utility capacity before plans would be approved, eliminating the need for any backup generators to run full time, all day. Middle Tennessee Electric would work with the data centers to determine the capacity needed, as well as providing the actual electrical service. In addition, the water and wastewater utility that serves the area in which any center would locate would also work with the facility to determine their water and wastewater needs. A public concern about data centers is noise and vibration from the centers, affecting homes, business and other structures. The committee discussed hiring an experienced acoustic consultant or engineer, as well as purchasing sound level detectors, rather than county employees being responsible for determining sound levels which exceed the limits set forth in the resolution. They discussed 40 dBA and 60 dBC as the maximum noise level. The 40 dBA is equivalent to a refrigerator hum, according to Decibelmeter.org. The American Academy of Audiology states that 60 dBC is equivalent to normal conversation or a dishwasher running. There would also be a timeline that the facility would be required to respond to the city for any noise or vibration complaint, the committee decided. The resolution states that the facility would have up to 48 hours from the time the notice of violation them to a complaint or noted an excessive noise level. Area governments, such as Rutherford County, have set their data center moratoriums at one year rather than the six months established in June by the Wilson County Commission. That one expires on Dec. 22, 2026. The next step is for the resolution to go to the county’s planning and zoning committee, whose next meeting will be in October. If it is delayed for any reason, the resolution could be passed after Dec. 22. The planning and zoning committee can recommend the commission extend the moratorium beyond that date in order for it not to expire before the resolution and subsequent ordinance are passed by the commission. That would be the last step and could take a few months for the commission to vote on the final resolution.
