artigo.texto: Almost two years after a fire at a battery storage site in Moss Landing, another one is smoldering. The fire resurfaces concerns about battery storage sites as the state charges ahead with clean energy goals. By Rachel Becker and Alejandra Reyes-Velarde, CalMatters This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters. The burned remains of the Moss Landing Power Plant battery energy storage facility caught fire again Friday morning, prompting Monterey County officials to issue a shelter in place order — less than two years after it became one of the largest battery storage facility fires in history. Workers for Vistra, the plant’s Texas-based operator, noticed a flare-up early Friday morning against the wall of a building that burned in the initial January 2025 fire. The cause: roughly 1,200 inaccessible battery modules, still charged, spontaneously ignited, said Chief Jess Cortez with the North County Fire Protection District. “They’re in the smoldering stage right now,” Cortez said at a briefing Friday afternoon, adding that at that point there was no active fire. “The incident is very dynamic. There could be possible flare-ups.” Local authorities lifted the order to shelter in place later Friday afternoon. Still, the flare-up reignites fears about battery storage facilities — even as California comes to increasingly rely on them. The state now has “the nation’s largest battery energy storage fleet,” the California Energy Commission announced in August. “If we had only known the worst-case scenarios of how not to build batteries, we wouldn’t have built Moss Landing,” said Dustin Mulvaney, a professor at San Jose State University in the school of planning, policy and environmental studies. “Because it keeps coming back to haunt us.” The incident also sharpens the tension between Gov. Gavin Newsom’s push to shortcut permitting for energy and other projects, and the communities hosting these facilities. Fire, rekindled In January 2025, residents watched large plumes of smoke and ash spewing from Vistra’s 300-megawatt battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County. It was the facility’s fourth safety incident, the third on the Vistra property, since 2019, according to a letter Assemblymember Dawn Addis, a San Luis Obispo Democrat, sent state regulators last year. The fire continued for days before crews could control it, then rekindled briefly a month later. Newsom called for a state investigation. The California Public Utilities Commission began with a site visit that month. Nearly two years later, that investigation is ongoing, with a root cause analysis underway in coordination with Vistra and an independent consultant, said Terrie Prosper, a spokesperson with the Public Utilities Commission. Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church expressed frustration about the delay. “Why it takes a year and a half to come up with an answer when everything is just about near the end of being cleaned up, I don’t know,” he said. Before the state approves any more of these facilities, he said, “It’s a good idea to know what’s causing these fires.” Safety rules, too late Unlike facilities built more recently, the Moss Landing site was built in an enclosed, aging building with older battery technologies crammed closely together — allowing fires to spread quickly, Mulvaney said. Denise Grab, the Clean Energy Law & Leadership project director for the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, agreed: The site is “one of the earlier battery storage facilities in the state and in the country, even. And the design is not up to par with current safety designs.” Battery plants still carry less overfall harm than fossil fuel plants, Grab added. “There are risks from other types of energy generation as well, particularly fossil fuel,” Grab said. “Asthma, premature death, heart attacks, lung disease from fossil fuel plants is significant, and (battery plants pose) a different kind of risk.” California passed a series of safety laws both before and after the January 2025 fire, including several laws from State Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, aimed at better planning for — and preventing — fires. A 2022 law by then-Sen. Ben Hueso required the California Public Utilities Commission to set new standards for battery storage facilities and boost oversight of their emergency plans. But the commission didn’t bring its proposal for implementing Hueso’s law to a vote until after last year’s Vistra fire. “We should have never built Moss Landing the way we did,” Mulvaney said. “We were too late with coming up with the standards and certifications, which make batteries much safer today.” Environmental health controversy Vistra says that the cause of last year’s fire is still unknown. The energy company commissioned a study finding that chemical concentrations in nearby soil or water posed no risk to humans or the environment. “As a result, no further human health or ecological risk evaluation related to the (Moss Landing fire) event is warranted,” the report read. But scientists’ findings and resident accounts suggest otherwise. As the fire blazed for days in January 2025, residents reported wheezing, coughing, headaches and eye irritation. Researchers presented additional findings at a symposium last month, including evidence from one UC Santa Cruz researcher of elevated exposure to battery-related materials in hair samples. Scientists with the San Jose State University’s Moss Landing Marine Laboratories have found high levels of nickel, manganese, and cobalt in soil around the facility. Ivano Aiello, the scientist who led the study, said Vistra’s recent report examined potential contaminants months after the fire was contained. The long-term health impacts of potential exposure remain unclear, and researchers continue studying the incident. artigo.texto: TERRY TURNER: Water concerns and data centers Published 7:11 am Monday, September 21, 2026 We in Georgia’s southwestern coastal plain sit atop two groundwater aquifers, the Floridan nearer the surface and the Claiborne deeper down. The depths of the aquifers are highly variable, but the Floridan’s average estimated depth goes to approximately 200 ft below the surface and the Claiborne continues down to an average of approximately 600 ft. The point is, southwest Georgia sits atop a lot of water. That said, it is not limitless. Major water withdrawals from the Floridan aquifer began in the 1970s with the advent of pivot irrigation systems for agriculture. Georgia’s Department of Natural Resources estimates that there are now between 10,000-13,000 pivot systems active in Georgia. Considering that one typical pivot system for a 100-acre field can require 500-1,000 gallons of water per minute when in use, the total number of active systems represents an enormous amount of water drawn out of what was once a largely unmolested aquifer. Georgians alert to the issue have often raised concerns about the current rates of water withdrawal because, if persisted in, they could have significant effects on our groundwater supply, a supply depended upon not only for agriculture but for homes, businesses, manufacturing, and even recreation. One point of obvious concern is that early pivot systems had wells with depths of only 60-200 feet deep into the Floridan aquifer to get an adequate water supply. Presently, it is not uncommon to have to bore to 500 feet to reach sufficient water. Similarly, private wells bored for homeowners once found adequate water for those needs at 50-100 feet. Today those wells typically have to go down 200-400 feet. Those data and others indicate a shrinking water base strongly correlated with the increase in the number of pivot irrigation systems, not only locally, but upstream of our aquifers’ natural water flow. These concerns plus the effects of a long-term drought had the state put a moratorium on new groundwater withdrawal permits in 2012. That ban was not lifted until 2025 with new rules to maximize pivot systems’ water-use efficiency and to better monitor their activity. The point here is that southwest Georgia has a history of awareness about the health of our groundwater resources. Now come the data centers. Data centers are high-tech marvels that run thousands of computers all at once to crunch an unimaginable amount of data so they can quickly provide answers to almost anyone on any subject. All those computers require enormous amounts of electricity, which generates heat, and enormous amounts of water to generate cooling. In southwest Georgia that water has to come from local aquifers already being reduced by large withdrawals for agriculture. A medium-sized data center can use an estimated 110 million gallons of water per year; a large center can use that much in a week at peak use. Data centers do not run sporadically like irrigation rigs; they run 24 hours per day, 365 days per year and would put a huge drain on aquifers already under stress. Data centers are not built thinking they might suddenly face severe water restrictions. So, what would happen if a data center were be established locally and environmental conditions like those in 2012 mandated a need for reduced water withdrawal from our aquifers? Local governments need to have thought this through. What counts more, one might ask, groundwater preservation to meet the needs of the local population and agriculture or the needs of a remote corporation hoping to profit off the natural resources of others? Political leaders make these decisions. Money is involved. One hopes they have their priorities straight. Terry Turner, a resident of Colquitt County, is professor emeritus of urology at the University of Virginia as well as author of books based on his experiences as an infantry officer in Vietnam.

artigo.texto: Brasília - Após o Redata virar lei na quarta-feira, 16 de setembro, uma divergência dentro do governo sobre se o gás natural também poderá ser usado como energia (além das fontes renováveis já previstas) para abastecer os data centers que terão direito a incentivos fiscais pode adiar ainda mais a implementação do programa no País. Ao NeoFeed, o Ministério da Fazenda admitiu que a expectativa é que o decreto, que o Executivo já prepara com essa e mais uma série de regulamentações do Redata, seja publicado até o fim deste mês. O documento estava previsto para sair no mesmo dia em que o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) sancionou a lei. Isso acontece pois há posições opostas dentro do próprio governo em relação às questões energéticas relacionadas aos projetos que receberiam as isenções de PIS, Cofins e IPI. E a tendência é que a Casa Civil tenha que arbitrar a respeito, segundo uma fonte a par das negociações disse ao NeoFeed. Em uma frente, os ministérios de Minas e Energia e o de Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) vêm sinalizando positivamente para o uso do gás como uma das fontes dos data centers. Quem tem defendido essa exceção costuma argumentar nos bastidores que a fonte seria complementar, uma vez que algumas energias renováveis são intermitentes - solar e eólica. De outro lado, no entanto, o Ministério da Fazenda já defende restrições e entende que apenas as fontes de energia limpas (hidrelétrica, eólica, solar) podem ser usadas para abastecer as estruturas de data centers, apurou o NeoFeed. Na verdade, a lei aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional no início do mês e sancionada em meados de setembro por Lula já prevê o uso de energias renováveis para alimentar os data centers. Mas toda a confusão se deu por uma mudança feita já quando o projeto tramitava pelo Senado: o texto substituiu a expressão “energias renováveis ou limpas” por “energias renováveis ou de baixa emissão de carbono”. Logo, o governo terá que definir também quais as condições seriam admitidas para essa baixa emissão. E caso o gás natural seja aceito como uma das fontes aptas a participar dos projetos de data centers, ainda assim o governo deve exigir compensação de emissão de carbono para o gás. Além do decreto, também será editada uma portaria interministerial. Além da Fazenda, do MME e MDIC, também vêm participando das discussões no governo os ministérios do Meio Ambiente, das Comunicações e de Ciência e Tecnologia. Além da questão energética, a regulamentação do Redata precisa indicar a lista de quais componentes e equipamentos poderão receber os benefícios fiscais e quais documentos as empresas precisam apresentar para se cadastrar no programa. Apesar da indefinição sobre as fontes de energia, a Pasta da Fazenda, responsável pela concessão dos benefícios fiscais, avalia que haverá tempo hábil, ainda em 2026 para que as empresas interessadas se habilitem para o programa. “Com a regulamentação lançada, dependerá da iniciativa das empresas. Mas haverá condições e tempo suficiente para fazer habilitações neste ano, se houver pedidos instruídos adequadamente”, respondeu o ministério. Procurado, o MME não respondeu aos contatos da reportagem. Acertos e urgências Affonso Nina, presidente da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais (Brasscom), admite que a lei, embora restritiva para algumas fontes de energia, foi positiva em trazer ganhos ambientais para os próximos projetos de data center no País. “Esperamos que o decreto seja o menos burocrático e saia quanto antes para habilitar as empresas este ano ainda”, afirma Nina, ao NeoFeed. “Mas estamos na expectativa de quando isso vai ser fechado e entendemos que o decreto ainda depende dessa definição da energia.” O executivo lembra que o gás natural representa 6% da matriz energética e mesmo que ele seja autorizado pelo governo a ser utilizado nos data centers habilitados pelo Redata ainda assim os projetos vão demandar necessariamente outras fontes de energia. Ele pondera também que os data centers têm um consumo “ínfimo de água”. Na leitura de Nina, porém, o Redata é apenas uma das necessidades do setor para destravar investimentos da ordem de R$ 90 bilhões durante os próximos cinco anos a partir de 2027. Para viabilizar esse montante de recursos, é necessária a redução de ICMS pelo Confaz no âmbito dos Estados e também reverter uma medida da Camex de fevereiro que aumentou as alíquotas de imposto de importação para vários itens úteis para os data centers”, pontuou. “Existe o apetite do investidor, o clima é positivo e digamos que já fizemos 1 a 0, mas precisamos de 3 a 0 para nos classificar no campeonato. Faltam ainda outros dois gols. O Redata sozinho não resolve”, afirma ele. “Enquanto tudo isso não acontecer, é possível que os investimentos em datacenters no Brasil não aconteçam nesse volume esperado. E enquanto isso o Redata perde muita eficiência”, complementa. A Frente Parlamentar pelo Brasil Competitivo (FPBC), que articulou pela aprovação do projeto no Congresso, também comemorou a sanção da lei do Redata, mas advertiu que a regulamentação precisa viabilizar os investimentos necessários. “Agora começa uma nova etapa: precisamos de uma implementação que dê segurança aos investidores e preserve a competitividade necessária para transformar o potencial brasileiro em projetos concretos”, diz Tatiana Ribeiro, secretária-executiva da FPBC e diretora-executiva do Movimento pelo Brasil Competitivo (MBC). A Frente defende neutralidade tecnológica, critérios objetivos de emissões e a possibilidade de diferentes fontes e soluções energéticas, inclusive de forma combinada. E diferentes modelos de suprimento, como contratação no mercado livre, autoprodução, geração própria ou dedicada e conexão ao Sistema Interligado Nacional. artigo.texto: - ABB introduces Infinitus, the industry’s first source-to-rack direct current portfolio for AI data centers designed for architecture flexibility - Breakthrough Infinitus solid-state transformers help maximize energy efficiency and reduce physical footprint, alongside DC power distribution and protection technologies to enhance overall system performance - Infinitus direct current portfolio expected to drive similar benefits across other industries including industrial buildings, manufacturing, renewables, and marine operations ABB today announced the launch of Infinitus, a portfolio of direct current (DC) solutions designed to manage the increasing power demands of AI data centers. The portfolio will accelerate the adoption of DC architectures in data centers improving energy efficiency and reducing power infrastructure footprint, while increasing available computing capacity. ABB expects other energy-intensive industries to make the same transition. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global data center electricity demand to more than double by 2030 and ABB estimates that approximately 25-40% of new capacity installed in 2030 could be using DC distribution. Next-generation AI chips are expected to draw 1 MW per rack and beyond, an increase from today's almost 200 kW, requiring a shift to DC architecture that can support performance while driving energy efficiency. With 800 VDC distribution, the footprint is more compact while eliminating redundant conversion steps and cutting heat losses of conventional alternating current (AC) systems. A recent BCG / ABB report calculated that DC distribution delivers energy efficiency gains of more than 5% and increases available space for compute racks. For a 500MW data center, a 5% efficiency gain can mean 25 MW more power for revenue-generating IT loads and more than US $300 million in potential additional revenue per year. With 5% efficiency gains for a 500 MW data center campus, the energy savings over one year would be equivalent to powering Washington D.C. for almost a full week. Giampiero Frisio, President of ABB’s Electrification business area, said: “ABB has pioneered DC technology for more than 25 years across several segments. We are working closely with chipmakers, hyperscale customers, supply partners and industry bodies to set the standards and the pace for the roll-out of high-efficiency DC architectures. Infinitus is the first portfolio providing the building blocks for any data center architecture - either DC native or hybrid AC/ DC - to power next-generation AI chips efficiently. This technology will bring similar energy efficiency gains to other energy-intensive industries such as large scale manufacturing, renewables and marine operations.” Infinitus is the industry's first integrated source-to-rack DC portfolio. At its core is ABB’s breakthrough Infinitus solid-state transformer technology, enabling sites to operate with a smaller footprint and greater energy efficiency. As the only major electrification supplier with both the world's first fully IEC-certified solid-state circuit breaker and an industry-first static medium-voltage UPS in production, ABB delivers a breadth of technology unmatched in the market. ABB’s Infinitus DC portfolio includes five key building blocks: - Medium Voltage Powertrains deliver stable resilient power from the grid or on-site generation; - DC Sources and Power Quality converts AC to DC removing conversion from white space; - DC Power Distribution delivers power safely and reliably, enabling higher power density in a smaller footprint; - DC Power Protection provides protection for operators, AI servers and hardware from DC overcurrents; - Cooling Optimization reduces energy consumption across grey and white space with DC connected variable speed drives and motors. ABB works with customers to design solutions tailored to their specific power demands, facility layout, and energy mix. This partnership approach ensures each deployment is optimized for maximum efficiency and reliability. The Infinitus portfolio complements traditional AC systems with DC flexibility that supports customers across all power architectures while also enabling unprecedented efficiency, reliability, and scalability for AI-era data centers. For next-generation data centers, this integrated architecture enables the high-density, high-efficiency power delivery that future AI chips demand. With a number of main components produced in the next twelve months, the first DC-native facilities using the complete Infinitus portfolio are expected to be installed and operational within two to three years. The portfolio launch extends support for ABB's continued collaboration with NVIDIA, first announced in October 2025, to develop 800 VDC power architectures for gigawatt-scale AI facilities. ABB brings more than 25 years of DC experience and over 700 patents spanning renewables, power generation, energy storage, motors and drives. ABB is a global technology leader in electrification and automation, enabling a more sustainable and resource-efficient future. By connecting its engineering and digitalization expertise, ABB helps industries run at high performance, while becoming more efficient, productive and sustainable so they outperform. At ABB, we call this ‘Engineered to Outrun’. The company has over 140 years of history and around 110,000 employees worldwide. ABB’s shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange (ABBN) and Nasdaq Stockholm (ABB). www.abb.com

artigo.texto: BYD India has said the Seal U SUV is the first model it is considering for its Indian plug-in-hybrid entry, with a launch targeted within 2026. The company has not announced an exact launch date. This is a PHEV, so it combines a rechargeable battery with a petrol engine. BYD describes DM-i as an electric-first system: the battery and electric motor handle most normal driving, while the petrol engine supports efficiency and extends range when required. How often the engine starts will depend on battery charge, speed, temperature and driving demand. BYD says DM-i vehicles can exceed 1,200 km using a full battery and a full fuel tank. The company also said it would publish the Seal U’s exact range when the model is announced. Until then, the figure should not be presented as an ARAI-tested India range or a guaranteed real-world result. A plug-in hybrid delivers its biggest daily-fuel benefit when the owner charges it regularly. BYD’s India executive said a person driving about 50 km a day with home or workplace charging could remain mostly in EV mode. Without regular charging, the petrol engine has to do more work. Overseas Seal U and Sealion 6 versions use different engines, batteries, drivetrains and equipment. Claims such as a 26.6kWh battery, 140 km EV-only range, 336hp output or a 15.6-inch screen describe particular global variants. BYD has not confirmed that complete package for India. BYD India confirmed that the Seal U would be imported, while declining to discuss future localisation. An imported launch can affect pricing, but no India price, variant list, battery warranty or homologated efficiency figure has been released. Buyers should wait for the official India specification sheet.

artigo.texto: SAUK CITY, Wis. — On a Saturday morning at the Sauk City farmers market, neighbors browse for food to bring home, catch up with friends and talk about the issues shaping their votes. Patricia and Lloyd Breunig are regulars at the market. Pat said they come nearly every week to talk with people in the community, where she has lived for 61 years. “It’s my hometown,” Lloyd said. The couple has watched Sauk City grow and change, and they say the cost of staying there has risen sharply. “Sixty years ago, we had our first house. Our taxes were $169. Now they’re over $5,000,” Lloyd said. For the retired couple, that increase is more than campaign rhetoric. It is part of household conversations and budgeting decisions. “It’s scary because you’re on a limited budget, and we’re both retired,” Pat said. “We try to get by as reasonably as we can, and our kids are great at helping us.” An August Marquette Law School Poll found inflation and the cost of living were voters’ top concerns. Property taxes, the Breunigs’ leading concern, also ranked among the issues voters identified. A Wisconsin Policy Forum report found property tax levies saw their largest increase in nearly 20 years. “We can’t afford higher taxes, pretty much,” Lloyd said. “Taxed out.” The Breunigs do not identify strongly with either major political party. “We’re not Democrat or Republican — independent,” Lloyd said. “We go with whoever we feel is a good candidate.” That independent streak is also apparent a few stalls away, where Julie Breunig — who is not related to Pat and Lloyd despite sharing their last name — sells goods at the market. “I’ve lived here all my life,” Julie said. She began selling jam with her daughter, Robin, at the Lodi Farmers' Market to help pay for college. The work grew into a regular market business. “Every vendor here is very community-based and trying to make good products for our community,” she said. Julie, who also identifies as an independent, said she remains undecided. “It’s really tough right now for me to think of what side’s better,” she said. She said candidates will need to demonstrate a commitment to the environment, farmland and future generations. “I need somebody to stand up for good water, good air and family farms,” Julie said. For her, those concerns include artificial intelligence and data centers. “We have to figure out how to deal with AI and the data centers,” she said. The August Marquette poll found 78% of voters said the costs of data centers outweigh their benefits. Sixty-seven percent said they would support banning data centers for at least a year. “They need to slow down and figure it out,” Julie said. In Sauk County, voters such as the Breunigs say they are looking beyond party labels and toward candidates they believe will follow through. “We like to see people that are honest in our politics, which is pretty hard to find these days,” Lloyd said. “They make a lot of promises, but when it comes to delivering, they fall a little short.” COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Data centers trocam água por químicos permanentes para resfriar I.A Publicado 21/09/2026 • 06:00 | Atualizado há 6 horas ALERTA DE MERCADO: KEY POINTS Foto: pexels A expansão da inteligência artificial aumenta a demanda por data centers e, com ela, a necessidade de sistemas para controlar o calor gerado pelos equipamentos. Nesse processo, os PFAS, conhecidos como “químicos eternos”, ganham espaço em tecnologias de refrigeração. Um relatório da organização ChemSec aponta que grandes produtores mundiais de PFAS estão ampliando a capacidade de produção diante da demanda relacionada à infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. Além disso, entre as empresas citadas estão a japonesa Daikin, a francesa Arkema e a americana Chemours. Leia também: Anthropic alerta para sistemas de inteligência artificial capazes de desenvolver novos modelos IA Segundo a Fortune, a demanda está concentrada principalmente em três áreas: refrigeração de data centers, fabricação de semicondutores e produção de materiais para baterias de íon-lítio. Os equipamentos utilizados para processamento de I.A geram grandes quantidades de calor. Dessa forma, para controlar a temperatura, sistemas mais recentes podem utilizar substâncias químicas fluoradas que incluem PFAS, em vez de água. A alternativa aparece enquanto o consumo de água se tornou uma das preocupações relacionadas à expansão dos data centers. Porém, os PFAS também geram questionamentos por sua resistência à degradação. As fortes ligações químicas dessas substâncias dificultam sua decomposição no ambiente. Essa característica favorece aplicações industriais, incluindo sistemas de refrigeração, fabricação de semicondutores e equipamentos industriais. Dados da Pesquisa Nacional de Saúde e Nutrição dos Estados Unidos, citados pela Fortune, encontraram PFAS no sangue de 97% dos americanos. O avanço da I.A também impulsiona a construção de data centers. Um estudo de 2026 da BOMA apontou que essas instalações representaram quase 46% da construção privada nos Estados Unidos em 2025. Uma década antes, a participação era inferior a 5%. Segundo dados da Statista citados pela Fortune, os gastos com construção de data centers passaram de US$ 1,8 bilhão (cerca de R$ 9,25 bilhões) em 2014 para US$ 41,1 bilhões (R$ 211,34 bilhões) em 2025. A ChemSec afirma que a Chemours produz ou utiliza mais substâncias PFAS do que qualquer outra empresa analisada pela organização. A companhia também desenvolve produtos para refrigeração de data centers e amplia a produção de refrigerantes à base de PFAS. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Leia também: Startup lança coleira com I.A que promete traduzir latidos e miados A organização estima que entre metade e dois terços da receita de US$ 5,8 bilhões (R$ 29,82 bilhões) da Chemours venham da produção de PFAS. A Daikin, segundo o relatório, pretende triplicar sua capacidade de produção em resposta à demanda do setor de semicondutores. A Arkema também iniciou uma expansão na América do Norte e na Ásia. Em julho, 17 organizações ambientais enviaram uma carta à Agência de Proteção Ambiental dos Estados Unidos (EPA) contra o pedido da Chemours para acelerar a aprovação do Opteon 2P50, composto PFAS destinado a sistemas de refrigeração de data centers. Os grupos afirmaram que a empresa teria subestimado possíveis riscos à saúde e ao clima e questionaram as evidências toxicológicas disponíveis. Segundo a carta, data centers de hiperescala podem armazenar dezenas de milhares de litros de fluido dielétrico em centenas de tanques. A Chemours contestou as preocupações. Segundo a empresa, o sistema funciona em circuito fechado e libera pouca quantidade de gás durante a operação. A companhia também lançou novos refrigerantes em agosto. Leia também: Teck Check: IA já virou obrigação, mas diferencial está nos dados e na estratégia, diz CEO da HSM Em janeiro, 192 cidadãos franceses e quatro organizações ambientais entraram com uma ação contra Arkema e Daikin por alegações de poluição relacionada a PFAS. A Arkema afirmou que se defenderá das acusações, enquanto a Daikin declarou que acelerou investimentos desde 2022 para controlar melhor suas emissões. Segundo uma análise da ChemSec de 2023, os maiores fabricantes de PFAS tiveram cerca de US$ 4 bilhões (R$ 20,57 bilhões) em lucros em 2022, enquanto os custos sociais associados às substâncias foram estimados em US$ 17,5 trilhões (R$ 89,98 trilhões) por ano. Assim, a expansão da I.A cria uma demanda adicional por sistemas de refrigeração capazes de lidar com o calor dos equipamentos. artigo.texto: Almost two years after a fire at a battery storage site in Moss Landing, another one is smoldering. The fire resurfaces concerns about battery storage sites as the state charges ahead with clean energy goals. By Rachel Becker and Alejandra Reyes-Velarde, CalMatters This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters. The burned remains of the Moss Landing Power Plant battery energy storage facility caught fire again Friday morning, prompting Monterey County officials to issue a shelter in place order — less than two years after it became one of the largest battery storage facility fires in history. Workers for Vistra, the plant’s Texas-based operator, noticed a flare-up early Friday morning against the wall of a building that burned in the initial January 2025 fire. The cause: roughly 1,200 inaccessible battery modules, still charged, spontaneously ignited, said Chief Jess Cortez with the North County Fire Protection District. “They’re in the smoldering stage right now,” Cortez said at a briefing Friday afternoon, adding that at that point there was no active fire. “The incident is very dynamic. There could be possible flare-ups.” Local authorities lifted the order to shelter in place later Friday afternoon. Still, the flare-up reignites fears about battery storage facilities — even as California comes to increasingly rely on them. The state now has “the nation’s largest battery energy storage fleet,” the California Energy Commission announced in August. “If we had only known the worst-case scenarios of how not to build batteries, we wouldn’t have built Moss Landing,” said Dustin Mulvaney, a professor at San Jose State University in the school of planning, policy and environmental studies. “Because it keeps coming back to haunt us.” The incident also sharpens the tension between Gov. Gavin Newsom’s push to shortcut permitting for energy and other projects, and the communities hosting these facilities. Fire, rekindled In January 2025, residents watched large plumes of smoke and ash spewing from Vistra’s 300-megawatt battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County. It was the facility’s fourth safety incident, the third on the Vistra property, since 2019, according to a letter Assemblymember Dawn Addis, a San Luis Obispo Democrat, sent state regulators last year. The fire continued for days before crews could control it, then rekindled briefly a month later. Newsom called for a state investigation. The California Public Utilities Commission began with a site visit that month. Nearly two years later, that investigation is ongoing, with a root cause analysis underway in coordination with Vistra and an independent consultant, said Terrie Prosper, a spokesperson with the Public Utilities Commission. Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church expressed frustration about the delay. “Why it takes a year and a half to come up with an answer when everything is just about near the end of being cleaned up, I don’t know,” he said. Before the state approves any more of these facilities, he said, “It’s a good idea to know what’s causing these fires.” Safety rules, too late Unlike facilities built more recently, the Moss Landing site was built in an enclosed, aging building with older battery technologies crammed closely together — allowing fires to spread quickly, Mulvaney said. Denise Grab, the Clean Energy Law & Leadership project director for the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, agreed: The site is “one of the earlier battery storage facilities in the state and in the country, even. And the design is not up to par with current safety designs.” Battery plants still carry less overfall harm than fossil fuel plants, Grab added. “There are risks from other types of energy generation as well, particularly fossil fuel,” Grab said. “Asthma, premature death, heart attacks, lung disease from fossil fuel plants is significant, and (battery plants pose) a different kind of risk.” California passed a series of safety laws both before and after the January 2025 fire, including several laws from State Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, aimed at better planning for — and preventing — fires. A 2022 law by then-Sen. Ben Hueso required the California Public Utilities Commission to set new standards for battery storage facilities and boost oversight of their emergency plans. But the commission didn’t bring its proposal for implementing Hueso’s law to a vote until after last year’s Vistra fire. “We should have never built Moss Landing the way we did,” Mulvaney said. “We were too late with coming up with the standards and certifications, which make batteries much safer today.” Environmental health controversy Vistra says that the cause of last year’s fire is still unknown. The energy company commissioned a study finding that chemical concentrations in nearby soil or water posed no risk to humans or the environment. “As a result, no further human health or ecological risk evaluation related to the (Moss Landing fire) event is warranted,” the report read. But scientists’ findings and resident accounts suggest otherwise. As the fire blazed for days in January 2025, residents reported wheezing, coughing, headaches and eye irritation. Researchers presented additional findings at a symposium last month, including evidence from one UC Santa Cruz researcher of elevated exposure to battery-related materials in hair samples. Scientists with the San Jose State University’s Moss Landing Marine Laboratories have found high levels of nickel, manganese, and cobalt in soil around the facility. Ivano Aiello, the scientist who led the study, said Vistra’s recent report examined potential contaminants months after the fire was contained. The long-term health impacts of potential exposure remain unclear, and researchers continue studying the incident. artigo.texto: Existing assets can provide crucial benchmarks for the vital task of correctly sizing a battery storage system and other crucial design decisions, writes Ashutosh Vats, head of BESS business development at 3E. Battery storage projects can start losing revenue as soon as they begin operating. The challenge is to learn from what happens in real-world operations and to use that information to improve the assumptions behind the next project. This article looks at why battery sizing assumptions can have a bigger impact on project economics than many developers realise, and how using real operational data alongside financial models can lead to more realistic and reliable investment cases and ultimately change what it means for a battery project to be ‘bankable.’ Battery storage is now the fastest-growing power technology in the world. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports 108GW of new capacity deployed in 2025, representing a 40% jump from 2024 and 11 times the installed base just four years earlier. Here comes the uncomfortable part for developers and IPP working on their first BESS projects: that financial model was built on assumptions and every one of them begins to drift the day the asset goes live. Consider how a typical battery sizing study works. To identify the best configuration, the model simulates how the battery would operate over several years, using detailed forecasts of electricity prices and renewable generation. It effectively assumes that the future is known perfectly. This is not a weakness of the approach. The aim is to establish a theoretical benchmark: the maximum revenue a battery could generate if it had perfect information and could always make the right decision. A financial model that assumes, say, 2% annual capacity fade but meets 4% in the field will overstate revenue every single year, compounding across the debt term. The gap can be the difference between a project that services its debt and one that does not. Yet most models still rely on manufacturer curves, and most operational platforms simply pass through the state of health (SoH) reported by the on-site battery management system (BMS), which is often supplied by the same OEM that issued the warranty in the first place. Therefore, the assumptions that determine whether a BESS project is financeable are often the ones that are hardest to assess from a datasheet. The most reliable evidence comes from batteries that are already operating in the market. This is where the feedback loop becomes important. It needs to be based on independent, physics-based measurements rather than on information provided by equipment suppliers. An independent digital twin can track how connected batteries actually perform over time. Instead of relying only on specifications, it can show how a battery is really behaving in the market: how its state of health changes, how different degradation mechanisms affect performance, how much revenue it captures, and how available it is during the periods when electricity prices are highest. This is the principle behind SynaptiQ, 3E’s asset performance platform: independently measure how batteries actually perform across an operating fleet and use that evidence to improve the models used for future projects. The same operational data can then feed back into 3E’s BESS sizing tool. This means that degradation assumptions are no longer based solely on manufacturer specifications. They can be informed by how batteries using the same chemistry have actually aged under comparable operating conditions, duty cycles and climates. Every new BESS project can ‘learn’ from what came before it At the development stage, investors can use the sizing tool to test different battery sizes and market strategies and assess how they would perform under different scenarios. The built-in optimisation process can then identify configurations that offer the best balance between technical performance and financial returns. In Spain, for example, where co-location development of PV plants and/or wind farms with battery storage is thriving, understanding how the different technologies will generate electricity in order to optimise revenue stacking through the right BESS size requires an optimisation tool capable of integrating numerous variables, go-to-market strategies and real simulation of how the different assets will operate through time. Over the last 2 years, simulations have increasingly shown a need for 4-hour batteries instead of 2-hour batteries to obtain optimal profitability and NPV. For investors and lenders, this changes the way we should think about bankability. A project will always depend on assumptions about future prices, degradation, availability and revenues. But those assumptions become more robust when they are continuously tested against the performance of real operating assets. The value of closing this loop is simple: every new BESS project can learn from the batteries that came before it. Operational data improves the models, better models lead to better sizing decisions, and those decisions provide investors and lenders with a more realistic view of the project’s potential performance. The BESS market is expanding rapidly, and large amounts of capital are being committed to new projects. artigo.texto: Despite stock stress, CATL likely to retain EV battery dominance in China, analysts say CATL’s tech edge and brand safeguard its EV battery lead, though carmakers are seeking alternative suppliers Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited’s (CATL) dominance in the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) market is unlikely to slump over the coming year given its brand recognition and edge in technology, analysts said, though its shares have already tumbled amid the battle with profit-squeezed EV makers. Chinese carmakers have been doubling down on efforts in recent weeks to reduce their reliance on CATL – in September, Xiaomi and Li Auto highlighted their partnership with tier-two battery manufacturers, including CALB Group, while Xpeng planned to make in-house battery packs this year. Amid concerns about a potential loss of market share, CATL’s Shenzhen-listed shares have lost 25.7 per cent since mid-August and 36.5 per cent from their all-time high seen in early May. On Monday, the equities of the Fujian-based firm fell by a further 1.6 per cent in Shenzhen and 0.59 per cent in Hong Kong.

artigo.texto: The US energy storage industry is targeting 225GW/1TWh of storage deployments by the end of 2032, according to an analysis published by the Energy Storage Coalition (ESC). Released this month (September), the report, titled The Terawatt-Hour Opportunity, said that battery energy storage systems (BESS) offer the speed to power, reliability and flexibility to address America’s energy demand challenge whilst fortifying energy security, provided policy and regulatory frameworks enable the industry to scale at the pace the US power system demands. The US energy storage industry has undergone one of the fastest expansions of any part of the American power sector. In just a few years, energy storage has moved from an emerging technology to what the ESC describes as a foundational backbone of the American power grid. Energy storage capacity has grown from 1.5GW at the end of 2020 to 52GW by mid-2026, with the industry now targeting 225GW by the end of 2032. This represents more than 300% growth in power capacity and 500% growth in energy capacity for energy storage resources over the next five years. Energy storage capacity will reach more than 20% of current US peak electricity demand, with energy storage resources operating in all 50 states. The 225GW of energy storage capacity is equivalent to peak power supply for Texas, California, Florida and Michigan combined. The deployment range scenarios through 2035 were assessed based on cumulative estimates from Wood Mackenzie, ACP, BNEF, McKinsey & Company, Baringa Partners, Aurora and E3. Drivers of market acceleration ESC identified three key factors driving the acceleration of the grid-scale energy storage market. Grid flexibility requirements: The power system has become more dynamic, with electricity supply and demand changing more rapidly, renewable generation expanding, and grid operators increasingly needing resources that can respond instantly, shift power across hours and provide capacity when most valuable. Storage is uniquely capable of doing all three. Urgent capacity needs: After decades of relatively flat electricity consumption, load growth from manufacturing, electrification, artificial intelligence (AI) and other large power users is creating an urgent need for new capacity. Storage can be deployed quickly, help unlock constrained grid capacity and make existing generation and transmission infrastructure work harder whilst longer-lead infrastructure catches up. Cost reduction: Storage can replace expensive peak power, reduce price spikes, defer costly grid investments and extract more capacity from infrastructure already paid for by consumers. Rather than solving each grid need with a separate investment, storage can provide capacity, energy, congestion relief and essential grid services from the same asset. Economic benefits The analysis projects that energy storage will generate more than US$250 billion in cost savings over the next decade by scaling deployment to 850+ GWh. The cumulative energy system cost savings average out to US$1,550 across all 160 million American ratepayers. BESS helps to deliver cost savings by efficiently boosting grid utilisation, avoiding more expensive or unnecessary infrastructure upgrades, lowering peak pricing and maximising the output of existing power generation resources on the grid. The analysis highlighted Texas as a case study demonstrating the dual benefits storage can deliver to boost reliability and lower costs. The state achieved US$1.5 billion in savings over summer and winter extreme weather events in 2024, whilst grid emergencies reduced from 13 in 2023 to zero in 2025. Similarly, in May, ACP published its second annual ‘State of Clean Energy Manufacturing’ report, which claimed the US can currently produce enough solar and BESS modules to meet domestic demand, stating, “Rapid growth in solar and storage production, sustained wind manufacturing, and rising investment in critical minerals are reshaping the nation’s energy supply chain.”

artigo.texto: Democrats are now running against data centers. This is smart politics, given how unpopular the internet warehouses have become. Whether this is smart policy, well, that’s a different matter entirely, one we’ll have to deal with another day. However, no policy gets made if candidates don’t get elected, so let’s look at what Democrats are saying — specifically congressional candidates Tom Perriello in the 5th District and Beth Macy in the 6th District, who have both now made data centers part of their campaigns. In both cases they have made specific charges about their Republican opponents — incumbents John McGuire and Ben Cline — that can be fact-checked. The charge: Perriello says ‘McGuire voted for a $362 billion corporate tax break for data centers.’ The facts: McGuire voted for a more general corporate tax break that data centers are using. This is one of those charges that is true but selective. Perriello is referring to tax breaks in HR 1, aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” These aren’t specific to data centers, they apply to any manufacturer — although Politico recently reported that tech companies have been the main beneficiaries of them. “The law made it possible for companies to frontload the deduction of the full cost of new equipment from their taxes, a huge benefit for technology companies known as ‘hyperscalers’ that are driving the data center boom across Virginia and the country,” a statement from Perriello’s campaign said. Here’s how Politico reports what’s going on: “The tech world is pouring oceans of money into chips, data centers, power supplies and other components of the artificial intelligence infrastructure. And that’s eligible for generous tax breaks on investments Republicans included in their 2025 tax cuts. The tax incentives weren’t designed with AI in mind specifically — they’re available for all kinds of business investments. But it’s the tech industry that’s making the most of them, putting a major dent in corporate tax receipts.” The Democratic criticism is that tech companies don’t need this tax break, that they’d be investing in AI-related technology anyway, so this tax provision amounts to a giveaway that is costing the national treasury and driving up the national debt. The National Association of Manufacturers backed HR 1, partly because of that provision, which it said would “supercharge manufacturing.” So far, that hasn’t happened, though. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that the number of manufacturing jobs in the U.S. is almost exactly the same as it was before the bill was passed. In Virginia, the number of manufacturing jobs has declined, from 239,100 in June 2025 (the bill became law the next month) to 229,300 in July 2026, the most recent statistics available. Data at the local level is harder to find, but the Federal Reserve says that manufacturing jobs have declined over the past year in the two biggest metro areas in the 5th District, Charlottesville and Lynchburg. This seems to be a case where the intent of the provision and its actual application are two different things. Its intent was to boost manufacturing; instead, it’s boosted tech companies — some of which are manufacturing companies, just not in ways we usually think of. We’ll come back to this point later, but it’s not as if there was a specific bill to give tax breaks for data centers that McGuire voted for. Instead, he voted for HR 1, which included a provision aimed at manufacturers that data center companies have used. The charge: Macy says Cline has “voted three times to let data centers pay no sales tax, sticking us with the bill.” The facts: That’s true. Those votes were also 10-18 years ago when the context was different. These three votes are all when Cline was in the General Assembly, not Congress. Now we’re getting back to the origin of the data center boom in Virginia. HB 1388 in 2008 was the first tax data center tax bill in Virginia. It was introduced by Del. Tommy Wright, R-Lunenburg County, when Virginia was in contention for an Apple data center that was looking at Mecklenburg County. Wright’s bill created a sales tax exemption for data centers that located “in a Virginia locality having an unemployment rate above 4.9 percent for the calendar quarter ending November 2007” and created “at least 100 new jobs paying at least twice the prevailing average wage in that locality.” The bill — framed as a way to lure a tech industry to an economically distressed part of rural Virginia — was so noncontroversial that it passed the House of Delegates 97-2 and the state Senate 40-0. Yes, even state Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, who has become the most vocal opponent of data centers, voted for it. Gov. Tim Kaine, a Democrat, signed the bill into law. Apple eventually passed over Mecklenburg in favor of North Carolina but the county did later land Microsoft. Virginia’s loss of Apple in 2009 spooked state leadership. There was a strong feeling that Virginia was falling behind North Carolina economically. The economy then was weak — this was the era of the Great Recession — and Republican Bob McDonnell won the 2009 governor’s race on the slogan “Bob’s for Jobs.” Come the 2010 General Assembly session, Del. John O’Bannon, R-Henrico County, introduced a bill — HB 302 — to expand the tax break for data centers statewide. This bill was also so noncontroversial that it passed the House 97-0 and the Senate 40-0 (again, with Lucas as one of those 40). McDonnell signed it into law. The intent was to make Virginia competitive in creating a technology economy and it worked — maybe too well, some might see it now. The state’s data center boom owes its origin to this measure. The third data center vote that Macy cites is SB 64 in 2016. That year, state Sen. Frank Ruff, R-Mecklenburg County, introduced a bill to extend the sunset date on the state’s tax break for data centers from 2020 to 2035. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- The 2026 IAA Transportation show ran from September 14 to 20 in Hannover, Germany. EVE Energy used the event to debut its Open Source Battery 4.0 (AI Battery) in Europe for the first time, signing strategic cooperation agreements with several industry partners totaling more than 30 GWh. Under the agreements signed on-site, EVE Energy's strategic partners include BMZ, Janus Electric, Morris Commercial, Sunswap, and WEG. The deals primarily focus on commercial vehicle battery solutions and integrated delivery capabilities. Image source: EVE Energy In terms of product and technology, EVE Energy showcased its Open Source Battery 3.0 and 4.0 series, featuring LMX chemistry cells such as the LM815, LM285, and V63, along with the LM815-641 kWh heavy-duty truck underfloor system and the B3E-LF206S bus system. Notably, the Open Source Battery 4.0 integrates a custom AI chip that enables active sensing at the cell level, real-time diagnostics, and intelligent optimization. Its LMX material system enhances low-temperature performance while retaining the high safety and stability of lithium iron phosphate (LFP), tailored to meet European regulatory standards and complex operating conditions. Electrification of commercial vehicles in Europe continues to accelerate. Stringent regional regulations and diverse, extreme cross-border operating conditions are raising the bar for power battery safety, environmental adaptability, and total cost of ownership. Leveraging a decade of technical expertise in commercial vehicle batteries, EVE Energy launched these solutions to address the core demands of the European market.

artigo.texto: Democrats try to ride data center backlash to election victory in rural US Midwest Mounting public anxiety about AI, cloud-computing infrastructure has transformed data center construction into a contentious midterm elections issue No company has announced plans for a data center in Defiance, a city of 17,000 people surrounded by soybean fields in northwestern Ohio. But people in the aptly named community are not taking any chances. After learning the county’s economic development group had fielded inquiries from tech companies, residents spent months gathering signatures for a November 3 ballot measure to ban all but the smallest data centers. City officials announced a six-month moratorium on new project approvals. The fight in Defiance is part of a broader political backlash throughout Ohio — and across the nation — where mounting public anxiety about AI and cloud-computing infrastructure has transformed data center construction from an economic success story into a contentious midterm elections issue. Many in Defiance were already concerned about the impacts of AI development on farmland, electricity demand and water consumption. Their misgivings deepened this summer after the release of state tax records showing Ohio had foregone more than $2 billion in sales-tax revenue through data-center incentives in 2024 and 2025, benefiting companies such as Amazon and Meta. Some 71% of Ohioans would now support a temporary ban on new data center construction, according to an August 31 poll from Bowling Green State University. "Most people feel preyed upon by big business," said Becca Rupp, founder of Citizens for Responsible Development - efiance. The groundswell building against data centers during election season has given Democratic candidates a new opening in the rural US Midwest, where they have struggled to compete during Donald Trump's presidency. Ohio is one of a handful of states with competitive races expected to decide control of Congress. Ohio's Republican Governor Mike DeWine has suspended new applications for data center tax exemptions pending legislative reforms, but state lawmakers did not act before summer recess, leaving the future of AI development in Ohio uncertain — and ripe for political attack. Clash over tax incentives Democratic US Representative Marcy Kaptur faces one of the toughest reelection races of her four-decade congressional career, in a newly redrawn district that includes Defiance and other conservative rural areas. She has leaned heavily into data-center messaging, running television ads accusing her Republican opponent Derek Merrin of supporting the unpopular tax incentives. In a statement, Kaptur linked data centers to rising utility costs and wider concerns about corporate influence. "Politicians are letting these companies pass the costs of their enormous energy and utility demands onto Ohio ratepayers, then handing them billions in tax breaks to sweeten the deal," she said. Residential electricity bills in Defiance rose 10% to 15% in June from a year earlier, according to utility FirstEnergy. Merrin did not respond to requests for comment. In a Facebook post last week, he said Kaptur was “blaming me for a tax break for data centers that was enacted BEFORE I was even elected to the Ohio legislature.” The issue has also featured prominently in the state's closely watched US Senate race, pitting Republican incumbent Jon Husted against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who lost his old seat in 2024. With recent polls showing Brown leading, Republican groups have poured $14 million into advertising in Ohio in the past week alone, hoping to boost Husted's chances. Brown has repeatedly criticized his opponent for promoting AI infrastructure development and tax incentives, describing him as "data centers' best friend." “Ohioans, not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends, should get to decide if data centers are built in their community,” Brown’s campaign said in a statement. Husted's campaign rejected the criticism, noting he has sponsored legislation that would require data-center operators to cover the cost of building more electricity generation and transmission. “Sherrod Brown had three decades in Congress to lead on this issue,” campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce said in a statement. “Instead, he did nothing and is suddenly pretending to care in the middle of an election year.” Tax subsidy disclosure galvanizes activists Lyn Cox, a leader of the local advocacy organization Conserve Ohio, said disclosure about the scale of tax subsidies transformed what had been a series of scattered zoning disputes into a statewide political issue. "I think it was a huge turning point," said Cox, who lives in rural Waterville Township, about 40 miles (64 km) from Defiance. She said candidates from both parties have been forced to engage with activists and develop formal policies on data-center development. Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who previously voiced support for attracting tech investment, released an "Ohioans First" data-center proposal that would eliminate local property-tax abatements for data centers, direct revenue toward homeowner rebates and require projects to cover incremental residential electricity costs. His opponent, Democrat Amy Acton, has proposed restricting tax incentives, requiring developers to pay for their own power infrastructure and mandating union labor standards. Both candidates have also called for limiting construction on productive farmland. Cox remains skeptical of campaign promises from both parties. "They're just words," she said. "They both came up with a policy because they're starting to understand this is a sleeper issue." artigo.texto: O olhar único que há 50 anos acompanha o que é notícia no Brasil e no mundo Data centers: nova lei abre caminho para investimentos, mas regulamentação é desafio O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sancionou na quinta-feira a lei do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), que concede incentivos tributários para empresas que instalarem ou ampliarem data centers no país. O projeto foi aprovado no Congresso durante a semana do esforço concentrado, no início de setembro. Na avaliação do Instituto Brasileiro de Telecomunicações e Soluções Digitais (IBTD), o Redata resolve uma parcela importante do custo de entrada ao suspender tributos federais incidentes sobre equipamentos. A competitividade brasileira, no entanto, dependerá também de outras condições, como regulamentação rápida e previsível, disponibilidade de energia, capacidade de transmissão, expansão de backbones, conectividade internacional, licenciamento e segurança regulatória. — Agora abre-se uma nova etapa voltada à regulamentação e à criação das condições necessárias para transformar o incentivo tributário em investimentos efetivos — salienta André Martins, presidente do Instituto Brasileiro de Telecomunicações e Soluções Digitais (IBTD). Com a publicação oficial da lei no Diário Oficial, deverão ser regulamentados os dispositivos operacionais e os requisitos de habilitação ao regime, além dos procedimentos a serem adotados pela Receita Federal e pelos órgãos competentes para a fruição dos benefícios, explica o IBTD. Com essas regras definidas, poderão ser anunciados os primeiros projetos de investimento por empresas interessadas. Um dos pontos de maior impacto do texto sancionado está na mudança da regra energética. Na versão aprovada pela Câmara, os empreendimentos deveriam atender à sua demanda por meio de fontes "limpas ou renováveis". No Senado, a redação passou a considerar fontes "renováveis ou de baixa emissão", alteração que abre espaço para a participação de fontes como gás natural e energia nuclear, além das hidrelétricas, salienta Alexei Vivan, sócio e head de Energia do CGM Advogados. A definição dos critérios para enquadramento será detalhada na regulamentação do Redata. O desafio agora é o regulamento, que precisa definir com clareza o que é baixa emissão para que a segurança jurídica prometida pela lei chegue, de fato, aos projetos, salienta Bruna Correia, sócia da área de Energia do BMA Advogados, que defende a inclusão das fontes de baixa emissão na nova lei. — É uma decisão acertada, porque o sistema elétrico é equilíbrio: solar e eólica são centrais para a transição, mas a segurança do suprimento depende de fontes despacháveis, que podem ser acionadas de imediato e não variam com o sol e o vento, e o gás natural cumpre esse papel. Para a advogada, o Redata acerta ao condicionar o benefício fiscal a contrapartidas que chegam à vida das pessoas. Segundo ela, a exigência de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão e o limite de consumo de água de 0,05 litro por kWh fazem com que o data center cresça sem disputar com as cidades vizinhas a água e o ar de que elas dependem. — Os aportes de 2% em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação financiam ciência feita aqui e ajudam a formar pesquisadores e engenheiros capazes de desenvolver tecnologia no Brasil, e não apenas operar a que vem de fora. E a oferta de ao menos 10% da capacidade ao mercado doméstico abre essa infraestrutura a startups, universidades e empresas brasileiras, que ganham acesso a processamento de dados no próprio país — esclarece.

artigo.texto: The United States Senate is made up of 100 members, two from each state. U.S. Senators serve staggered, six-year terms. The powers of the Senate are outlined in the Constitution. You can learn more about those powers here. Mark Warner (D) has served as senator since 2008 and was the governor of Virginia from 2002 to 2006. He is being challenged by Bert Mizusawa (R). This is Mizusawa’s second bid for senate, after failing to qualify for ballot in the 2018 Republican primary. Charlottesville Tomorrow designed a questionnaire for the candidates based on responses we received from our voter survey. They provided answers below, listed in the order they were received. Energy In our survey, many 5th District voters voiced concerns over expanding data centers, rising power costs and transmission projects like Valley Link, citing the potential impact on land rights and regional resources. Others welcomed such projects, particularly data centers, for the new jobs they can bring to communities. Although local and state officials decide where individual projects can be built, federal lawmakers hold power over how fast and far local development can expand by controlling the regional power grid. Federal leaders set the national rules and funding mechanisms that dictate how this multi-state grid operates. In your view, what, if anything, should the federal government do to manage rapid energy growth, and what would your priorities be in Congress? Mark R. Warner: Artificial intelligence will reshape nearly every aspect of our economy and society. The only question is whether Congress is going to do something about it or try to play catch up. My comprehensive AI legislative framework addresses four key priorities: building AI infrastructure responsibly; promoting competition and safety; preparing workers for economic disruption and technological change; and strengthening America’s national security advantage. Data centers use enormous amounts of power* and water.** Virginians deserve to know the impact a new data center will have on their community, and companies shouldn’t be able to hide those details behind secret deals. I’ve introduced legislation to require greater transparency about energy and water use and other impacts, make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they require instead of passing those costs on to residents, and condition valuable tax benefits on meeting strong efficiency standards.*** Editor’s notes: * In 2023, data centers consumed approximately 4.4% of all electricity in the United States and by 2028, this is expected to increase to between 6.7% and 12% in 2028, according to a 2024 study published by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. ** Scientists at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that in 2023 U.S. data centers used about 228 billion gallons of water, with about 17 billion gallons used for cooling servers and 211 billion gallons used to generate the electricity that powered them. Those researchers project the water usage might grow to between 469 billion and 844 billion gallons by 2028. However, precise predictions are challenging because technology companies do not release detailed data on their water and energy usage. Read more about what that means in this article published by CBS News. *** Sen. Mark Warner introduced new legislation related to data centers on July 21, 2026. Bert Mizusawa: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a disruptive frontier for technology and, as Americans, we should not cede the lead to any other nation, especially potential adversaries. Unlike technology breakthroughs of the past, such as electricity, nuclear power and the Internet, AI has the potential to reinvent itself — without human intervention — with potentially catastrophic outcomes.* While the federal level of government must focus on the technology itself, I will support the ability of local communities, who will bear the costs,** to veto having data centers that serve AI forced on them by Richmond or Washington, DC. Data centers can and should be located in remote areas. For energy, I support the rapid deployment of newer nuclear reactors to provide cheaper, cleaner, and safer electrical energy*** for both commercial and residential uses. Editor’s notes: * Some artificial intelligence systems work autonomously with little to no human intervention, called agentic AI. In July 2026, tech company Hugging Face reported a hacking incident that turned out to be a result of its own AI agents. This and similar scenarios have fueled calls for AI restrictions and oversight. See this article from Politifact for more information. ** Most data centers “are simply hooked up to the local water mains, meaning most data centers’ cooling water comes from potable (drinking-quality) sources like treated municipal water or groundwater,” said this report from the University of Georgia Cooperative Extension. *** Nuclear reactors are like the “boiler” of a nuclear power plant. One of the newer models of these are called microreactors, small nuclear reactors designed to generate electricity for facilities such as data centers, industrial sites and remote communities. You can read more about them in this April 27, 2026 edition of Today in Energy, a daily publication authored by the U.S. Energy and Information Administration. Nuclear power plants as a source of energy have a variety of pros and cons related to affordability, sustainability and safety. Here is more information from the Encyclopedia Britannica on the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear energy. Housing In our survey, 5th District voters expressed competing concerns over housing. While many families face rising rents and high home prices, others, particularly rural residents, worry that new housing developments are destroying farmland and overloading roads. County and city boards decide where new housing can be built, but federal decisions on things like road funding, housing grants and tax credits can heavily influence regional g

artigo.texto: Aolani planeja implantar 22.000 chips Nvidia Blackwell Ultra, acelerando a expansão de data centers de IA no Sudeste Asiático A provedora singapuriana Aolani firmou parceria estratégica com a Nvidia para implantar 22.000 GPUs Blackwell Ultra em fábricas de IA na Malásia e nas Filipinas até o início de 2027, elevando o total para mais de 48.000 unidades. A colaboração utiliza compartilhamento de receitas e suporte de crédito para mitigar pressões de capital. Embora o projeto fortaleça a infraestrutura de IA no Sudeste Asiático, impulsionado por investimentos regionais bilionários, sua execução e o sucesso comercial dependem de financiamento, fornecimento de energia, entrega de equipamentos e demanda de mercado. TradingKey - A provedora de serviços em nuvem de IA de Singapura Aolani anunciou uma parceria estratégica de capacidade computacional com a Nvidia (NVDA), com previsão de implantar 22.000 GPUs Blackwell Ultra em duas fábricas de IA na Malásia e nas Filipinas no início de 2027. Após a conclusão dessa implantação, o total de GPUs implantadas pela Aolani ultrapassará 48.000 unidades, com a capacidade total das fábricas de IA excedendo 100 megawatts, ampliando ainda mais a escala potencial de implantação do Blackwell Ultra no Sudeste Asiático. Quais empresas usarão 22.000 chips Blackwell Ultra? A Aolani foi fundada em 2023 e ingressou no Nvidia Cloud Partner Program no mesmo ano, oferecendo principalmente serviços em nuvem de GPU para empresas de IA, startups, desenvolvedores e clientes institucionais. O Blackwell Ultra foi projetado para cargas de trabalho como pré-treinamento e pós-treinamento de modelos, inferência e IA agêntica. A Aolani usará essas GPUs para expandir seus serviços de computação acelerada no Sudeste Asiático, fornecendo aos clientes locais recursos de computação em nuvem baseados na plataforma Nvidia. A expectativa é que essas GPUs sejam implantadas no início de 2027. As duas partes não divulgaram o valor da aquisição, as configurações específicas do sistema, as listas de clientes ou os contratos relacionados. O progresso do projeto dependerá de financiamento, entrega de equipamentos e construção de data centers. Por que a Nvidia adota modelos de compartilhamento de receita e suporte ao crédito A Nvidia está adotando esse modelo principalmente para expandir a escala de implantação da infraestrutura de IA e vincular as vendas de produtos ao uso de serviços em nuvem. Além da receita tradicional de produtos, a Nvidia também pode participar de uma parcela da receita de serviços em nuvem gerada pela capacidade computacional fornecida, aumentando a receita recorrente atrelada ao uso. A Aolani declarou que as duas partes adotarão um modelo de compartilhamento de receitas e suporte de crédito para alinhar a implantação da infraestrutura à demanda dos clientes. De acordo com a explicação da Nvidia sobre o modelo, os provedores de serviços em nuvem para IA compram a infraestrutura da Nvidia para fornecer serviços computacionais externamente, permitindo que a Nvidia obtenha receita com a venda de produtos, além de uma parcela da receita de serviços em nuvem. O suporte de crédito ajuda os provedores de serviços em nuvem para IA a obter financiamento para projetos, aliviando a pressão de capital durante as fases iniciais de implantação em grande escala. As duas partes ainda não divulgaram o montante do financiamento, os provedores de suporte de crédito, os percentuais de divisão de receita ou os termos de assunção de riscos para essa colaboração. A eficácia real desse modelo dependerá dos custos de financiamento, da demanda dos clientes e das taxas de utilização de GPUs. Por que o investimento em infraestrutura de IA está se aquecendo no Sudeste Asiático? Segundo relatos, grandes provedores globais de serviços em nuvem já investiram um total de mais de US$ 50 bilhões em data centers de IA e infraestrutura em nuvem no Sudeste Asiático, sendo a Malásia um dos principais mercados a concentrar os investimentos em data centers na região. O Google (GOOGL) planeja investir US$ 2 bilhões para construir seu primeiro data center e região do Google Cloud na Malásia; a Microsoft (MSFT) também investirá US$ 2,2 bilhões ao longo de quatro anos para expandir a infraestrutura local de computação em nuvem e IA. O mercado de data centers nas Filipinas é relativamente pequeno. A Aolani afirmou que sua fábrica de IA projetada deve se tornar uma das primeiras plataformas de infraestrutura de IA em grande escala do país, fornecendo recursos de computação de alto desempenho para clientes corporativos, desenvolvedores e institucionais. A demanda por serviços digitais no Sudeste Asiático continua a crescer, com diversos países expandindo o desenvolvimento de energia, computação em nuvem e data centers. O avanço dos projetos relevantes permanece sujeito à capacidade de fornecimento de energia, velocidade de conexão à rede elétrica, condições de resfriamento, regulamentações de dados e políticas de exportação de chips avançados. Se o projeto da Aolani poderá entrar em operação dentro do prazo depende de financiamento, entrega de equipamentos e construção de engenharia; seu desempenho comercial após o início das operações dependerá da demanda dos clientes, da precificação dos serviços e das taxas de utilização de GPUs. Se o projeto avançar conforme o planejado, ele ampliará ainda mais a escala de implantação da Blackwell Ultra da Nvidia no Sudeste Asiático. Este conteúdo foi traduzido por IA e revisado por humanos. Ele é fornecido apenas para fins informativos e de referência, não constituindo aconselhamento financeiro ou recomendação de investimento.

artigo.texto: Brown targets data center tax breaks and rising electric bills in Ohio COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — A political clash over data centers, electric rates and tax breaks is heating up as Sherrod Brown meets with Ohioans in Westerville on Friday. Brown said he wants to hold Jon Husted accountable for rising costs affecting families. While talking with reporters, Brown raised concerns about Husted's support for data centers. "He's simply not a voice. He's voted for higher electric rates for these data centers. He was the point man for more than 200 of them coming into Ohio with big tax breaks, with no local input and higher electric rate. So that's not what people want. They know that I will stand up. I'll stand up to Big Tech. I'll stand up to the oil companies," Brown said. Brown argued that local communities should have more say in where these tech projects are built, that companies should use union labor and that out-of-state corporations should not benefit from Ohioans paying higher electric bills. He said, "To me it's this, we need to make sure that there's local input on these locations of these, that they use union labor when they build them, that we don't use over-the-top tax breaks for these big tech companies and that people's electric bills, that people in Ohio shouldn't pay the electric bills for these out-of-state corporations," Brown said. He also expressed skepticism about large AI and tech companies demanding tax breaks and pushing aside local interests. "I start with this, that I have a healthy skepticism of big corporations that come into Ohio and demand tax breaks and then override any local concerns and then try to raise our electric rates. I think you need reasonable regulation on any companies that come in, but you start with the fact that you need to be skeptical of these big companies that are buying their way into Ohio with low local income," Brown said. Amy Natoce, a spokesperson for Husted's campaign, pushed back on Brown's charges in a statement. She says as lieutenant governor Husted had no authority to grant tax breaks. "After failing Ohio families during his 32 years in Washington, Sherrod Brown is once again resorting to lies instead of facing his abysmal record head-on. The House overwhelmingly passed Sen. Husted’s bipartisan legislation requiring data center companies to pay for the power they use, but Senate Democrats blocked it. Sherrod Brown and his friends would rather play politics and stick Ohio families with higher electric bills than pass a commonsense solution. It’s despicable," Natoce said.
