artigo.texto: Galesburg wants to get ahead of data center development before it starts. The City Council takes up a first-reading ordinance tonight establishing a 180-day moratorium on new data center permits, giving the city time to set its own rules before any project arrives. The moratorium, running through April 3, 2027, is one of several items on a council agenda tonight that also includes the retirement of a longtime police K9, a $3.2 million transit fleet grant, and two transportation grant applications worth a combined $3.373 million. Eric Hanson, Galesburg city manager, joined Galesburg’s Morning News on Monday, Sept. 21. Listen to the full interview below. Data center moratorium The city says it has no active data center proposals on file, but has been contacted by interested parties. City Manager Eric Hanson said the pause is meant to give Galesburg time to watch for potential state legislation on data centers, expected either during this fall’s veto session or next spring’s general session, before setting its own rules. “We want to be able to control what the future looks like and make sure that any development that comes here related to technology is something that is in the best interest of our residents,” Hanson said. He said the biggest concerns are the electricity and water demands data centers place on local infrastructure, and the potential for higher utility costs for residents. K9 Dax’s retirement Also on tonight’s agenda: the retirement of Galesburg Police K9 Dax, a five-year veteran of narcotics detection and evidence recovery. Dax was purchased by the department in 2021 at a year and a half old and is now 7 â old enough, city officials say, that retraining him with a new handler isn’t practical. He’ll retire to live with his longtime handler, Officer Jacob Thompson, as a family pet, with Thompson covering all future expenses. “It’s great to have these exceptionally trained animals available,” Hanson said. “And then obviously to the officers who take the time and commitment that it takes to be a K-9 officer is significant.” Transit fleet and grant applications Council will weigh a $3.2 million grant application to replace and expand the city’s public transportation fleet â 22 vehicles in all, including one minivan, 14 medium-duty paratransit vehicles and seven super-medium-duty vehicles. No local match is required. Hanson credited Transit Manager Kraig Boynton for identifying the funding opportunity, saying the upgrade supports the city’s push to take transit countywide and would replace aging vehicles, including several Gillig buses he described as “well past their prime.” Council will also consider two Illinois Transportation Enhancement Program grant applications. One would put $920,000 toward a $2 million project completing sidewalk, lighting and crosswalk improvements on Simmons Street between Cherry and Prairie streets and between Kellogg and Seminary streets â filling gaps on either side of a middle section the city finished previously. If awarded, Hanson said preliminary engineering could begin next year, with construction in 2028. The second application seeks $350,400 toward Phase II engineering for a shared-use path and sidewalk project on East Main Street, from Grand Avenue to east of Walnut Street. The city has also applied for a competing Highway Safety Improvement Program grant covering the same engineering costs; only one of the two would be awarded. Hanson said grant decisions typically take four to six months, with an answer likely by spring. Treat Street and bicycle disposal Also on tonight’s consent agenda: a resolution closing Main Street from Chambers Street to the public square for Treat Street on Halloween. The road will close from 10 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., with the event running 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. This year’s citywide trick-or-treat hours are 5 to 8 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31. Council will also consider a first-reading ordinance changing how the city disposes of abandoned bicycles held by the police department. Because bicycle listings on Purple Wave Auctions no longer draw enough bidders to be cost-effective, functional bikes will now be donated to charitable organizations, with inoperable bikes scrapped. City officials say the change has no budget impact. The Galesburg City Council meets tonight at 6 p.m. at Galesburg City Hall. artigo.texto: BRICK – The governing body introduced an ordinance that defines data centers and clarifies that they are a distinct land use that is not included in any existing township category. Every piece of property in a town is zoned in a specific category. This determines what is allowed to be built there. The proposed ordinance, recommended by the township’s Land Use Committee, defines data centers and specifies that they are precluded from the Warehouse, Distribution, Storage, Office, Light Industrial or related Land Use categories. “Data centers are not allowed in any zone,” said Council Vice-President Derrick Ambrosino. “They haven’t been – the amendment eliminates any developer calling a data center a warehouse.” There are no data centers in Brick, and none have been proposed, but “the Land Use Committee had concerns about rising electric bills, groundwater depletion, noise, noise pollution, wildfire risks and industrial overdevelopment,” Ambrosino said. A data center is a dedicated building that houses computer systems, networking equipment, servers and data storage drives to store, process and share digital information. They represent a unique and evolving land use category that differs substantially from traditional land uses listed above. Data center buildings house rows of computers and equipment for storing, processing and transmitting data for major technology companies, private enterprises, banks, hospitals, government agencies and everyday businesses. They typically have minimal windows, high gates, security cameras and biometric screening. The computers require a lot of electricity to prevent the equipment from overheating and huge amounts of water for specialty air conditioning and ventilation requirements. The International Energy Agency says one large data center uses the same amount of electricity as it takes to power 400,000 electric cars, and tech companies are increasingly using data centers to train and operate artificial intelligence systems, which require additional computing power. Increasing demand for artificial intelligence has created a massive wave of new data center construction across the country, resulting in a strain on power grids. During the most recent council meeting, Councilman Gregory Cohen said he would vote in favor of the ordinance but said the problem is “unpassing it or changing it in the future” becomes more difficult. “I totally agree that these data centers really do not belong in our township at this point in time, nor do we really have any place to put it,” he said. Cohen said he was concerned that closing the door on data centers could also close the door on future revenues, which he said could “bring in a lot of money in taxation…we need to keep those things in mind that these things can change in the future. The footprint of a data center can change…reactors the size of a table are in the near future.” Councilwoman Lisa Reina agreed with Cohen. “At this time, data centers do not appear to fit the unique needs of Brick Township,” she said. “There is always an opportunity to amend an ordinance or create a new ordinance in the future as Land Use did here, if and when it is appropriate to do so.” Data centers are a somewhat partisan issue, as Republicans nationwide are more in favor of data centers than Democrats. Reina and Cohen are two of the three Republican members of the council, the rest of whom are Democrats. However, the all-Republican governing bodies in towns such as Manchester and Jackson have unanimously banned data centers as well. The Brick Township Council was unanimous in passing the introduced ordinance. In May, Governor Mikie Sherrill issued a press release announcing a four-part statewide plan to address the growing impact of data centers on energy demand, resource use and local communities. The measure will help to hold data centers accountable “while still positioning New Jersey to lead in AI innovation,” she said. The plan establishes strong guardrails to “protect communities, strengthen transparency, ensure these facilities invest in New Jersey’s energy infrastructure and deliver good-paying jobs,” she said. The next council meeting will be held on Tuesday, September 22 at 7 p.m.

artigo.texto: (Eveo/Divulgação) Publicado em 19 de setembro de 2026 às 01h04. Por Francisco Werneck Maranhão e João Rafael Gândara de Carvalho, sócios do Pinheiro Neto Advogados O Senado Federal aprovou o REDATA - Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, que concede incentivos fiscais para projetos de instalação e de modernização de data centers no País. Espera-se que a lei seja sancionada nos próximos dias. Em um mundo em que os dados viraram o “novo petróleo”, os datacenters aparecem como as “grandes refinarias” de dados. Eles são a infraestrutura necessária para processar os dados brutos, colhidos na internet, e transformá-los em produtos e serviços de alto valor agregado (streaming de voz e dados, aplicações de IA, armazenamento na nuvem, internet das coisas, carros inteligentes). Foi-se o tempo em que os data centers eram apenas galpões com computadores. Eles são hoje centros de servidores e equipamentos de rede de alta tecnologia, que podem custar bilhões de dólares. Estruturas fundamentais para o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura tecnológica brasileira e aprimoramento da inclusão digital do País. O Brasil pode oferecer o que as grandes empresas de tecnologia atualmente procuram: grandes espaços livres para instalação dos data centers, matriz energética predominantemente limpa e renovável, estabilidade geológica e geopolítica, um mercado consumidor amplo altamente digitalizado e elevada conectividade internacional proporcionada por cabos submarinos. Portanto, enquanto Estados Unidos e Europa enfrentam gargalos de energia para sustentar a demanda de inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem, o Brasil reúne condições que poucos países conseguem oferecer atualmente. O potencial brasileiro não é meramente teórico. Na nossa atividade profissional, temos assessorado empresas com grandiosos projetos de data centers nas mais diversas regiões do país. O principal desafio enfrentado por esse setor, no entanto, são os custos fiscais atrelados a esses investimentos. Estudo da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV) revela que construir um data center no Brasil custa quase 30% a mais do que nos Estados Unidos - e a tributação responde por fatia expressiva desse diferencial. Estudos apontam para uma carga tributária de cerca de 60% do valor dos bens utilizados nos data centers. Isso significa que para cada dois data centers construídos, no Brasil, as empresas precisam pagar o equivalente a um data center em tributos. É precisamente esse cenário que mostra a necessidade de aprovação do REDATA, que estabelece suspensão de PIS, COFINS, II e IPI para a aquisição, no mercado interno ou por importação, de componentes eletrônicos e equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados a data centers, observadas algumas condições.Trata-se de uma desoneração fiscal pontual para os investimentos em CAPEX, assim como outras indústrias que dependem fortemente de investimentos como a indústria do óleo e gás (REPETRO) ou mesmo os projetos de infraestrutura (REIDI). Mas o REDATA não é uma desoneração fiscal pura e simples. Ele pressupõe uma série de contrapartidas exigidas das empresas. E esse ponto precisa ser frisado, já que o projeto, infelizmente, não tem sido bem compreendido na sua integralidade. Muitas das críticas feitas ao REDATA não parecem sequer considerar as contrapartidas existentes no projeto, que vão justamente ao encontro de reivindicações legítimas feitas por vários grupos organizados da sociedade civil. No plano ambiental, a habilitação exige que o beneficiário atenda a demanda energética do data center com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão e mantenha eficiência hídrica igual ou inferior a 0,05 L/kWh, aferida anualmente - padrão rigoroso que impõe tecnologias avançadas de resfriamento e circuitos fechados de reutilização de água No plano econômico, a obrigação de destinar ao menos 10% da capacidade instalada ao mercado interno cria ainda um compromisso de que parte da infraestrutura digital subsidiada ficará acessível a empresas brasileiras, universidades e ao poder público. Na prática, isso pode significar capacidade de processamento de alto desempenho a menor custo para pesquisadores, pequenas empresas de tecnologia e projetos governamentais de inteligência artificial, benefícios que dificilmente surgiriam sem a contrapartida regulatória, mas que também dependerão dos critérios de oferta, contratação e fiscalização definidos na regulamentação complementar. Do ponto de vista tecnológico, é obrigatório que 2% do valor dos bens adquiridos por meio do REDATA sejam destinados a projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação – PD&I em parceria com instituições brasileiras. Isso permite que parte do valor que seria arrecadado com tributos, de forma difusa, seja diretamente aplicado no desenvolvimento tecnológico brasileiro. A governança complementa o desenho: relatório obrigatório de sustentabilidade com indicadores de eficiência hídrica e energética, acompanhamento contínuo pelos Ministérios do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços e da Fazenda, e uma lógica sancionatória clara: descumpridas as condições, os tributos suspensos serão exigidos com juros e multa, a habilitação poderá ser cancelada e o beneficiário ficará impedido de nova adesão por dois anos. O REDATA opera, portanto, por suspensão condicionada - e não por isenção pura, preservando o crédito tributário da União e criando incentivo real ao cumprimento. O êxito do REDATA não será medido apenas pelo volume de novos investimentos anunciados, mas pela capacidade de não socializar custos ambientais e fiscais desproporcionais. A aprovação do REDATA é um passo relevante, mas seu resultado dependerá da regulamentação, da fiscalização e da articulação com as políticas fiscal, energética, ambiental e de conectividade. artigo.texto: The Data-Center Debate Is Divorced From the Facts All those scary numbers aren’t what they seem. As the build-out of AI data centers has accelerated, the public has tended to focus on every possible downside of these industrial projects. Some wariness—about the developments and the companies behind them—is sensible. As with almost any new industrial development, and depending on where they are built and how they are powered and cooled, data centers pose risks of excessive carbon-dioxide emissions and noise pollution. But the panic about the harms of these projects has well outpaced the evidence. In my years researching and reporting on AI and the environment, with support from a grant from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), I’ve noticed that misconceptions abound. This panic, moreover, is leading communities to forgo massive amounts of tax revenue—largely because of threats that are inflated, confused, and sometimes nonexistent. The trade-offs are real. In June, a Massachusetts city near where I grew up blocked a data center, in large part out of concern over the amount of water the development would use and pollute. Data centers do need a lot of water to cool their equipment, and—as with most industrial building projects—constructing these developments can introduce chemical additives into the local wastewater. But there are no confirmed cases of this data-center pollution harming people, and this city specifically has abundant fresh water. Most of the fear about water seems to be the product of misunderstood details from news reports, spread like a game of telephone. The New York Times published a story last year about a Georgia couple whose water taps at home went dry after Meta broke ground on a $750 million data center nearby. The couple suggested that Meta’s construction created a buildup of sediment in the water, which caused water-pressure problems and damaged their well (many homes in the area use well water). Whether the construction actually caused these problems remains unclear, but the story is often read as evidence of the harms of data centers. Yet sediment buildup in groundwater is a standard construction risk, and most places don’t ban large buildings over it. Almost all stories about the harms of data centers cite such construction-related problems. As for the concern that data centers add toxic “forever chemicals,” known as PFAS, to local water sources, this seems to involve some confusion over how centers use water to cool the machinery. Some systems use fluorinated fluids classified as PFAS to help cool servers and prevent fires, but these are designed as closed loops that stay contained in equipment. There’s always the threat of a leak, but contaminating local waterways is a risk of any major industrial project. One known exception in which a data center was linked to a water-pollution problem was in Oregon, where Amazon data centers used groundwater that was already contaminated from decades of local agriculture and food processing. Because much of the water used to cool equipment ends up evaporating during the process, the wastewater that left the data center had a higher concentration of nitrates, which exacerbated the contamination problem in the local groundwater. Amazon agreed to settle the matter for $20.5 million without admitting guilt. The company accurately noted that the area had been suffering from polluted water for decades, even if the data center made it worse. The data-center debate includes plenty of dauntingly large numbers without context, such as that they consume millions of gallons of water a day. This is a significant amount, but also comparable to the water use of other industries. The data center with the highest known water consumption, Google’s development in Council Bluffs, Iowa, consumes about 1.3 billion gallons a year. That sounds massive, but so is the amount of water used to irrigate Iowa’s corn crops. If Google had bought a cornfield four to six times as large as the data center’s plot, or about eight square miles (roughly 0.04 percent of the total area Iowa uses for corn), the company would consume the same amount of water irrigating it. All American data centers together will consume about 1 percent of the water that America uses to irrigate corn. This is not nothing, but hardly horrifying in context. Another misconception is that data centers consistently raise local electricity prices. There is no clear positive relationship or broad pattern between data centers and household electricity prices, but people are happy to spread misleading claims on the subject. A common statistic that critics bandy about is that electricity costs near data centers have skyrocketed by as much as 267 percent in five years. Senator Elizabeth Warren cited this number in an op-ed earlier this year. But the figure comes from a Bloomberg analysis of wholesale electricity prices at specific nodes on the grid, not the prices that households pay. Although wholesale prices influence residential prices over time, residential prices are largely insulated from wholesale spikes and drops, and American-household bills have not risen anywhere near 267 percent during the data-center build-out. When price hikes have been linked to data centers, the amount looks more like 10 percent. Perhaps the most pernicious misunderstanding of the facts involves the claim that data centers don’t pay taxes. Early reports about the sales-tax exemptions on machinery and equipment that data centers enjoy in most states have somehow morphed into a sweeping assumption that data centers are actually depriving states and municipalities of tax revenues. The reality is that data centers are a reliable and lucrative source of tax revenue wherever they are built. Real-estate and personal-property taxes ensure that the tax burden on these developments is high, regardless of sales taxes. artigo.texto: The data center backlash is reshaping American politics — one community at a time With striking speed, the widespread debate around data centers has become a fault line in American communities, cutting across political parties, splitting constituencies and forging unexpected alliances. In city halls and county commission chambers, east to west and north to south, people are squaring off against their local representatives. It starts with distrust Data centers have "upended politics as we know it," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. It's more than a not-in-my-backyard issue, he says — it also reflects existential fears that artificial intelligence will take jobs or eliminate humanity entirely. "People just feel like they no longer have control over the technology, [and] that worries them," West says. "This is a real grassroots movement. It's ordinary people all across the country, both Republicans and Democrats." For this story, NPR traveled to data center hot spots and spoke to dozens of activists, politicians, developers and everyday Americans. The picture that emerges is complicated. Data centers have been an economic boon for some communities, helping to lower land taxes and providing jobs. At the same time, the proliferation of secretive deals that often involve elected officials signing nondisclosure agreements has exacerbated suspicions. A recent poll by The Economist and YouGov of nearly 1,600 adults found that about two-thirds of Americans oppose new data center construction in their communities. A rare cocktail of concerns has fueled the opposition, according to Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University. "It's aligning interests in ways that aren't traditional," he says. "If you're in power right now and you are dealing with this issue, you have a target on your back." Elected officials have had to scramble to recalibrate. "It's a recognition that the ground shifted under their feet and they were not ready for that to happen," Borick says. Parties are divided In Loudoun County, Va., data centers are driving a wedge between fellow Democrats. On one side is Juli Briskman, a member of Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors, who has led efforts to slow further data center development. On the other is Phyllis Randall, also a Democrat and the board's chair, who has argued in favor of data centers for the tax revenue they bring into the county, even while acknowledging they are "a double-edged sword" for nearby residents. Briskman is running to unseat Randall in next year's primary. She says her opposition to data centers dates back to 2020, when the board was seeing land-use cases seeking to convert residential and flex-industrial properties into the centers. "I feel like I have been singing this song for a while, and now all of a sudden everyone's grabbing my music and singing along with me," Briskman says. Randall did not respond to NPR's request for comment. Briskman is tapping into a sentiment in her area. Kasey Hatch lives near Loudoun County's Vantage VA2 data center, which is powered by eight natural-gas-fired turbines. Residents say the turbines produce a constant low-pitched rumble along with a high-frequency whine that has become a major source of noise complaints in the surrounding neighborhoods. Hatch, an IT infrastructure engineer for a bank who uses AI in her job, says she and her staunchly Republican cousin "never saw eye to eye on politics." But to her surprise, the last time they met, they were "on the same page about everything" when it came to data centers. At the grassroots level, that translates into Democrats and Republicans working together on an issue of mutual interest. Nusheen Farahani also lives near VA2 and is part of a group of women organized against the facility who regularly show up at public hearings. "I'm a liberal and I'm a Democrat, and the people that are in our little team … not all of them are liberals or Democrats," Farahani says. A similar story is playing out in Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Indiana, to name just a few, where locally organized groups are uniting against data centers — and elected officials. According to the Data Center Opposition Report, which tracks grassroots nonprofits on the issue, some 640,000 people are active in the anti-data center movement and 220 new groups sprang up in just the three months from June through August. They are driven by a feeling that government is part of the problem, according to Ben Green, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan's School of Information. With that comes a real sense of abandonment, he says. "If the policymakers, if my city council or zoning board or township board and governor, if they're on the side of the companies, who's standing up for me?" The economic impact Data centers have been around for a lot longer than the recent AI hype, quietly humming along in the background of the modern internet, powering cloud computing and storing vast amounts of data. AOL set up in Loudoun County, for example, back in the 1990s, giving the tech industry an early beachhead in the county that has only grown due to demand from government agencies in nearby Washington, D.C. To be sure, these facilities have brought economic benefits to the counties where they are located by creating billions of dollars in private investment, construction jobs and a limited number of well-paying positions at the data centers themselves, all the while providing an infusion of tax dollars that have stabilized and even lowered the tax burden for ordinary property owners. And among the many people NPR spoke to for this story who oppose data centers, nearly all acknowledge using AI in their daily life. Farahani, for example, says she "begrudgingly" uses chatbots for certain tasks "to make things easier." artigo.texto: Preservação florestal sustentável, abrindo caminho para um mercado de créditos de carbono. TPO - Graças aos esforços conjuntos da população, grandes áreas de florestas de madeira estão sendo expandidas em Da Nang, preservando não apenas a terra e a água, mas também com a expectativa de criar uma fonte de créditos de carbono no futuro. Báo Tiền Phong•20/09/2026 Grandes florestas Certa manhã, na aldeia de A Duong (comuna de Dong Giang, cidade de Da Nang ), o Sr. Bnuoch Ngang caminhava pela floresta de quase 3 hectares de sua família. As árvores de canela e teca, cuidadas ao longo de vários anos, erguiam-se imponentes, com sua folhagem exuberante destacando-se em meio à vasta floresta montanhosa. Após muitos anos plantando acácias, ele decidiu converter 1 hectare de área florestal para o plantio de árvores de grande porte para produção de madeira, principalmente canela e teca. Para ele, embora essa área florestal não gerasse um lucro econômico constante a cada poucos anos como as acácias, ela traria um valor maior e mais sustentável para as gerações futuras. O Sr. Bnướch Ngang pertence à etnia Cơ Tu. Anteriormente, sua família e as famílias vizinhas plantavam principalmente acácias. Essas árvores crescem rapidamente e podem ser colhidas após um curto ciclo, mas o preço da madeira de pequeno porte não é alto e depende do mercado. Há cerca de 5 anos, após ser informado e orientado por funcionários florestais e autoridades locais, ele começou a mudar seus métodos de plantio florestal. “Além do plantio de acácias, as pessoas agora estão desenvolvendo florestas de grande porte com espécies nativas, como teca e canela. O período de plantio é mais longo, mas contribui para a proteção da floresta, a conservação do solo e a retenção de água durante a estação chuvosa, limitando deslizamentos de terra e enchentes repentinas. A longo prazo, o plantio de árvores de grande porte também ajuda as pessoas a desenvolverem meios de subsistência sustentáveis sob a copa das árvores”, disse Bnướch Ngang. Há mais de uma década, na comuna montanhosa de Hiep Duc (cidade de Da Nang), os agricultores locais começaram a gerir as florestas, plantando árvores de grande porte e colhendo de forma sustentável as madeiras das florestas plantadas, contribuindo assim para o enriquecimento das florestas naturais. Eles fundaram a Cooperativa Agrícola Hiep Thuan com pouco mais de 50 famílias para aprenderem juntos a plantar florestas de acordo com padrões internacionais, incorporando conceitos que eram muito novos na época, como manejo florestal, certificação de manejo florestal sustentável (FSC) e florestas certificadas. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Huu Duong, Presidente do Conselho e Diretor da Cooperativa, a população local está acostumada ao método antigo de plantio de florestas, por isso a mudança não é fácil. Foram necessários vários anos, até que as florestas plantadas com certificação FSC gerassem altos retornos econômicos, para que a população local começasse a mudar seus hábitos. Até o momento, a cooperativa conta com 260 famílias envolvidas no reflorestamento, cultivando quase 1.500 hectares de floresta de acácias e coordenando esforços para proteger mais de 1.000 hectares de floresta natural. “Atualmente, a cooperativa continua a ‘digitalizar’ a gestão florestal, utilizando GPS e software de mapeamento para coletar coordenadas… Gerenciar áreas florestais em mapas digitais facilita a inspeção e o patrulhamento da floresta pela cooperativa, além de permitir a identificação de áreas ambientalmente sensíveis. Essa é a base para que possamos almejar conquistar o mercado de créditos de carbono em um futuro próximo”, compartilhou o Sr. Duong. Ao longo dos anos, a cidade de Da Nang tem se concentrado no desenvolvimento de plantações florestais de grande porte, incentivando as pessoas a plantar e colher acácias de forma sustentável e convertendo parte das plantações de acácias em áreas de plantio de espécies nativas de árvores de grande porte. Você também pode gostar Os agricultores florestais estão gradualmente mudando sua mentalidade; o valor das florestas não é medido apenas pela quantidade de madeira colhida, mas também por sua capacidade de reter água, prevenir a erosão, proteger o solo, conservar a biodiversidade, manter o ar limpo... e, além disso, pela expectativa de obtenção de créditos de carbono. Da Nang está considerando "vender o ar". Após a fusão, Da Nang tornou-se uma das localidades com uma grande área florestal, aproximadamente 745.000 hectares, dos quais mais de 241.000 hectares são florestas plantadas. Isso representa um enorme potencial para a cidade desenvolver uma economia florestal sustentável, criando uma base para a entrada no mercado global de carbono. Além das políticas que incentivam a expansão das áreas de plantações florestais de grande porte, a localidade também está se esforçando para apoiar as pessoas no desenvolvimento de meios de subsistência sustentáveis sob a copa das árvores, como: pagamento por serviços ambientais florestais, desenvolvimento do cultivo de plantas medicinais de alto valor sob a copa das árvores, etc. Recentemente, o Comitê Popular da Cidade de Da Nang emitiu a Decisão 3688, aprovando o Projeto de Desenvolvimento e Gestão de Créditos de Carbono Florestal na cidade para o período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão até 2035. O projeto abre uma nova perspectiva sobre como as cidades valorizam as florestas. Além da madeira, dos produtos florestais ou dos benefícios ambientais diretos, a capacidade das florestas de absorver e armazenar carbono também é considerada um recurso que pode gerar valor econômico. É por isso também que, no período de 2026 a 2030, Da Nang pretende concluir o levantamento e a revisão do estado atual das florestas; calcular e determinar as reservas de carbono; e classificar 100% das áreas florestais com potencial para a implementação de projetos de carbono florestal. artigo.texto: Raritan Township adopts ordinance banning data centers RARITAN TOWNSHIP, N.J. (Hunterdon county) — Data centers are now prohibited throughout Raritan Township after the Township Committee recently adopted an ordinance amending the municipality’s Land Development Code. The ordinance adds data centers to the township’s list of prohibited uses, banning them in all zoning districts. The amended code also specifies that warehouses, flex spaces and research facilities cannot include data centers. The ordinance establishes a distinction for businesses and other permitted uses that use computer servers as part of their regular operations. Accessory server rooms remain permitted when they are located within a principal building and used solely to support the principal use of the property. The server space cannot exceed 10% of the building’s gross floor area or 2,000 square feet, whichever is less. Mayor Brad Perry and the entire Township Committee supported the ordinance, according to the township. Township officials said the ordinance is part of Raritan Township’s broader approach to land-use planning and establishing regulations that reflect the community’s long-term planning objectives.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no LAWINFRA SUMMIT: Risco institucional é maior que o tecnológico no armazenamento de energia, diz juiz federal Antônio Cláudio Macedo da Silva Publicado 19/09/2026 • 18:28 | Atualizado há 2 dias ALERTA DE MERCADO: KEY POINTS O principal risco para o avanço dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia no Brasil não está na tecnologia, mas no ambiente institucional e regulatório. A avaliação é de Antônio Cláudio Macedo da Silva, juiz federal da 1ª Região. Em entrevista ao Times Brasil — Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC durante o LAWINFRA SUMMIT Brasília 2026, o magistrado afirmou que o armazenamento terá papel central na estabilidade do sistema elétrico, especialmente em momentos de pico de consumo ou de necessidade de recomposição da rede. Segundo ele, os sistemas permitem guardar energia em períodos de maior disponibilidade e utilizá-la quando houver necessidade, ajudando a garantir maior segurança operacional. “O armazenamento é a pedra angular, a pedra de toque, que vai dar confiabilidade e estabilidade ao sistema de energia”, afirmou. Macedo da Silva destacou que o valor econômico desses sistemas depende não apenas do custo e da tecnologia das baterias, mas também das regras que determinarão como o armazenamento poderá atuar no mercado. “A bateria não gera energia, ela desloca no tempo”, explicou. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Segundo o juiz, o avanço tecnológico tende a contribuir positivamente para o setor, com soluções capazes de reduzir custos, ampliar a capacidade de armazenamento e diminuir o uso de recursos naturais. “O risco principal nesse campo não é o risco tecnológico. O grande problema que a gente precisa controlar é o risco institucional”, afirmou. artigo.texto: Illinois is one step closer to a cleaner, more resilient power system after its first state-mandated battery auction secured 600 megawatts of storage. The amount was below what regulators wanted, but it still gives Illinois a significant boost in a fast-growing technology that can supply power when wind and solar output dips. Here's what to know According to Capitol News Illinois, the inaugural battery procurement required by the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act will add enough utility-scale storage by 2030 to serve roughly half a million homes. The new total would also be a major increase over Illinois' current 141 megawatts of utility-scale battery storage, based on Solar Energy Industries Association data. The auction was designed to secure 1,038 megawatts overall. In central and southern Illinois, in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator region, results beat expectations, with 520 megawatts from four projects. Northern Illinois, part of the PJM Interconnection territory, fell far short of its goal, with a single project providing 80 megawatts. For households looking beyond grid-scale solutions, going solar is one of the best ways to save money on home energy. You can explore EnergySage to get free solar installation estimates and compare quotes. Supporters nevertheless called the first round encouraging. Brett Sproul, Advanced Energy United's Illinois policy advocacy lead, said: "Despite not hitting the initial procurement target, the 600 megawatts of storage, regardless, in and of itself, is a huge step forward for Illinois, and definitely a really great success for affordability and reliability in the state." More background As wind and solar make up a larger share of electricity generation, battery storage is becoming more important. It allows power to be saved for times when sunlight and wind are unavailable, reducing dependence on dirty fuel power plants and helping stabilize costs for ratepayers. "My sense is that we just had a mismatch between the commercial operation date this procurement was seeking, and the status of project development in the PJM queue," said James Gignac, Midwest Policy Director at the Union of Concerned Scientists. A major challenge in PJM has been long interconnection delays, which have made it tougher for new projects to connect to the grid on schedule. Procurement rounds planned for 2027 and 2028 are expected to give the Illinois Power Agency more flexibility, and the next round may also permit projects that pair batteries with solar or wind. The law is also helping push residential efforts ahead. It enabled "virtual power plant" programs, including Solrite Energy's new option that combines rooftop solar with home batteries so households can lower their bills while sending electricity back to the grid during times of high demand. What's being done? Illinois still must add at least 3,000 megawatts of storage by the end of 2030, so this first auction is the first phase of a much larger expansion. "I think that the paired solar and storage market is really aggressive and optimistic for the future for Illinois," said Andrew Linhares, Director of Midwest State Affairs at the Solar Energy Industries Association. More From EnergySage 💡Go deep on the latest news and trends shaping the residential solar landscape For anyone considering rooftop solar, EnergySage's solar map shows the average cost of a home solar panel system state by state, along with details on solar panel incentives for each state. Together, these resources can help readers get the best price for rooftop solar panels and access available incentives. EnergySage's free services also make comparison shopping easier, and with EnergySage's help, the average person can save up to $10,000 on solar purchases and installations. Adding battery storage to a solar setup is one of the best ways to protect your home during outages, save money on energy, and go off-grid. Home batteries can also help you hang onto the power your panels generate instead of sending it all back to the grid. You can explore EnergySage for information about home battery storage options, including competitive installation estimates. "It's exciting to see real-life projects and programs being implemented as a result of the legislature's leadership. Implementation is not an easy process, but there's a lot of good people working on it," Gignac added. Where can I learn more? artigo.texto: What's The Difference Between Data Centers And Crypto Mining? Almost everybody has a personal computer, but it's the servers that keep their modern services running. You pay a subscription for a streaming app? Servers house all the shows and movies you watch. You play games like "Final Fantasy XIV" and "Fortnite"? All your progress and ability to communicate with other players relies on servers. However, not all servers are built the same, and the differences are best illustrated by comparing data centers and crypto mining operations. The differences start with the purposes. Crypto mines produce currency (depending on your definition) by solving complicated math problems. The more problems a mining program solves, the more "money" it generates. Meanwhile, data centers support AI models, from their computations to their learning. Furthermore, while multiple users can access data centers and the AI models they house, each crypto mining operation is reserved for one user. The differences branch out from there. All data centers and crypto mines rely on components operating in parallel, with countless operations carried out at the same time. The more components an installation uses, the more calculations it can handle. Crypto miners primarily rely on GPUs (what few there are after the crypto market sank). These rigs still need CPUs and RAM — only enough to maintain multitasking — but the graphics cards are the main draw. Data centers, meanwhile, use the same components, and while GPUs still do most of the heavy computational lifting, data centers need way more RAM than crypto miners to provide a near-constant stream of data and then send the results to users. The price of doing business At the end of the day, both data centers and crypto mining rigs perform innumerable computations in parallel, but the same could also be said of modern computers. What truly sets them apart is the requirements needed to maintain their performance. While both data centers and crypto mines are energy intensive, AI models require way more power than crypto. For example, two crypto facilities in Sandersville, Georgia consumed enough energy to power around 110,000 households, whereas two similar data center facilities in Atlanta gorged themselves on enough electricity to keep about 458,000 houses lit. And yet despite that electricity going to large corporations, the average citizen is still paying ever-increasing power bills. An exponential power drain isn't the only side effect of running data centers and crypto mining facilities. People complain about the harm these locations cause, from noise pollution to water contamination, but again, data centers cause more harm than crypto mines. AI servers require more effort to stay cool — mostly because they are more sensitive to temperature changes — and thus require more water and electricity to achieve that goal. Somewhat ironically, data centers generally use more sophisticated cooling solutions than crypto mining buildings, which can rely on cheap fans yet still function. But this design makes crypto miners generate more noise, which is saying something since data centers often produce noises up to 96 decibels — well beyond the threshold of sounds harmful to human hearing.

artigo.texto: CLARENCE, N.Y. (WBEN) - Not that there is one in its economic development pipeline, but Clarence would likely shoot down any data center project - should one arise. Clarence is like many municipalities both regionally and across the country that are not welcoming the development of a data center. The issue continues to be an economic development talking point with the City of Buffalo later this month expected to see its Common Council back a two-year moratorium on data center-anchored projects. "These projects make more noise than the Buffalo airport," said Clarence Supervisor Pat Casilio. In July, Gov. Kathy Hochul issued a one year statewide moratorium on data center projects. Data center developments remain key discussion points in the Town of Tonawanda and City of Niagara Falls - among other municipalities. Casilio said no developer has ever approached Clarence about a data center and there are none on its development log. Casilio said there is a proper location for data centers - just not in his town. The supervisor said rock quarries might make a good location because of environmental issues like noise and water usage. In fact, environmental issues are key reasons why Casilio thinks data centers would be a bad fit for Clarence. Chief among his concerns: noise, electrical and water usage. ""We don't have enough power to support one," Casilio said. "And, I do have concerns about the noise." But, data center advocates say the buildings can produce large scale tax dollars to aid financially ailing communities. The Data Center Coalition reports that in 2024, more than $200 billion in tax dollars were created by data centers. "We don't have financial issues," Casilio said. "But, I can see where, financially, a data center may make sense in some cities." For now, Clarence has no plans to even consider data centers, Casilio said. "It takes a special place to develop a data center and Clarence isn't that place," Casilio said. If a data center project was proposed for Clarence, it would be shot down

artigo.texto: Virginia Curbs State Support for Large Data Centers, Plans Tighter Rules Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger barred new large data center projects from specified state development and expedited-review programs, taking immediate action while laying out broader restrictions on the industry’s electricity costs, environmental impacts and local approvals. Executive Order 22, signed September 18, excludes new projects with anticipated peak electricity demand of at least 25 megawatts from assistance provided by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership through its Business Ready Sites Program and similar discretionary development or expedited-review programs. The order also restricts new nondisclosure agreements involving agencies under the governor’s supervision. The measures accompany a wider Data Center Accountability Framework that Spanberger plans to advance through agency action and the 2027 General Assembly session. Its proposals include requiring local approval for facilities using more than 25 megawatts, stronger upfront financial commitments from developers and allocating more electricity generation and transmission costs to large users. Those proposals are not all requirements already in force. The initiative addresses a central tension for Virginia: data centers bring construction spending and local tax revenue, but their growing electricity needs require costly infrastructure. A December 2024 study by the state’s Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission identified Northern Virginia as the world’s largest data center market. That study found utility rates at the time appropriately allocated costs to data centers and other customers. It nevertheless warned that expansion would raise system costs, estimating that generation and transmission expenses could add $14 to $37 to a typical Dominion Energy (NYSE: D) residential customer’s monthly bill by 2040, excluding inflation. The commission also estimated the industry contributed $9.1 billion annually to Virginia’s economy, with most benefits arising during construction. The order directs the chief energy officer to work with utilities, the State Corporation Commission and regional grid operator PJM Interconnection on assigning costs driven by large data center loads to those customers. It does not itself establish a new electricity rate. Its transparency provisions also have limits. Agencies must honor existing contracts and nondisclosure agreements. Future agreements that prevent disclosure of material information about proposed commercial data centers are prohibited, absent extraordinary circumstances such as national security. The immediate restriction applies to bodies and employees under the governor’s supervision. Environmental measures largely initiate reviews and accelerate rulemaking. Within 180 days, the Department of Environmental Quality must submit findings on the cumulative effects of data center backup generators, including localized air pollution and options for cleaner equipment. The agency must also provide accelerated work plans for noise regulations and rules governing areas where evaporative cooling could threaten water supplies. The order directs that the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area be designated a cooling water scarcity area. These deadlines concern findings and regulatory plans, rather than requiring every facility to install new equipment within six months. The broader framework proposes limiting on-site natural gas generation and prioritizing grid access for facilities meeting stronger clean-energy and emissions conditions. Spanberger’s administration will seek legislation to put additional provisions into law in 2027. The order also creates an artificial intelligence task force to develop executive and legislative responses to risks including job displacement, privacy violations and cyberattacks. It must examine existing enforcement powers and coordinate with leading AI developers. Another initiative, called VA-LEAD, would evaluate facilities through a tiered system covering resource use, infrastructure impacts, employment and community benefits. Proposed criteria and an implementation plan are due by the end of 2027, leaving important details of the administration’s longer-term approach still to be developed.

artigo.texto: A data center has been proposed for Grady County near Amber, Oklahoma. The center is still in the early planning phases and has not broken ground yet. MORE: Grady County landowners raise concerns over proposed data center What to know about the Grady County data center - Company: Aligned Data Centers - Proposed to be in Amber, Oklahoma - Expected to sit on 800 acres of land Is the Grady County data center built? The data center has not been built yet. Aligned Data Centers, the company behind the project, said that the data center is still in the planning phase. Land for the center has been purchased, but construction has not begun. In a September meeting, Grady County leaders said they did not have the legal authority to pause plans for the data center development near Amber. County commissioners said they cannot issue a moratorium on private property. RELATED: Grady County commissioners to hold special meeting on planned data center Who is Aligned Data Centers? Aligned Data Centers is the company working to bring the data center to Grady County. They have more than a dozen data centers throughout multiple countries. The company said its facilities use a closed-loop cooling system designed to minimize water use.

artigo.texto: Entrou em vigor a lei que concede incentivos fiscais para empresas instalarem ou ampliarem centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. Para o ambiente virtual existir, é preciso uma obra de engenharia bem concreta: um data center. “Qualquer vídeo a que a gente assista, quando a gente faz uma transação via PIX, por exemplo, no segmento financeiro, é porque tem um data center como esse sustentando toda essa operação”, afirma Marcos Siqueira, vice-presidente de empresa de data center. São prédios onde ninguém mora, mas que guardam dados de praticamente todo mundo. No caso de nós, brasileiros, muitas informações estão em data centers fora do país, porque aqui faltam centros de processamento que deem conta de toda a demanda. São bilhões de dólares para construir e equipar um data center, e o setor diz que aliviar os impostos diminui bem esse custo. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, o Redata, suspende a cobrança do Imposto de Importação, do PIS/Cofins e do IPI na compra de componentes eletrônicos e bens de tecnologia da informação e comunicação. Entram em vigor regras para ampliação de data centers no Brasil; veja vantagens e riscos desse mercado na era da IA — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução Segundo cálculos do setor, a estrutura de um data center padrão de IA custa, em média, US$ 1 bilhão. Os equipamentos são a parte mais cara: US$ 4 bilhões a US$ 5 bilhões. O benefício fiscal é aplicado nessa fase. “É 26% mais caro instalar um data center no Brasil do que um investimento do mesmo porte nos Estados Unidos. Com a aprovação do Redata, essa desvantagem cai para 17%”, afirma Tatiana Ribeiro, diretora-executiva do Movimento Brasil Competitivo. O Brasil tem cerca de 200 data centers. A inteligência artificial trouxe a necessidade de novos centros. O data center padrão de IA pode consumir 15 vezes mais energia do que outros centros processadores do mesmo tamanho. A nova lei determina que as empresas devem usar energia de fonte renovável ou de baixa emissão. Entre as contrapartidas, 10% do serviço do data center devem ser destinados ao mercado interno. O setor avalia que o Brasil tem duas vantagens: uma matriz elétrica renovável e tecnologia para usar pouca água. “Foi adotado como tecnologia padrão, o sistema de refrigeração de circuito fechado, que funciona como um motor de carro. Então, eu não consumo água no data center. Essa tecnologia no Brasil responde por mais de 90% a 95% de todos os data centers já construídos, e todos os novos trabalham com circuito fechado. O Redata vai atrair novos investimentos. E a gente tem a possibilidade de, até 2030, quadruplicar ou quintuplicar o parque instalado de data centers no Brasil, que hoje é em torno de 1 gigawatt de carga de TI instalada”, explica Luís Tossi, vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center. artigo.texto: Mombak anuncia novo fundo e passa a contar com Salesforce como compradora de créditos de carbono A startup brasileira Mombak lançou seu segundo fundo de reflorestamento com meta de US$ 150 milhões e crédito de R$ 200 milhões do BNDES para restaurar a Amazônia. Além disso, fechou um contrato de venda de créditos de carbono com a Salesforce, somando-se a clientes como Google e Microsoft. Com a expansão do mercado, impulsionada pelas emissões da infraestrutura de IA, a empresa e o BNDES preveem uma demanda ampliada para além das big techs, atraindo setores como mineração, petróleo e siderurgia. A startup brasileira de remoção de carbono Mombak anunciou nesta segunda-feira que concluiu o primeiro fechamento de seu segundo fundo de reflorestamento e assinou um novo contrato de compra antecipada de créditos de carbono com a Salesforce , ao mesmo tempo em que aposta que a demanda se expandirá para além das empresas de tecnologia que ajudaram a construir o mercado. A empresa informou que o "The Amazon Reforestation Fund II" tem como meta arrecadar US$150 milhões para financiar projetos de restauração na Amazônia brasileira e terá acesso a uma linha de crédito de R$200 milhões do Fundo Clima, operado pelo BNDES . Os investidores estão de olho nas tendências de demanda no mercado emergente de remoção de carbono, onde empresas como Google , Microsoft e Meta surgiram como grandes compradoras, à medida que buscam lidar com as emissões ligadas à rápida expansão da infraestrutura de IA. "A gente só está conseguindo fazer a captação desse segundo fundo porque a gente conseguiu provar ao longo desses últimos cinco anos que existe um business, existe uma indústria. Esse produto que a gente se propôs a criar, essa solução, tem um mercado para ela", disse o presidente-executivo da Mombak, Gabriel Silva, à Reuters. O primeiro fundo da Mombak arrecadou US$120 milhões de investidores, incluindo um fundo da AXA , a CPP Investments e a Bain Capital, financiando projetos de restauração em 15 fazendas na Amazônia, onde a empresa plantou quase 15 milhões de árvores nativas. A empresa também anunciou um contrato plurianual de compra de créditos de remoção de carbono com a Salesforce, adicionando a empresa de software a uma lista de compradores que já inclui Google, Microsoft e McLaren Racing. O acordo segue a primeira emissão de créditos de remoção de carbono por reflorestamento da Mombak, realizada no início deste ano. A empresa espera uma segunda emissão, maior, de aproximadamente 80 mil toneladas métricas até o final de 2026. SURGIMENTO DE NOVOS COMPRADORES Embora as grandes empresas de tecnologia tenham ajudado a estabelecer o mercado para remoções de carbono de alta qualidade, tanto a Mombak quanto o BNDES esperam que a demanda se expanda para novos setores. "Ao longo do tempo, eu acho que você pode até esperar que a gente volte com anúncios de empresas que não são essas big techs", disse Silva, acrescentando que ganhos de produtividade e técnicas aprimoradas de reflorestamento estão reduzindo os custos e tornando os créditos acessíveis a uma gama mais ampla de compradores. A diretora socioambiental do BNDES, Tereza Campello, disse que as empresas de tecnologia estão reavaliando suas metas climáticas à medida que os custos associados a data centers com alto consumo de energia ficam mais claros, enquanto o interesse de setores como petróleo, mineração e siderurgia se intensificou. "A gente tem sido procurado por outros setores que não estavam com tanto apetite para a área de crédito de carbono, que têm se mostrado muito interessados", disse ela. Os créditos de carbono permitem que as empresas compensem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa por meio do financiamento de atividades que reduzam ou removam emissões em outros locais.

artigo.texto: Libraport registra alta nas cargas para data centers (Foto: Divulgação Libraport) A movimentação de cargas destinadas a projetos de data centers na Libraport Campinas alcançou US$ 520 milhões no primeiro semestre de 2026, valor 35,8% superior aos US$ 383 milhões registrados em todo o ano de 2025. De acordo com a empresa, o resultado acompanha a expansão da infraestrutura digital no Brasil, impulsionada pela demanda por computação em nuvem, processamento de dados e aplicações de Inteligência Artificial. Entre os produtos movimentados estão servidores, racks e outros componentes de infraestrutura de tecnologia. Em comunicado, a companhia apontou que a logística tem papel estratégico nesse processo, já que os equipamentos destinados aos data centers apresentam elevado valor agregado e, em muitos casos, características que demandam procedimentos específicos de recebimento, inspeção, armazenagem, movimentação e transporte. Nesse cenário, a Libraport vem ampliando a atuação no segmento de cargas de alta tecnologia. A estrutura da empresa permite o atendimento a diferentes etapas da operação de comércio exterior, desde o recebimento das cargas até a liberação e expedição para os destinos finais. Para o diretor-presidente da Libraport, Bruno Barbosa, o desempenho do primeiro semestre da empresa mostra que a expansão dos data centers já está produzindo efeitos concretos sobre a cadeia de comércio exterior e logística. “Em apenas seis meses, movimentamos um valor de cargas superior ao registrado em todo o ano passado, o que demonstra não apenas o crescimento desse mercado, mas também a importância de contar com uma estrutura preparada para atender produtos de alto valor e operações que exigem segurança, agilidade, equipamentos adequados e precisão”, apontou.

artigo.texto: As one data center bill stalls, more proposals to protect consumers from rising energy costs are brought forward in Congress Plus, answers to the most important questions about the high-tech facilities that have become a major flashpoint in American politics. A bipartisan data center bill passed by the House earlier this week hit a roadblock in the Senate on Thursday, opening room for more debate among lawmakers over how far Congress should go to shield Americans from increased electricity costs associated with facilities being built across the country. The Ratepayer Protection Act (RPA), which was approved by the House on Wednesday with an overwhelming 417-3 majority, would compel state utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard under which large data centers would cover the extra costs of upgrades. An effort to fast-track the passage of the bill in the Senate was derailed by New Mexico Democrat Martin Heinrich, who said it doesn't go far enough. "When I open my mail, unfold my electricity bill, and read how much I owe, it doesn't say I 'may' or 'should' pay that amount. … I have to pay it," he said on the Senate floor Thursday. "The same needs to be true for AI data centers." Heinrich's objection doesn't mean that the RPA is dead, but it does mean it will have to go through a more time-consuming process that will likely table it until after the midterms. With the RPA stalled, several senators have pushed for separate legislation that represents much more aggressive efforts to curb data center-related utility costs. Heinrich has proposed a bill that would empower federal regulators to force tech companies to cover certain costs that come from connecting their data centers to the grid. A separate bipartisan bill, the GRID Act, would go even further by requiring all new data centers to have their own independent power supply that's completely separate from the public grid. Progressive lawmakers Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a full, nationwide moratorium on new data centers "until strong national safeguards are in place." The mounting pushback against data centers on Capitol Hill puts Congress on the opposite side of the issue from President Trump, who has been a vocal advocate for building more of the facilities in the United States. Trump recently warned communities that oppose them that they will end up "backwards and poor" if they block new data centers from being built. "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," he wrote on Truth Social in late August. "The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame." Trump's full-throated data center advocacy is at odds with the views of most Americans. Recent polls show that a strong majority of those surveyed oppose a new data center being built in their communities, while only a small percentage strongly support the idea. Even Republican voters are largely against data centers. A few years ago, the typical American hardly ever thought about data centers. But they've become a major political issue seemingly overnight. We've seen local lawmakers lose their jobs over their support for new data center projects. Candidates in some of the most pivotal races in this year's midterms have angled to position themselves as the voice of the people's opposition to the data center boom. New York recently became the first state to ban new data center projects. Similar proposals have been put forward in more than a dozen other states. All this is happening at a time when the president and the country's biggest tech companies are saying that the U.S. needs to dramatically increase its data capacity in order to build the economy of the future. With that in mind, here are answers to some of the most important questions you may have about data centers, including why we need them, why thousands more are being built and what it means for local communities when a new data center comes to town. What are data centers? Data centers are often called the "physical infrastructure of the internet." They are facilities where the servers, networking equipment and storage systems that allow digital data to be processed, stored and transmitted are housed. Why do we need data centers? At a fundamental level, the modern internet simply cannot exist without them. Every email, social media post, video or news article that you can find online runs through a data center. How many data centers are there? There are an estimated 3,000 data centers currently operating across the United States, according to a Pew analysis of industry data. The facilities aren't evenly distributed, though. Virginia has nearly 400, while data centers in some states number in the single digits. How many more are being built? There are roughly 1,500 new data centers in "various stages of development" nationwide, according to Pew. Other estimates suggest there could be as many as 3,000. But that doesn't just mean more of the same types of facilities that already exist are being built. Some of the proposed data centers are much larger than anything that's currently in operation. According to the power market tracking company Clearview, the biggest active data center in the U.S. has a power capacity of 750 megawatts. A single data center that's been proposed in Utah would have an estimated capacity of nearly 9,000 megawatts. Data centers aren't just getting bigger. They're also being built in new places. Right now, the vast majority of active data centers are in urban areas, according to Pew. More than two-thirds of the incoming data centers will be in rural areas. Why do we need so many more data centers? The more we ask the internet to do, the more computing power is needed to meet our demands. artigo.texto: Following seven fact-finding meetings over nine months, Gov. Tina Kotek’s Data Center Advisory Committee is asking the public to weigh in on a report detailing its findings. The 20-page “preliminary learnings and questions” report that the seven-member, governor-appointed group posted Friday includes more considerations than conclusions, and is a departure from the cost-benefit analysis of data centers in the state it was tasked with providing by mid-September. That charge changed recently when Kotek instead directed the group to synthesize its findings for the public before providing her with final recommendations by the end of the year — and after the November election. The public has until Oct. 24 at 5 p.m. to submit comments based on the report. Although the report does not include distinct policy recommendations, the group seems to have found consensus around a need for more responsible oversight of the data center industry and a more centralized information repository about Oregon data centers’ type, their water and energy use and the tax breaks they receive each year through state incentive programs. The committee’s findings land as the growth of the data center industry in the state has become a lightning rod in the Oregon governor’s race amid growing public backlash. Kotek and her Republican challenger, state Sen. Christine Drazan of Canby, have tried in recent months to paint themselves as the lone force to stop the industry’s proliferation in the state. Last week, Kotek shared her support for a statewide data center moratorium at a rally at the Oregon Capitol and unveiled a roughly one-year pause on approvals for any requests to develop data centers on state land or in state buildings. She also insisted that the state lacks the authority to mandate an all-out moratorium. Findings The committee has fielded more than 700 written comments, along with nine hours of verbal comments, since it first met in February. Roughly 90% of commenters expressed opposition to data centers. Utility affordability was the single most frequently listed concern. Most comments came from the Portland metro area, with relatively few from eastern Oregon counties, with substantial ongoing and proposed data center development, according to the report. “Our state has hosted data centers since the earliest generation of internet infrastructure, and these facilities have contributed to the prosperity of urban and rural communities alike across the state,” members wrote. “At the same time, the current unprecedented scale and speed of data center development has raised serious concerns for many Oregonians.” Oregon is among the top ten markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research, and has for more than 20 years attracted massive server facilities due to a lack of sales tax, moderate climate, relatively cheap electricity and generous property tax incentives for industrial development. But the widespread use of non-disclosure agreements and corporate secrecy around tech companies’ data centers means there is a considerable lack of information about their operations. An ECOnorthwest analysis found the state now hosts between 123 and 144 facilities, a massive increase from the eight data storage facilities in Oregon 25 years ago. The consulting firm found that almost 1 in every 100 jobs in Oregon is related to data centers. The committee wrote that the number of data centers is slated to grow significantly in the years ahead, with approximately 9,000 acres proposed for data center development. Much of that land is in rural areas or on the outskirts of cities. Most data centers in Oregon are small, “non-AI-oriented facilities” used for data storage, payment processing, cloud computing, content streaming, telecommunications and social media, according to the report. But of the 31 data centers in the process of getting sited in Oregon today, eight are hyperscale data centers meant for companies that do large-scale data storage and AI processing, the group wrote. Water, energy, tax breaks Beyond the difficulty of gathering information about the data centers, committee members enumerated what they’d learned about data centers’ growing energy, water and land demands. Committee members consider water quantity for data centers as a bigger issue than water quality, despite concerns from environmental and community groups that the facilities are pumping out water laced with forever chemicals, among others. The committee members found that seasonal water demands for irrigation in some parts of the state mean data centers are becoming unwelcome competition for resources that are already overallocated. When it comes to energy use, the members said the central questions are not only how much electricity Oregon data centers are consuming but how the industry can be leveraged to stimulate more investment in clean energy, grid modernization and other energy development in the state. The state’s lack of accounting for the property, income and other tax breaks data centers are receiving through industrial enterprise zone programs continues to be an issue, according to the report. Local and statewide tax experts and watchdogs who presented to the committee indicated that Oregon is being overly generous to data centers and the tax breaks are not necessary to keeping the facilities in the state. For instance, Morrow County’s assessor told the committee that the $7.2 billion estimated value of tax-exempt property owned by data centers in the county in 2025 was $3 billion more than the combined value of the Morrow County property subject to property taxes. The advisory group did not share any thoughts on whether Oregon’s tax programs should be scaled back for data centers. Instead, it posed a question that has come up repeatedly in meetings during the past nine months: “What should Oregon provide to attract data center investment,” the members wrote, “and what should Oregon and its communities receive in return?” Resour

artigo.texto: As fazendeiras Ida Huddleston e sua filha, Delsia Bare, recusaram uma oferta conjunta de aproximadamente US$ 26 milhões (cerca de R$ 133 milhões) para vender suas terras agrícolas no Condado de Mason, estado do Kentucky, nos Estados Unidos. A proposta foi feita por uma empresa anônima listada na Fortune 100uma das maiores gigantes de inteligência artificial (IA) do mundo, para a construção de um data center de IA. A recusa firmou a posição da família em preservar a propriedade histórica, mas a atitude dividiu opiniões entre moradores, críticos econômicos e defensores da agricultura local. As informações foram divulgadas pelas emissoras norte-americanas LEX18 e WKRC/Local 12. Seguir Enquanto proprietários rurais nos EUA analisam as vantagens de negociar suas terras, o avanço desses empreendimentos ganha forte apoio governamental com a aprovação do ReData no Senado, projeto de lei que cria incentivos fiscais para atrair grandes investimentos em infraestrutura de data centers no Brasil, que superou o México na corrida por data center de IA. Oferta para data center de IA foi 10 vezes maior que o valor de mercado A proposta apresentada pela corporação superou de forma expressiva as avaliações locais. No Condado de Mason, a média de preço de uma terra agrícola gira em torno de US$ 6.000 por acre. A empresa ofereceu valores muito acima do padrão da região: - Propriedade de Ida Huddleston: A mãe recebeu uma oferta de US$ 60.000 por acre em sua área de 71 acres, totalizando cerca de US$ 4,26 milhões. - Propriedade de Delsia Bare: A filha recebeu uma oferta de US$ 48.000 por acre por seus 463 acres, somando mais de US$ 22 milhões. Mesmo com cifras multiplicadas por até dez vezes o valor real de mercado, mãe e filha optaram por manter as propriedades. Críticas ao projeto e acusação de “assédio” para data center de IA Ida Huddleston classificou a insistência do grupo empresarial em adquirir a área como uma pressão descabida sobre a família. “O que eles propuseram e levaram adiante não é um acordo comercial, é assédio psicológico”, disse Huddleston à rede LEX18. Ela ressaltou a preocupação com o impacto ambiental na comunidade e demonstrou receio quanto à contaminação da água e ao desabastecimento de alimentos. A agricultora também rebateu os argumentos de que a chegada do centro de dados traria desenvolvimento econômico. Em entrevista à WKRC/Local 12, Huddleston questionou as promessas de novos postos de trabalho trazidas pelo empreendimento e classificou as projeções da empresa como “uma fraude”. Tradição familiar que atravessou a Grande Depressão Para Delsia Bare, a recusa se fundamenta no valor histórico e na utilidade produtiva da fazenda, cultivada por gerações de sua família. “Meu avô, meu bisavô e vários outros familiares viveram aqui por anos, pagaram impostos e alimentaram uma nação com a terra”, relatou Bare à Local 12. Ela relembrou que a propriedade produziu trigo para abastecer a população durante o período da Grande Depressão econômica nos EUA. Bare comparou sua ligação com o solo ao apego da personagem Scarlett O’Hara no clássico E o Vento Levou. “Fiquem, mantenham a posição e alimentem a nação, 26 milhões de dólares não significam nada”, destacou à LEX18. A resistência não se restringe às duas mulheres. Em dezembro, os proprietários vizinhos Andy Grosser e seu pai, Timothy, também rejeitaram uma proposta de quase US$ 8 milhões para vender a fazenda da família no mesmo local planejado para o complexo de IA. Decisão divide opiniões e gera debate sobre desapropriação A recusa das produtoras rurais abriu um debate sobre a gestão de patrimônios milionários. Críticos da decisão apontam o movimento das fazendeiras como arriscado do ponto de vista financeiro. O repórter da publicação Reason, Billy Binion, opinou publicamente que a recusa foi uma atitude imprudente. Segundo ele, propostas no valor de dez vezes a avaliação da terra não costumam se repetir no longo prazo. Binion alertou ainda para o risco de o governo recorrer a mecanismos de desapropriação no futuro para viabilizar obras ou infraestruturas, pagando indenizações substancialmente menores às famílias. Por outro lado, defensores do setor produtivo local apontam que o avanço desmedido de infraestruturas tecnológicas sobre áreas rurais consolidadas ameaça a segurança alimentar e destrói um patrimônio agrícola que, uma vez pavimentado, não pode ser recuperado.

artigo.texto: CALEXICO — Calexico has now become the first city in Imperial County, and the third city in the entire state of California, to enact a permanent data center ban. Following several months of discussion, the Calexico City Council voted on Wednesday, Sept. 16, to permanently prohibit the establishment of data centers citywide. This decision adopts an ordinance that adds Article XII to Chapter 17.11 of the city’s Municipal Code, outlining the definition of data centers and allowing a citywide ban to be established. Four-Month Procedure The process to ban data centers in Calexico can be traced back to June 3, 2026, when the council directed staff to return with an item for consideration regarding a potential data center moratorium during its meeting. On July 1, 2026, staff came back and recommended the adoption of an interim urgency ordinance pursuant to California Government Code section 65858, establishing a temporary moratorium while the city evaluated appropriate long-term land use regulations. The council, however, declined to pursue the moratorium, and instead directed staff to prepare a permanent amendment to the city’s Municipal Code that prohibits the establishment of new data centers within the city. Following procedure, on Sept. 2, 2026, the council introduced and conducted the first reading of the ordinance prohibiting data centers within the city. A vote was held to advance the ordinance for a second reading and consideration of adoption, which passed unanimously. The second reading was held on Sept. 16, 2026, where the council voted to adopt the ordinance. Applause was heard throughout the council chambers once the vote passed 3-0, as Mayor Pro Tem Lorenzo Calderon and council member Adriana Marquez were absent. The enactment of the data center ban cements Calexico as the first city in the Imperial Valley to ban data centers entirely, and in the state of California, Calexico is the third city that has implemented a permanent ban following Monterey Park’s decision in June 2026 and Coachella’s decision in August 2026. Article XII Chapter 17.11 of Calexico’s Municipal Code has been amended by adding Article XII, which clarifies that data centers are not a permitted land use within the city. Article XII includes several outlining paragraphs, and the subjects are as follows: - 17.11.1210 – Purpose - 17.11.1220 – Definition - 17.11.1230 – Prohibition - 17.11.1240 – Exemption - 17.11.1250 – Enforcement According to Article XII, the council has determined that data centers are not consistent with the city’s long-term planning objectives, infrastructure planning assumptions, environmental sustainability goals, economic development priorities and community vision. Article XII also outlines what constitutes a data center – a building, dedicated space within a building or group of structures used to house a large group of networked computer systems used for data storage and processing for off-site and on-site users, to be used for data storage, processing or distribution of large amounts of data. Such facilities may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, back-up batteries, fire suppression systems, enhanced security features and other associated utility infrastructure to support operations. The ordinance becomes effective 30 days after adoption, and it will be published in accordance with California Government Code Section 36933.
