artigo.texto: Greene County says no permit for data center submitted The above video is our WITN+ livestream and may not reflect the content in this story. GREENE COUNTY, N.C. (WITN) - One Eastern Carolina county is sharing an update on the possibility of a data center coming to the area. Friday, Greene County Government shared there’s currently no pending or submitted building permit for a data center in the entire county, namely at Burnette Road. It says there have been questions and concerns about a possible data center coming to Greene County. The county also says the Burnette Road site is still available and is actively being marketed for industrial development. The county says it developed the site to attract major new investment, create jobs, grow Greene County’s tax base and strengthen its economy. “Any data center or other major industrial development considered at Burnette Road or elsewhere in Greene County will be carefully evaluated for its impact on our community,” the county said in a Facebook post. “That includes water and electricity needs, roads and infrastructure, nearby homes and farms, environmental impacts, jobs, investment, and the long term impact on Greene County.” Some have shared concerns about cemeteries on the Burnette Road site, and the county says archaeological and historical work identified and documented the cemeteries. That information was reported to the North Carolina State Historic Preservation Office, who recommended a protective buffer of around 100 feet for the cemeteries, which the county says it intends to respect as planning continues. Greene County says any development needs to make sense for it and the people who call the county home. “Greene County can welcome new technology, responsible investment, and good jobs while protecting our water, infrastructure, taxpayers, and quality of life,” the county says. “Those goals should go hand in hand as we plan for Greene County’s future.” Copyright 2026 WITN. artigo.texto: RWE builds one of the Netherlands' largest battery systems RWE has made the final investment decision to build one of the largest battery storage systems in the Netherlands. Published on September 21, 2026 Team IO+ selects and features the most important news stories on innovation and technology, carefully curated by our editors. RWE has made the final investment decision to build one of the largest battery storage systems in the Netherlands: a 400 MW/1,100 MWh battery at the power plant in Moerdijk. The system will consist of 208 containers with lithium-ion batteries and will be able to deliver its full capacity for nearly three hours. Construction will begin shortly, and commissioning is scheduled for the second quarter of 2028. Nikolaus Valerius, CEO of RWE Generation SE: “This battery represents an important milestone for a reliable power supply and for relieving the strain on the power grid in North Brabant. As one of the largest and most powerful battery systems in the Netherlands, it will be able to meet the peak evening demand of approximately 500,000 households for nearly three hours. At the same time, it can absorb excess electricity from the grid within seconds. Battery storage plays a crucial role in building a resilient energy system that accommodates a growing share of renewable energy sources.” Mark Lentjes, Regional Director of TenneT South Netherlands: “We are pleased that RWE in West Brabant intends to contribute to a more efficient use of the power grid with a large-scale battery that acts as a congestion reliever. RWE’s large-scale battery is located near the 150,000-volt Moerdijk-Noord high-voltage substation and helps alleviate the bottleneck there, which in turn reduces congestion throughout North Brabant.” Alleviating congestion on the power grid The new battery system will make optimal use of the existing infrastructure: it will be connected to the national power grid via the existing substation at the RWE power plant in Moerdijk. Through capacity management agreements with grid operator TenneT, the battery will be used to alleviate congestion in the North Brabant region. Thanks to this development, space will be created on the grid for parties on the waiting list who wish to purchase electricity. TenneT, together with the regional grid operator Enexis, will investigate what this means for whom and when in the coming period. The grid operator will incorporate this development, along with other developments in the region, into the reassessment of the congestion management study December 2026. The new battery system will be able to provide advanced grid services, such as immediate reserve (inertia). The Moerdijk site already hosts the first synthetic inertia battery connected to the continental European grid, with a capacity of 7.5 MW/11 MWh. Linking offshore wind energy to onshore flexibility The 795 MW offshore wind project by RWE and TotalEnergies off the Dutch coast is designed to combine offshore wind power generation with onshore flexibility solutions that help align renewable energy production with electricity demand. In Moerdijk, the battery projects play a key role in this by storing electricity when wind production is high and feeding it back into the grid when needed. This helps smooth out fluctuations and optimize the use of renewable energy. Together with technologies such as electrolysis, e-boilers, and EV charging, this supports OranjeWind’s ambition to integrate offshore wind energy more effectively into the Dutch energy system.

artigo.texto: US Department of Energy Selects Coreshell Technologies for $50 Million Award to Scale Domestic Battery Manufacturing with Metallurgical Silicon (MGS) Anodes Award will fund expansion of production capacity, creating more than 100 operational jobs and strengthening U.S. supply chain independence for American mobility and defense applications SAN LEANDRO, Calif., Aug. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Coreshell Technologies announced that it has been selected by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Manufacturing Deployment Office (MDO) for a $50 million award under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The award will fund the expansion of Coreshell’s manufacturing facilities, establishing the first U.S. gigafactory dedicated to producing lithium-ion batteries with anodes made entirely from metallurgical silicon (MGS) that supplants graphite, the most challenging Chinese critical mineral to remove from battery supply chains. Coreshell’s patented technology leverages abundant MGS to completely replace graphite, a critical mineral that is heavily concentrated in China (>93% of global supply). Coreshell pairs this innovation with dry-coating cathode technology developed with subrecipient AM Batteries. Together, the two companies will build out approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of electrode manufacturing capacity and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of cell assembly capacity. The project is expected to create more than 100 domestic jobs across production, technical, and administrative roles, with hiring phased alongside construction and equipment ramp-up. These batteries will not only comply with the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), but they will be the first scalable cells in the US to fully eliminate supply chain vulnerabilities from China. Jonathan Tan, CEO and co-founder of Coreshell, said: This award is about more than building a factory. It’s about liberating the batteries that power America from a supply chain we don’t control, “Today, the anode material in nearly every lithium-ion battery traces back to Chinese graphite processing. By proving that domestically sourced metallurgical silicon can replace that graphite at scale, we’re giving the U.S. automotive and defense industries a path to energy storage that isn’t hostage to a foreign supply chain. This DOE award lets us build that capability right here in the US.” Domestic mineral producers, including Coreshell’s supply partner Ferroglobe, already produce more than 100,000 tons of MGS per year, giving Coreshell’s approach a secure, scalable U.S. feedstock in a segment of the battery supply chain that is almost entirely foreign-controlled today. By anchoring both anode active material and cell production onshore, the project is designed to reduce U.S. reliance on foreign batteries for the electric vehicle industry while also supporting specialized applications for the U.S. military, where secure, domestically sourced battery supply chains are a growing national security priority. AM Batteries will contribute its Powder-to-Electrode™ dry coating process for cathode manufacturing as a subrecipient, eliminating solvent-based wet coating and the associated solvent-recovery and management infrastructure. AM Batteries’ dry electrode manufacturing reduces capital costs, operating costs, and safety risk while enabling higher performance cells. Hieu Duong, CTO of AM Batteries, said: This project is about proving that a 100% domestically produced high-performance battery cell can be cost-competitive with mass-market cells from Asia. “The U.S. will not win by simply replicating existing technologies or the status quo; we must create fundamental advantages in manufacturing and materials. By combining AMB’s platform with Coreshell’s MGS anode technology, we can lower cost, improve performance, and help build a globally competitive battery industry in the West.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market US Department of Energy Selects Coreshell Technologies for $50 Million Award to Scale Domestic Battery Manufacturing with Metallurgical Silicon (MGS) Anodes, source

artigo.texto: IN SUMMARY - Almost two years after a fire at a battery storage site in Moss Landing, another one is smoldering. - The fire resurfaces concerns about battery storage sites as the state charges ahead with clean energy goals. The burned remains of the Moss Landing Power Plant battery energy storage facility caught fire again Friday morning, prompting Monterey County officials to issue a shelter in place order — less than two years after it became one of the largest battery storage facility fires in history. Workers for Vistra, the plant’s Texas-based operator, noticed a flare-up early Friday morning against the wall of a building that burned in the initial January 2025 fire. The cause: roughly 1,200 inaccessible battery modules, still charged, spontaneously ignited, said Chief Jess Cortez with the North County Fire Protection District. “They’re in the smoldering stage right now,” Cortez said at a briefing Friday afternoon, adding that at that point there was no active fire. “The incident is very dynamic. There could be possible flare-ups.” Local authorities lifted the order to shelter in place later Friday afternoon. Still, the flare-up reignites fears about battery storage facilities — even as California comes to increasingly rely on them. The state now has “the nation’s largest battery energy storage fleet,” the California Energy Commission announced in August. “If we had only known the worst-case scenarios of how not to build batteries, we wouldn’t have built Moss Landing,” said Dustin Mulvaney, a professor at San Jose State University in the school of planning, policy and environmental studies. “Because it keeps coming back to haunt us.” The incident also sharpens the tension between Gov. Gavin Newsom’s push to shortcut permitting for energy and other projects, and the communities hosting these facilities. Fire, rekindled In January 2025, residents watched large plumes of smoke and ash spewing from Vistra’s 300-megawatt battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County. It was the facility’s fourth safety incident, the third on the Vistra property, since 2019, according to a letter Assemblymember Dawn Addis, a San Luis Obispo Democrat, sent state regulators last year. The fire continued for days before crews could control it, then rekindled briefly a month later. Newsom called for a state investigation. The California Public Utilities Commission began with a site visit that month. Nearly two years later, that investigation is ongoing, with a root cause analysis underway in coordination with Vistra and an independent consultant, said Terrie Prosper, a spokesperson with the Public Utilities Commission. Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church expressed frustration about the delay. “Why it takes a year and a half to come up with an answer when everything is just about near the end of being cleaned up, I don’t know,” he said. Before the state approves any more of these facilities, he said, “It’s a good idea to know what’s causing these fires.” Safety rules, too late Unlike facilities built more recently, the Moss Landing site was built in an enclosed, aging building with older battery technologies crammed closely together — allowing fires to spread quickly, Mulvaney said. Denise Grab, the Clean Energy Law & Leadership project director for the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, agreed: The site is “one of the earlier battery storage facilities in the state and in the country, even. And the design is not up to par with current safety designs.” Battery plants still carry less overfall harm than fossil fuel plants, Grab added. “There are risks from other types of energy generation as well, particularly fossil fuel,” Grab said. “Asthma, premature death, heart attacks, lung disease from fossil fuel plants is significant, and (battery plants pose) a different kind of risk.” California passed a series of safety laws both before and after the January 2025 fire, including several laws from State Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, aimed at better planning for — and preventing — fires. A 2022 law by then-Sen. Ben Hueso required the California Public Utilities Commission to set new standards for battery storage facilities and boost oversight of their emergency plans. But the commission didn’t bring its proposal for implementing Hueso’s law to a vote until after last year’s Vistra fire. “We should have never built Moss Landing the way we did,” Mulvaney said. “We were too late with coming up with the standards and certifications, which make batteries much safer today.” Environmental health controversy Vistra says that the cause of last year’s fire is still unknown. The energy company commissioned a study finding that chemical concentrations in nearby soil or water posed no risk to humans or the environment. “As a result, no further human health or ecological risk evaluation related to the (Moss Landing fire) event is warranted,” the report read. But scientists’ findings and resident accounts suggest otherwise. As the fire blazed for days in January 2025, residents reported wheezing, coughing, headaches and eye irritation. Researchers presented additional findings at a symposium last month, including evidence from one UC Santa Cruz researcher of elevated exposure to battery-related materials in hair samples. Scientists with the San Jose State University’s Moss Landing Marine Laboratories have found high levels of nickel, manganese, and cobalt in soil around the facility. Ivano Aiello, the scientist who led the study, said Vistra’s recent report examined potential contaminants months after the fire was contained. The long-term health impacts of potential exposure remain unclear, and researchers continue studying the incident. artigo.texto: New Hampshire’s Republican majority will pursue a moratorium on AI data centers, marking a policy shift after two new data centers were proposed in the capital region in recent weeks. Senate President Sharon Carson, a Londonderry Republican, announced on Thursday that the Senate would explore legislation to “protect New Hampshire taxpayers from shouldering the costly demands of data center development and ensure our communities are not left to pay the price.” She echoed recent sentiments from Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who said this summer that she supports a moratorium after public opposition to data center proposals continued to grow across the state. “Large scale facilities can place significant demands on electricity and water, create noise and environmental impacts and require substantial infrastructure,” Carson said in a statement on Thursday. “While we can embrace technological innovation, we agree with Governor Ayotte that it cannot be at the expense of Granite State families.” Two proposed data centers are on New Hampshire’s radar right now: one at the former Merrimack Station power plant in Bow and one at a vacant lot in East Concord. An unofficial plan for a data center in Nottingham was withdrawn in May after widespread public opposition. Resistance to AI data centers is largely bipartisan, according to a recent UNH Survey Center poll, which found that 67% of New Hampshire residents either strongly or somewhat oppose local construction of data centers. New Hampshire already has several data centers, though none are in the capital region. Earlier this year, Republicans watered down a Democratic bill that would have imposed design and noise requirements on data centers and codified towns’ ability to adopt their own regulations. The bill, SB 439, ultimately did not pass. “Republicans in the State House took that bill and gutted it, handing that power to developers instead of the people who actually live next to these projects. I watched them do it,” state Sen. Debra Altschiller, the Stratham Democrat who proposed that bill, said in a statement. “Now, eight months later and weeks before an election, they want credit for caring about the exact thing they tried to take away.” New Hampshire’s next legislative session begins in January 2027.

artigo.texto: TERRY TURNER: Water concerns and data centers Published 7:11 am Monday, September 21, 2026 We in Georgia’s southwestern coastal plain sit atop two groundwater aquifers, the Floridan nearer the surface and the Claiborne deeper down. The depths of the aquifers are highly variable, but the Floridan’s average estimated depth goes to approximately 200 ft below the surface and the Claiborne continues down to an average of approximately 600 ft. The point is, southwest Georgia sits atop a lot of water. That said, it is not limitless. Major water withdrawals from the Floridan aquifer began in the 1970s with the advent of pivot irrigation systems for agriculture. Georgia’s Department of Natural Resources estimates that there are now between 10,000-13,000 pivot systems active in Georgia. Considering that one typical pivot system for a 100-acre field can require 500-1,000 gallons of water per minute when in use, the total number of active systems represents an enormous amount of water drawn out of what was once a largely unmolested aquifer. Georgians alert to the issue have often raised concerns about the current rates of water withdrawal because, if persisted in, they could have significant effects on our groundwater supply, a supply depended upon not only for agriculture but for homes, businesses, manufacturing, and even recreation. One point of obvious concern is that early pivot systems had wells with depths of only 60-200 feet deep into the Floridan aquifer to get an adequate water supply. Presently, it is not uncommon to have to bore to 500 feet to reach sufficient water. Similarly, private wells bored for homeowners once found adequate water for those needs at 50-100 feet. Today those wells typically have to go down 200-400 feet. Those data and others indicate a shrinking water base strongly correlated with the increase in the number of pivot irrigation systems, not only locally, but upstream of our aquifers’ natural water flow. These concerns plus the effects of a long-term drought had the state put a moratorium on new groundwater withdrawal permits in 2012. That ban was not lifted until 2025 with new rules to maximize pivot systems’ water-use efficiency and to better monitor their activity. The point here is that southwest Georgia has a history of awareness about the health of our groundwater resources. Now come the data centers. Data centers are high-tech marvels that run thousands of computers all at once to crunch an unimaginable amount of data so they can quickly provide answers to almost anyone on any subject. All those computers require enormous amounts of electricity, which generates heat, and enormous amounts of water to generate cooling. In southwest Georgia that water has to come from local aquifers already being reduced by large withdrawals for agriculture. A medium-sized data center can use an estimated 110 million gallons of water per year; a large center can use that much in a week at peak use. Data centers do not run sporadically like irrigation rigs; they run 24 hours per day, 365 days per year and would put a huge drain on aquifers already under stress. Data centers are not built thinking they might suddenly face severe water restrictions. So, what would happen if a data center were be established locally and environmental conditions like those in 2012 mandated a need for reduced water withdrawal from our aquifers? Local governments need to have thought this through. What counts more, one might ask, groundwater preservation to meet the needs of the local population and agriculture or the needs of a remote corporation hoping to profit off the natural resources of others? Political leaders make these decisions. Money is involved. One hopes they have their priorities straight. Terry Turner, a resident of Colquitt County, is professor emeritus of urology at the University of Virginia as well as author of books based on his experiences as an infantry officer in Vietnam.

artigo.texto: Moss Landing shelter-in-place and road closure lifted after battery storage fire Firefighters responded Friday morning to a fire at the Moss Landing battery storage facility operated by Vistra Energy, the same facility damaged in a major battery fire in January 2025. The North Monterey County Fire District was dispatched shortly after 6:15 a.m. Crews arrived to find smoke and flames coming from the facility’s north side. The fire involved 1,500 batteries that were still energized inside a structure damaged during the 2025 fire. Officials said Friday’s fire was not comparable to the January 2025 fire in scale or complexity. They anticipate it could burn itself out over the next 24 hours. Everyone working at the facility has been accounted for, and no injuries have been reported. The incident is being managed under a unified command that includes the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office. The county’s Emergency Operations Center has also been activated. The Sheriff’s Office lifted the shelter-in-place order for the area within one-third of a mile of 7301 Highway 1, known as Zone PAZ-1. The hard closure of Dolan Road between Highway 1 and Via Tanques Road has also been lifted. Highway 1 remains open. The EPA is monitoring air quality in the area. KSBW 8 contacted the EPA and Vistra Energy for additional information but had not received a response. The North Monterey County Unified School District said its shelter-in-place order had been lifted. Schools and activities will continue as scheduled, and air-quality readings were in the normal range. Assemblymember Dawn Addis said she was “frustrated and deeply concerned” about the fire. “I'm frustrated and deeply concerned by the repeat fire at Moss Landing. Early this morning I received initial briefings on the Moss Landing battery energy storage fire. Although initial cleanup and battery removal, under the supervision of the federal EPA, were completed two weeks ago, 1,500 hard-to-access batteries remain in the damaged area of the facility. This incident is ongoing, and we don't yet know all details. I strongly ask surrounding communities to follow all safety instructions from emergency services." Additional information will be provided as it becomes available.

artigo.texto: A new aluminum coating could simplify how battery components are manufactured by protecting the metal during forming while adding properties needed inside electric vehicle and energy storage systems. Novelis is expanding its portfolio of coated aluminum solutions for battery applications, targeting components including battery enclosures, casings and electrical connectors known as bus bars. The approach combines automotive-grade aluminum sheet with surface treatments designed to improve corrosion resistance and formability. The company says the coated material can also be engineered to provide electrical insulation for specific battery applications. A key part of the technology is a water-based coating applied to aluminum coils before they are formed into components. The coating is designed to remain effective after stamping, potentially allowing manufacturers to remove some processing steps used with untreated aluminum. Coating simplifies battery production Battery components must withstand demanding manufacturing and operating conditions. Aluminum is attractive because it is lightweight, durable and recyclable, but components may require additional surface treatments to protect them from corrosion or provide electrical insulation. Novelis says its pre-applied coating can address some of those requirements before the aluminum reaches the forming stage. Because the coating is already on the coil, manufacturers may be able to reduce reliance on external lubrication and additional e-coating processes. “Leveraging decades of automotive expertise, we have developed aluminum solutions that combine advanced surface technologies with high-performance sheet products for demanding battery applications,” says Milan Felberbaum, Director R&D, Novelis Europe. “By integrating these capabilities, we help customers improve manufacturing efficiency while supporting battery performance and durability.” More from Energy See All The company says the coating has already been proven and is in use on its advanced coating line in Germany. Its ability to withstand stamping is important because battery components often need to be shaped into complex forms after the coating is applied. Aluminum targets tougher battery demands The coated aluminum can be used for battery enclosures and casings, where corrosion protection can help improve component durability. It can also be tailored for electrical insulation, a property that can be useful for components that need to prevent unwanted electrical contact. The technology is aimed at both electric mobility and stationary energy storage. That gives the material a role across different battery systems rather than limiting it to automotive applications. Novelis is also emphasizing the use of recycled aluminum. The company says high-recycled-content, low-carbon aluminum can support efforts to reduce the environmental impact of battery supply chains. Closed-loop recycling could allow aluminum recovered from products to be returned to the manufacturing cycle. The announcement is therefore focused less on changing battery chemistry and more on changing the material and manufacturing process around the battery. By combining aluminum’s low weight with a pre-applied coating, the company is targeting a way to make battery components easier to manufacture while meeting durability and insulation requirements. Fewer steps for battery makers The approach could also help manufacturers reduce manufacturing complexity if fewer coating and lubrication stages are required. However, the announcement does not provide quantified figures for cost savings, production-time reductions or improvements in battery performance. Novelis is positioning the expanded portfolio for the growing battery and energy storage markets, building on its experience supplying aluminum products to the automotive industry.

artigo.texto: New Hampshire’s Republican majority will pursue a moratorium on AI data centers, marking a policy shift after two new data centers were proposed in the capital region in recent weeks. Senate President Sharon Carson, a Londonderry Republican, announced on Thursday that the Senate would explore legislation to “protect New Hampshire taxpayers from shouldering the costly demands of data center development and ensure our communities are not left to pay the price.” She echoed recent sentiments from Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who said this summer that she supports a moratorium after public opposition to data center proposals continued to grow across the state. “Large scale facilities can place significant demands on electricity and water, create noise and environmental impacts and require substantial infrastructure,” Carson said in a statement on Thursday. “While we can embrace technological innovation, we agree with Governor Ayotte that it cannot be at the expense of Granite State families.” Two proposed data centers are on the capital region’s radar: one at the former Merrimack Station power plant in Bow and one at a vacant lot in East Concord. An unofficial plan for a data center in Nottingham was withdrawn in May after widespread public opposition. Resistance to AI data centers is largely bipartisan, according to a recent UNH Survey Center poll, which found that 67% of New Hampshire residents either strongly or somewhat oppose local construction of data centers. New Hampshire already has several data centers, though none are in the capital region. Earlier this year, Republicans watered down a Democratic bill that would have imposed design and noise requirements on data centers and codified towns’ ability to adopt their own regulations. The bill, SB 439, ultimately did not pass. “Republicans in the State House took that bill and gutted it, handing that power to developers instead of the people who actually live next to these projects. I watched them do it,” state Sen. Debra Altschiller, the Stratham Democrat who proposed that bill, said in a statement. “Now, eight months later and weeks before an election, they want credit for caring about the exact thing they tried to take away.” New Hampshire’s next legislative session begins in January 2027.

artigo.texto: A criação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) abre uma nova etapa na tentativa do Rio Grande do Norte de atrair investimentos em centros de processamento de dados. A Lei nº 15.504/2026 reduz o custo de implantação desses empreendimentos ao suspender tributos federais sobre máquinas e equipamentos, mas especialistas do setor avaliam que a vantagem tributária, sozinha, não garante a escolha do Estado por grandes operadores. A legislação suspende PIS, Cofins, IPI e, no caso de bens sem produção nacional, o Imposto de Importação. O efeito ocorre principalmente sobre o custo de capital dos projetos, que demandam grandes volumes de equipamentos de tecnologia. Como o regime vale nacionalmente, entretanto, a desoneração também beneficia concorrentes do RN. Leia também: Lei do Redata abre espaço para data centers no RN Para Darlan Santos, do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia (Cerne), a medida retira uma barreira financeira dos projetos, mas não cria uma vantagem tributária exclusiva para o Rio Grande do Norte. “Como o Redata é uma lei federal de alcance nacional, ele promove uma desoneração uniforme e não gera, isoladamente, um privilégio competitivo exclusivo ao RN perante os demais Estados. O ganho real do Estado decorre da equalização das condições tributárias com o mercado internacional, permitindo que o nosso principal ativo (abundância de energia renovável) atue como diferencial competitivo no custo operacional (opex) das empresas”, afirma Santos. Marcello Cabral, diretor de Novos Negócios da Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (ABEEólica), faz avaliação semelhante. Para ele, o benefício federal melhora as condições brasileiras, mas a definição do local onde cada empreendimento será instalado continuará submetida a fatores regionais. “O Redata reduz um dos principais componentes do custo de implantação dos data centers ao suspender PIS, Cofins, IPI e, para bens sem produção nacional, o Imposto de Importação incidente sobre equipamentos. Isso melhora a competitividade do Brasil e, consequentemente, do RN”, afirma. “Entretanto, o Redata é um incentivo nacional, não assegura que o investimento venha para o RN. A decisão continuará dependendo de licenciamento ambiental, conexão elétrica, fibra óptica, segurança jurídica, água, terrenos e eventuais incentivos estaduais.” O Estado entra nessa corrida tendo a produção de energia renovável como um dos principais ativos. Segundo Cabral, o RN produz dez vezes mais energia do que consome, com partes significativas de eólica e solar. A oferta ganha peso porque o Redata exige que a demanda elétrica dos empreendimentos seja atendida por contratos ou autoprodução de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. “Pesa significativamente, sobretudo porque o Redata exige que a totalidade da demanda elétrica dos empreendimentos seja atendida, por contratos ou autoprodução, por fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão”, afirma Cabral. “O RN produz dez vezes mais energia do que consome, o que lhe oferece um argumento relevante. Entretanto, disponibilidade de geração não equivale à disponibilidade de conexão. É necessário também firmeza do suprimento, estabilidade elétrica, ponto de conexão e a capacidade da rede”, acrescenta. Leia também: FIERN defende data centers: RN produz 10 vezes mais energia do que consome A vantagem, portanto, não significa que toda essa energia esteja imediatamente disponível para um data center. Os empreendimentos funcionam 24 horas por dia e exigem fornecimento contínuo. A geração eólica e solar é variável e precisa ser combinada com o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), armazenamento, redundância e outras fontes de segurança. Darlan Santos, presidente do Cerne, chama atenção ainda para os cortes de geração determinados pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), conhecidos como curtailment. “A abundância renovável é uma condição necessária, porém insuficiente. Embora o RN tenha ampla oferta eólica e solar, o curtailment (cortes de geração pelo ONS) evidencia uma saturação de rede, e não um desconto automático na tarifa. A energia cortada só se torna um ativo atrativo se houver arranjos regulatórios e físicos específicos”, explica. O tratamento concedido pelo Redata às regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste acrescenta outro componente à competição. Nessas áreas, a obrigação de destinar capacidade computacional ao mercado interno cai de 10% para 8%, enquanto o investimento obrigatório em Pesquisa, Desenvolvimento e Inovação passa de 2% para 1,6% do valor dos equipamentos. Para Cabral, a diferenciação ajuda a reduzir custos, mas não elimina as vantagens acumuladas por regiões que já possuem infraestrutura digital consolidada. “Essa diferenciação reduz contrapartidas, mas não amplia diretamente a desoneração tributária. Portanto, ajuda, mas não compensa sozinha diferenças em conectividade, infraestrutura elétrica, disponibilidade de terrenos, licenciamento, proximidade de clientes e segurança jurídica.” Rede elétrica e fibra condicionam projetos Transformar a disponibilidade de energia em capacidade para receber grandes centros de dados exigirá investimentos adicionais. A avaliação do Cerne é de que o sistema elétrico potiguar não possui capacidade instalada imediata para absorver empreendimentos hyperscale sem obras em transmissão e distribuição. “O sistema elétrico potiguar não possui capacidade instalada imediata para absorver grandes data centers (hyperscale) sem investimentos adicionais em transmissão e distribuição”, afirma Darlan Santos. Segundo ele, a conexão de cargas dessa dimensão exige “novas subestações de seccionamento, ampliação das redes de distribuição locais e construção de linhas de transmissão dedicadas”. artigo.texto: A new study by Portland consultancy ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia reveals Oregon has two distinct data center profiles based on geography. “We don’t just have one Oregon data center story; we have two Oregon data center stories,” says Terry Wirkkala, project director at ECOnorthwest, which on Thursday released a 135-page study intended to provide Oregonians and policymakers with reliable information on an exceedingly controversial subject. “The data center debate can quickly get reduced to a single number, whether it’s tax incentives, land use, jobs, or electricity use, but none of those measures tells the whole story.” East of the Cascade Mountains, Oregon has a mature data center market dominated by massive hyperscale facilities. Of the 2,630 people employed in Oregon’s data center industry, 2,205 live on the east side of the mountains; 67 of 70 data centers in Eastern Oregon are considered huge “hyperscale” facilities. And based on analysis by S&P, the state is projected to see a 12% increase in square footage by 2030 and nine more facilities. But west of the Cascades, Oregon has a less-developed data center market consisting mainly of retail and telecommunications-type facilities. It employs 425 direct staff but expects an 80% increase in square footage by 2030 with 23 new facilities in the development pipeline. Data center development has expanded rapidly in Oregon to where there are now 111 operational data centers across 22.1 million square feet in Oregon and 32 proposed facilities at some stage of development. But they’re also now subject to major public backlash in Oregon and beyond, with opponents on either side of the political divide. One common argument against data centers is that aside from initial construction and despite their massive cost, they employ relatively few people. Data centers account for 0.2% of statewide employment and 0.5% of statewide wages. By comparison, the semiconductor industry accounts for 2.2% of statewide employment and 5.4% of statewide wages. The study, which was funded by the Lemelson Foundation, determined the data center industry’s true fiscal impact is elusive due to fragmented evidence and inconsistent terminology. “While tax abatements are common, it’s unclear if these incentives are the primary driver for site selection over other factors like climate or power access,” Wirkkala says. Beyond the information presented, the study identifies key gaps in information available to policymakers, noting a significant lack of precise data regarding water use and electricity consumption. Other gray areas include the full fiscal relationship between data centers and host communities, and payments and investments made by data centers. A day earlier, on Wednesday, the Portland City Council approved a resolution that urges the city administrator not to enter into nondisclosure agreements with data center developers. An amendment to the resolution states the council intends to pursue “moratorium or zoning restriction on all hyperscale data centers at the earliest time and to consider additional approaches for large-load data centers.”

artigo.texto: System integrator Fluence and lithium-ion battery OEM Eve Energy have struck a massive 206GWh battery supply framework agreement for 2027-31, one of the largest deals of its kind ever announced. The firms have committed to 16GWh of capacity in 2027, with 190GWh reserved for 2028-2031, Eve Energy announced in a filing on the Shenzen stock exchange last week (18 September). China-based Eve Energy said it could not yet estimate the boost to its finances that the deal would bring, but its share price saw a sharp 6-7% jump when it made the announcement. Eve added that framework agreement was subject to change, including from industry policies or market conditions which could prevent the co-operation proceeding as expected. It mainly attributed this to delays in its US manufacturing ramp-up. Its US manufacturing ecosystem is key to delivering on US BESS projects, following the past few years of increased tariffs on Chinese batteries and new Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) rules meaning that projects using Chinese battery tech cannot avail of clean energy tax credits. Fluence has positioned itself as a first-mover on securing a fully FEOC-compliant battery and BESS supply chain. Fluence hasn’t communicated anything to the market regarding the Eve deal, so nothing is certain, but its agreement with Eve would therefore presumably cover projects outside of the US. While it has increasingly focused on the US, Fluence still has lots of business elsewhere, including two projects totalling 1.1GW/4.4GWh on which it started construction for power firm LEAG in Germany recently. Eve Energy mainly manufactures in China, with its only non-China facilities to-date serving the EV market. The firm is one of the more recent entrants to the BESS space but it has aggressively moved into the top three BESS cell suppliers in the past few years, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

artigo.texto: LAWINFRA SUMMIT: Data centers envolvem segurança nacional e exigem prevenção à judicialização, diz a desembargadora Mônica Sifuentes, presidente do TRF6 Publicado 19/09/2026 • 18:15 | Atualizado há 2 dias Desembargadora afirma que expansão de data centers no Brasil é necessária para proteger dados e reduzir dependência de estruturas no exterior. Presidente do TRF6 alerta para consumo de energia e água e defende planejamento de longo prazo. Mônica Sifuentes avalia que incentivos tributários e novas regras para o setor podem gerar disputas judiciais. A instalação de data centers no Brasil deixou de ser apenas uma questão de infraestrutura e passou a envolver também segurança nacional e proteção de dados, afirmou Mônica Sifuentes, desembargadora federal e presidente do Tribunal Regional Federal da 6ª Região (TRF6). Em entrevista ao Times Brasil — Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC durante o LAWINFRA SUMMIT Brasília 2026, Sifuentes afirmou que o avanço da inteligência artificial aumenta a necessidade de estruturas de armazenamento instaladas no próprio país. Segundo a desembargadora, manter capacidade doméstica de processamento e armazenamento é importante para reduzir a dependência de data centers no exterior, especialmente diante da crescente quantidade de informações sensíveis produzidas pelo setor privado e pelo próprio Poder Judiciário. Para Sifuentes, o tema ultrapassa a segurança jurídica e alcança a proteção estratégica dos dados brasileiros. Na avaliação dela, a expansão desse tipo de infraestrutura será inevitável nos próximos anos. Ao mesmo tempo, a presidente do TRF6 chamou atenção para os impactos da instalação de grandes centros de processamento, especialmente sobre o consumo de energia e de recursos hídricos. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Segundo ela, o país precisa construir uma política de longo prazo para evitar que a expansão acelerada provoque dificuldades futuras no fornecimento de energia ou na gestão de recursos necessários para manter essas estruturas em funcionamento. “Temos de realmente pensar numa política de longo prazo para que isso não cause um caos, um apagão, um problema lá na frente que seja difícil de se gerenciar”, afirmou. Em parceria com o Times Brasil — Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC, o LAWINFRA SUMMIT Brasília teve cobertura completa do canal. Entre os temas abordados nos chamados Grandes Painéis estiveram data centers, armazenamento de energia, transmissão e segurança jurídica. artigo.texto: Senate Democrat blocks data center electricity costs bill WASHINGTON - A Senate Democrat on Thursday blocked a Republican-led effort to unanimously pass a bill aimed at shielding Americans from higher energy electricity and grid infrastructure costs associated with data centers. The blockage comes one day after the bill secured widespread bipartisan support in the House in a 417 to 3 vote. The bill, the Ratepayer Protection Act, seeks to make data centers or tech companies pay for increased electricity costs of new energy infrastructure, rather than pass those costs on to consumers. However, it does not require states to adopt any such standards or force tech companies to cover the costs. Senate Democrat blocks data center bill Big picture view: On Thursday, Senate Democrat Martin Heinrich blocked Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted’s effort to approve the legislation under unanimous consent. "Mr. President, America is expected to build the equivalent of 1,000 major data centers during the next five years," Husted said ahead of the vote. "And we need to protect American ratepayers from footing the bill." However, New Mexico Sen. Heinrich blocked Husted’s effort to pass the bill, arguing that the measure doesn’t go far enough. Sen. Martin Heinrich blocked an effort to fast-track the Ratepayer Protection Act in the Senate, saying it does not go far enough. (Credit: Getty Images) "The Ratepayer Protection Act falls short of what we need to do to respond," Heinrich said, adding, "I don’t think it’s enough to just take their [tech companies’] word for it. It’s not enough for us to tell states to consider making data centers pay for grid updates. Rather than voluntary pledges or suggestions to states, Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth." After objecting to Husted’s unanimous-consent request, Heinrich sought unanimous consent to pass his GRID Savings Act, but Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, objected. Heinrich said the GRID Savings Act would "require large load customers like data centers to pay for the facilities needed to connect them to the grid, not to consider it, not to make pledges, to actually do it, to pay for the upgrades they need." Following the Senate’s blockage of the bill, Husted said, "It is a shame that this opportunity has been missed today, but I will be back to push this issue forward. We have a bipartisan opportunity to get this done; we should do it immediately." About Ratepayer Protection Act Dig deeper: In its current form, the Ratepayer Protection Act does not seek to ban data centers, set limitations on their expansion or even set regulatory guidelines for them. Instead, it amends existing energy law, the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act (PURPA), so states must consider a federal standard. Large data centers that consume 100 megawatts or more would pay the full extra cost of the generation, transmission and distribution upgrades built to serve them. Companies would also be required to make financial assurances in the event a project is canceled or moved to prevent communities from being left holding the bill. RELATED: Trump says he is banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from White House Its sponsor, Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., framed it as a needed step toward keeping data center energy costs from spilling over to local communities. "As America races to lead the world in AI, we must build the energy infrastructure needed to support this innovation and stay ahead of competitors like communist China," Evans said in a statement earlier this year. "But Colorado families, farmers and small businesses should not be forced to cover the costs of new power generation driven by these developments. The Ratepayer Protection Act is a bipartisan, commonsense solution that protects everyday Americans and ensures our nation can continue to win the AI race." Husted introduced the bill on July 16, 2026. The Source: The information for this story was provided by statements made by Senate Democrat Martin Heinrich and Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Congress, FOX News contributed. This story was reported from Los Angeles.

artigo.texto: This year's Congressional Black Caucus Annual Legislative Conference, which wraps Sunday, has taken on a different feel than its usual college homecoming vibe. The event, which has drawn thousands of attendees to Washington, took on a more serious tone with briefings and conversations focused on artificial intelligence opportunities and regulation amid escalating concern about threats posed by the technology. "I stand 100%, and so does the CBC on regulation," CBC Vice Chair Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., told CNBC. "I think we need guardrails, I think we need transparency, I think we need to prepare and protect the community from the potential ills that come with it." Carter said at least 60 of the 62 members of the CBC would vote for a bill to regulate artificial intelligence, creating guardrails and placing guidelines on human safety. He added that competition with China should not be a factor in any legislation. "I'm not going to run and race with China, they're not doing it the right way. They are not protecting communities," he said. "Our race should be enhanced innovation, advanced technology, while we simultaneously protect the rights of the American people." The CBC is an influential group whose members include 29% of Democrats in the U.S. House. As Democrats aim to take control of the House in November's midterm election, the caucus's standing could rise. The CBC's tackling of AI came amid the backdrop of Open AI becoming the latest company to report an incident where AI agents conducted what they call 'concerning model behavior,' It's one of a growing number of so called 'jailbreaks,' the slang term for when models bypass guidelines and perform unauthorized actions. "The message they wanted me to bring is how we can do this in a way that protects our communities but do not put us in a position to lose in a national security race," said X. Eyee, an AI expert and Army veteran, who spoke with CBC members about striking a balance between putting boundaries on the technology without inhibiting innovation. "To do that, it does require addressing some of these areas where algorithms are being used with little boundaries around them." Carter said he is talking with voters about how important the upcoming midterm elections are for AI regulation. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., this month asked that the House stay in session to find a way to legislate AI safeguards. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., after President Donald Trump called AI-safety concerns a "hoax," countered that "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people." "They're not bringing it to the floor because I'm not sure that they want the regulation that we want," Carter said of Republican House leadership. "I've heard them say pump the breaks. I've heard them say let's let innovation handle it on its own, but we can't afford to do that." With AI skepticism high in the caucus, the AI and tech industries also showed up for the CBC's Washington gathering. Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick touted the economic benefits of data centers and the AI buildout they power. Meta is building the Hyperion data center project in Louisiana, and its hyperscaler rivals, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, are all also in the data center expansion race. "Technology and AI are the economic revolution of our generation," Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., a former CBC chair who now leads its technology committee, told CNBC. "That means that as Black Americans, we cannot allow this innovation to pass us by." Horsford spoke about the importance of helping shape the energy-intensive AI buildout on a panel with Exelon CEO Calvin Butler. Exelon provides power and grid services for the Philadelphia, Chicago, Baltimore, and Washington areas, and Butler said he is having continuing conversations with lawmakers about the potential impact on energy prices and residents' quality of life. "AI is a real conversation because people are trying to figure out where they fit in and can have a voice," Butler told CNBC. "What they are saying is we can't sit on the sidelines and let our constituents be impacted, and you as energy companies have a role in helping us solve this problem." Data centers, the CBC and redistricting The debate over AI regulation and data centers took on greater urgency because congressional redistricting could affect CBC members. The Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais will make creating "minority-majority" districts difficult and have major ramifications for the 2028 election and 2030 census, according to the Harvard Kennedy School. CBC Chair Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., estimated earlier this year that as many as 19 seats held by CBC members are at risk due to redistricting. Carter said that while that number is lower now after court challenges to redistricting plans, the impact on the Black community remains. "This is not just about congressmen," he said. "This is about school boards. This is about legislative seats." Horsford echoed concerns about threats to minority representation in Congress. "This has never been about protecting any one district, and it is absolutely not about protecting one party or another," he said. "It's about protecting the voters' right to pick their representatives, and not the representatives being able to pick which voters they serve. And as long as we keep that at the center of the work, then we're honoring what our democracy is supposed to be about."

artigo.texto: Advait Battery Ecosystem has signed a 1 GWh LFP cell supply deal with China’s Hithium for its upcoming Gujarat BESS facility. The agreement was signed on 18 September 2026. Under its terms, Advait can buy up to 1 GWh worth of battery cells from Hithium over the next one year. In simpler terms, this deal locks in a steady supply of the raw battery cells Advait needs, instead of the company having to source them on a case by case basis as demand comes in. Hithium will supply its 314 Ah LFP prismatic cells, a format that is widely used across the global energy storage industry. On pricing, the first 350 MWh of cells under this deal have been fixed at $49.5 per kWh. That covers roughly a third of the total order. Pricing for the remaining volume has not been finalised yet and will depend on how Advait’s future project orders shape up. This cell supply deal is a building block for something larger. Advait is setting up a 2.5 GWh battery energy storage system, or BESS, assembly facility at Gangad in Gujarat. Once up and running, this plant will handle everything from assembling battery modules and packs to container integration and final system commissioning, turning raw cells into storage units that utilities and industries can actually use. This is not Advait’s first move to build out this ecosystem either. The company had earlier partnered with Adaptive Engineering to handle engineering design and energy management system architecture for its BESS business. With Hithium now on board for cell supply, two of the more critical pieces of the puzzle are in place. Bhushan Shahane, Chief Operating Officer of Advait Battery Ecosystem, said the company is looking to work with dependable, high quality partners as it scales up the Gujarat facility. Hithium is recognised as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 manufacturer and already supplies battery cells and storage systems to clients across utility scale, industrial and residential markets globally. Taken together, the agreement points to Advait’s broader push to build a more self reliant, India based battery manufacturing chain, one that depends less on last minute sourcing and gives the company more control over how quickly it can scale up. artigo.texto: Oregon Data Centers Now Consume 23% of State Electricity - Oregon's data center industry currently accounts for nearly one-quarter of all retail electricity sold in the state, with 111 operational facilities supporting 2,630 jobs and projected to demand up to 32% of the state's electricity by 2030. Nearly one-quarter of all retail electricity sold in Oregon now powers a data center. That figure comes from a new ECOnorthwest and University of Virginia report, funded by the Lemelson Foundation, giving state officials their first comprehensive count of Oregon's data center footprint and what it demands from the grid. 111 Facilities, 2,630 Jobs, and a Grid Under Pressure The scale of Oregon's data center industry is now documented in one place for the first time, and the numbers are harder to ignore than the abstract headlines. Oregon currently has 111 operational data centers occupying roughly 22.1 million square feet, according to the report hosted by the Oregon Department of Energy. Another 32 facilities are under construction or in planning, adding an estimated 6.9 million square feet once built. That physical footprint sits in sharp contrast to the sector's direct employment. All 111 facilities together support an estimated 2,630 workers, per the ECOnorthwest–UVA report. The electricity numbers reveal the sector's true weight on the grid. ECOnorthwest economist Pedro Ferreira stated plainly in an interview with OPB: "By the end of 2025, data centers were already a big user of electricity in Oregon, accounting for almost 23% of all the electricity demand in Oregon, and we expect this number to grow up to 31, 32% by 2030." Toward One-Third of Oregon's Grid by 2030 Projections show data center demand could reshape Oregon's entire electricity system within five years, regardless of how aggressively the sector grows. The report projects data center electricity demand could reach approximately 25 terawatt-hours per year by 2030, according to ECOnorthwest–UVA modeling cited in the Oregon Data Center Advisory Committee meeting summary. Mashable's coverage frames that figure as roughly 31 to 32 percent of total state electricity demand, equivalent to the annual consumption of about 2.5 million homes. That percentage could climb higher depending on how fast other sectors grow alongside data centers. Per the DCAC meeting summary, if other electricity demand remains relatively flat, 25 terawatt-hours could represent closer to 40 percent of Oregon's current consumption. Even conservative projections carry weight. Oregon Department of Energy documents presented to the DCAC note that a scenario with 50 percent lower data center growth still raises overall state electricity loads by more than 25 percent by 2030. The report authors state the infrastructure stakes directly: "Data center electricity demand is increasing substantially…accommodating large-load growth will require new electricity resources, transmission capacity, and coordinated infrastructure planning," according to "Understanding Oregon's Data Center Industry," published by ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia and hosted by the Oregon Department of Energy. Oregon's Policy Response: Making Data Centers Pay for What They Use Oregon is already treating large data centers as a distinct class of electricity customer, with rate structures designed to shield households and small businesses from grid-expansion costs. Oregon's POWER Act (2025) and the ongoing work of the Data Center Advisory Committee reflect a deliberate effort to move beyond treating large data centers as ordinary industrial users. If your utility is Portland General Electric, that shift is already reflected in your bill. PGE's new rate class for facilities above 20 megawatts raises data center electricity bills by roughly 30 percent. Residential bills edge down approximately 1.3 percent and small-business bills drop about 3.7 percent, because data centers now bear full responsibility for new grid infrastructure costs tied to serving them, according to Portland Civic Lab's analysis of the rate order. Contracts run 10 to 30 years and include 90 percent minimum demand charges. Facilities above 100 megawatts pay a 1-cent-per-kilowatt-hour surcharge directed toward efficiency programs for energy-burdened households. Competing Views on Oregon's Data Center Bargain Supporters and critics agree the sector is growing; they disagree sharply on whether Oregon is getting a fair return. Supporters of data center growth point to the tax base, high-value capital investment, and a rate structure that now shifts grid-expansion costs away from households. Critics counter that electricity consumption is outsized relative to direct job creation, and that siting incentives have not always delivered commensurate community benefit. Mashable reports that other U.S. states are now restricting new data center construction amid similar concerns about grid strain and climate commitments. Oregon's report provides, for the first time, a factual foundation for that debate: concrete counts, verified projections, and a state advisory process already using the data to shape energy strategy.

artigo.texto: Redata amplia vantagem do Nordeste com data centers A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) marca um importante passo para a competitividade nacional em infraestrutura digital. Contudo, para que o País continue avançando nessa área, é fundamental a aprovação de convênio no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) que autorize os Estados a reduzirem o ICMS incidente sobre equipamentos de infraestrutura de Tecnologia da Informação (TI) destinados a esses centros. A proposta está pendente de deliberação desde março, quando ainda aguardava a aprovação do Redata. Na última reunião do Confaz, realizada em 4 de setembro, a análise do texto foi novamente adiada. Na avaliação do Conselho de Economia Digital e Inovação da Federação do Comércio de Bens, Serviços e Turismo do Estado de São Paulo (FecomercioSP), a adoção da iniciativa, agora com o Redata sancionado, poderia proporcionar condições mais competitivas aos Estados na atração de novos empreendimentos. O ICMS representa uma parcela expressiva da carga tributária incidente sobre os equipamentos de TI necessários à operação de data centers. Para se ter uma ideia, no Brasil, a tributação sobre esses itens é até 33% superior à observada em outros países. Ao combinar o regime federal com uma redução do ICMS, os custos de investimento poderiam cair em até 21%, enquanto os benefícios relacionados aos tributos federais, isoladamente, produziriam uma redução estimada de até 4%. Além disso, para os Estados, o convênio representaria uma oportunidade concreta de desenvolvimento econômico e regional, já que esses empreendimentos mobilizam fornecedores e ampliam a demanda por infraestrutura energética e de telecomunicações. Esse movimento também pode estimular a formação profissional, a criação de empregos, a geração de receitas e o desenvolvimento da atividade econômica. O Brasil já reúne vantagens naturais, como amplo mercado consumidor, conectividade robusta, disponibilidade territorial e oferta de energia renovável. Ainda assim, o País não conseguiu transformar plenamente essas condições em vantagens concretas para se posicionar melhor na corrida pelo processamento de dados e pelo desenvolvimento de novas tecnologias, como a Inteligência Artificial (IA). artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – An east Tennessee family said Friday they are asking Cleveland officials to delay action on a proposed data center project. Project River is a private 850-acre, $11.3 billion industrial campus located in Charleston, about 45 minutes east of Chattanooga. The Wright family is proposing a data center powered by a power plant that will use a combination of forest biomass and natural gas, according to information provided by the developers. It will provide up to 1,500 megawatts of power and will only need electricity from the Tennessee Valley Authority as a backup. The tax benefits to the community are unprecedented and could fund schools, teacher salary increases and first responder increases, Lukas Salyer, a member of the Wright family and president of Wright Industrial Group, told The Center Square in an interview. The Wright family was negotiating a planned unit development agreement with the city of Cleveland that would have mitigated noise, barred any direct connection to the Hiwassee River, and generated 90% of the data center's water onsite. The family also agreed to fund a new fire and emergency medical services facility near the site. Hundreds have shown up at community meetings, most opposing the project. The Wright family said in a statement on Friday that nothing is more important to them than being a good neighbor. "To that end, with the community’s best interest in mind, the Wright family has requested that the city of Cleveland temporarily delay further action on Project River until the Wright family can onboard a third-party team of technical experts to review every aspect of this project and address concerns raised through public engagement over the last few weeks," the family said in the statement. The Center Square was unsuccessful prior to publication getting a response from the city. Project River is not the first data center project halted in Tennessee. In Nashville, a battle is ongoing between the Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County, and Atlanta-based D.C. Blox, which is proposing a data center near the Nashville Zoo. The conflict has spilled over to the courts. D.C. Blox is suing the government, saying Metro officials are refusing to process the company's permits in what it calls in court documents a "targeted attack" that violates federal constitutional protections. The case is still pending.

artigo.texto: Redata abre caminho para atrair data centers ao Brasil Novo regime reduz desvantagens do país, mas avanço depende de regulamentação, ação dos Estados e energia competitiva O Brasil tem diante de si uma oportunidade importante para ampliar sua participação na economia digital. Os investimentos globais em data centers, inteligência artificial e capacidade computacional estão crescendo rapidamente e a disputa pela atração desses recursos já está em curso há algum tempo. Nesse cenário, a recente aprovação do Redata pelo Congresso e sua sanção presidencial representam um passo importante para que o país ganhe competitividade em relação a outros mercados. A relevância desse avanço está no papel estratégico que os data centers desempenham na economia atual e futura. Essa infraestrutura é essencial para o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e de outras atividades intensivas em capacidade computacional. Por isso, a discussão sobre o novo regime vai além da instalação de novos empreendimentos. Trata-se de criar condições para que o Brasil amplie sua capacidade computacional e, a partir dela, desenvolva e atraia atividades de maior valor agregado, além de estimular investimentos associados em energia, equipamentos e serviços. A dimensão dessa oportunidade é expressiva. Os anúncios de investimentos internacionais em infraestrutura digital alcançaram US$ 270 bilhões em 2025, segundo relatório da UNCTAD, colocando o setor à frente até mesmo das energias renováveis. O Brasil já está no radar de grandes empresas globais de tecnologia, mas participa dessa disputa com uma desvantagem relevante. Sem os efeitos do Redata e uma resposta tributária também dos Estados, o custo para construir um data center no Brasil pode ser cerca de 34% superior ao observado nos Estados Unidos e em países vizinhos da América do Sul, segundo análises da Brasscom. O Redata é, portanto, um passo relevante. Mas sua efetividade dependerá agora da implementação. A regulamentação federal precisa assegurar critérios objetivos, procedimentos céleres e previsibilidade para os investidores, preservando o espírito do texto aprovado pelo Congresso. Será igualmente importante avançar em convênio do Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária para reduzir substancialmente a carga tributária estadual. Essa combinação aproximaria custos brasileiros dos concorrentes e destravaria projetos concretos. Entre as vantagens do Brasil, a energia é central. Data centers são intensivos em consumo energético e precisam operar 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Demandam, portanto, energia contínua, confiável e a preços competitivos. O Brasil parte de uma posição privilegiada por ter uma matriz predominantemente renovável e potencial para combinar diferentes fontes. Os próprios data centers podem estimular novos investimentos em energia limpa e contribuir para a expansão da oferta. Há também uma dimensão estratégica para a relação entre Brasil e Estados Unidos. Os 2 países têm integração relevante em serviços digitais, computação em nuvem, tecnologia e equipamentos, justamente os segmentos em que o Brasil busca atrair investimentos para agregar valor. O Redata pode favorecer essa cooperação e, embora as discussões tarifárias sigam uma agenda própria, investimentos em infraestrutura digital ajudam também a construir uma agenda bilateral positiva, baseada em tecnologia e inovação de longo prazo e estratégica. O Redata, portanto, não é um ponto de chegada, mas um 1º passo. Se vier acompanhado de regulamentação eficiente, ação dos Estados e maior cooperação internacional, o Brasil terá condições de disputar uma parcela maior dos investimentos globais em infraestrutura digital. Mais do que atrair data centers, a oportunidade é ampliar nossa capacidade computacional, desenvolver tecnologia interna e criar empregos qualificados e de alta remuneração.

artigo.texto: Two dozen years ago, Gina and Darin Madsen bought a house in Monrovia, a small community in Morgan County, planning to stay there through retirement. But their peace and quiet has been disrupted by the construction of a massive data center virtually on their doorstep — something they didn’t want and didn’t even know about until it was too late. “We really didn’t have a lot of time to even react to it,” Gina Madsen said. “Even if we had reacted, which some people did ... voices were not heard.” Like other Monrovia residents, the Madsens received little notice about the 400-acre data center plans before the deal was signed and sealed. And it would be months before they discovered that the builder was Google, one of the wealthiest and most powerful companies in the world. That’s because of a non-disclosure agreement signed by the Morgan County Board of Commissioners, promising to keep the owner’s name private until the transaction was complete. Research by the Arnolt Center for Investigative Journalism and the Limestone Post found such agreements are not unusual. The Arnolt Center and the Limestone Post researched 46 AI data centers identified by the Indiana Citizens Action Coalition as existing, proposed, or withdrawn, and found seven projects where an NDA was used. The center then filed records requests with 26 communities either with active data sites or ones under development and found: - Officials in New Carlisle in northwest Indiana and in Morgan County signed NDAs - 12 communities denied having any responsive records - 12 communities never responded to records requests New proposals continue to proliferate across the state as Indiana’s business-friendly environment has made it a magnet for data centers. As of February 2026, the state has 38 operational data centers and 54 planned data centers, according to the Pew Research Center. Opposition to the centers spans the political spectrum, as residents worry about the environmental impact on their communities and the relatively small number of permanent jobs planned for such large-scale projects. Some communities, including Indianapolis, are weighing regulations to block data center projects. “Signing an agreement that prevents them from disclosing to the very public they serve [is] really important information, right? I find that hugely problematic,” said Pat Garofalo, director of state and local policy at the American Economic Liberties Project. “I think, in terms of just democracy and our understanding of how American democracy is supposed to function, it simply should not be allowed for a public official to sign away their right to communicate with their constituents, to a private corporation.” ‘Already set in stone’: Monrovia development moves forward The Madsens received a letter from the Morgan County Economic Development Corporation on January 24, 2025, informing them of a community meeting February 10 about a potential data center development in Morgan County. Gina Madsen said the meeting was informational and people could speak up and ask questions. At that meeting, the Morgan County Plan Commission announced plans for “Project Louie,” a large data center project on West Keller Hill Road in Monroe Township, close to Monrovia. The Morgan County Economic Development Corporation had made a rezoning request for the 391-acre site on behalf of an unnamed company. Despite opposition from community members, on February 18, the Morgan County Board of Commissioners unanimously approved a rezoning request for the site from agricultural to a planned unit development, laying the groundwork for the construction of the data center. “It was already set in stone. Man, went from day one, it’s a done deal,” Darin Madsen said. In October 2025, Google issued a written statement announcing it was the previously unnamed developer of the data center. That same month, the Morgan County Commissioners voted to approve the rezoning of an additional 158 acres, bringing the total for the site to 549 acres. As of April 2026, the town of Monrovia initiated proceedings to annex land to the east, including the entire site data center site, allowing the town to receive additional tax revenue. Emails leaked to the Morgan County Correspondent said that Google offered Monrovia $12 million in wastewater treatment plant upgrades if the Town Council dropped its bid to annex the land that includes the data center. The Morgan County Commissioners in June proposed a tax increment financing district that would include the Project Louie site. The Morgan County Redevelopment Commission voted unanimously in favor of the TIF at a July 15 meeting. The site of the Monrovia data center in mid-June, looking northeast. The Indianapolis skyline can be seen faintly on the horizon in the top right corner. The Madsens are devastated about the sudden disruption to their retirement plans. “We were looking out over a nice field and a nice sunset for 23 years,” Gina said. “We have a front porch we love to sit out on and have that view, and that’s gone, that will never be back.” NDAs keep key details, developers shielded Indiana is attracting a large number of data centers, according to the available data from the Data Center Map. Nationwide, Virginia and Texas lead with 685 and 466 data centers [operational or planned] respectively. Indiana State Representative Matt Pierce, a senior lecturer in The Media School at Indiana University, said it is difficult for the public to get information about data centers when public officials sign non-disclosure agreements. “The problem is when the public comes to the public hearing, or they’re discussing whether or not to approve the data center, the local officials can’t have a complete discussion,” he said. “They can’t really inform the public about all the impacts of data centers that they’ve signed a non-disclosure agreement that says they can’t tell the public about the information they have.” As the number of data centers grows, concerns about ND

artigo.texto: Sherrill: ‘Towns can make their own decision’ on data centers New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) is making her case against a statewide moratorium on data centers, pledging to enforce a new suite of regulations on the facilities even as state lawmakers introduce more bills to slow down their construction. In an interview with POLITICO's Energy podcast, she said she favored letting local governments make their own decisions rather than putting a blanket moratorium on the hot-button projects, as New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) became the first governor to do in July. "If they want a moratorium, there are certain towns where it's probably not appropriate to build data centers," Sherrill said. "There are other towns where it probably makes sense." New Jersey lawmakers have announced plans for more than a dozen bills on data centers so far this session, including one introduced last week that would put a six-month moratorium on data centers over 10 megawatts. Sherrill, who campaigned heavily on energy bill affordability and froze utility rate increases via executive order on her first day in office, is trying to boost electricity generation to ease data center-driven supply constraints across the Northeast states' shared grid. But she said state and local officials could negotiate effectively to manage data centers' impacts. She signed two laws to that end last month: one requiring them to periodically report water and electricity usage to the state and another ending a two-year old, $500 million tax credit program to encourage their development. "If corporations make all the decisions, look, it's cheaper to just dump all of your pollution into the local river instead of treat it and protecting people," she said, a reference to a diesel spill last week from a data center into a tributary of the Hackensack River. "That's where government comes in." "We've built a new rate class for our data centers so that they don't drive up costs for ratepayers," she said. "We've made sure that they're using good union labor, so they're getting good jobs into the community. Community benefits agreements, so that towns can make their own decision." "If a data center says, 'Look, this is what we're proposing in this industrial park, and we're also going to invest in your K-12 curriculum, or we are going to build a community center, we'll do that,' that's something the towns can determine." Sherrill said she had discussed her state's plans with Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D), whose state has the highest concentration of data centers in the world and last week announced new restrictions on them, including a ban on nondisclosure agreements and limits on the type of power generation they can use on-site. She acknowledged Virginia is "in a very different space on data centers. In fact, I've been frustrated with Virginia because they're sucking all the power out of PJM and seeing rates go up. But I think as Abigail's taken her seat, she's been very thoughtful about how she is going to approach data centers. I've talked to her about our data center plan and what she's thinking of enacting there." Sherrill signed a law in April lifting the state's moratorium on nuclear power. She sounded an optimistic note on the energy source, as well as on the Trump administration's willingness to subsidize projects' financial risk. "When you look at the cost overruns in Georgia, much of that had to do with building a new full-scale nuclear power plant — that hadn't been done in a generation — and finding the workforce to do that in rural Georgia. We don't have that problem here in New Jersey," she said. "Where the federal government needs to come in is to sort of build that economy of scale. The Department of Energy also has the ability to take on the fiscal responsibility for a lot of this and make sure they're backstopping all the funding, so they take on the risks, so the states don't have to." She added that she was planning to visit a company this week that's deploying nuclear fusion technology developed at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory. "This new technology that could be almost unlimited power at no emission," she said. "This is the kind of thing that government does when it works at its best."
