artigo.texto: Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has concluded a cooperation agreement with Battery Manufacturing in Egypt (BME) to support battery pack production in the country. BME will fund and develop the planned facility, source battery cells from CATL, and supply the assembled packs directly to local automakers. Under the deal, CATL will provide licensing for its battery pack technology alongside production equipment and technical instruction, while BME bears full responsibility for facility investment. The arrangement aims to build Egypt’s domestic battery manufacturing capability and supports the broader electrification of local commercial vehicle fleets. The facility is planned for initial annual production of 1 GW/h, with a focus on packs for heavy commercial vehicles. BME intends to expand capacity to 5 GW/h in the longer term, extending its product scope to cover passenger vehicle battery applications and stationary energy storage for solar and wind. BME was established by Egyptian commercial vehicle manufacturer MCV and automotive solutions provider Auto D. CATL’s contribution extends beyond cells to encompass technology licensing, production equipment, and engineering support. The Egypt partnership forms part of CATL’s broader approach of deploying its battery technology through licensing agreements across multiple markets. Source: CATL

artigo.texto: O presidente Lula afirmou, em ato de campanha em Santa Catarina, que o Redata deve atrair R$ 500 bilhões em investimentos. Segundo ele, a oferta de energia renovável pode tornar o Brasil um grande polo de data centers. Lula disse que empresas interessadas em instalar data centers no país terão de investir na construção de usinas de energia renovável. Segundo o presidente, a geração de energia não poderá ser destinada exclusivamente aos centros de dados. O candidato também destacou minerais críticos e terras raras e defendeu investimentos em pesquisa e formação de profissionais. Lula afirmou que o objetivo é ampliar a produção nacional de chips, baterias, tecnologia e conhecimento. O ministro Nunes Marques, do STF, avalia participar da análise do pedido de investigação contra André Mendonça por suposto abuso de autoridade na condução do Caso Master, segundo o Metrópoles. Nunes se declarou impedido de julgar pedido semelhante contra Alexandre de Moraes, mas tem dito a interlocutores que a decisão não se aplica automaticamente ao caso de Mendonça. O ministro ainda não definiu se votará. O presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), enfrenta cobranças do governo e da oposição para avançar com pautas represadas no Congresso, segundo o Metrópoles. Lula cobra a votação da PEC que reduz a jornada máxima de 44 para 40 horas semanais e prevê dois dias de descanso. O texto já passou pela CCJ, mas ainda aguarda análise do plenário. O cientista político Steve Levitsky, professor da Universidade Harvard e autor de Como Morrem as Democracias, afirmou que existe uma “boa probabilidade” de Donald Trump não reconhecer uma eventual vitória de Lula (PT) nas eleições brasileiras. Em entrevista ao jornalista Jamil Chade para o portal ICL Notícias, o pesquisador avaliou que o risco de contestação do resultado por parte do presidente dos EUA é real. Levitsky também afirmou que a eleição de representantes do movimento bolsonarista seria “muito arriscada” para a democracia brasileira. Arthur Lira (PP) registra 41,2% das intenções de voto ao Senado em Alagoas, considerando a soma do primeiro e segundo votos, segundo levantamento do Paraná Pesquisas divulgado nesta segunda-feira (21). Marina JHC (PSDB) tem 37,8% e Renan Calheiros (MDB), 34,6%. Os três estão empatados dentro da margem de erro. Davi Davino Filho (Republicanos) aparece com 25,7%. O candidato à Presidência Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) afirmou neste domingo (20) que pretende cortar as emendas parlamentares impositivas, rever incentivos fiscais e reduzir gastos dos Poderes caso seja eleito. Caiado também propõe uma PEC, com duração de 24 meses, para limitar o crescimento das despesas do governo a 50% da expansão do PIB.

artigo.texto: This story was originally published by Mother Jones and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. While tech oligarchs grandstand about the existential danger AI superintelligence poses to humanity, former Environmental Protection Agency officials say we should be worried about a more immediate threat to our health: the data centers that power those AI models. The former EPA researchers, now working with the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network, are warning in a new report that since January 2025, Donald Trump’s EPA has embarked on a systematic weakening of pollution safeguards, permitting processes, inspection norms, and other guardrails — at least 30 different actions — that could increase the health risks associated with the data center boom. There are currently about 3,000 data centers in the United States, and more than 1,500 new centers are in the planning stages. But as developers build out this vast, energy-hungry infrastructure, the country is losing the government regulatory safeguards that are needed to ensure that expansion is done safely, the ex–EPA officials say. Dan Costa, who spent 35 years at the EPA studying air pollution, noted that for decades the environmental agency, which was established in 1970, had a large and committed cadre of researchers who investigated emerging sources of pollution and new environmental threats. “Over the decades, toxicologists, chemists, atmospheric scientists, modelers, and engineers worked in concert with academic colleagues on behalf of the American people — not on behalf of industry,” Costa said in a press briefing last week. “We wanted to carry out EPA’s mission of protecting people’s health from industrial air pollution.” Now, though, that workforce has been gutted. The Trump administration has dismantled EPA’s main research office, and the agency’s priorities have shifted away from strict enforcement of pollution standards. “Transforming the nation’s energy system, while diminishing its scientific capacity to understand what the impacts are going to be, makes no sense,” Costa said. But that appears to be the direction the country is heading in. President Donald Trump is “positioning America as the global leader in AI,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin wrote in a memo last year. The agency is “committed to bolstering” those efforts, Zeldin said, by “cutting heavy-handed regulations to ensure America can build and power the data centers essential to Making America the AI Capital of the World.” Since Trump returned to the White House, data center developers have seized the opportunity to expand at a rapid pace, helped by the administration’s moves. In some cases, that deregulation has involved keeping old coal-fired plants online past their planned decommissioning times in order to power data centers; other times, it has meant easing regulations on the use of onsite fossil fuel-powered turbines to power hyperscale data centers like xAI’s Colossus. The agency has proposed a rule change that would let developers begin constructing data centers and their associated power plants before they get air pollution permits. And it has directed the agency’s enforcement staff to avoid any action that could “unduly burden or significantly disrupt” energy production or power generation. According to one study the former EPA researchers cited in their new report, pollution associated with the AI boom may lead to 1,300 additional deaths per year. Physician and former EPA administrative official Lynn Goldman said some health impacts of increased data center pollution might be felt quickly — for example, heart attacks or premature births associated with particulate exposure. Others, such as cancer, might take years to emerge. “The AI industry’s race for advantage should not be a matter of life or death,” Goldman said at the press conference. “Families shouldn’t have to pay for the AI boom with their health.”

artigo.texto: The Scoop The data center buildout is driving a rush of venture capital investment in clean tech, breathing new life into startups that were at risk of being steamrolled by the Trump administrationâs pullback on climate policy. Global climate tech venture investment hit $26 billion in the first half of this year, 55% above the previous year, according to climate tech finance tracker Currence.ai. Data centers and the products and services that help them operate are in particularly high demand, with startups in the sector seeing their fundraising and valuations jump. Itâs an opportunity to push some new carbon-cutting tech across the âvalley of deathâ between pilot and commercial scale, to the benefit of the global energy transition at large â but also links clean techâs fortunes to a digital infrastructure buildout whose ultimate scale remains uncertain. âVenture capital sees the data center opportunity, and is focused on it,â Frank OâSullivan, managing director for energy at VC firm S2G Investments, told Semafor. âThereâs an opportunity over the next little while to see a lot more clean tech success stories emerge. The risk is that the driver of all of this â the data center bubble â might pop.â In this article: Timâs view This week, climate tech investors will descend en masse on New York for Climate Week, a forum for a vast range of cutting-edge firms to show off and find money. As political support for decarbonizing the existing energy system has dried up, data centers have emerged as a new center of financial gravity, drawing in unprecedented billions from the biggest tech and Wall Street firms. Much, perhaps most, of that investment is going into conventional energy assets that are not necessarily climate-friendly. But with AI companies under intense pressure to reduce their resource consumption â for reasons of cost, if nothing else â a lot is trickling down to tech originally conceived for the energy transition. âWeâre experiencing a very hot time for a bunch of the stuff we were already in,â said Tom Chi, founding partner of clean tech investor At One Ventures, which focuses on deep tech innovations with environmental benefits. Thatâs setting up potential new windfalls for shops like his: One company in Chiâs portfolio, Blue Energy, a startup building low-cost modular components for advanced nuclear plants aimed at drastically cutting the amount of time needed to build them for data centers, has seen its pre-IPO valuation shoot up by orders of magnitude. That type of growth acts like a beacon to other non-energy investors, and suddenly Chi has found his companiesâ funding rounds increasingly crowded. âItâs a really weird moment because weâre having a bunch of tourists come in,â he said. âWeâre investing alongside firms that have spent their entire history doing enterprise SaaS, and now theyâre sitting here trying to understand desiccants for cooling systems.â Conversely, the focus on AI-relevant technologies is pushing climate tech VCs to look in unusual directions: S2G recently invested in Alliance North America, which makes high-end, low-emissions diesel generators. A technology that facilitates fossil fuel consumption âdoesnât seem like it would be in our bailiwick,â OâSullivan said. But because of its use for powering data centers more efficiently, âthat has mushroomed into an enormous opportunity, and suddenly youâre decarbonizing by stealthâ relative to conventional generators. Room for Disagreement More capital is usually welcome, Chi said. But firms with less experience, and less in-house engineering expertise, can have unrealistic expectations about the time, capital, and skill required to bring a novel hard tech to scale and profitability compared to software â which could ultimately lead to disappointment and cutbacks. Itâs also likely that as the space becomes more crowded, more mistakes will be made, inflating the valuations of companies that donât really have a strong business model when you get down to the nuts and bolts, and creating conditions for spectacular failures. And if clean tech startups are only valuable when they have data centers as primary customers, some technologies that are important for emissions reduction will fall through the cracks: VC investment in carbon management tech and low-carbon fuels both plummeted this year, according to Currence.ai. Notable - Republican regulators in North Carolina moved to block a gas-fired power plant for an Amazon data center. The project would run contrary to Trumpâs Ratepayer Protection Pledge, they said.

artigo.texto: (Bloomberg) -- Opposition to data centers continues to mount in the US. Most Read from Bloomberg That's according to research group Data Center Watch, which said some 45 data center projects worth $68 billion were blocked or delayed by local pushback between April and June this year. Communities across the country are now pushing through moratoriums on new construction, often before developers can apply for permissions. Some 30 statehouses introduced or adopted rules pertaining to issues such as data center siting, electricity and water, the group said in a report Monday provided to Bloomberg News. The research quantifies growing concern about the rapid pace of expansion of artificial intelligence, both in the construction of new computing clusters and its proliferation into daily life. There are now 843 opposition groups across 49 states, with Hawaii the exception. "New groups continue to emerge, opposition is appearing across a wide range of states and jurisdictions, and online petition signatures continue to grow," lead analyst Miquel Vila said. Data Center Watch is a project from AI intelligence company 10a Labs. Home to the biggest investors in AI infrastructure, the US is experiencing a bipartisan backlash against facilities that critics say harm the environment and siphon away resources in order to fuel AI systems that many fear will imperil jobs and livelihoods. Tech giants like Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Alphabet Inc. — the so-called hyperscalers — argue they need the facilities to win a race against China to develop potentially world-changing AI. President Donald Trump has dismissed opposition to data centers and concern about advances in AI as a "sick conspiracy," saying "the only one that is happy about it is China." The number and value of disrupted projects fluctuates by quarter, with the first three months of this year seeing 75 cases worth roughly $130 billion facing opposition in the US. The 45 projects affected during the second quarter represented more than half of all new large-scale developments Data Center Watch began tracking during the period. Opposition by public figures and the use of social media are amplifying concerns. One petition against a project in Tennessee garnered over 500,000 signatures on online activism platform Change.org, accounting for more than one third of those on the service during the quarter, Data Center Watch said.

artigo.texto: WILMINGTON — Debate over data centers has increased significantly in recent years in Massachusetts and beyond, but as Wilmington Planning and Development Director Valerie Gingrich told the Select Board, they aren’t exactly new. “They’ve been around for quite some time. When you think about the cloud, whether it is iCloud or if you use Gmail, the cloud is actually a physical place where all of that is stored,” Gingrich said Tuesday, citing services that have been around for many years. The difference now, Gingrich said, is artificial intelligence. “What has changed is that there is a greater demand for large hyperscale data centers for AI development and training. They use a lot more power and resources than the traditional data centers that have been around for a long time,” said Gingrich. With the AI industry growing at a rapid pace, and the large amount of land, electricity and water resources needed to run it, communities without large-scale data centers, like Wilmington, have begun having conversations about getting policies in place to govern data centers of that scale before one is proposed there. In Wilmington that has taken the form of a proposed bylaw that would effectively prohibit large-scale AI data centers from operating in the town. Discussion of the bylaw for the town began in May, and since then there have been multiple moves by Gov. Maura Healey addressing data centers statewide. In June her administration suspended the sales tax exemption data centers in the state received while setting requirements that the operating companies cover the full cost of their own energy supply, which must come from clean energy resources. Earlier this month Healey also issued an executive order that mandated local approval for data centers in the form of a community benefit agreement. The best way to implement local data center regulation, Gingrich told the board, is zoning, but the town does not currently have data centers as a land-use category in its bylaws. They could already technically be banned for that reason, as there is a clause in place that prohibits any land uses not specifically permitted within a given zone, but it could be challenged under the current wording, Gingrich said. “The goal is to be very clear in our bylaw how we want to regulate data centers,” she said. The proposed bylaw now being reviewed by the Planning Board, with a public hearing for it scheduled for Sept. 29 at 7 p.m., would be similar to one approved by the town of Mansfield and the Attorney General’s Office. The new bylaw would allow for small data center facilities that draw less than 2 megawatts of power in the highway industrial district and general industrial district zones, while anything larger than that would be outright prohibited. Facilities with data center being their primary use would face these restrictions, but other types of businesses that have accessory data centers on their properties would still be allowed to use them. Proposed data centers under the maximum allowed power usage and in the correct zoning would be required to go through the special permit process, which would look at factors like noise generation, water use and power use. That permit would be good for five years with reporting requirements, and would have to be renewed. Select Board member Jacob Gearwar, who noted that he helped create the bylaw, expressed support for it as it is currently written. “I think it is great the way it is written, I think it will get through the AG’s Office easily. It makes a lot of sense,” said Gearwar.

artigo.texto: Jackie Venson to headline Austin anti-data center fundraiser AUSTIN, Texas — Austin guitarist and singer Jackie Venson will headline an Oct. 7 benefit concert at Radio East supporting efforts to increase oversight of data center development across Central Texas. The show, titled CTRL-ALT-DEL, is organized with Save Our Springs Alliance and will raise money for legal advocacy and community organizing around proposed large-scale data centers. Garage-punk trio Subpar Snatch and Austin hip-hop artist Blakchyl are also scheduled to perform. The event runs from 7 p.m. to 11 p.m. at Radio East, 3504 Montopolis Drive. The concert responds to concerns about data centers’ water use, energy demands and the limited public notice surrounding proposed projects, organizers say. Save Our Springs Alliance says the facilities can require large quantities of water for cooling while Texas communities face drought and water restrictions. Venson said she began following the environmental effects of data centers nearly five years ago, but her sense of urgency grew as proposed developments moved closer to her community. “I happen to live in the area that’s going to be directly affected,” Venson said. “But really, all of Austin, Texas, is going to be affected because all of Austin, Texas, is in a water crisis.” Venson said that the Austin City Council’s approval of the proposed Dog’s Head development left her feeling that residents’ concerns were being disregarded. “It did feel like a complete betrayal from the City Council,” Venson said. Venson, an Austin native known for blending blues guitar, soul, pop and electronic influences, has shared stages with Gary Clark Jr. and Melissa Etheridge. She also performed at the 2023 CMT Music Awards alongside Alanis Morissette and Lainey Wilson. She said the benefit concert can start important conversations while raising money for legal action and other efforts to oppose developments that environmental groups believe could threaten local resources. “The number one purpose of this show is to raise awareness of the issue,” Venson said. “The more people know about it, the more minds we have on it and the more we can start taking action that really means something.” Venson described the event’s mission as “awareness and then action.” Environmental and community organizations will provide information at the concert for attendees interested in learning more or getting involved. “We can all come together and we can just put our heads together,” Venson said. “Dance first, then fight the good fight.” Save Our Springs Alliance is working with groups including Sunrise Movement, the Data Center Action Coalition, PODER, Extinction Rebellion and Public Citizen. The benefit comes after the alliance filed a lawsuit in July on behalf of the Data Center Action Coalition and several landowners challenging tax abatements and development agreements connected to the proposed Palomino Alpha and Cloudburst data centers in Guadalupe County. Proceeds will support the alliance’s legal efforts and its work opposing similar developments across Texas. Tickets and additional information are available through Radio East and Save Our Springs Alliance.

artigo.texto: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger ordered the state government to take steps that could empower local communities to have a larger say in data center development and slow down approvals in a state that is already home to the data center capital of the world. Virginia governor creates an AI task force and moves to restrain data centers Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order addressing data centers and AI risks. Executive Order 22 bans executive branch officials from signing nondisclosure agreements for data center projects, requires expedited noise regulations, and requires a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers, among other requirements. The order also establishes an AI task force responsible for evaluating how the state government can address risks to Virginians like workforce displacement and data privacy issues, and determining how existing law can be applied to AI harms. The order represents the latest signal that states are taking data center and AI policy into their own hands as Congress and President Donald Trump have been slow or resistant to sweeping changes. Also on Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order convening experts to tackle AI safety issues, and earlier, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott have both taken executive action to rein in rapid data center development. In addition to Virginia’s new executive order, Spanberger unveiled a new “Data Center Accountability Framework” for the state, which lays out additional priorities. These include eliminating “by-right approval,” like the kind that existed in Loudoun County for many years allowing developers to build on certain land without additional approvals, removing some state subsidies, establishing environmental guardrails, and safeguarding residents against increased energy prices that are associated with data centers. A press release for the actions includes many statements from environmental groups praising Spanberger’s approach, but others reportedly wish she’d gone even further. Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), for example, is a nonprofit that has advocated for a moratorium on new development to deal with existing concerns, and PEC president Chris Miller said in a statement that “It largely addresses standards on new data centers and does not deal with what’s already built and in the pipeline, along with the ongoing impacts piling up in communities now.”

artigo.texto: Artificial intelligence has seemingly, overnight, integrated into our daily lives. From requesting a recipe to a Fortune 500 company automating tasks, we have come to rely on AI for its efficiency, convenience and productivity. With growing demand for AI technologies comes a stark question – where will the data centers that fuel AI be built, what are their potential impacts and how can those impacts be mitigated? Digital backbone Data centers power AI systems by providing the computing, storage and networking necessary to process vast amounts of data. These facilities accommodate thousands of servers that train AI models and generate responses. AI tools like ChatGPT rely on data centers to perform the calculations required to understand prompts, retrieve information and produce responses in real time. Demand has grown rapidly as businesses, governments and consumers increasingly adopt AI-powered tools. Community impacts As demand for data centers grows, so do public concerns about their potential impacts. Among the most commonly cited concerns: Electricity demand: Data centers require substantial electricity. A single ChatGPT response uses 10 times more electricity than a Google search; using generative AI in each Google search would consume the annual output of four to five nuclear reactors. Water usage: Data centers use significant quantities of water to cool their machines. A medium-sized data center can consume approximately 110 million gallons annually, while larger facilities can use up to 5 million gallons per day. Noise: Data centers produce persistent noise from cooling equipment and backup generator testing. Without adequate mitigation, data centers can disturb nearby residents who face elevated risks of annoyance and sleep disturbance. Pollution: Data centers connected to an electric grid increase emissions from fossil-fuel power plants, including fine particulate matter, nitric oxide and sulfur dioxide. Emissions from diesel backup generators include nitrogen oxide and particulate matter. Zoning controls Municipalities administer zoning laws that control where and how data centers can be built and operated, placing them at the forefront of weighing data center benefits against their potential impacts. The benefits of data centers should not be ignored — they generate substantial property tax revenue, garner private investment and create construction and permanent technical jobs. On a national scale, AI can bolster American business competitiveness and enhance U.S. military capabilities. Developers, municipalities and interested parties alike should be attuned to how data centers can and have been regulated. Municipalities that do not enact data center-specific regulatory standards risk forfeiting control over their development. For example, Stratos, a 40,000-acre data center project in Box Elder County, Utah — covering an area roughly the size of Manhattan — is moving forward with minimal local government oversight because the county had not established zoning regulations before the project was proposed. To plan for data centers, municipalities have certain land use controls at their disposal. One tool is a zoning moratorium, which temporarily suspends a particular type of development while local officials establish regulations governing that use. In May, for example, the town of Morris, Connecticut, enacted a one-year moratorium prohibiting data center development. Moratoria, however, must be limited in duration and scope, making them a short-term solution to a long-term planning need. Another tool is zoning regulations. The town of Groton has developed regulations that limit data center size and proximity to other data centers, restrict cooling infrastructure and fuel sources, and establish noise mitigation, fire suppression, utility agreement and buffer requirements to protect nearby residential districts. Other municipalities have imposed outright bans or restrictions. Mansfield, Massachusetts, for example, recently banned data centers requiring more than 10 megawatts of electricity. While data centers may be an emerging land use, developers should anticipate a regulatory process akin to other complex proposals, which can include layers of oversight from municipal, state and federal government agencies. Andrew R. Morin is an associate in the Real Estate group at law firm Hinckley Allen.

artigo.texto: The combined Harmony City Council, EDA and Planning and Zoning once again reviewed a revised draft of their proposed data center ordinance September 16 The group met in the gymnasium of the Harmony Community Center to provide more room for the ever-increasing public audience. At the beginning of the meeting, Mayor Steve Donney announced the three goals of the meeting: to review the draft, to see if the group at the table had any other suggestions and to allow public comment if there was time. Attorney Soren Mattick of Campbell Knutson in the Cities, reviewed draft 6 of the ordinance, highlighting changes made since the last draft. One change in the ordinance was to further clarify the closed loop system. A description of the closed loop and its technology would be included in the application, including identification of any water or liquid discharge that will occur during the system startup and operation. A third party soils and geotechnical study will be required. A 3D acoustic model will be required to assess whether the data center noise levels will comply with MPCA standards. In addition, an annual study will check for continued compliance, The maximum height of a center was changed from the original 60 feet to 40 feet. Shipping containers will not be allowed as a construction material for the center. Water may be used for the initial startup of the closed loop system and as necessary for ongoing maintenance, but ongoing water use would not be allowed during industrial operation. The setback from agricultural property lines was changed to at least 400 feet. All compliance monitoring and inspection costs will be the responsibility of the data center developer or operator. The city will be authorized to establish and set fines that may be assessed if any violations occur. The city will not enter into any NDAs and will process applications with complete transparency. Mattick reminded the group that the ordinance would state that a data center could be built if it met the requirements set down in the ordinance. He detailed the primary ways to enforce an ordinance, stating that the moment a CUP (conditional use permit) is violated, the company would lose that CUP and no longer have the ability to conduct business. The city might need to sue the company to enforce that action. Mattick stressed that the ordinance was not up for approval at this time. There is still time to make desired changes. “This is the beginning of the discussion – not the end,” Mattick pointed out. Councilman Keith McIntosh asked, “What if we decide not to do an ordinance at all?” Mattick answered that if they passed an ordinance that says no data centers for a time period, there would be no path. A developer could come in and present their own ordinance; the city would then be under the gun to respond in a certain time period. Mattick shared that more communities are deciding they want to determine the criteria themselves. With an ordinance in place, the council would be able to deny applications that do not meet their criteria. Public Comment The public was given time to ask questions; Mattick responded to the questions once all citizens were given a chance to speak. For clarity, Mattick’s answers are included after specific citizen comments. One question from the public was, “Who’d be responsible for the property if the data center closes?” Mattick answered that the property would still be owned by the company which could reuse or repurpose the building just as in any case. Necessary applications would need to be made to the city for any alternative uses requiring such applications. Another citizen asked several questions. Could they restrict data centers to just one? Who will ultimately be the owner? Would liquid discharges be identified as well as how liquids are discharged? Who would be reporting the electrical use – MiEnergy or the data center? Mattick responded that they could take a look at limiting to just one data center. At the time of application, the owner or end user is often not known. He pointed out that liquid discharges will be through the city system as will the incoming water. The data on electrical use of the center will come from the bills from the provider, in this case, MiEnergy. Aaron Bishop asked if there would be an opportunity between the Planning and Zoning meeting and the City Council meeting for citizens to say yes or no to the data center ordinance. The opportunity for public input will come at the public hearing which will be the same night as the Planning and Zoning meeting. A question was asked about how the normal operations of a data center would sound day-to-day rather than just the peak sounds of the generators at 100% operation. Mattick noted that the section about noise does talk about studies to show daytime and nighttime noise levels at different distances as well as including the peak noise levels of generators. A homeowner in Harmony commented that she felt this was not a good use of prime farmland. She also questioned the use of metal as a building material. Michael Himlie commented that he’d gone door-to-door knocking to learn public opinion. He saw a “severe disconnect between citizens and the elected officials” and strongly advised a citywide survey of the residents. Walker Ward shared that he thinks of Harmony as a booming small town with a charming community. Ward asked, “Does this fit our style? What is the future of Harmony 20 years down the line? Does the impact of this limit us? Is this focusing too much on the data center?” Mattick noted that the need for a data center and whether it was appropriate was a question for the people of Harmony and not himself. He did say that the ordinance could eliminate metal as a building material if the group wished. Citizens were encouraged to submit further comments via email to the city; the comments will be shared with the entire group. After discussing logistics, Planning and Zoning set their next meeting to be held October

artigo.texto: Chinese battery maker CATL has developed a "tall" battery design for the US pick-up truck market despite trade barriers to entering the country, reported the Financial Times. The newspaper, citing CATL international business unit CTO Zhu Lingbo, reported that US carmakers have already tested the batteries, although the companies were not identified. According to the report, Zhu said CATL could license the technology to companies in the US for local production, in a model like existing arrangements with Ford and Tesla for EV battery manufacturing in the country. Speaking at CATL's headquarters in Ningde, Zhu said the US remained a market with potential for "huge business" for the company "even with this kind of very intense geopolitics". The remarks were made before a planned summit in Washington involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well as an earlier scheduled meeting in New York between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng. The Pentagon, US Department of Defence headquarters, named CATL last year as a company with alleged military ties, a claim the firm has denied. Chinese battery and EV manufacturers are continuing to face tariffs, localisation requirements and possible bans from Washington on national security grounds, which has made exports to or investment in the US largely impractical. Last week, organisations representing the US automotive industry asked Trump to maintain measures aimed at preventing Chinese carmakers and their supply chains from entering the US market. That followed Trump's statement that he would "be OK" with China establishing car plants in the US if American workers were employed. In April, CATL introduced a new fast-charging EV battery. The company launched the third-generation "Shenxing" lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery, which it said can charge from 10% to 98% in six minutes and 27 seconds under moderate temperatures. "CATL develops US-specific battery despite trade restrictions – report" was originally created and published by Just Auto, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: Trump-Xi summit underscores risk of outright data center bans Former senators urge Congress to avoid ‘misguided panic’ in order to allow America to win AI race As President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet later this month, much of the attention will center on trade, tariffs and security. Behind those issues lies a larger competition that will determine the economic and military balance of power for decades to come: leadership in artificial intelligence (AI). While Beijing remains the top threat to American leadership in AI, an equally concerning wave of state and local data center bans is undercutting the infrastructure American AI and our digital lives require. These measures, while well-intentioned and based on real concerns that require a serious response, threaten our national security. In fact, more than 300 communities across 44 states have adopted moratoriums or bans on data centers, including one in five counties in Georgia. In July, New York became the first state to halt permits for large facilities. Texas has paused new grid connections while regulators audit the backlog. State legislatures have filed nearly 2,000 bills regulating AI. Meanwhile, China has made its intentions clear. Beijing’s new five-year plan sets a $1.4 trillion target for its AI industry and is preparing to double its national data center capacity by 2030. From our experiences on the Senate Intelligence and Budget Committees, we saw firsthand how our adversaries use technology to plot against us and how innovation drives our economy. Between us, we spent four decades in the Senate, a Georgia Republican and a North Dakota Democrat, and we disagreed on plenty. But we agree on this: outright bans on data centers pose an existential threat to American competitiveness and national security. A ban here does not stop AI from being built. It just means that communities will forfeit thousands of construction jobs, millions in tax revenue, and the economic growth a data center brings. To be sure, the communities enacting these restrictions have honest concerns about water usage, electricity consumption and siting issues associated with new data centers. Those anxieties are understandable and deserve straight answers and assurances from developers. But the good news is that the facilities being built today are increasingly environmentally efficient and effective job creators. For example, newer data centers employ closed-loop recycled water systems, which cut freshwater use by up to 70 percent. Microsoft’s latest data centers use the same amount of water annually as a single restaurant. The same principle applies to power. Initiatives like the Ratepayer Protection Pledge ensure that tech and data center developers, not residents, bear the burden of extra energy costs from data center infrastructure. The fears that AI will destroy employment opportunities overlook the massive blue-collar boom these facilities generate. Don Slaiman from the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) wrote in the New York Times that data center work will double union hours, and The Economist found that data center construction has helped create hundreds of thousands of new jobs since 2023, with many installation and maintenance positions paying roughly 40 percent more than comparable work elsewhere. Additionally, Meta’s $115 million investment in its Workforce Academy is helping train the workforce of the future. In Indianapolis, Baton Rouge, Houston and Columbus, alumni who entered the program with no previous experience are now working on critical job sites. Now, Lowe’s, Nvidia, Bank of America and more are teaming up to train 1 million plumbers, electricians and other skilled trade workers over the next decade. These investments are revitalizing the American workforce in communities that haven’t seen this kind of investment in decades. But private companies cannot overcome public policy barriers. Training workers can only create jobs if there are projects to put those skills to use. It’s time for all levels of government to work with the private sector instead of proposing bans on data centers. - To start, Congress should codify a unified national AI framework into law to prevent a patchwork of 50 conflicting state rules. - Next, federal and state agencies must fast-track the grid upgrades and data center permits that allow our new workforce to build the digital backbone of the future. - Finally, all levels of government must prioritize grid modernization. This includes onshoring turbine and transformer production, securing the grid from physical and cyber threats, streamlining permitting and expanding transmission capacity to build the AI infrastructure necessary to maintain American leadership. Winning the AI race will strengthen America’s economy, national security and technological independence for decades. We cannot let misguided anti-data center panic surrender our advantage. Kent Conrad represented North Dakota in the Senate from 1987 to 2013 as a Democrat. Saxby Chambliss represented Georgia in the Senate from 2003 to 2015 as a Republican. Both serve as advisers to the American Edge Project, which is supported by Meta and other domestic tech organizations.

artigo.texto: This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist's weekly newsletter here. ______ Georgia's Public Service Commission, or PSC — the group that has final say over how the state's largest electric utility generates electricity and how much it charges customers — regularly hears from members of the public during its meetings. But because those meetings are almost always in Atlanta, many of the commenters typically come from the metro area. Since the spring, commissioner Alicia Johnson, one of two recently-elected Democrats, has been pressing the commission to meet in a different part of the state as a way to open the floor to different commenters. On Tuesday, the PSC finally did that. "For over 100 years, the Public Service Commission has met in Atlanta and rarely, if at all, has meetings across the state," Johnson, whose PSC district includes Chatham and Effingham counties, said. "This was an opportunity for me to have our commissioners come out and actually speak with their constituents outside of Atlanta to move away just from hearing the voices of interveners or advocates." The commissioners traveled to Savannah to hear from coastal residents. Following a brief administrative meeting and a presentation on the PSC's recent actions on data centers, including approval of Georgia Power's contract with OpenAI and new protections for regular customers, the floor opened for public comments. Many of those who spoke voiced concerns over the OpenAI data center that is planned for Effingham County, just outside of Savannah, and called for more transparency around the company's contract with Georgia Power — the largest for a single customer since the utility started reporting its contracts in 2024. "There's a reason you're named the Public Service Commission and not the Georgia Power service commission or the OpenAI service commission," said Bill Wright of Pooler, a city northwest of Savannah. "Your name tells you where your loyalty should lie." The commissioners clarified the limited scope of their involvement with data centers: They oversee the making and selling of electricity only if a data center chooses Georgia Power as its utility. They encouraged attendees to take up their concerns with local elected officials. Commenters also criticized the commission over power bills. Michael Hawthorne, an organizing strategist with the Sierra Club, argued the commission is supposed to set reasonable rates for electricity. Then he posed a question to the room at large. "Does anybody feel like everything's reasonably priced?" he asked. The audience replied with a resounding "No." Read Next: The rush to power data centers is weakening the Clean Air Act, Emily Jones The frustration and anger from the Savannah crowd wasn't surprising, Johnson said. "It's what I've heard since running for office, and so I'm just glad that our other commissioners got to hear some of it, too," she said. Jason Shaw, a Republican from a south Georgia district and the PSC chair, said the meeting reinforced what he's heard from constituents as well. In an interview after the meeting, Shaw said transparency has been a core issue with the OpenAI data center in particular, starting at the local level. But he said Georgia Power needs to share more information about its data center contracts, too. "We've got to do a better job of forcing the company to be able to present more to us that's not redacted," he said. "And I think that's something that we're working really closely on." Some commenters accused the commissioners of failing to represent the interests of the public that elected them — and reminded them another election is coming up in November. "If you truly want to be on this board, it's time to step up and protect the people," said Corey Foreman, a candidate running for the state senate from a coastal district. "If you can't do that, I will be more than happy to help remove you." All five members of the PSC were Republicans from 2006 until the start of this year, when Peter Hubbard and Johnson took office after unseating two Republican incumbents in an election that focused largely on power bills and the commission's recent history of rate increases. The two Democrats have cast dissenting votes several times and closely questioned Georgia Power officials. But both have also been candid that their ability to shift policy on emissions, rates, data centers, and other issues is limited while they are in the minority on the PSC. The District 3 seat currently held by Hubbard and the District 5 seat recently vacated by Republican Tricia Pridemore are both on the ballot in November. If the Democratic candidates win both seats, the party would hold a majority on the commission for the first time in decades. Hubbard was elected to a one-year term last year and is now facing former Republican commissioner Fitz Johnson in a rematch election for a six-year term. In District 5, Democrat Shelia Edwards is running against Republican Josh Tolbert. While the candidates have to live in their districts, both races are statewide. Early voting begins October 13. ______ This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/energy/in-savannah-georgia-psc-faced-public-wrath-over-data-centers/. artigo.texto: A Fraunhofer IEE study, commissioned by BSW-Solar, identifies 150 GW of additional PV potential in Germany with the addition of BESS across 1,313 substations Batteries can shift solar output away from periods when transformers reach their operating limits, according to the study The modeled 150 GW potential would require around 60 GW/240 GWh of battery storage under the study’s reference scenario Germany could potentially accommodate 150 GW of additional solar PV through the use of smart battery storage at existing substations, according to a Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Economics and Energy System Technology (IEE) study, commissioned by the German Solar Association (BSW-Solar). Currently, the country targets to achieve 215 GW of solar PV capacity by 2030. It exceeded 129 GW at the end of August 2026 (see Germany’s August 2026 Solar Installations Exceed 1.6 GW). The study identifies this technical potential across 1,313 rural substations with high renewable generation. It estimates that around 60 GW/240 GWh of battery storage would be needed under its reference scenario. The analysis starts from the observation that transformers do not operate at their rated capacity throughout the year. Moreover, electricity demand, wind generation and solar output vary by time, leaving transmission capacity unused during many periods. Intelligently controlled large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) located directly at a substation could then charge when local solar generation pushes power flows toward the transformer limit. It could then release the stored electricity later. This, according to the analysts, would allow more efficient use of existing transformer capacity, relieving the load on the substations. As a result, on an annual average, only about one percent of the additionally generated solar power would need to be curtailed due to transformer capacity limits, according to the study. The analysts offer this conclusion after analyzing data from 20 transformers at 13 substations operating in the networks of Pfalzwerke Netz and Westnetz. The transformers had capacities ranging from 15 to 80 MVA, with simulations based on hourly data for 2025. “If storage systems charge where and when peaks in solar power generation occur, they can specifically alleviate grid bottlenecks and enable the integration of additional solar power. This could lead to savings of billions in grid expansion costs, among other benefits,” said Carsten Körnig, CEO of BSW-Solar. The association says the findings are relevant to the Bundestag’s proposed Grid Package which aims to better coordinate renewable energy, storage and grid expansion. BSW-Solar argues that the government must ensure that existing grid capacity is used more efficiently alongside further grid expansion. It also wants the administration to designate grid bottleneck areas only after grid operators have implemented digitalization of medium- and high-voltage networks and conducted feasible storage tenders.

artigo.texto: Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today! In 2004, Microsoft’s future chief sustainability officer, Melanie Nakagawa, co-edited a law journal issue on Indigenous peoples’ right to prior informed consent. This month, as a data center developer routed around exactly that standard in New Mexico, she didn’t answer whether it applies to her own company’s work. Ask Google, Amazon, and Microsoft whether they consult Native nations before building a data center, and you’ll get the same answer: silence dressed up as sustainability commitment — as if the law here were unsettled, rather than two centuries old. Chief sustainability officers operate by ESG (environment, sustainability, governance) principles that imply tribal consultation, typically executed either to pacify objecting community members or to comply with an environmental review process. ESG reports are meant to define a company’s community impact but instead serve as shields for deals structured to sidestep responsibility. Project Jupiter, a 1,400-acre Oracle and OpenAI hyperscale data center under development in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, is leased by these tech titans from BorderPlex and Stack: two companies handling physical infrastructure, simultaneously distancing the lessees from responsibility for their environmental and tribal impacts. On August 23, the New Mexico Supreme Court temporarily halted construction for air quality review and ordered a state engineer to diminish water use. Oracle has forecast its use of 11 million gallons of water for an initial fill, plus roughly 168,000 gallons per year in ongoing maintenance. Sen. Melanie Stansbury has separately put the figure at “over a million gallons a day” — a gap neither company nor state officials have reconciled. Lisa Henne, general counsel for the Interstate Stream Commission, told Truthout the water used for construction is purchased from an existing water right holder, not a new appropriation, and that New Mexico’s Pueblos — all located upstream of Elephant Butte Reservoir — aren’t affected, since Jupiter sits in the Lower Rio Grande, a separate hydrological zone. That leaves an open question: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, based across the state line in Texas, sits in the same Lower Rio Grande stretch, closer to the site than any New Mexico Pueblo. Asked whether the Commission had been in contact with the Pueblo, Henne confirmed it had not. She added, though, that the Commission “would not expect” the project to affect it, based on the same reasoning she applied to New Mexico’s own Pueblos. In other words: no contact, but a conclusion about impact reached anyway. Even that thin standard assumes someone’s title implies responsibility. OpenAI has no chief sustainability officer at all. The closest approximation would have been the company’s Head of Data Centers Chris Malone, who just left the company in August amid a wave of executive departures, leaving infrastructure decisions split across engineers with no explicitly named party responsible for considering environmental or community impact. Zephyr Jaramillo of Isleta Pueblo, speaking for Youth United for Climate Crisis Action at the Santa Fe County hearing, put it plainly: “Communities are already considering considerable harm … We look forward to engaging with communities throughout this process.” Whether that engagement extends to Project Jupiter and the Pueblos with senior water rights along its stretch of the Rio Grande, remains an open question that no one — not Oracle, not OpenAI, and not the state — has yet answered. Amazon is the sole data center builder that appears to uphold a minimal standard of tribal consultation. Teara Farrow Ferman, the program manager for the Department of Natural Resources’ Cultural Protection Program, says, since 2019, the company has held monthly meetings with the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation (CTUIR), signing a memorandum of understanding with the tribes in 2023, and funding cultural mitigation projects and community programs. But even here, true prior informed consent remains out of reach: CTUIR learns of new projects only once Amazon’s internal site-review process is already underway, after land and design decisions are effectively locked in. What’s more, the relationship only works because Amazon builds exclusively on private and municipal land. The company’s data centers sit on what the tribes call aboriginal, or ceded, territory. But under the Stevens Treaties, hunting and gathering rights attach only to land that remains publicly owned and “open and unclaimed,” not to land that’s since been privately developed. Fishing rights at usual and customary places are broader and persist regardless of ownership. But hunting and gathering rights are narrower, and it’s those rights — not fishing — that might otherwise compel something more than a courtesy conversation on land like this. On these specific parcels, the broader treaty obligation simply doesn’t reach. Amazon’s relationship with CTUIR isn’t uniformly cooperative, either. When Amazon made the announcement of plans for small modular nuclear reactors near Hanford to help power its Umatilla and Morrow County data centers, CTUIR issued a formal statement opposing any “expansion of nuclear energy” unless developers actually sought permission through the CTUIR government, Oregon Public Broadcasting reported in January 2025. When asked whether Amazon has a company-wide tribal consultation policy that applies before site selection, or whether the CTUIR agreement is a template used elsewhere, Amazon spokesperson Margaret Callahan said only that the company’s “partnership with the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation reflects years of direct collaboration in eastern Oregon … grounded in listening and long-term partnership.” Her response did not answer the question directly. artigo.texto: - A judge will allow a 75-megawatt data center project to move forward in Chatham County despite a local moratorium. - Superior Court Judge John Morris awarded summary judgment to Eco TIP West in its lawsuit against the county. - The company argued that Chatham County violated property rights by using a February moratorium to block an $11 million project that had been under way for months. A judge will allow a Chatham County data center project to move forward despite the county’s moratorium on new data centers. Eco TIP West had sued the county in April. The company argued that its project already was under way when county commissioners voted in February to block new data centers for a year. Superior Court Judge John Morris issued his ruling Thursday, a little more than two weeks after holding a hearing in the dispute. “After careful consideration of the file, counsels’ legal briefs, Plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment, and the exhibits and arguments of counsel during the August 31 hearing, the Court finds that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that Plaintiff is entitled to a judgment in its favor as a matter of law,” Morris wrote. Morris awarded attorney’s fees to Eco TIP. Plus “the determination and award of Plaintiff’s damages is reserved for further proceedings,” according to the order. “The Moratorium, and the County’s refusal to recognize that Eco TIP’s existing data center project is exempt, has and continues to cause Eco TIP substantial financial and other losses,” the company’s lawyers wrote on Aug. 27. “The County did not simply make one mistake but violated almost every applicable statute and governing legal principle. In short, the Moratorium is a legal trainwreck that should have never been approved, and never been applied, to take away Eco TIP’s property rights in its project.” Development company Eco TIP spent $11 million on the 750-megawatt data center project at Chatham County’s Moncure megasite, according to the court filing. “The Data Center Project is currently a use permitted by right under the Chatham County Zoning Ordinance in the Heavy Industrial district,” Eco TIP’s lawyers explained. “This means there are no additional approvals required to develop and operate that use. Multiple County officials, including the County Manager, the County Attorney, and the County Planning Director have been aware of the Data Center Project and Eco TIP’s efforts toward development since at the very latest, October 2025.” County officials issued a document giving the company “statutory vested rights in the Data Center Project under N.C. Gen. Stat. §160D-108 and § 143-755, which are protected property rights under the state and federal Constitutions,” according to the court filing. “Then, in early January 2026, County officials made a hurried decision to enact the Moratorium and block development of all data centers in the County for at least one year,” Eco TIP’s lawyers wrote. “The decision to undertake this course of action was made without input from, or notice to, Eco TIP. In fact, public records show that one of the Moratorium’s primary purposes was to stop the Data Center Project because TIP West was the only viable location for a data center in Chatham County at that time. The Moratorium was also rushed, which resulted in a sloppy and poorly drafted document which violated almost every statutory mandate.” The company’s request to have its exemption recognized by county commissioners “was not even acknowledged,” according to the brief. “A subsequent letter to the County Attorney again asking for the exemption was summarily denied with no explanation or analysis. The County also unlawfully refused to process Eco TIP’s pending site plan application for the Data Center Project, citing only the Moratorium as a reason.” “Eco TIP realizes that data centers are a controversial topic and that at least thirty North Carolina local governments have passed similar moratoria,” the company’s lawyers wrote. “This does not, however, mean these moratoria are legal or that all data centers should be stopped in their tracks. Eco TIP’s Data Center Project is located in exactly the place in Chatham County where these types of uses are intended to go, and the location the County itself chose to not only allow that use, but to encourage and recruit intense industrial uses. There was simply no reason to apply the Moratorium to Data Center Project, other than political cover.” “Eco TIP filed this lawsuit to enforce its rights, recover its damages and attorney’s fees, and force the County to follow the law,” according to the brief. “Plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment presents a straightforward question: does Plaintiff have a legal right to proceed with its proposed data center despite the County’s moratorium? The answer is no,” Chatham County responded in its own Aug. 27 brief. “The moratorium was validly adopted and is not an unlawful down-zoning. Plaintiff has no vested right to construct a data center, having never obtained a development approval authorizing that use.” “Plaintiff cannot establish that the moratorium was adopted in bad faith or deprives it of all economic value so as to violate the ‘Law of the Land’ Clause,” the county argued. “Plaintiff is not entitled to permit choice, having neither submitted a complete application before the moratorium’s effective date nor exhausted its administrative remedy for the County’s inaction. And in any event, discovery remains necessary to test whether Plaintiff’s claimed expenditures were made in good-faith reliance on any qualifying approval, making summary judgment premature under Rule 56(f).”

artigo.texto: The threat of a data center being built in Beacon Falls has proven so unpopular with residents that they’re objecting even before any formal proposal comes forward. Homeowners are organizing lawn sign displays and a social media campaign, while three separate online petitions got under way this summer urging town leaders to kill the idea immediately. “We should say ‘no’ to this. We have a beautiful, peaceful town. We want to keep it like that,” longtime resident Brian Hourigan said Wednesday. “What would it do the water supply? What about the environmental impact — and the noise? They run 24/7.” The response is a dramatic turnaround from four years ago, when the town appeared eager to get a smaller data center on the same property. It was never built. Now, following the lead set by data center opponents in West Haven, Groton, Morris and other communities, a group of Beacon Falls residents is calling on their town to pass a moratorium. Officials of the 6,000-population town in the Naugatuck Valley convened a public information meeting in August to emphasize that there’s no formal application pending. But residents countered that recent commercial real estate ads are promoting the property with the phrase “Largest data center in Connecticut.” The listings speak of a “100MW green-powered data center” and a 294,000-square-foot building, and include computer renderings of a massive structure marked “Beacon Falls Technology Center.” An online listing by The Agency, a California-based real estate brokerage, states “Beacon Falls presents a rare, clean slate opportunity to develop a purpose built digital infrastructure campus across 49 acres with up to 100MW of utility power in place – one of the most compelling and supply constrained sites available in the Northeast. “For equity partners and co-developers, the asset offers significant long term appreciation potential in a sector where institutional appetite continues to substantially outpace available product.” The listing also states the project would ultimately have 33 fuel cells on site. Torrington-based O&G Industries, among New England’s most powerful construction and paving companies, is listed as the developer of the project. O&G owns 49 acres of woods and former gravel pits off Lopus Road. “We are presently marketing 1 Lopus Road as a data center,” company President David Oneglia wrote in an email Thursday. The controversy illustrates just how deeply public opinion has switched against data centers. Across the country, many communities were trying to lure data center projects, drawn largely by the prospect of major new revenue from taxes and fees. In Beacon Falls, for instance, residents at a town meeting in 2022 unanimously authorized selectmen to sign a contract for a 32MW data center on the same parcel off Lopus Road. The agreement would have given the town $6 million over the first three years, and more than $2.5 million a year after that. But that project never went forward. The mood was vastly different when selectmen met Monday night: Several residents spoke against allowing any data center in town, and at least two asked about imposing a moratorium against them. Nobody spoke to support a data center or raised the issue of revenue. When the Economic Development Commission hosted a public meeting Aug. 24, the message was about the same: Nearly a dozen people spoke opposing data centers in town, while none endorsed the idea. Selectmen have repeatedly said that nobody has applied to build a data center in town, and that they have to avoid premature decisions. In a July 31 social media post, Selectman Peter Betkoski urged the public to be patient and rejected complaints that town leaders have been secretive. “What I find most concerning are the accusations that there have been ‘backroom deals’ or that elected officials have somehow hidden information from the public. Those are serious allegations. They don’t just question opinions — they accuse public officials of improper or even illegal conduct,” he wrote. On Thursday, Betkoski told The Courant that it’s too early to offer opinions. “It’s simple: there is no application. When there’s an application we can talk about the pros and cons and make a fair decision. I can’t now because the decision would become prejudiced,” Betkoski said. “So there’s really no comment.” First Selectman Gerard Smith was away this week; a message referred callers to Selectman Michael Krenesky. Krenesky did not return two calls this week. Online petitions signed by more than 3,000 people are pushing for more transparency about what’s happening — and a hard line against data centers. “In our tranquil community of Beacon Falls, a storm is brewing. Plans for a colossal data center — slated to become the largest in our state — threaten to overshadow our town’s serene landscape and delicate ecosystem,” reads one. “Our elected officials owe us transparency and action,” says another petition on the topic. “As residents, it’s our duty to stand up for the environment we cherish and the financial well-being of our community. We must demand comprehensive evaluations and clear communication before any irreversible steps are taken.”

artigo.texto: LOS ANGELES (CNS) -- Los Angeles County's planning director Thursday ordered an immediate prohibition on the development of large-scale data centers that power artificial intelligence in unincorporated areas of the county. Department of Regional Planning Director Amy Bodek issued the directive in a memorandum Thursday, saying it is intended to serve as interim guidance for planning staff while the county moves toward codifying the prohibition in its zoning regulations. Los Angeles County Board Chair and First District Supervisor Hilda Solis said she introduced a motion in April addressing public health and environmental concerns surrounding data centers. The motion was unanimously approved by the Board of Supervisors. "I introduced it in response to concerns raised by San Gabriel Valley residents who were understandably concerned about the effects of data centers in their communities, concerns that have since been reflected nationwide," Solis said in a statement Thursday. "As a necessary next step to address these concerns, the county's report back on that motion identified zoning changes that would prohibit these facilities. The need for such a ban has only been further underscored by alarming developments from the AI sector on catastrophic impacts the technology may have on humanity," Solis added. Solis said she intends to bring additional actions before the Board of Supervisors to implement recommendations from the departments of Regional Planning and Public Health to amend the county's zoning code and prohibit data centers powering artificial intelligence in unincorporated areas. In the meantime, the Department of Regional Planning's guidance will prohibit such facilities while the zoning amendment process moves forward, Solis said. She thanked county departments, residents and other stakeholders who raised concerns about data centers and said she remains committed to ensuring technological growth does not come at the expense of public health, environmental protections or residents' quality of life. In January, a group of Monterey Park residents participated in a community meeting hosted by San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, which bills itself as a "grassroots, community-driven organization focused on environmental justice, transparency, and equitable development in the San Gabriel Valley." The organization says it is not affiliated with any political party, according to its website. At the time, the group and residents criticized a proposal to build a massive data center by SDCF Monterey Park, LLC, as reported by LA Public Press. The project was introduced in 2024. The applicant proposed to demolish vacant commercial buildings at 1977 Saturn St. and construct a 218,400 square foot single-story data center on 15.8 acres of land. Residents had shared environmental concerns about living next to a data center, such as the potential pollution of air, land and water. Ultimately, in response to concerns from residents, the Monterey Park City Council imposed a 45-day moratorium on data centers and later extended it while city staff worked to codify planning and zoning codes to ban data centers outright. In June, Monterey Park voters approved Measure NDC, amending the land use element to prohibit all data centers unless repealed by future voters. Monterey Park's measure to ban data centers was a first of its kind in California. The City Council of neighboring Industry unanimously approved a change in zoning laws in February, allowing the construction of a battery storage site. The action sparked criticisms from city residents and people living nearby in La Puente and the unincorporated communities of Rowland Heights, Avocado Heights, Hacienda Heights and South San Jose Hills. Concerned residents expressed concerns that Industry was creating a pathway for a new data center that would take over its mostly vacant Puente Hills Mall. The No Data Centers SGV coalition opposed the project, which consists of members from the San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, Avocado Heights Vaquer@s, Puente Hills Community Preservation Society, SGVoices, Party for Socialism and Liberation and No Data Center Monterey Park. In late April, the city councils of El Monte and Baldwin Park also voted to implement a yearlong ban on data centers proposed within their city limits. Data centers have existed in the country before, and the construction of them has increased in recent years. These facilities run AI technology and California has at least 287 data centers. In 2024, data centers provided more than 665,000 jobs in the state and generated $14.1 billion in state and local taxes, according to a report from The Data Center Coalition, which bills itself as "the trade association for the data center industry with members that own data centers operate and maintain data center infrastructure both nationally and globally."

artigo.texto: Covenergo and Delta Capacity have started construction on the AKKU One battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Lapinlahti, Finland. The site will feature a stand-alone battery with a capacity of 125MW and an energy storage capability of 300MW-hours (MWh). The companies expect to commission the facility in the fourth quarter of 2027 (Q4 2027). The AKKU One project was acquired as a ready-to-build asset from Helios Nordic Energy. Covenergo holds the majority ownership and expects to use its experience in renewable energy development, project finance and asset management to support the scheme. Delta Capacity is responsible for securing offtake agreements, delivering construction and handling long-term management of the asset as the engineering, procurement and construction management contractor. It will work alongside Covenergo's team. According to Covenergo, the move supports the company's strategy of expanding its flexible asset portfolio and increasing its involvement in the Nordic energy market. Covenergo CEO František Kalivoda said: "This partnership and acquisition is an important step forward for Covenergo's flexible asset portfolio and reinforces our growing footprint in the Nordic energy market. We remain fully committed to delivering high-quality, investment-ready projects that support Europe's energy transition." For Delta Capacity, AKKU One is its second BESS storage project in Finland. Earlier this year, the company completed the 70MW/160MWh Ånge BESS in Sweden, reflecting its increased activity in the Nordic region. Delta Capacity CEO Patrik Hes said: "AKKU One once again reaffirms our belief in the Nordic market and our expertise in delivering high-quality battery storage projects – including as a trusted partner for developers like Covenergo. We are proud to bring the same speed and execution that delivered Ånge to our new project in Finland." A Nordic team is providing support throughout construction and for future operations. Rejlers, an engineering consultancy, is delivering technical project support. Sungrow will supply the battery system, following a 1GW-hour framework agreement with Delta Capacity signed earlier this year. NYAB is conducting balance of plant works, and Ampner is responsible for grid connection studies and compliance. GreenPowerMonitor will provide energy management and supervisory control and data acquisition systems for operational monitoring and control. Once operational, the AKKU One project is expected to deliver flexibility services to the Finnish electricity network, including frequency regulation and balancing, as the country expands its wind and solar generation. "Covenergo, Delta begin construction on AKKU One BESS in Finland" was originally created and published by Power Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: - NVIDIA (NasdaqGS:NVDA), Google, and Emerald AI have created the AI Energy Management Alliance to coordinate electricity use in AI data centers. - The alliance has started building what it calls the first purpose-built power-flexible AI data center, designed to adjust consumption with grid needs. - AEMA plans to publish shared frameworks for grid-responsive data centers with input from utilities, regulators, and large AI infrastructure users. - The formation of AEMA and the power-flexible data center project is worth weighing against the rest of our NVIDIA findings. We have also flagged 2 warning signs (1 major) for NVIDIA. NVIDIA is far from the only company exposed to this push toward grid-aware AI infrastructure, so it is worth scanning 88 AI infrastructure stocks. NVIDIA operates as a data center scale AI infrastructure provider across the US, Asia, Europe, and other regions. As a result, any shift toward power-flexible facilities directly affects how its hardware and software fit into future grid-aware computing projects. 4 things going right for NVIDIA that this headline doesn't cover. Why does a power-flexible data center matter for NVIDIA investors? Electricity availability has become a practical ceiling for AI data centers, so any credible way to align compute usage with grid conditions directly supports NVIDIA's AI infrastructure ambitions. If AEMA can show that GPU heavy sites can flex demand without hurting performance, it helps keep large AI deployments politically and operationally acceptable. Does this shift the NVIDIA Narrative or mostly reinforce it? The existing Narrative highlights "rising data center constraints" and power bottlenecks as risks to long term AI infrastructure spending. AEMA leans into that by treating power flexibility as part of the full stack, alongside GPUs, networking and software. Rather than changing the story, it backs the catalyst that NVIDIA can sell more energy efficient, grid aware architectures into those constraints. See how these catalysts shape NVIDIA's path to a $303 fair value. What has to happen next for this alliance to really matter for NVIDIA? The inflection point is whether the first power-flexible facility in Manassas actually secures faster grid interconnection terms or preferential tariffs by late 2026. Concrete regulatory wins or standardized "grid responsive" design templates would show AEMA is more than marketing and could influence how future DSX style AI factories are specified and approved.

artigo.texto: Anitta é coroada rainha de bateria da Grande Rio; veja Artista ocupa o posto antes ocupado pela influenciadora Virginia Fonseca; a cantora também assina um dos samba-enredos que competem na grande final deste domingo (20) A cantora Anitta, 33, foi coroada Rainha da Bateria da escola de samba Acadêmicos do Grande Rio no início da noite deste domingo (20). A coroação acontece durante a grande final de samba-enredo da agremiação em Duque de Caxias, na Baixada Fluminense. A artista recebeu a coroa diretamente de Eloína dos Leopardos, travesti pioneira e considerada a primeira rainha de bateria da história do Carnaval brasileiro. Veja galeria de fotos acima. Com a coroação, Anitta assume o posto antes ocupado pela influenciadora Virginia Fonseca, 28. Anunciada como a nova rainha em setembro, Anitta afirma que o enredo da escola se conecta com o momento atual de sua carreira musical. Neste ano, Anitta lançou o álbum "Equilibrium", que retrata sua conexão com a ancestralidade e espiritualidade por meio de sua religião, o candomblé. Em 2027, a escola vai levar para a Marquês de Sapucaí o enredo "Sankofa Tabon - Os Retornados da Costa do Ouro e a Estrela Negra da Liberdade", para contar a trajetória de africanos escravizados que, após a liberdade, retornaram ao continente africano. A cantora, inclusive, assina uma composição de samba-enredo ao lado de Arlindinho, Igor Leal, Fred Camacho, Fabian Juarez e Diego Nicolau. Veja o momento da coroação a seguir: HISTÓRICO! Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, a artista disse que o enredo escolhido pela Grande Rio para falar sobre fé e ancestralidade teve uma conexão imediata com o seu momento de vida e carreira. "Sabendo a importância do carnaval na vida de tantas milhares de pessoas, e para a história de um povo lutador que há décadas faz dos desfiles um ato político e revolucionário. E por isso nada na minha presença pode ser maior do que a escola, o desfile, a comunidade e os profissionais que trabalham nesse espetáculo", afirmou ela. Substituindo o reinado da influenciadora Virginia Fonseca, 27, a cantora garantiu ainda que, como tudo o que faz, se esforçará para dar o seu melhor, mesmo com a agenda cheia e a rotina agitada. *Com informações de Carolina Ferreira, da CNN Brasil
