artigo.texto: Ohio Supreme Court blocks citizen-led data center referendum from appearing on ballot in Wilmington A ballot initiative that would have allowed Wilmington residents to weigh in on new regulations for data centers will not be appearing before voters this fall. The proposed initiative brought by Wilmington resident Quintin Koger Kidd would have created new rules for data centers built within city limits, addressing concerns about noise, water usage, and generators. On Friday, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled on Friday that the Clinton County Board of Elections was legally justified this summer in blocking the referendum. The ruling was 6-1, with the majority maintaining that the referendum would have allowed citizens to sue data centers over zoning violations, which is not permitted under Ohio law. "While (the Ohio Revised Code) provides 'municipal corporations' independent power to 'abate any nuisance and prosecute' any person responsible therefor, it does not authorize a municipal corporation to essentially delegate that power to its citizens by way of a civil action," the justices wrote in their majority opinion. "The proposed ordinance at issue here purports to create a new cause of action and therefore is not within the municipality’s power to enact; consequently, relators have not established a clear legal right to compel the board to certify relators’ proposed ordinance for placement on the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot." The majority went on to add that complainants failed to provide sufficient legal rationale that the referendum would create "a new cause of action" that did not fall under the existing precedent, as Kidd and those backing the ballot initiative had previously argued before the court. However, in his lone dissent, Justice Patrick Fischer said that the decision should not be left up to individual election boards to determine which citizen referendums make the ballot, and that such a decision should be determined solely by a judge. "Even if the proposed ordinance is outside the municipality’s authority to enact, that is a legal determination that must be made by the judiciary in the postenactment process," wrote Fischer in his dissenting opinion. "We have long held that courts lack the authority to judge the legality of proposed legislation. See Pfeifer v. Graves, 88 Ohio St. 473 (1913), paragraph five of the syllabus. 'Just as we cannot stop the General Assembly from considering a proposed law, we cannot allow an elections board to interfere in the legislative process initiated by the people.'" Justice Jennifer Brunner, the court's lone Democrat, concurred with the majority while also noting that she was sympathetic to the arguments made by Fischer. However, Brunner noted that "there is public expense for elections that will ultimately be invalidated" at a later date, leading to her to side with the majority. Brunner added that courts should continue to retain their existing power to serve as checks on local election boards if they overstep their authority. The proposed regulations come as Amazon is seeking to build a massive new data center within the city, a project that has been marred by repeated legal setbacks and intense resident backlash over the past year.

artigo.texto: The developer of at least one of the 22 data center campuses proposed for Northeastern Pennsylvania doesn’t expect the executive order Gov. Josh Shapiro signed in August to slow down the project. The Nebius AI cloud campus project in Butler Twp., Schuylkill County, is on track, John Sutter, vice president of U.S. Public Affairs at Nebius, said in a written statement in response to an inquiry. “(We) are committed to developing data centers responsibly and in close coordination with local communities — an approach consistent with the executive order’s focus on responsible development and local engagement,” Sutter said. Shapiro’s Aug. 18 order, which contains safeguards he has touted as “the strictest guardrails in the nation” for data centers, requires developers to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Requirements or risk losing a 6% state sales tax exemption. The order removes all current and future data centers from the PA Permit Fast Track program designed to streamline and accelerate state government permitting for high-impact economic development and infrastructure projects and requires developers to secure all local approvals before the state will even begin to review permit applications. Operators must invest in local economies, create jobs and negotiate community benefit agreements, as well. The newspaper reached out to eight developers or their attorneys behind 12 data center campus projects in Lackawanna, Luzerne and Schuylkill counties to ask how the executive order would affect project timelines, if at all, and only Nebius and one other developer responded. An Amazon spokesperson didn’t directly answer the question for its projects in Hazle and Salem townships in Luzerne County and in Kline Twp. in Schuylkill County, but the spokesperson did indicate that the company was complying with at least one directive in the executive order – job creation. “In 2025, Amazon made a deep commitment to Pennsylvania – a $20 billion planned data center investment that’s expected to create at least 1,250 new high-skilled jobs while supporting thousands of other jobs in the data center supply chain in the Commonwealth,” the spokesperson said. “This builds on our existing footprint of more than 31,000 full- and part-time employees and an economic presence that supports over 20,000 additional jobs across industries like construction, logistics, and professional services. We’re committed to being good neighbors in the communities where we build and operate, and will continue working with state and local leaders to invest responsibly and create good jobs,” the spokesperson concluded. Nebius’ Sutter promised local cooperation and community involvement, as well. “We’re grateful for early support from Butler Township leaders and we will continue working closely with community members and state officials throughout the development process,” Sutter said. Here’s a look at where data center projects are at in Lackawanna, Luzerne and Schuylkill counties. Schuylkill County Project: Nebius AI cloud campus Location: Highridge Business Park, Butler Twp. Developer: Nebius AI of the Netherlands Operator: Nebius AI of the Netherlands Number of centers: 2, with future plans for 4 more Acreage: 600 Status: Preliminary approval from township supervisors, final plan pending, construction expected to begin in late 2026. Power: Dedicated, developer-funded infrastructure agreement with PPL pending state permits Cooling: Closed-loop, air-cooled system Project: Amazon Web Services Location: Kline Twp. Developer: Amazon Operator: Amazon Number of centers: 9 Acreage: 380 Status: Proposed Power: PPL and diesel generators Cooling: Water from Kline Twp. Municipal Authority Luzerne County Project: Project Hazelnut Location: Hazle Twp. Developer: Northpoint Development, Kansas City, Missouri Operator: Amazon Number of centers: 15 Acreage: 1,250 Status: Plans denied by township supervisors. Appeal pending in Commonwealth Court Power: PPL with backup generators Cooling: Treated sewage from Greater Hazleton Joint Sewer Authority Project: LBT Sugarloaf Location: Sugarloaf Twp. Developer: LBT Investment Group, LLC, Chicago, Illinois Operator: Unknown Number of centers: 6 Acreage: 185 Status: Company seeking amendment to township zoning in Luzerne County Court Power: Unknown Cooling: Unknown Project: Hollenback Location: Hollenback Twp. artigo.texto: Another fire burning at battery storage facility in Moss Landing September 18, 2026 By KAREN VELIE A fire is burning at the Vistra lithium-ion battery storage facility in Moss Landing leading Monterey County to recommend residents close their windows and doors and turn off their air systems.Residents are asked to shelter in place. Shortly after 7 a.m., the Monterey County’s North County Fire Protection District sent out an alert about the fire burning at the facility off Highway 1. In 2025, a large fire at the Vistra battery storage facility resulted in the evacuations of thousands of residents. For years, research scientists at San José State University’s Moss Landing Marine Laboratories have monitored marsh soil properties as part of a program for the Elkhorn Slough estuary. Soil tests performed following the 2025 fire showed a dramatic increase in nickel, manganese and cobalt, was found. Scientists studied soils in an approximately two-miles radius of the Vistra battery storage facility. Vistra had planned to construct and operate a 600-megawatt battery storage facility in Morro Bay. However, mutiple residents voiced concerns the facility will endanger the public while negatively impacting tourism and the fishing industry. In Oct. 2025, Vistra Energy informed the California Energy Commission it is no longer “advancing the project.” A month earlier, Vista withdrew its application from the California Independent System Operator queue.

artigo.texto: The Chinese company sees an opportunity in America despite trade barriers, with local production through licensing as a possibility. - CATL says U.S. automakers have already tested its new batteries designed specifically for American pickups. - CATL hasn't disclosed the batteries' specifications, production timeline, or which U.S. automakers tested them. - Licensing could allow American companies to manufacture the batteries domestically. Chinese battery giant CATL wants in on the American electric pickup market, and it has already developed batteries specifically for the job. Getting them into trucks, however, will be tricky and likely require American companies to manufacture them locally. Zhu Lingbo, the chief technology officer of CATL's international business unit, told the Financial Times that the company has created "tall" batteries specially designed for American pickups. U.S. automakers have already tested them, he said, without naming the companies. The CATL executive spoke Sunday at CATL's headquarters in China, saying that America offered "huge business" despite "very intense geopolitics." He noted that licensing the technology to U.S. manufacturers could provide a way in. - CATL's New Electric Truck Battery Is Coming For Diesel's Biggest Advantage - This New CATL Battery For Delivery Vans Can Recharge In 7 Minutes - CATL Says Ultra Fast Charging Won't Kill Its New Battery - CATL Reveals Game-Changing Leap In Battery Endurance However, the FT report contains no specifics regarding the batteries' chemistry, dimensions, performance, or production time frame. It also doesn't point to an actual customer that has agreed to use them. We do know that Ford's upcoming Fathom electric pickup will use Michigan-made LFP cells built with CATL technology. It's unclear whether Ford's cells relate to the newly disclosed design, but the arrangement shows how CATL's technology could reach American pickups. CATL's American ambitions also predate this announcement. Company chairman Robin Zeng had previously expressed willingness to build a U.S. factory, if it were allowed. Tesla provides another licensing precedent, although its Nevada LFP production serves officially manufactures cells for energy storage products, not cars. Developing batteries specifically for American pickups suggests CATL still sees a market worth pursuing despite the obvious obstacles. Yet political resistance remains strong, with very high tariffs, strict localization requirements, and potential security bans constraining Chinese companies' access to the American market, regardless of their cost and technology advantages.

In lawsuits filed Wednesday in Montgomery County Court of Common Pleas, O’Neill said Upper Merion officials have stated in recent years that data centers — which house the equipment that powers AI — qualify as warehouses and are therefore permitted under its zoning code. They changed their tune, according to O’Neill’s team, only after residents pushed back against the plans. “The township issued a zoning officer’s determination letter that the proposed use was a permitted use, and then when the people started to bombard them, they did a 180,” said Marc Kaplin, an attorney representing O’Neill. “This is what happens when there is public pressure.” Township Manager Anthony Hamaday said Thursday that Upper Merion officials had been informed of O’Neill’s land-use appeals but that the documents had yet to be delivered to them. They declined to comment, pending a full review of the filings. O’Neill is asking a judge to reverse the supervisors’ denial, give his plans preliminary approval, and appoint an independent third-party “referee” to conduct an evidentiary hearing and oversee the rest of the process. In the lawsuit, O’Neill says the board acted in bad faith and denied his plans over “minor technical items.” At a contentious Aug. 13 meeting, the supervisors unanimously rejected O’Neill’s five data center plans on the grounds that the proposals lacked specificity, including on fire-safety-related issues, and did not meet zoning requirements. They said O’Neill’s team failed to address their many questions and concerns during the review process. » READ MORE: King of Prussia data center complex is rejected by Upper Merion Township officials O’Neill had said his team needed more time to respond and requested an extension until Sept. 30, a request township officials denied. A day before the supervisors’ vote, the developer sued the township, its planning commission, and its board of supervisors, saying they violated his legal right to an extension. In response, Montgomery County Court Judge Garrett D. Page ordered a pause on township proceedings and decisions related to the data centers. That decision was vacated the next day, just hours before the supervisors’ vote on Aug. 13. Neighborhood pushback O’Neill, a longtime real estate developer in the region, is fighting to build a data center complex on five of his properties in a swath of Upper Merion Township between West Conshohocken and Bridgeport. The developer has declined to specify who would operate the centers, though he indicated the facilities would fuel AI-powered biotech to complement his existing life-sciences complex, Discovery Labs. O’Neill has said the centers would emit little light and noise, operate on a closed-loop system that requires no outside water, and provide their own power. They would also be an economic engine for Montgomery County, according to O’Neill, who released an economic impact study saying the project would result in more than 10,000 jobs during construction, more than 700 permanent jobs, and more than $55 million a year in local tax revenue. Neighborhood groups have rallied against O’Neill’s plans, organizing on social media, packing township meetings, and displaying bright orange lawn signs opposing the project. About 18,000 people had signed a Change.org petition against the Upper Merion data centers as of Friday. Opponents have expressed concerns about pollution, light, noise, electricity prices, property values, and quality of life. » READ MORE: Human reporters explain why AI data centers are so controversial in the Philly suburbs and beyond The pushback in Upper Merion mirrors the opposition seen across the Schuylkill River in Plymouth Township, where O’Neill has spent a year trying to get the OK to build another 2 million-square-foot data center on a shuttered steel mill outside Conshohocken. The project was set to be the subject of a Plymouth Township Zoning Hearing Board meeting on Thursday, but the meeting was canceled due to what the township called “an administrative oversight.” Plymouth Township officials failed to post the meeting agenda 24 hours in advance, in violation of the Sunshine Act. “Out of an abundance of caution and in the interest of legal compliance and public transparency, the board will not convene as scheduled,” Plymouth Township officials said Thursday in a statement, adding that the meeting will be rescheduled. O’Neill has also faced off with Plymouth Township officials in recent months. In July, he filed a legal challenge to the Plymouth Township zoning ordinance, which prompted township leaders to accuse O’Neill of “throwing a tantrum” in an attempt to bully and intimidate them. O’Neill called their statements “a bald-faced lie.” News of O’Neill’s actions in Plymouth Township prompted a rebuke from Gov. Josh Shapiro, who had previously encouraged data center development. Weeks later, the governor signed an executive order restricting data center development in Pennsylvania, including by requiring projects to get local approval before receiving state permits. » READ MORE: In a major shift, Gov. Josh Shapiro restricts data center development in Pennsylvania Fears about AI The debate over artificial intelligence has intensified in recent weeks, with executives at some of the country’s largest AI companies urging a slowdown of the technology amid fears that it may eventually wipe out humanity. artigo.texto: Infra em 1 Minuto: uso de gás em data centers divide governo Pedro Rodrigues defende critérios de emissão no Redata e liberdade para investidores escolherem a matriz energética O Poder360, em parceria com o CBIE (Centro Brasileiro de Infraestrutura), lança neste sábado (19.set.2026) o 180º episódio do programa “Infra em 1 Minuto”. No vídeo, o especialista em energia Pedro Rodrigues, sócio do CBIE, analisa a divergência no governo sobre a inclusão do gás natural entre as fontes que poderão abastecer data centers beneficiados pelo Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter). O programa é publicado semanalmente no canal do Poder360 no YouTube. Assista ao vídeo (2min6s): O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sancionou na 3ª feira (15.set.2026) a lei que institui o Redata. O regime suspende a cobrança de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, modernização e ampliação de data centers no país. Para receber os benefícios, os empreendimentos deverão comprovar que toda a demanda de energia elétrica será atendida por contratos de fornecimento ou autoprodução de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A lei não especificou quais tecnologias poderão ser classificadas como de baixa emissão. A definição será feita por uma portaria interministerial. GÁS NATURAL NO REDATA A versão aprovada pela Câmara exigia que os data centers usassem energia 100% renovável. O Senado acrescentou as fontes consideradas de baixa emissão. A mudança abriu espaço para a inclusão do gás natural, a depender da regulamentação. O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) defende que o combustível seja contemplado. Segundo o ministério, o gás pode assegurar o fornecimento firme exigido pelos centros de processamento de dados, que funcionam continuamente e consomem grande quantidade de eletricidade. O Ministério da Fazenda ainda não definiu uma posição. O secretário-executivo, Rogério Ceron, afirmou que o governo discute o alcance da expressão “baixa emissão”. Entre as alternativas estão exigências de compensação para fontes emissoras, como a compra de créditos de carbono. Rodrigues afirma que condições adicionais podem reduzir a competitividade do gás na geração de energia para os empreendimentos. “Não faz sentido dar incentivo fiscal para baratear o equipamento e, ao mesmo tempo, encarecer a energia, que é a base de tudo”, declarou. ENERGIA FIRME Segundo Rodrigues, os data centers precisam de fornecimento ininterrupto de eletricidade. Falhas podem comprometer serviços de armazenamento, processamento de dados e inteligência artificial. As fontes solar e eólica variam conforme as condições climáticas. As usinas termelétricas a gás, por sua vez, podem ser acionadas seguindo a necessidade do sistema. Para o especialista, a regulamentação deveria estabelecer critérios objetivos de emissão, sem determinar antecipadamente as tecnologias que poderão ser usadas. “Data center não pode piscar. Precisa de energia firme, 24 horas por dia”, afirmou. Rodrigues defende que os investidores escolham a combinação de fontes considerando custos, segurança do fornecimento e parâmetros ambientais estabelecidos pelo governo. “Quem escolhe a fonte é o investidor, não o regulador”, disse. artigo.texto: A Wilson County data center zoning ordinance is one step closer to becoming the rule after the county’s data center committee worked out the final details and passed the resolution during its Sept. 15 meeting. The committee went through the initial resolution section by section, evaluating what information Wilson County Planning Services Director Christopher Lawless included in the ordinance. The committee members then made changes as they worked through the draft ordinance. Among the details they discussed were berm height and vegetation; noise and vibration from the data center; third-party plan review; parking spaces; size classifications and property line distance; distance from location where people assemble; eliminating possible interference of public electricity, gas, water, sewer and internet; and generators which the data centers could use in an emergency. Berm height would be determined at 40 percent of the height of the building and would have state-approved vegetation such as maple, oak or magnolia trees on it to help deter the noise affecting any other structures. The data centers would have to have utility capacity before plans would be approved, eliminating the need for any backup generators to run full time, all day. Middle Tennessee Electric would work with the data centers to determine the capacity needed, as well as providing the actual electrical service. In addition, the water and wastewater utility that serves the area in which any center would locate would also work with the facility to determine their water and wastewater needs. A public concern about data centers is noise and vibration from the centers, affecting homes, business and other structures. The committee discussed hiring an experienced acoustic consultant or engineer, as well as purchasing sound level detectors, rather than county employees being responsible for determining sound levels which exceed the limits set forth in the resolution. They discussed 40 dBA and 60 dBC as the maximum noise level. The 40 dBA is equivalent to a refrigerator hum, according to Decibelmeter.org. The American Academy of Audiology states that 60 dBC is equivalent to normal conversation or a dishwasher running. There would also be a timeline that the facility would be required to respond to the city for any noise or vibration complaint, the committee decided. The resolution states that the facility would have up to 48 hours from the time the notice of violation them to a complaint or noted an excessive noise level. Area governments, such as Rutherford County, have set their data center moratoriums at one year rather than the six months established in June by the Wilson County Commission. That one expires on Dec. 22, 2026. The next step is for the resolution to go to the county’s planning and zoning committee, whose next meeting will be in October. If it is delayed for any reason, the resolution could be passed after Dec. 22. The planning and zoning committee can recommend the commission extend the moratorium beyond that date in order for it not to expire before the resolution and subsequent ordinance are passed by the commission. That would be the last step and could take a few months for the commission to vote on the final resolution.

artigo.texto: This article was produced by Capital & Main, an award-winning publication that reports from California on economic, political, and social issues. It is co-published here with permission. In January, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wisconsin) called data centers “exciting new technology” and voted for a federal bill to speed their construction. But by May, as he was running for governor of Wisconsin, he was promising to repeal the state tax breaks that lure them. And within a week of the Aug. 11 Democratic primary in the Badger State, Tiffany’s campaign was on the air branding his opponent “Data Center David Crowley”—a Republican attacking a Democrat for being too cozy with Big Tech. The ad focused on a statement Crowley gave at a candidate forum in November 2025 that Wisconsin had the opportunity to become a major artificial intelligence and data center hub “not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe and really sets us apart in making sure that we continue to invest in businesses and companies here.” But early this summer, Crowley began insisting that local communities should have absolute veto power to reject any such project and that data center developers should pay for all grid and infrastructure upgrades. Voters in the battleground state’s most important race could be forgiven for experiencing whiplash. Data centers are now what the Wisconsin Examiner called the biggest issue in the governor’s race, and the public has turned on them faster than on anything the state’s leading pollster has measured in 15 years. And Tiffany has navigated that turn to outflank Crowley with tougher rhetoric, his own reversal notwithstanding. A longtime fossil fuel supporter, Tiffany is also using the unpopularity of data centers in service of a much older fight against renewable sources of energy such as wind and solar. He recently called for the state to not close coal-fired plants, arguing that they “are a backbone of baseload power, and cannot simply be replaced with intermittent generation provided by wind and solar.” Nothing Has Moved This Fast “It’s been one of the fastest changes in public opinion that we’ve seen in Wisconsin,” Charles Franklin, director of the Marquette Law School Poll, told Capital & Main. “We’ve been doing the Marquette poll for 15 years, and in that time nothing else has moved this fast.” When Marquette first asked about data centers last October, 55% of registered voters said the costs of data centers outweighed the benefits. By February it was 70%, and by August 78%. What struck Franklin more was the absence of a partisan split: 54% of Republicans, 55% of independents and 56% of Democrats were all opposed last fall. “Almost nothing we see in Wisconsin shows that small a partisan gap,” Franklin said. That backlash reshaped the Democratic gubernatorial primary. At a Milwaukee town hall the week before the vote, five candidates competed to out-tough one another on the developers dubbed “Big Tech oligarchs” by Francesca Hong, a Democratic state representative who is also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America party and a gubernatorial candidate. Hong made a one-year moratorium on data centers the centerpiece of her campaign, but she lost the primary to Crowley. “Data Center David” Tiffany, who had reportedly hoped to run on economic issues, moved fast to claim the voters Hong had galvanized. He pledged to end the sales tax exemption the state legislature adopted for data centers—a break the Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimated could cost the state more than $2 billion. Crowley countered with accountability framing. “They have to pay their own way,” he said. “They need to pay for their own infrastructure, and they need to bring their own new clean energy.” Behind the ad copy, the two men actually agree on a lot. Neither supports Hong’s proposed moratorium. Both back the same guardrails: a ban on nondisclosure agreements between data center companies and local governments, a local veto over whether a project gets built and protection for residential rates. The general election is a contest over credibility and degree, not direction. What Crowley won’t do is promise to claw back the existing tax breaks, and that is the detail that Tiffany has zeroed in on. Tiffany’s central claim—that Crowley is “funded by the people building” data centers—is easy to misinterpret. The more than $350,000 in campaign contributions that an unnamed Tiffany spokeswoman cited to the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel came largely from building trades unions whose members would pour the concrete for data centers, not the tech companies that own the buildings. “David Crowley is honored to have the support of thousands of hard-working union members who are suffering from the affordability crisis MAGA extremist Tom Tiffany and Donald Trump created,” an unnamed Crowley spokesperson said in an email to Capital & Main. Tiffany, meanwhile, accepted $5,000 in June from Robert Marchant, a lobbyist for the Wisconsin Data Center Coalition, which fought the nondisclosure agreement ban and lobbied for the same tax exemption that Tiffany now vows to repeal. Campaign finance reports also showed donations to him from lobbyists for OpenAI and Oracle and a donation from Amazon, which is actively building data centers across the country. Capital & Main has reached out to the Tiffany campaign for comment. artigo.texto: Keeping Up with Data Centers From the Western Ag Network, I’m Bob Larson. More data centers are bringing new challenges for utilities across rural America. Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, says as electricity demand continues to rise, utilities will need both new and existing resources to maintain reliability … MATHESON … “It’s going up, and it's going up a lot, and it requires a significant amount of new generating capacity to meet that need. It also requires us to stop shutting down power plants that still have useful life, which public policy has been encouraging over the last few years in this country, and we've got to stop doing that because we need to make sure we can keep the lights on at an affordable price." Despite the growing debate around data centers, Matheson says the issue is not whether or not communities should support data centers, because that’s not the right question … MATHESON … “But what we are for is making sure that our utilities have the ability to make the decision that's right for them in their local community. We don't like one-size-fits-all mandates on data centers or any other policy, quite frankly, that's out there. Because different geographic locations have different characteristics, different capacities, different needs, and different challenges. And the extent that you can maintain that autonomy and local control in making decisions from an electric cooperative standpoint, that drives through all of our policy advocacy that we do.” Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association.

artigo.texto: Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) is going all-in on artificial intelligence (AI), investing billions in data centers to expand its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure business and provide the computing power needed to train and run AI models. That is great news for Vertiv Holdings (NYSE: VRT) and Caterpillar (NYSE: CAT), two industrial stocks that could help power this huge building boom. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Vertiv powers and cools the AI data center boom AI makes data centers much more power-hungry and harder to cool, and Vertiv sells the infrastructure needed to solve both problems. Demand is already fueling a major order cycle for the company. In the second quarter, it reported net sales of around $3.27 billion, up 24% year over year. To meet growing demand from data centers, Vertiv announced four new or expanding factories to increase capacity for power management and infrastructure products. The company said the investments will support the continued expansion of AI factories. Also, as AI chips become more powerful, cooling is becoming one of the biggest physical challenges. To address it, Vertiv announced a $50 million investment in Ohio to expand production of liquid-cooling and chilled-water systems. These are designed for high-density computing, and the Ironton factory expansion in particular is expected to be operational in the second quarter of 2027. Management has also acquired companies like PurgeRite to further strengthen its fluid management services. So, while Oracle supplies the cloud capacity, Vertiv provides much of the infrastructure that gets electricity to the AI chips and removes the heat they generate. And another player is helping hyperscalers like Oracle secure huge amounts of power. Caterpillar powers data centers when the grid falls short Grid connections can take years to complete, but hyperscalers want new computing capacity as soon as possible. To address this problem, Caterpillar supplies natural gas generators, gas turbines, and other power equipment that can provide electricity directly to data centers. Management says that data center demand is a key driver for its power generation business, with the company expecting continued strength as demand grows. Building new grid connections can take too long, so off-grid solutions are a faster way to power data centers. Caterpillar is already putting more capacity behind this. For example, it announced a $725 million expansion of its large-engine manufacturing footprint, citing rising energy demand and the growing opportunity around AI and data centers. It is also moving beyond backup generators toward providing on-site power for data centers. Caterpillar entered into an agreement with Joule Capital Partners to power a high-performance computing campus in Utah, with 4 gigawatts of total energy supported by a fleet of Caterpillar natural gas generators. And Caterpillar and Vertiv announced a collaboration combining the former's power generation equipment with the latter's power distribution and cooling systems. The goal is to create integrated solutions that help data centers be deployed faster and be powered up sooner. So, as Oracle builds out its data centers, Caterpillar can help provide the on-site power to get them up and running before grid connections are available. With many investors still focused on chips and memory, it's easy to overlook other opportunities such as these two that could offer greater upside. Why AI requires more than just chips The data center boom creates opportunities beyond chipmakers, with insatiable demand for power, cooling, and other infrastructure, and Vertiv and Caterpillar are stepping up to meet it. As hyperscalers build more data centers, Vertiv provides the power management and cooling systems, while Caterpillar delivers on-site power generation for applications where the grid can't keep up. With both companies supporting this expansion, these two stocks could be some of the best ways for investors to bet on Oracle's hundreds of billions in data center commitments. artigo.texto: Lula: não vamos deixar que nossa energia seja usada para data center O candidato à reeleição, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, disse, durante ato de campanha em Santa Catarina, que o programa de incentivo ao desenvolvimento de data centers, o Redata, deve atrair investimentos da ordem de R$ 500 bilhões. Segundo ele, o País tem tudo para ser um grande polo desse setor por ser abundante em energia renovável. Mas ele ressaltou que, pelo projeto, as empresas que vierem para o Brasil terão que construir as suas usinas para abastecer os seus centros. “Não vamos deixar que a energia produzida vá somente para o data center, quem quiser vir pra cá terá que investir na construção em energia renovável”, disse. Lula também exaltou a sanção da Lei de Minerais Críticos e terras raras e disse que o Brasil conhece apenas 30% de seu território e mesmo assim é a segunda maior reserva de terras raras do mundo, perdendo apenas para a China. “Mas não temos tecnologia para explorar, por isso, temos que ter cursos em nossas universidades, para ter mais capacidade do que o chinês. Queremos vender chip, bateria, queremos exportar inteligência, conhecimento. Por isso temos que ter informação e investimento em pesquisa”, disse. “Prometo a você e à minha consciência que em 10 anos esse País não estará devendo nada para formar um engenheiro ou cientista, não queremos ficar na guerra entre China e EUA, queremos formar os jovens.” Lula também falou das políticas que seu governo fez para o agronegócio e disse que abriu 693 mercados para o setor, dentre eles, para a produção de proteína animal. Santa Catarina é um dos Estados que mais produzem carnes suína e de frango. “Sabe quantos mercados eu abri para carne de aves e derivados? 34 novos mercados de exportação. Para carnes suínas e derivados, 25 mercados para vender os nossos produtos, bovinos e derivados, 37, pescados, 22 novos mercados. Somando as 4 proteínas aqui em Santa Catarina, foram 118 mercados que o Lulinha, que eles não gostam, abriu para venderem os seus produtos. O problema com agronegócio é porque eu sou nordestino, não por dinheiro. Porque nunca houve tanto crédito para o agro como agora.” Segundo ele, a escolha do candidato Gelson Merísio ao governo estadual pelo PSB foi feita para dialogar com o agronegócio. Mais uma vez, Lula chamou a militância para entrar mais firme no debate há duas semanas do primeiro turno das eleições. “Agora é a hora da verdade. Nada de fazer lacração. Não tem que votar por você, vote pelo seu neto, filho, pelo futuro do País. Não fiquei sentado. Se a gente tem a chance de escolher o melhor, vamos escolher. Por que deixar o pior entrar em campo?” Assuntos continue lendo - Moraes se torna relator de pedido que envolve esposa, Vorcaro e filho de Lula Nícolas Robert · há 32 minutos - Crise no STF: Mendonça tem até hoje para se manifestar sobre acusações de Moraes Jovem Pan · há 2 horas - Governo Lula demite Eduardo Bolsonaro da PF por abandono de cargo Nícolas Robert · há 2 horas - Paraná Pesquisas: JHC lidera corrida contra Renan Filho para o governo de AL Jovem Pan · há 3 horas

artigo.texto: Desde 2014, o Brasil tem aprovado uma série de legislações para regular o uso da internet em território nacional, com destaque para o Marco Civil da Internet (que trata da neutralidade da rede, a liberdade de expressão e a privacidade), a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (que determina como empresas e órgãos públicos podem coletar, armazenar e usar informações pessoais), o Projeto de Lei 2030/2020 (que exige transparência das plataformas e responsabiliza provedores por conteúdo impulsionado) e o ECA Digital (que estabelece regras rígidas para redes sociais, aplicativos, jogos e plataformas de streaming a fim de garantir a segurança de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente virtual). Entretanto, nem todas as normas em pauta no Congresso Nacional atuam em benefício da população. É o caso do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center no Brasil (Redata). Sancionado na última terça-feira (15/09) pelo presidente Lula, o Redata nasce com o objetivo de estimular a implantação, ampliação e manutenção de data centers, além de impulsionar a economia digital no país. Para isso, o programa reduz os custos para as Big Techs, garantindo a isenção de tributos como PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI na compra de equipamentos de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação. Como contrapartida, as empresas beneficiadas são obrigadas a investir 2% do valor dos produtos que adquirirem em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação dentro do setor digital brasileiro. A expectativa do governo é atrair R$2 trilhões em investimentos ao longo de 10 anos por meio do programa. Um dos principais argumentos da gestão Lula é a criação de empregos que a construção de data centers traria ao Brasil. Segundo reportagem investigativa do Business Insider, porém, esses centros operam, em grande parte, de forma autônoma e não geram muitos empregos permanentes em tempo integral. Uma análise aprofundada de alvarás de construção e divulgações de empresas revelou que mesmo os maiores data centers das gigantes de tecnologia, como Google, Amazon e Meta, geralmente empregam menos de 150 trabalhadores permanentes, com alguns casos de instalações que operam com apenas 25 funcionários. Ainda de acordo com a reportagem, a grande maioria das vagas criadas ocorre durante as obras: cerca de 80% dos empregos gerados por data centers nos últimos anos concentraram-se na construção civil. Além disso, esses empregos são temporários, muitas vezes durando apenas algumas semanas ou menos de um ano (um período muito inferior à duração das isenções fiscais, que podem se estender por décadas). Diante disso, economistas e pesquisadores afirmam que o número de empregos de longo prazo não compensa o alto custo das isenções tributárias. Segundo Timothy Bartik, economista sênior do WE Upjohn Institute for Employment Research, por exemplo, as estimativas feitas pela própria indústria de tecnologia costumam exagerar significativamente e podem representar até o dobro do impacto real na geração de empregos a longo prazo. O governo federal também defende que a construção desses data centers contribuiria para uma das pautas mais relevantes do chamado Lula 3: a soberania nacional. Desde o tarifaço imposto pelos Estados Unidos de Donald Trump, com apoio do ex-deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro, a gestão tem insistido na defesa da soberania, sem interferência externa (principalmente dos estadunidenses) em solo tupiniquim. O argumento tem sido utilizado para convencer parte significativa do eleitorado, que já embarcou nessa narrativa desde agosto de 2025. Mas será que esse é, de fato, o motivo central? Superados os principais argumentos do governo a favor da expansão dos data centers no Brasil, é necessário abordar o problema mais sensível dessas estruturas: o impacto ambiental. Esse impacto se manifesta, sobretudo, no enorme volume de água, muitas vezes potável, exigido por esses centros. Com uso intensivo voltado ao resfriamento das máquinas, essas estruturas podem comprometer recursos hídricos e agravar crises de abastecimento para a população local, mesmo em regiões com forte disponibilidade de água. Outro efeito relevante é o impacto sobre a infraestrutura energética. Nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo, o Departamento de Energia estimou que, impulsionado pela Inteligência Artificial, o consumo dos data centers pode saltar de pouco mais de 4% (em 2023) para até 12% do consumo total de eletricidade do país em um futuro próximo. Para suportar esse aumento expressivo de demanda, concessionárias precisam construir novas linhas de transmissão e usinas, com a conta recaindo sobre a população. De acordo com estudo da Faculdade de Direito de Harvard, as empresas lucram “forçando o público a pagar por infraestrutura projetada para abastecer um pequeno grupo de corporações extremamente ricas”. E esse impacto não atinge apenas os cidadãos comuns: a gigante do varejo Walmart já reclamou oficialmente que o aumento das contas de luz, impulsionado pela demanda dos data centers, está colocando em risco a expansão de suas próprias lojas. Isso sem contar outros impactos ambientais, como a geração de lixo eletrônico, a poluição, a intensificação da extração mineral, a poluição sonora e o aquecimento do ambiente ao redor. É importante pontuar que o Redata é fruto de uma corrida global pela Inteligência Artificial. O rápido desenvolvimento da IA tem acelerado drasticamente a construção de novos data centers, não apenas no Brasil, mas em todo o mundo. O próprio Projeto de Lei 2338/2023, que busca regular a Inteligência Artificial no país, aponta como diretriz o incentivo governamental à ampliação de data centers de alta capacidade para apoiar o setor produtivo e a pesquisa científica nacional — demanda à qual o Redata procura responder diretamente. O poder desse lobby a favor das Big Techs e da Inteligência Artificial não pode ser subestimado, mas chamam a atenção as recorrentes tentativas de venda do Brasil, feitas por um governo que se diz defensor da chamada “soberania nacional”.

artigo.texto: - GOP attack ad suggests Democratic governor candidate Jocelyn Benson could get rich off data centers - The ad points to her husband’s work for a company that helped bring a controversial data center to Saline Township - Benson’s husband announced he’s switched roles and is no longer working on Michigan projects. Firm say he made no commission Proposed data centers have sparked controversy in cities and towns across Michigan and emerged as a key issue for campaigns leading up to the November election. That’s true in the Michigan governor’s race, where both major party candidates have responded by proposing temporary moratoriums. A recent advertisement from a super PAC supporting Republican John James claims Democrat Jocelyn Benson’s husband could make millions on the most controversial data center in the state, the $43 billion hyperscale data center in Saline Township. Benson’s husband, Ryan Friedrichs, worked on the project as senior vice president-Michigan for Related Companies, which is helping develop the facility, and vouched for the project before Saline Township officials. His work on the project wasn’t widely known for much of last year, while Benson was campaigning for governor. Now, the company says Friedrichs didn’t earn a commission on the project and is no longer working on it. Benson’s campaign has gone further, saying her “family has not made any money from data centers” at all. Claims about Benson’s family connection to the Saline Township data center are among several that Bridge Michigan is reviewing in the state’s gubernatorial race between James, a Republican, and Benson, a Democrat. The winner will succeed Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who is term-limited. The claim The 30-second TV ad from the Mission Michigan super PAC opens with a narrator defending James against criticism of his stock trades, a frequent attack by Democrats, before claiming Benson is the one “using government to get rich.” “Her lobbyist husband could profit tens of millions” of dollars from the Saline Township data center, the narrator says while recreated images of news stories flash on the screen, including one claiming Friedrichs could receive $70 million. That figure stems from an estimate of private equity commission rates that a former management consulting firm employee delivered in a state House subcommittee meeting. But Friedrichs won’t make any commission from the project, Related Companies spokesperson Natalie Ravitz told Bridge. The $70 million estimate cited in the ad was “a number that was seemingly made up,” she said in an email. In a statement to Bridge, Joanna Burgos, chief strategist for Mission Michigan, wrote that “Jocelyn Benson looked Michigan in the eye and said no one in her family is profiting from data centers. Then she signed a disclosure putting $370,000 a year from the developer into her own household. He is a paid lobbyist for the company. He stood up and spoke for it after the township voted it down.” Rajan Srinivasan, a spokesperson for Benson’s campaign, called the ad “deceptive” and “false” in a statement to Bridge in which he also criticized James for taking campaign contributions from data center companies. “Jocelyn is the only candidate who has called for a moratorium on data centers until we can get guardrails in place to protect Michiganders that create well-paying union jobs, pay for their own power, and ban them from getting tax breaks or abusing our water,” Srinivasan wrote. Alyvia Bailey, a spokesperson for James’ campaign, did not return a message seeking comment. What we know Ravitz told Bridge that Friedrichs is an employee of Related Companies, an affiliate of Related Digital, and that he “receives a standard salary and bonus like all members of our team.” He earned $370,000 in 2025, according to a financial disclosure Benson filed in May. Friedrichs had previously registered as a lobbyist for Related Companies in Michigan, but he terminated that registration in May 2025. Ravitz added that Friedrichs “receives zero commission or compensation from the Related Digital data center project.” The data center was one of at least three projects he was working on during that stretch, she added. Prior to a switch earlier this year, Friedrichs “focused on stakeholder engagement” and he “was never a senior leader or developer on the Saline project,” she wrote. Friedrichs’ work on the data center began in early summer of 2025 and ended in February, Ravitz told Bridge. During that time, he spoke as a representative of Related Digital during a Nov. 10, 2025, public meeting in Saline, saying that as he “saw the data centers coming to Michigan, I wanted the right ones coming.” Days later, Michigan Advance reported that Friedrichs would recuse himself from any projects in the state if Benson won the general election. But in March, Friedrichs announced on LinkedIn that he was changing roles at Related Companies and would no longer be working on any projects in Michigan. That lines up with the timeline that Ravitz provided. The bottom line There’s no evidence Benson’s husband could make millions of dollars on the Saline Township data center, as the attack ad claims. But the Benson campaign’s claim that her family has “not made any money from data centers” omits the fact that her husband earned $370,000 from his employer last year — at least in part for his work on the project.

artigo.texto: Company offers exclusive look inside its Bloomington data center BLOOMINGTON (25News Now) - Pearl Technology is an IT services and technology solutions provider in Central Illinois that has owned and operated its own data centers in Peoria and Bloomington for the last 13 years. 25News was given a tour of the company’s data center in Downtown Bloomington, which according to its leaders, operates around the clock to ensure the safety of sensitive information belonging to clients, including local small businesses, banks and hospitals. Most large-scale data centers are known for producing a constant humming noise. However, outside Pearl Technology’s smaller, roughly 30,000-square-foot data center, it is silent. Once you make it through the second set of doors, however, the humming from the data center starts to make its way through the walls. Consuming roughly the same amount of energy as a grocery store during its peak season in the summer, the data center has a maximum power capacity of 2 megawatts. Through the security doors are 260 racks, with 80 of them currently storing data from Pearl Technology’s customers. The data center’s second floor has room to expand to fit 200 more racks. “What we have here is a layered approach for customers that want to have their data secure and accessible in the event of some sort of disaster or power failure throughout the city. Folks want to know that their critical infrastructure is safe and that’s what we do here,” said Pat Venditte, an account executive for Pearl Technology, speaking just slightly louder as he stood in front of the racks inside the data center. Above the racks are carefully positioned thick wires carrying power from the mechanical room behind them. The power is then distributed to boxes above the racks, which provide the necessary amount to each one. “Power comes into this room from the mechanical room, through these conduits and into this cutoff. So, each one of these cutoffs feeds one of the overhead distribution rails and those distribution rails provide tap boxes that have different amperage and voltage drops for each rack depending on the clients’ requirements,” said Rob Judd, Pearl Technology’s director of data operations, standing in front of the machinery that transfers the power. Besides the racks necessary to store sensitive information, which Judd helped build from scratch, the room has visible components designed to ensure the systems stay dry. “Think of it as like your laptop — if your laptop gets wet, that thing is probably done,” said Venditte, standing in front of one large and one small clean-agent fire suppression cylinder. “Same with the infrastructure in here, it needs to be dry and that’s what our fire suppression system is able to do. Keep our technology dry even in the case of an emergency.” Their small-scale data center consumes only 10 gallons of water a year through a closed-loop system, while the cooling room regularly remains at around 70 degrees Fahrenheit. A key component of the data center is the amount of redundancy built into the facility. With more than 3,500 pounds of batteries and two cooling systems, if one system fails, there are multiple backups behind it. “What this does is it takes the hot warm air that’s coming from the inside of the data room, brings it through the coolant system and keeps it on that continuous loop,” said Venditte. Right beside the main cooling system, Judd monitors the temperature in the mechanical room. “So, it’s not just raw water, it’s a mixture of glycol, or antifreeze, and water that we keep in big 250-gallon reservoirs. So, it cycles through pumps, and it comes in refrigerated and usually at 48 degrees, and the air heats that glycol and pushes it back out to the chiller to be chilled again,” said Judd. As the debate about data centers continues, Pearl Technology leaders said regional facilities play an important role in supporting local businesses and protecting their data. “At first glance, a data center might look like nothing more than rows of cabinets. But behind those doors, there’s an enormous amount of data moving, electricity flowing, and technology working together,” said Pearl Technology President Anthony Mini. “When you peel back those layers, you realize just how remarkable this facility really is.” Mini added that the company is beginning to see increased demand for regional data centers like Pearl Technology’s. According to Mini, companies “want more direct control over their data, their security, and their technology,” adding that he expects demand to continue growing as businesses adopt AI and look for places to store information. Regional data centers offer another advantage: placing computing and storage closer to the people and businesses using it. “Local services are usually provided by local data centers,” said Judd. “You don’t necessarily want things to come from 2,000 miles away when latency is an issue. artigo.texto: While local governments are increasingly strapped for cash under Senate Enrolled Act 1, the city of Hobart is swimming in funds as a result of an Amazon data center project still under construction. Speaking to the Post-Tribune this week, Mayor Josh Huddlestun detailed Hobart’s financial windfall and how the “economic impact payments” are being doled out for the benefit of the local community while beefing up city coffers. The city initially received $47 million, with another $10 million arriving last week, according to Huddleston. He expects another $45 million in-hand by the end of 2026, with a $43 million payment scheduled to arrived in 2027. Under the agreement, the city will receive approximately $40 million in both 2028 and 2029 and approximately $52 million in 2030 when the 723-acre project is expected to be completed. The payments from Amazon effectively double the city’s general fund budget year over year, according to Huddlestun. He said that Hobart will receive approximately $52 million per year over the next 35 years. He explained that the city negotiated a plan for direct payments, thus granting Amazon a 35-year tax abatement on personal property (equipment on site) and a 10-year abatement on real property (buildings). Huddlestun sees direct payments from Amazon as a better long term deal for the city, explaining that tax assessments and the resulting proceeds can vary over time. He noted that there is no tax abatement on land, describing a “negligible” assessment. Because the development falls within a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district, any tax proceeds would have been delegated to improvements within that legally defined area, though Indiana has widened the scope of acceptable TIF uses to include public safety. The data center encompasses a 555-acre parcel located south of 61st Avenue, east of Colorado Street and north of 69th Avenue, known as Hobart Tech Park, which is owned by Amazon Web Services. The other parcel, described as the Ewen Farm property, encompasses 168 acres and is located southeast of 61st and Arizona Street. The data center facility will have 26 buildings spread out across the two sites, with six at the 61st Avenue location and 20 at the Colorado Street location. Spending has already started Hobart homeowners are already realizing the benefits from Amazon’s payments to the city through a new program establishing $10,000 50/50 matching grants for residential exterior home improvements. Another 50/50 matching grant program provides homeowners with $5,000 for energy improvements, such as the purchase of more efficient furnaces and central air conditioning units. The Hobart City Council will appropriate the funds, including $16 million earmarked for improvements to Festival Park. Huddlestun said the city is making funding available to struggling nonprofit groups and has established a $500,000 revolving loan fund to support improvements for downtown businesses. Hobart’s general fund will enable long overdue infrastructure projects involving road repairs, mitigating drainage issues and replacing sidewalks, and the city is shopping for a new fire truck and two ambulances. Huddlestun termed the influx of funding as “generational” wealth, but cautioned that the city will be measured with how the money is spent. “We want to make sure is that this is beneficial to our city and are trying to touch as many of the community members as we can,” he said. “I think this puts us in position to really soar in the next chapter of Hobart’s life, be able to give back to the community and deliver on good projects while being very selective on about the developments that come into our city. Hobart’s future is drastically positive.” Hurdles still exist Continued public opposition to the project aside, one remaining critical issue involves an air permit application, which the Ramboll Engineering firm filed with Indiana Department of Environmental Management on Amazon’s behalf on July 24. According to the permit application, the facility would host 808 fuel storage tanks, storing more than 5.46 million gallons of diesel fuel. At the 61st Avenue location, Amazon plans to build 170 emergency backup diesel generators, while 612 emergency backup generators will be installed at the Colorado Street facility. the total power capacity combined for both sites is 2,119 megawatts. On September 4, the Hobart Plan Commission tabled action until October on final plat approval of the development, requesting that Amazon make minor revisions to requested site improvements. According to Hobart City Engineer Alex Metz, the revisions include recording a legal description for a dedicated of a right-of-way involving a new pedestrian walkway around of the perimeter of the development, primarily along 61st Avenue and connecting to the local neighborhood. Jim Masters is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

artigo.texto: Carillon Tower Advisers, an investment management company, released its second-quarter 2026 investor letter for the "Carillon Eagle Small Cap Growth Fund". The letter can be downloaded here. Small-cap stocks rallied broadly in the second quarter, with the Russell 2000 Growth Index (+25.71%) outpacing Value +17.24%). Information Technology (+46.79%) led all sectors, supported by solid gains in Real Estate (+25.91%), Industrials (+25.80%), and Health Care (+25.54%). Consumer and defensive sectors lagged, while Energy (-2.40%) was the sole sector in the red. Following a strong quarter, the outlook for equity markets remains positive, supported by robust corporate profits and economic growth. However, midterm election uncertainties could introduce volatility, especially around data center development, a key economic driver. The $1 trillion data center spending boosts corporate earnings and supports ongoing AI infrastructure investments. Additionally, reviewing the Fund's top five holdings could help identify its best picks for 2026. In its second-quarter 2026 investor letter, Carillon Eagle Small Cap Growth Fund highlighted SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM). SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) designs and develops solutions for silicon timing systems, which contributed 1.68% to the fund's returns this quarter. On September 18, 2026, SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) closed at $614.27 per share. Over the past month, SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) returned 5.73%, and its shares are up 102.14% over the past year. SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) has a market capitalization of $18.40 billion, and its stock has traded within a 52-week range of $243.68 to $901.81. Carillon Eagle Small Cap Growth Fund stated the following regarding SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) in its Q2 2026 investor letter: "SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM), a provider of precision timing semiconductors, delivered earnings results well above expectations, driven by modern AI data center demand for AI-processing semiconductors, optical components, and network switches and servers. The company announced a plan to acquire the precision timing business of a competitor, strengthening SiTime's competitive position, gaining scale, and providing the company with a new installed base of customers to whom it can cross-sell its products." SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) is not on our list of the 40 Most Popular Stocks Among Hedge Funds. According to our database, 76 hedge fund portfolios held SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) at the end of the second quarter, compared to 54 in the previous quarter. While we acknowledge the potential of SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ:SITM) as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. If you're looking for an extremely undervalued AI stock that also stands to benefit significantly from Trump-era tariffs and the onshoring trend, see our free report on the best short-term AI stock.

artigo.texto: A flurry of legal activity during the past two weeks has surrounded a hyperscale data center under construction in Birmingham’s Oxmoor Valley neighborhood. Two new lawsuits related to the controversial project were filed last week, and on Thursday a judge consolidated three existing ones. The consolidated lawsuits allege the city of Birmingham illegally granted permits for the data center, which is being built in a mixed-use zoning district near homes and a school, and ask for a permanent end to the project. Residents and the Greater Birmingham Humane Society filed those suits. The humane society had planned to build a medical facility for traumatized animals on land adjacent to the data-center site. “There are a number of issues that are common to all the lawsuits, so it makes sense to have the same judge decide those common issues,” said Mark Parnell, an attorney for the residents. Jefferson County Circuit Court Judge Javan Patton Crayton has set the next hearing in the case for March 8. Meanwhile, construction at the 80-acre site is taking place six days a week, for 12 hours per day, with completion slated for 2028. Parnell said the consolidation won’t slow the judge’s decision. She had already scheduled the same hearing date for the case that had progressed furthest through the court system. Rob and Gail Sansome, a couple living near the site, filed that lawsuit and finished presenting evidence in court last month. Defendants in the lawsuit include data-center developer Nebius, the city of Birmingham and Hoar Construction. The two new lawsuits deal with the sale of the site and a billion-dollar tax abatement the Birmingham Industrial Development Board granted to Nebius. A Regions Financial shareholder filed the suit related to the property sale. Regions Bank is a former owner of the main parcel that became the Nebius data-center site, and James Anderson’s lawsuit alleges three transactions in just one day improperly inflated the price of the land. Anderson is suing a slew of people and companies on behalf of Regions. Last fall, Regions sold the property. Two subsequent sales of the same land on the same day raised its price by $66 million. Anderson alleges Regions executives acted negligently in not obtaining fair market value for the land. And that Nebius and companies involved in the sales transactions actively concealed from Regions that a pre-arranged deal was already in place to resell the property at a much higher price. The suit Anderson filed in Jefferson County Circuit Court claims that $66 million, plus interest and damages, are owed back to Regions. It names as defendants Regions executives, Nebius and three companies and their leaders who were involved in the sales transactions. Birmingham resident Terri Michal filed the other lawsuit, also in Jefferson County Circuit Court. It alleges the Birmingham Industrial Development Board held an illegal special meeting in May to award a 30-year, $3.2 billion tax break just before new state laws that limit such incentives went into effect. According to the lawsuit, the board failed to provide required public notice of the meeting, exceeded its authority in forgiving state and county taxes and didn’t conduct an independent cost-benefit analysis. Michal is asking the court to cancel the deal. Board chair David Perry has defended the deal as a win for the community. He said property taxes from the site were $200,000 a year before the Nebius project and will increase to $87 million a year.

artigo.texto: South Bend, Indiana Mayor James Mueller last week issued an executive order prohibiting city staff from entering into non-disclosure agreements about data centers. Mueller's order came a week after common council members Oliver Davis Jr. and Sherry Bolden-Simpson filed a bill banning NDAs. That came after Bolden-Simpson learned that Mueller's public works director, Eric Horvath, declined her invitation to speak to a council committee about the contents of wastewater that the Amazon data center is sending to the city's sewage treatment plant. Mueller said he didn't know until recently that Horvath and city engineer Kara Boyles had signed the agreements with Amazon in 2023. But he said he wasn't bothered because unlike St. Joseph County, the city has a limited role in the project and he says the agreement with Amazon has cleared the Board of Public Works process. "People get ideas when they hear the term but in actuality nothing was prevented from being released by this agreement," Muller said. Still, Davis says he'll push the bill, which is set for first reading Sept. 28. If it passes, Mueller says he'll veto it because the council, as city government's legislative branch, would be exceeding its statutory power in trying to tell the mayor, the executive branch, how to execute contracts. artigo.texto: In a move that challenges Orange Juicer and Buick Electra for the highly coveted Best Name in the EV Business title, a new venture between CATL and Octopus Energy called “Swaptopus” has been formed to build out a European battery swap network for commercial trucks. First announced at Octopus Energy’s Energy Tech Summit back in June, the Swaptopus concept got a bit of a boost at last week’s IAA Transportation event in the form of TECTRANS II, a next-generation commercial vehicle battery solution built specifically to serve as a modular, universal electric truck platform that promises to eliminate long charge times and battery life concerns that have remained key barriers to commercial fleet electrification. According to the original CATL press release for TECTRANS II, the new battery system improves fleet economics in three ways: - Higher energy density – boasting a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, around 13% above the industry average, the battery enables vehicles to carry approximately 0.6 tonnes of additional payload at the same battery capacity. - Longer Range, Faster Charging – its maximum configuration offers up to 1,000 km of range and 80% charging in 25 minutes with megawatt-level fast charging, minimizing downtime on long-haul routes. - Higher energy efficiency – the world’s first full-tab low-impedance design enables 96% system round-trip efficiency (RTE), reducing charging losses and delivering more usable energy for daily operations. “Commercial vehicle electrification will unfold over more than a decade,” said Zhu Lingbo, CTO of CATL Global Business Unit. “With our deep technological expertise and long-term commitment, CATL is ready to be the most reliable partner for customers worldwide and for the global electrification of freight transport.” Once in full swing, CATL and Octopus claim their proposed network could support 300,000+ electric trucks and unlock more than £30 billion in private investment while creating jobs and reducing Europe’s dependence on imported oil by replacing fossil fuels with sustainably produced electricity. It takes a village Along with Octopus, CATL announced that it’s signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with global shipping giants DHL Group that aims to accelerate the electrification and decarbonization of road freight transportation across Europe by engaging a broad coalition of industry stakeholders that includes Xiaomi-backed mobile power plant specialists Quibo Energy and FleetBoost, who provide mobile charging and battery energy storage systems (BESS), including the “FleetBooster” trailer (shown, above) which integrates CATL battery technology. This level of collaboration points to an industry united in a single goal: avoiding high fuel prices decarbonization. Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business, emphasized that sort of “holistic” approach to fleet decarbonization, saying, “by combining real logistics demand with vehicles, charging, energy storage, battery swapping and lifecycle services, CATL plans to work with DHL and other ecosystem partners to create practical and scalable solutions for zero-emission freight.” For DHL Group, the partnership is a critical next-step toward its corporate goal of achieving net-zero logistics-related emissions by 2050, following other steps we’ve covered in these pages here and here. artigo.texto: Lais Carregosa, Marisa Wanzeller e Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA Grandes consumidores, em especial data centers, têm procurado as redes de distribuição para se conectar ao sistema elétrico e evitar a competição por margem de escoamento na transmissão, em uma espécie de “drible” no ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico), afirmaram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Com esse movimento, os agentes conseguem evitar o pagamento de garantias prévias antes da certeza de que conseguirão espaço na rede elétrica. O aumento dos casos tem chamado a atenção do operador e do planejamento, por meio da EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética), que relataram a situação à ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica). A suspeita é que haja também um movimento especulativo, em que os agentes reservam capacidade na rede de distribuição, sem garantia de que os projetos de fato se viabilizarão. O ONS e a EPE defendem a compatibilização da conexão na distribuição com a transmissão, que tem uma política de acesso própria, a Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) – criada em dezembro de 2025. Nesse caso, seria preciso alterar as regras dos procedimentos de rede, o Prodist, o que exige atuação da ANEEL. Gargalos Do ponto de vista dos agentes, o movimento é uma consequência direta da criação de uma política pública estabelecida sem conversar com o setor da economia afetado. Para Luciano Fialho, vice-presidente da Scala Data Center, essa falta de diálogo levou a uma “solução que não resolve nada”. Com isso, os empreendedores estão buscando formas de solucionar os problemas que enfrentam. Ele aponta que a Pnast impõe dois grandes gargalos aos projetos de data center: 1) aportes milionários de garantias prévias, sem a certeza de conexão dos empreendimentos; 2) poucas janelas para solicitar conexão ao sistema, as chamadas temporadas de acesso, que não acompanham a celeridade necessária para o setor digital. Fialho destaca ainda que nem todos os empreendimentos têm a possibilidade de se conectar às distribuidoras, sendo uma alternativa apenas para cargas menores. Além disso, ele reforça que as próprias distribuidoras podem negar a conexão se o ONS constatar que não tem espaço na rede de transmissão. Assim, a solução passaria por acelerar as obras e entregar mais linhas de transmissão, aponta. Para João Carlos Mello, CEO da Thymos, “o todo não está bem desenhado” e é necessária uma costura mais efetiva das regras de conexão, com participação “mais efetiva” da EPE. Ele aponta que a transição do modelo de conexão antigo para a Pnast foi “muito abrupta” e causou estranhamento no setor. “Ninguém tem espaço infinito na rede para as cargas entrarem, mas acho que tinha que dar uma melhorada nesse protocolo. O que era antes organizado pelo MME [Ministério de Minas e Energia], ONS, ANEEL e EPE, agora ficou só com o ONS”, pondera. Capacidade limitada A entrada de grandes cargas na distribuição depende da capacidade contratada, já que as concessionárias de distribuição também celebram CUSTs (Contratos de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão). Segundo as regras, as distribuidoras não precisam competir por margem, tendo o acesso assegurado. No entanto, como destaca o CEO da PSR, Luiz Barroso, à Agência iNFRA, já há casos de negativas de aumento dos montantes de capacidade contratados por falta de margem no sistema. “Muita carga se conectando diretamente nas distribuidoras faz com que elas necessitem solicitar ao ONS aumentar o sua contrato de uso do sistema de transmissão, o que pode ser um problema”, ressaltou Barroso. “O tradeoff entre conectar na distribuição ou na transmissão é bem relevante e economicamente importante para as cargas e o sistema”. Um interlocutor com conhecimento do assunto afirma que, com o aumento de carga na rede de distribuição, as concessionárias estão tendo que pagar penalidades de ultrapassagem do montante contratado junto às transmissoras. O executivo destaca que, por conta dessas restrições, grandes cargas podem ter o seu pedido de acesso na distribuição negado. Regulação A ANEEL disse que tem trabalhado em aprimoramentos regulatórios a fim de dar “sinais adequados para que os consumidores optem por determinado sistema de acesso considerando seus diferentes requisitos”. Em nota enviada à Agência iNFRA, a reguladora aponta que as mudanças também visam garantir a efetiva implantação dos empreendimentos para dar previsibilidade ao planejamento do setor e evitar ocupação ineficiente da capacidade das redes. O tema está na Agenda Regulatória 2026-2027 e tem sido tratado em diferentes processos, também passando por tomada de subsídios. A agência destacou que está acompanhando as discussões setoriais sobre o tema e que, até o momento, tem sido pautada pela análise dos casos concretos, “considerando que o atendimento por redes de distribuição continua sujeito a limitações técnicas, critérios regulatórios de conexão e, quando aplicável, à participação financeira do acessante nas obras necessárias”. Trabalho duplo O presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, defendeu a necessidade de compatibilização de acesso em evento no Rio de Janeiro na última semana. Ele destacou que a quantidade de pedidos de conexão de data centers na distribuição tem se aproximado dos números do sistema de transmissão. Isso leva as distribuidoras a procurar a EPE solicitando estudos de expansão, o que, segundo Thiago, causa um trabalho “duplo” do planejamento. “Posso estar trabalhando duas vezes porque vou estar trabalhando para expandir a transmissão, […] mas esses estudos estão concorrendo com os estudos de expansão [solicitados pela] distribuidora, porque ela celebra esses acordos de acesso, mas sem necessariamente ter uma garantia financeira”, afirmou.
