artigo.texto: A Fort Worth-area Texas lawmaker plans to introduce legislation on a hot button topic: data centers. After co-authoring laws regulating the use of artificial intelligence within state and local government agencies, state Sen. Tan Parker, R-Flower Mound, is crafting bills relating to the fast-growing technology hubs. Public outcry around the data centers has led the Fort Worth City Council to vote for a moratorium, and Gov. Greg Abbott has introduced a temporary moratorium. Though he did not provide any specifics, Parker said at the Fort Worth Chamber of Commerce Leaders in Government series on Sept. 17 that the legislation will be informed by his experience during the Barnett Shale natural gas drilling growth in the early part of this century. Then, Parker was representing communities in north Tarrant and Denton counties. “One of the bills I will carry next session will be a framework that is based on historical experience with other industries,” he said. That initial experience with the oil and gas industry setting up drilling sites in populated areas was not good, he said. “They came in arrogant, out of touch, tone deaf,” he said. “They were not paying attention to local interests.” Parker said he worked with the oil and gas industry to change that behavior and get them involved with and answering community questions. Parker also authored an amendment to a bill requiring oil and gas companies to publicly disclose the chemicals used in fracking. Parker said he plans to write data center legislation that establishes public discussion and transparency requirements. “I don’t mandate things on business,” he said. “It will incentivize them. I will encourage good behavior, and that’s what we did at that time (during the Barnett Shale).” While Parker works on plans to file a bill when the Texas Legislature meets starting Jan. 12, he also made clear he believes data centers are key to the future success of the state. “I’ll be very direct and I’ll be very candid,” he said. “I believe that we must continue to develop data centers in Texas and, frankly, across the country. Why? Big picture, it’s essential to our survival.” Parker said national security and economic security require the state and the nation to take a leadership role in data centers. “If we don’t win, if we’re not dominant when it comes to technology, we will lose this state and we lose this nation,” he said. Steve Montgomery, president and CEO of the Fort Worth Chamber of Commerce, said Parker’s role in the legislature is key to the city’s economic future. “From a public policy perspective, state Sen. Parker sits at the intersection of transportation, education and workforce — three areas that are fundamental to Fort Worth’s long-term economic growth and prosperity,” Montgomery said. “He is a strong champion for our region and for the economic future of Texas.” Parker is no stranger to crafting technology-related legislation. In the past two legislative sessions, Parker, along with state Rep. Giovanni Capriglione, R-Southlake, has authored bills related to artificial intelligence. Last session, Parker authored and Capriglione co-sponsored Senate Bill 1964 that established Texas’ first comprehensive artificial intelligence governance framework for public agencies, which was later signed into law. As chair of the Senate Committee on Transportation, Parker is key to helping the state transportation system keep up with its growth. There are big hurdles to clear in transportation, he said. “We have many tens of billions of additional investment we need to make in our transportation infrastructure over the course of the next decade,” he said. That money has not been found yet, he said. “We’re going to live within our means, but we’re going to grow our way out of that problem, and we’re going to find creative ways to continue to invest in that transportation infrastructure for the good of the state of Texas,” he said. Parker, who grew up in Fort Worth and graduated from Nolan Catholic High School was first elected in 2006 to the House and was elected to the Senate in 2022. Bob Francis is business editor for the Fort Worth Report. Contact him at bob.francis@fortworthreport.org. News decisions are made independently of our board members and financial supporters. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no LAWINFRA SUMMIT 2026: data centers podem consumir 30% da energia do país, diz Marcio Rea, diretor geral do ONS Publicado 18/09/2026 • 18:29 | Atualizado há 3 dias ALERTA DE MERCADO: KEY POINTS Os pedidos para instalação de data centers recebidos pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) entre 2025 e 2026 chegam a quase 20 GW, volume equivalente a cerca de 30% da energia do país, afirmou Marcio Rea, diretor-geral do ONS, em entrevista nesta sexta-feira (18) durante o Lawinfra Summit Brasília 2026, evento em parceria com o Times Brasil – Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC. Segundo Rea, a expansão da inteligência artificial tende a acelerar ainda mais a procura por infraestrutura de data centers, levando o operador a analisar a capacidade da rede e as regiões com condições para receber os novos empreendimentos. “A questão de data center, nós tivemos aproximadamente quase 20 gigas de pedido de 2025 para 2026 no ONS. Isso representa 30% da nossa energia. É muito bom para o Brasil”, afirmou. Para o diretor-geral do ONS, o crescimento da demanda por data centers é um movimento estrutural, que acompanhará a expansão das aplicações de inteligência artificial e exigirá preparação do sistema elétrico. “Hoje em dia, com o avanço da IA, da inteligência artificial, serão muito demandados os data centers. Na medida do possível, nós estamos vendo na nossa rede as possibilidades nas regiões para a gente instalar os data centers”, explicou. Rea afirmou que o processo de preparação da rede está avançando e classificou a expansão desse tipo de infraestrutura como uma transformação sem perspectiva de reversão. “Está caminhando bem, é um avanço que a gente vê que não tem mais retorno. Esse é o futuro do país”, disse. Além do crescimento do consumo de energia, o ONS acompanha os possíveis impactos do El Niño sobre a operação do sistema elétrico brasileiro. Segundo Rea, equipes do operador já trabalham há algum tempo na preparação para o fenômeno climático. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC “Certamente vai ser um período não muito simples, complicado até, posso dizer. A temperatura está mudando muito”, afirmou. Entre as principais preocupações estão chuvas intensas, tempestades e ventos fortes capazes de atingir a infraestrutura de transmissão. Rea citou episódios com ventos de até 200 km/h como exemplo do risco enfrentado pelas redes. “A gente tem exemplos de chuvas e tempestades, com ventos de 200 quilômetros por hora. Isso prejudica as nossas linhas de transmissão, as nossas torres”, explicou. O diretor ressaltou que o ONS trabalha com previsão e antecedência para reduzir o tempo de resposta diante de eventuais danos. “A gente vem acompanhando passo a passo e sempre trabalhando com previsão e com antecedência para poder, o mais rápido possível, consertar essas redes quando elas estiverem sendo danificadas”, acrescentou. Rea também apontou a aproximação entre o setor elétrico e o Judiciário como uma ferramenta para solucionar pendências que podem atrasar decisões e projetos. Segundo ele, algumas questões permaneceram sem solução durante anos e começaram a avançar com maior diálogo institucional. “A aproximação nossa com o Judiciário, o Judiciário conosco, tem resolvido muitas pendências que vinham sendo arrastadas por anos”, afirmou. O diretor citou uma iniciativa realizada no centro de operação do ONS em Brasília, que recebeu representantes do Tribunal Regional Federal da 1ª Região (TRF1) para apresentar as dificuldades enfrentadas na operação cotidiana do sistema elétrico. Rea acrescentou que o operador pretende ampliar esse diálogo institucional e levar integrantes do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) para conhecer de perto os desafios operacionais do setor, permitindo maior compreensão das questões técnicas envolvidas nas decisões que afetam o sistema elétrico. 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parabólicas canal 562 🔷 ONLINE: www.timesbrasil.com.br | YouTube 🔷 FAST Channels: Samsung TV Plus, LG Channels, TCL Channels, Pluto TV, Roku, Zapping | Novos Streamings

artigo.texto: State Rep. Phillip Ensler says his record of working across the aisle and focus on pocketbook issues can help him reach Alabama voters who might not typically consider a Democrat in a statewide race. Ensler, a Montgomery Democrat and candidate for lieutenant governor, pointed to his legislative work on taxes, mental health and public safety as he makes his case to voters ahead of the November election. “The case is that I’ve been in the Legislature, I’ve gotten things done,” Ensler told 256 Today. “I have sponsored legislation to cut people’s taxes. I have my efforts to expand access to mental health services, so I know what it takes to get things done.” Ensler said affordability is at the center of his campaign, including eliminating the remaining state sales tax on groceries, cutting income taxes for working- and middle-class Alabamians and restoring an exemption on overtime pay. “The biggest thing is putting more money in people’s pockets, and there are a lot of ways we can do that,” he said. His other priorities include expanding access to health care and mental health services, investing in public safety and increasing support for public education. Ensler said Medicaid expansion could provide additional support to hospitals, particularly those serving rural communities. On education, he called for teacher pay raises, expanded access to literacy coaches and additional college and career counseling. Data centers and Flock cameras Ensler has also called for a moratorium on new data centers until Alabama establishes additional protections addressing their effects on surrounding communities. “I’m all for technology and data centers are something that we need to have, but put more guardrails in place to make sure that it’s not hurting people’s electrical rates, their water and noise pollution,” he said. Ensler said he has heard concerns in rural communities about noise, wildlife and other potential effects of large data center developments. “People who live in rural areas, they have chosen to live there for a reason, and they don’t necessarily want the noise pollution,” he said. “They don’t want it hurting the wildlife there.” He also raised concerns about nondisclosure agreements involving local officials during the recruitment of data center projects. “I’m not opposed to having them entirely, but at least having more parameters in place,” Ensler said. “The fact that local officials are signing non-disclosure agreements where they’re then keeping things secret, I mean, that’s crazy. If you want to be an elected official, you have to respond. You have to give information to your constituents.” Ensler said he favors a similar guardrail approach to Flock license plate reader cameras. While he cited concerns about misuse of the technology and the handling of data by private companies, Ensler said license plate readers have also proven useful to law enforcement in cases involving kidnappings and other serious crimes. “It is a helpful tool for law enforcement,” Ensler said. “So similar to data centers, we should have guardrails in place. The Legislature should pass legislation that regulates them more, but doesn’t completely ban them.” “The biggest thing for me is that hearing from law enforcement who have or are using it in the right ways, I wouldn’t want to take the tool completely away from them,” he added. “But people do have very real legitimate concerns, and we have to do better than what it is right now.” Working across the aisle Ensler is facing Republican John Wahl in the lieutenant governor’s race. While the two agree on eliminating the remaining state grocery tax, Ensler pointed to his experience as a public school teacher, attorney and state legislator and said he feels Wahl lacks the experience needed for the office. “I’ve worked on legislation for years, have been in the Legislature where I’ve gotten things done for people,” Ensler said. “You know, I love butterflies. They’re beautiful creatures,” he said. “But being a butterfly farmer is not necessarily relevant experience to get things done in the Legislature,” Ensler said, referring to Wahl’s background as a professional butterfly farmer in western Limestone County. With Republicans holding large majorities in the Alabama Legislature, Ensler said relationships he has developed across party lines would be central to advancing his priorities as lieutenant governor. He pointed to his work with Republican lawmakers on Bo’s Law, dealing with animal cruelty, and legislation banning Glock switches. “I have the relationships on the Republican side and definitely with Minority Leader Bobby Singleton and rank and file,” Ensler said. “I would go in, not even on day one in January, but November 4th, be ready to hit the ground running because I have those relationships on both sides of the aisle.” Ensler also said he believes increased Democratic engagement in Alabama this year will carry into the general election. He said his campaign is traveling to all 67 counties and trying to reach voters across party lines. “I get everywhere I go, I hear from Republicans who say, ‘I voted for Donald Trump. I had to vote Republican, but I am going to cross over and vote for you,’” Ensler said. He said data centers and utility costs are among the issues he hears about from those voters. “People are hurting. They’re having a hard time,” Ensler said. “They’re tired of things that aren’t working in their favor.” Got a tip for OTR? artigo.texto: LAHORE: Pakistan’s rapidly expanding solar energy sector, investment opportunities in solar photovoltaic (PV) and battery energy storage systems (BESS), evolving net-metering policies and the challenges facing the renewable energy industry will come under discussion at the 3rd International SolarPower Conclave and Solar Technology Excellence Awards 2026, scheduled to be held on September 24, 2026, in Lahore. The conclave will bring together policymakers, government representatives, energy experts, solar industry leaders, technology providers, investors, consultants and other stakeholders to discuss the changing dynamics of Pakistan’s energy sector and the growing role of solar power and energy storage in the country’s future energy mix. Governor Punjab Sardar Saleem Haider Khan will attend the event as chief guest. The gathering will also feature senior representatives and leading professionals from the government, academia and private sector, providing a platform for dialogue on policy, investment, technology and the future direction of Pakistan’s solar industry. The event will feature two key panel discussions. Panel Discussion I, titled ‘Investment Opportunities in Solar PV and Battery Storage System (BESS)’, will focus on the growing investment potential in solar generation and energy storage, emerging business models, commercial and industrial applications, financing opportunities and the role of BESS in improving energy reliability and flexibility. Panel Discussion II, titled ‘Solar in Pakistan — Challenges, Policy Reforms & the Way Forward’, will examine the key challenges confronting the solar sector, including regulatory and policy issues, market developments, grid integration and the evolving framework for distributed generation and net metering. Industry experts will also discuss possible policy reforms and pathways for sustainable growth of the solar market. The conclave will also feature technical discussions focusing on the latest solar technologies, Battery Energy Storage Systems, system efficiency, grid integration, energy management and technological developments shaping the next phase of Pakistan’s renewable energy transition. The event will also host the Solar Technology Excellence Awards 2026, recognising companies and professionals for their contributions to the development, deployment and advancement of solar energy technologies and solutions in Pakistan. The awards will provide an opportunity to acknowledge innovation, technological excellence and industry contributions across the country’s growing renewable energy ecosystem.

artigo.texto: By Siddarth Sivaraman Voters in 18 Ohio municipalities and townships will decide the future of data centers in their communities this Election Day. The deadline to file charter amendment petitions with Ohio’s city councils in time to make the Nov. 3 ballot passed Sept. 4. Registered voters in charter cities can file charter amendment petitions at any time, but if the next regular election is less than 60 days or more than 120 days away, a special election is held instead. Nine petitions — in Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, and Upper Sandusky — mirror a statewide effort to ban data centers that draw over 25 megawatts of energy per month. Organizers with Conserve Ohio are hoping the statewide petition will make the 2027 ballot after missing a signature deadline in July. “Conserve Ohio is continuing to organize with many more communities across Ohio to enact local data center bans and to create local government structures that are by the people and for the people,” the group said in a statement Tuesday. Piqua petition organizer Alisha Lange said she became politically engaged in 2023, when a battery plant approved by the city gave her and others living nearby long-term health issues. She pleaded with politicians who represented Piqua, including U.S. Rep. Mike Carey, with little success. Now, she says those private meetings are a waste of time. After Meta announced plans for a data center in Piqua that would demand around 1,400 megawatts of power, she gathered enough signatures for a petition to recall Piqua’s mayor and two city commissioners, she said. Two more petitions filed Monday would change the city’s signature requirements for recalls to match state law and strike down a city agreement to power the data center. “When we’re out getting signatures, people come up, and they all want to share something. They’re all upset,” she said. “It’s like some fellowship … Even though the data centers are driving us apart, the petitions are bringing us together.” Ohio has the fourth-most operational data centers in the country, according to an analysis by Pew Research Center published in April, and tech giants and data center developers want to build dozens more across the state. 14 of the 18 communities with petitions filed for the November election have received formal proposals for new data center projects. A Gallup poll in May found that over 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their area, and a Bowling Green State University poll found that a similar percentage of Ohioans support a data center moratorium. Opponents list a variety of grievances, like rising utility bills, negative effects on the environment, or concerns about artificial intelligence. Different petitions tackle the issue in different ways. While gathering signatures for the 25-megawatt petition, many Piqua residents told Lange they would rather ban data centers entirely. That became another petition, and it now has enough signatures for a special election, she said. Urbana voters will decide on a charter amendment to ban data centers that draw over 7.5 megawatts of power, and Hubbard is the only Ohio city that will vote on a full ban this November. Pleasant Township resident Jen Belt lives within two miles of a proposed data center in Grove City. She was part of a petition drive to make any new heavy industrial project in Grove City — not just data centers — subject to a citywide vote. While she signed the statewide Conserve Ohio petition, Belt said Grove City organizers decided against advocating for a local data center ban because they were worried about litigation. “If the state would just ban these hyperscale facilities in general, that would be awesome,” she said. “ … I just feel like they need to sell it to us and come here responsibly.” Two Adams County townships located on the Ohio River will vote on zoning plans meant to preserve their “rural and agricultural character” in response to a potential data center that would use more than 20 times as much power as the county itself. Two counties over, Wilmington residents proposed a 33-page zoning ordinance after Amazon Web Services announced plans for a $4 billion data center on land next to a local subdivision. Residents have filed multiple federal lawsuits over the city’s handling of the project, and four referendums on Wilmington’s November ballot would strike down zoning ordinances passed by the city. The city’s alternative zoning ordinance is the fourth ballot measure related to data centers to go in front of the Ohio Supreme Court in the last month. A referendum against a proposed data center in Ashville and a 25-megawatt data center ban in Trenton will be on the general election ballot after legal battles, and a trio of Sidney petitions related to data centers will likely become a special election after the state’s highest court ruled that the city clerk illegally blocked them. The Clinton County Board of Elections rejected Wilmington residents’ petition to put the zoning ordinance on the ballot after determining that it would create new ways for residents to sue, which would go beyond Wilmington’s municipal power. Wilmington resident Quintin Koger Kidd, a longtime IT professional who helped write the ordinance, said the disputed clause only restates existing state and local law. If the court rules against residents in their lawsuit challenging the board of elections’ decision, Koger Kidd said he plans to circulate new petitions without the clause. artigo.texto: Why this conservative Maine town is trying to ban data centers DOVER-FOXCROFT — Dover-Foxcroft is the latest town in rural Maine that may pass a ban on building large-scale data centers as backlash against big tech sweeps the state. Developers are unlikely to build such a project in the town, which has limited infrastructure and ordinances already on the books to regulate development. But with support from a statewide environmental group, the rural community’s Select Board is on track to pass a six-month ban on large-scale data center development by the end of September. It’s another in a string of small, conservative towns backing temporary bans of data centers, a movement that sprouted up on the left but has quickly become more bipartisan. Maine has few data centers, the warehouse-like facilities that provide computing power for a variety of uses, including AI. News stories from away have Mainers concerned that such centers may crop up and use significant amounts of water and electricity, driving up utility prices. Since Gov. Janet Mills vetoed legislation that would have created a statewide moratorium on some new data center projects this spring, towns are taking up the issue themselves. Dover-Foxcroft is no exception. Select Board Chair Stephen Grammont said despite the low odds of a data center being built in town, jitters about the projects are “not a make-believe concern.” “We’re not high up on the mega data center list of places to locate,” Grammont said. “I think what’s concerned a lot of people is that there have been some surprises.” It wouldn’t be the first Maine town to be surprised by plans for a data center; officials in Jay only found out about a proposed project after the plan was well underway and reported on by the Bangor Daily News. Dover-Foxcroft’s proposed ban was pushed in part by Carole Boothroyd, chair of the town’s Climate Action Advisory Committee and wife of a Democratic candidate for state Legislature. Boothroyd sought and received advice from Maine Conservation Voters, an environmental group, as she drafted the proposed ordinance. The group worked closely with legislators during the last session to pass the statewide moratorium that Mills ultimately vetoed in the spring. As towns began weighing moratoriums this summer, the group posted on its social media accounts asking local officials to contact them if they needed advice drafting policy. “We were very, very disappointed by the governor’s veto of that bill, because we know that we need time to understand the impacts of these large-scale data centers,” Maggie Somers, the group’s outreach director, said. “That’s really when this got kicked into high gear, and I started working closely with these communities to see how we could help.” Boothroyd and Somers said Dover-Foxcroft’s proposed ban, which could be extended beyond six months, is meant to give the town cover while the state’s Data Center Advisory Council studies ways to regulate the projects, a process Maine Conservation Voters is involved in. “We’re already gearing up for this next [legislative] session and making sure that we have legislation prepared,” Somers said. Whatever bills on data centers are passed will not have to go through Mills, who is retiring. Those running to replace her, Republican Bobby Charles, Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett, have all said they would sign data center moratoriums. In Dover-Foxcroft, Grammont said it isn’t just Boothroyd and the conservationists who are supportive of a local ban. “I think it’s across the board,” he said. “We want to make sure that we, the town’s people, don’t get screwed.” Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

artigo.texto: Vena Energy’s Tailem Bend BESS 3 in South Australia and EnergyAustralia and Banpu Energy Australia’s Wooreen BESS in Victoria have both entered the Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) Market Management System (MMS). This is according to Geoff Eldridge of GPE NEMLog, who tracks project data across Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM). Both units, known in AEMO’s system as TB3B1 and WOORB1 respectively, entered the MMS on 15 September 2026. Eldridge noted that MMS registration is not the same as full commercial operation but marks a step that allows a unit to move into testing and commissioning ahead of normal market operation. Tailem Bend BESS 3 is registered with an operating maximum of 204MW, a registered capacity of 263MW, and 408MWh of storage, giving it a two-hour storage duration and a ramp rate of 82MW per minute. Tailem Bend BESS 3 extends Vena Energy’s cluster of South Australian projects Tailem Bend BESS 3 is located around 2.5km southeast of the town of Tailem Bend and approximately 89km east-southeast of Adelaide, connecting to the NEM through ElectraNet’s nearby Tailem Bend Substation. It sits alongside two existing Vena Energy assets at the same site. Vena Energy, the renewable energy development arm of Singapore-headquartered Vena Group, began construction of the standalone project in December 2025, with commissioning scheduled for 2027. It is the developer’s third BESS project in Australia, following the 100MW/150MWh Wandoan South BESS in Queensland. The project follows Vena Energy’s completion of a smaller battery at the same location. Vena added a 41.5MW battery to its existing 87MW solar plant at Tailem Bend in January 2025, completing what the company calls its Tailem Bend 2 Hybrid Project and lifting the combined grid output of its two co-located solar plants from 182MW to 223.5MW. South Australia sources around 75% of its annual electricity demand from wind and solar, and is targeting 100% net renewable energy by the end of 2027. Wooreen BESS advances toward 2027 as Yallourn’s replacement in the Latrobe Valley Wooreen BESS is being developed at Hazelwood North in Victoria’s Latrobe Valley, adjacent to EnergyAustralia’s existing Jeeralang Power Station and approximately 138km east-southeast of Melbourne, placing it within a growing cluster of storage and network infrastructure across Gippsland. EnergyAustralia, an Australian energy generator-retailer, reached financial close on the project in February 2025 and began construction days later, with the battery storage system designed to enter service before the retirement of its 1,450MW Yallourn coal-fired power station, scheduled for mid-2028. In July 2025, EnergyAustralia sold a 50% share in the project to Thailand-based Banpu Public Company, trading in Australia as Banpu Energy Australia, in a deal worth in the region of AU$700 million (US$490 million). Finnish marine and energy technology group Wärtsilä was contracted to supply the battery hardware, engineering, commissioning and a 15-year service agreement, using its Quantum High Energy units and GEMS Digital Energy Platform. Wärtsilä completed delivery and installation of all 1,038 Quantum units at the site in July 2026, with the system designed to operate in grid-forming mode to provide synthetic inertia as coal-fired generation retires from the Victorian grid. Zenviron, a joint venture between engineering group Monadelphous and renewable energy developer ZEM Energy, was awarded the balance-of-plant contract for the project in February 2025, covering design, construction, installation and commissioning. Tilt Renewables is the project’s developer and commercial operations for Wooreen are targeted for 2027. Never miss an Australian energy storage story. artigo.texto: Politics & Government Calls Intensify For AI Data Center Ban In Newark, Local Groups Push For Moratorium Data centers will make an already heavy environmental burden worse, while offering little benefit to the people who live there, critics say. NEWARK, NJ — Calls for a temporary ban on artificial intelligence data centers continue to grow louder in New Jersey’s largest city. Two local advocacy groups – the South Ward Environmental Alliance (SWEA) and the Ironbound Community Corporation (ICC) – are asking for a one‑year moratorium on AI data center development in Newark. Supporters of data centers say they’re needed to keep the state competitive in the rapidly growing artificial intelligence industry. But critics allege that they consume too much power and water – jacking up utility bills for local residents. Find out what's happening in Newarkfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The campaign from advocates comes as the Newark City Council moves towards a possible ban. Earlier this month, the city council voted in favor of a resolution that supports a 12-month moratorium on the development or expansion of data centers in Newark. For now, the resolution doesn’t make any changes to city code, which would have to be approved through a local ordinance. READ MORE: Newark City Council Takes Stance On Data Centers With New Resolution Find out what's happening in Newarkfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The move was a step in the right direction, advocates said. According to the SWEA and ICC, a temporary ban would allow time for more research into the potential impact on the local community. It would also give the public a chance to give feedback, and for the city to roll out “clear, protective standards” for any future data center proposals. Here’s why advocates are calling for a ban, they said: “AI data centers–particularly large‑scale, AI‑focused facilities–pose significant risks to overburdened communities. These facilities consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, generate substantial air and noise pollution, and often operate with limited transparency. Newark’s frontline neighborhoods, including the South Ward and Ironbound, already face some of the nation’s worst cumulative environmental burdens, including elevated asthma rates, cardiovascular illness, and chronic exposure to industrial emissions.” “Newark’s frontline neighborhoods have long been asked to absorb the harms of polluting industries,” said Leah Owens, ports and policy analyst at the SWEA. “AI data centers threaten to intensify those burdens while offering little benefit to the people who live here,” Owens said. Alejandra Torres, assistant director of advocacy and organizing at the ICC, said a moratorium is essential for studying the potential added environmental harms on already overburdened communities. “Industrial development that exposes our communities to more pollution must be seriously contended with to ensure it does not sacrifice our communities’ health,” Torres said. South Ward Councilman Patrick Council – a supporter of the city council’s resolution – said he stands with the two groups in their fight to temporarily put the brakes on data centers in Newark. “This moratorium is an essential step toward protecting Newark residents, our environment, and the future of our neighborhoods while we fully examine the potential impacts of data centers,” he said. Newark wouldn’t be the first New Jersey city to pass a local law prohibiting data centers. Dozens of municipalities in New Jersey have passed full or partial bans in the past year, including Jersey City and Union. Send local news tips and correction requests to eric.kiefer@patch.com. artigo.texto: Gerando resumo Anitta foi coroada rainha de bateria da Grande Rio no último domingo, 20, durante evento realizado na quadra da escola, em Duque de Caxias, na Baixada Fluminense. A cantora foi ovacionada pela comunidade da agremiação e recebeu a coroa das mãos de Eloína dos Leopardos, considerada a primeira rainha de bateria do carnaval brasileiro. Leia mais - Grammy Latino 2026: Anitta, Marina Sena e Ana Castela são indicadas; confira brasileiros na lista - Thiago Lacerda e Vanessa Lóes se separam após 25 anos: ‘Além do luto há uma jornada linda’ - Ludmilla diz que vai à Justiça após áudio enviado a fãs ser divulgado fora de contexto; escute A cerimônia ocorreu durante a final da disputa pelo samba-enredo que a escola levará à Sapucaí em 2027. Anitta assume o posto que foi ocupado por Virginia Fonseca no carnaval 2026. Antes da coroação, a cantora fez uma apresentação preparada para a ocasião, com troca de figurino, bailarinos e performances. O show começou com Você Já Sabe, faixa do álbum Equilibrivm II. Depois, ela cantou Meia-Noite e Feitiço, parceria com Mart’nália. “É muito emocionante. Tem tantos anos que eu não venho aqui em Duque de Caxias. Voltar desse jeito está sendo uma emoção que vocês não podem imaginar”, afirmou a cantora após a coroação. Na sequência, Anitta também agradeceu à comunidade da escola e falou sobre sua permanência no posto de rainha de bateria. “Se algum dia vocês acharem que não é isso, eu vou sair com a mesma gratidão e felicidade. Mas, se vocês quiserem que eu fique, vou ficando o quanto vocês quiserem”, declarou. Mudança na passagem da coroa A coroação também marcou uma mudança no protocolo tradicional da escola. Virginia Fonseca, que deixou o posto após o carnaval 2026, havia se colocado à disposição para participar da passagem de coroa, mas a cerimônia não contou com a presença da influenciadora. Segundo a assessoria de Virginia, a alteração ocorreu a pedido de Anitta. “Houve uma exigência da próxima rainha para que a passagem de coroa não acontecesse, e a escola optou por acatar. Desde sempre, Virginia respeitou a soberania da escola e assim seguirá”, declarou a equipe da influenciadora. Anitta também disputou samba-enredo Além da coroação, a cantora participou da disputa pelo samba-enredo da Grande Rio para o carnaval 2027. Ela é uma das compositoras de uma das quatro obras que chegaram à final. No entanto, a escola ficou com a composição de Deré & Cia e levará para a Avenida o enredo Sankofa Tabon – Os Retornados da Costa do Ouro e a Estrela Negra da Liberdade, que aborda a história de africanos escravizados que conquistaram a liberdade no Brasil e retornaram ao continente africano. A cerimônia teve ainda uma encenação sobre a trajetória de Anitta, com a participação de personagens representando orixás. Entre os famosos presentes estavam Brunna Gonçalves, Bruna Griphao, Alane Dias, Quitéria Chagas, Jaquelline Grohalski, Adriana Bombom, Mariana Goldfarb e David Brazil.

artigo.texto: Data centers: Brasil precisa resolver o gargalo da infraestrutura elétrica Em artigo à CNN Infra, João Carlos de Oliveira Mello alerta que, se conexão à rede demorar, investimentos podem procurar outros destinos A inteligência artificial colocou os data centers no centro de uma disputa global por investimentos. Países capazes de oferecer energia competitiva, segurança de suprimento, conectividade e regras previsíveis terão vantagem na economia digital. O Brasil reúne atributos importantes nessa corrida, em especial uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável. Porém, hoje há um descompasso entre a velocidade dos investimentos digitais e a expansão da infraestrutura necessária para atendê-los. Um data center pode entrar em operação em cerca de dois anos. Os reforços na estrutura do sistema de transmissão podem exigir de cinco a sete anos. Para projetos que disputam capital em escala global, essa diferença é decisiva. Se a conexão à rede demora, o investimento procura outro destino. O problema não está na falta de energia. O Brasil dispõe de grande potencial de geração renovável, mas enfrenta restrições na rede, tanto para escoar a produção quanto para conectar novas cargas. A chegada de empreendimentos que demandam centenas de megawatts e alta confiabilidade exige que o planejamento elétrico incorpore uma realidade que muda rapidamente. O país passou a adotar regras mais rigorosas para o acesso ao sistema de transmissão. O objetivo é legítimo: impedir que agentes sem projetos consistentes reservem uma capacidade escassa para fins especulativos. A questão é encontrar o equilíbrio. Garantias financeiras elevadas, exigidas quando ainda existem definições importantes sobre o empreendimento, podem afastar também investidores com projetos sólidos. A regulação precisa ser capaz de distinguir essas complexidades e diferenças. Critérios como maturidade do projeto, capacidade financeira, experiência de investidores e consistência técnica podem contribuir para a seleção de empreendimentos com condições reais de implantação sem impor a todos o mesmo nível de exigência. A tributação é outra questão que pode se tornar outro obstáculo. Equipamentos representam parcela relevante do investimento em um data center, e a diferença de custos em relação a outros mercados reduz a competitividade brasileira. Medidas tributárias capazes de corrigir essa desvantagem são importantes, mas precisam fazer parte de uma estratégia mais ampla e holística. A agenda digital deve estar alinhada ao planejamento do setor elétrico, à política tributária e às regras para infraestrutura tecnológica e tratamento de dados. O país não pode tratar cada uma dessas questões de forma isolada. A conexão entre elas é crucial. Também é necessário aproximar os horizontes de planejamento. O setor elétrico trabalha com obras de longa maturação por razões técnicas, ambientais e regulatórias. A economia digital opera em ciclos muito mais curtos. Essa diferença não desaparecerá, entretanto, a adoção de processos mais eficientes, planejamento antecipado e soluções de transição podem reduzir seus efeitos. Data centers são parte da infraestrutura que sustentará computação em nuvem, serviços digitais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Os países que atraírem esses investimentos ampliarão sua capacidade de processamento e sua inserção nas cadeias tecnológicas globais. O Brasil ainda pode ocupar uma posição relevante nesse mercado. Para isso, precisa oferecer um caminho previsível entre a decisão de investir e a conexão à rede. Regras devem afastar a especulação sem transformar a falta de infraestrutura em uma barreira adicional. A corrida global por capacidade computacional já começou. Se a rede elétrica brasileira não acompanhar a velocidade dessa transformação, o investimento encontrará outro destino. * João Carlos de Oliveira Mello é CEO e fundador da Thymos Energia

Due to recent legal risks and litigation trends associated with the California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA), we have reluctantly chosen to restrict access to our primary web platform for residents or visitors within your state. Originally passed in 1967 to prevent unauthorized wiretapping, CIPA has recently been applied by trial attorneys to standard web technologies. Under these modern interpretations, common tools like security analytics, contact forms, chat widgets, and customer support plugins can be claimed as technical violations. Because these interpretations carry severe statutory penalties regardless of intent, we cannot safely serve California residents without facing substantial legal vulnerability. We deeply regret this disruption to your browsing experience. This restriction is entirely due to systemic litigation risks, not because we do not value your business. If you believe that businesses should be able to safely use standard web security and analytics software without fear of predatory lawsuits, we encourage you to make your voice heard. Please reach out to your California State Assembly Member and State Senator to encourage them to pass reasonable amendments to CIPA. artigo.texto: Flow Power has broken ground on its 100MW/223MWh Bennetts Creek battery energy storage system (BESS) in Victoria, marking construction start on the renewable energy generator and retailer’s first large-scale standalone battery project. Bennetts Creek is located near Hazelwood North in Victoria’s Latrobe Valley, a region historically associated with coal mining and coal-fired power generation in the state. Flow Power reached financial close on the project in December 2025, with financing provided by banks Westpac and SMBC Australia. The company did not disclose the terms of that financing, but said its majority shareholder, Canadian pension trust OPSEU Pension Plan Trust Fund (OPTrust), supported the transaction. The project is expected to be completed in 2028. The company owns a 100% renewable energy generation fleet of wind and solar assets and structures its retail offering around wholesale market exposure, including a residential feed-in tariff of AU$0.45/kWh (US$0.32/kWh) between 17:30 and 19:30, when solar generation tails off and evening demand peaks. System integrator Wärtsilä Energy Storage will supply battery storage equipment and control systems for Bennetts Creek. Flow Power has also engaged Zenviron, a joint venture between engineering group Monadelphous and renewable energy developer ZEM Energy, as balance-of-plant contractor for Bennetts Creek. Zenviron previously delivered balance-of-plant works on the 100MW/200MWh Latrobe Valley BESS for developer Tilt Renewables, inaugurated by Victoria’s Minister for Climate Action, Energy and Resources, Lily D’Ambrosio. Elsewhere in Victoria, the State Electricity Commission (SEC) is investing up to AU$43 million for a stake in the 400MW/1.86GWh Baranduda Electrical Energy Reserve near Wodonga, alongside superannuation fund Aware Super and developer Birdwood, securing 50% of that project’s output through a 15-year agreement. The SEC has applied a similar minority-stake model to the 600MW/1.6GWh Melbourne Renewable Energy Hub, developed with Equis Australia. Corporate offtakers have also moved into standalone battery storage in Victoria without relying on state involvement. Anza Power, backed by global infrastructure investor I Squared Capital, signed a tolling agreement with Amazon Australia for the 50MW/200MWh Bairnsdale BESS in East Gippsland. That was described as Amazon’s first standalone battery storage tolling deal in the Asia-Pacific region and the first agreement of its kind in Australia for a non-energy business contracting a standalone battery storage system directly. Bennetts Creek differs from both models. Flow Power is financing and developing the project independently through bank debt and shareholder support, rather than through a state equity stake or via a corporate offtake agreement, adding a third financing pathway to the cluster of battery storage projects concentrated around the Latrobe Valley as the region’s coal-fired generation continues to retire. artigo.texto: Leapmotor has unveiled two major technologies that will underpin its next generation of electric vehicles, beginning with models scheduled to launch from 2027. The Chinese EV manufacturer introduced the LEAP 5.0 New Mobile Space Architecture and its latest Cell-to-Chassis (CTC) 3.0 High-Low Fusion Battery at the 2026 Leapmotor Tech Day, held at the company’s Hu Zhou Battery facility in Hangzhou on September 16. Both technologies are designed to fundamentally change how Leapmotor vehicles use interior space and manage electrical power. The company describes the development as a major shift comparable to the transition from traditional feature phones to smartphones. LEAP 5.0 Architecture Focuses on Interior Space The LEAP 5.0 New Mobile Space Architecture has been developed specifically for Leapmotor’s next-generation vehicles, with the first models using the platform expected to be revealed in 2027. According to Leapmotor, the architecture achieves 100% space efficiency compared with its previous vehicle architectures while integrating vehicle control systems into a centralized configuration designed to support modern electric and increasingly automated vehicles. One of the biggest changes comes from combining the air-conditioning system with a rear-mounted powertrain. Previously separate components are integrated into a more compact arrangement, increasing available cabin length by 19%. The design also reduces the number of components by 18% and cuts the amount of required piping by 30%. The front suspension layout has also been redesigned. A new vertical shock absorber arrangement with an aluminum tower reduces the amount of hardware intruding into the passenger compartment while increasing front-row lateral legroom by 37.5%. A Taller, More Open EV Interior Leapmotor is also using the architecture to rethink the traditional EV cabin. A new skateboard-style platform allows the company to combine a higher roof with a completely flat floor. Leapmotor says this increases interior height by 63.7%, creating a more open, loft-style cabin with enough space for full standing height. The approach could give future Leapmotor EVs significantly more usable interior space without requiring a corresponding increase in the vehicle’s exterior dimensions. The LEAP 5.0 architecture is intended to serve as the foundation for the company’s next generation of vehicles, with the first production models arriving from 2027. Leapmotor CTC 3.0 Battery Eliminates the Traditional 12-Volt Battery The second major technology unveiled at Tech Day is the Cell-to-Chassis 3.0 High-Low Fusion Battery. It represents the latest development of Leapmotor’s package-less battery and power supply technology, integrating battery components directly into the vehicle chassis. More significantly, CTC 3.0 can supply both high- and low-voltage electrical functions. Leapmotor says the system has achieved a seven-fold increase in low-voltage capacity and functionality compared with its previous generation. That capability allows future vehicles using the technology to eliminate the conventional 12-volt lead-acid auxiliary battery. The 12-volt battery has traditionally supplied power to many of a vehicle’s electrical systems, including lighting, windshield wipers, infotainment, HVAC controls, security systems and other functions. In conventional vehicles, it has remained a separate part of the electrical architecture even as high-voltage battery systems have become increasingly sophisticated. Leapmotor’s CTC 3.0 technology instead integrates these functions into a unified battery and power distribution system. High- and Low-Voltage Systems Share the Same Battery Hardware The CTC 3.0 system removes the need for separate battery modules by integrating the cells and modules directly into the chassis. High- and low-voltage functions use the same battery cells and modules, while also sharing thermal management and energy distribution systems. This creates a more integrated electrical architecture and reduces the number of separate components required. Leapmotor says the technology can deliver the equivalent low-voltage power traditionally supplied by a 12-volt battery while removing the auxiliary battery itself. The company claims that its next-generation vehicles will therefore be the first road-going vehicles in more than 70 years to operate without a conventional lead-acid auxiliary battery. Potential Environmental and Ownership Benefits Removing the traditional 12-volt battery could have benefits beyond vehicle packaging. Lead-acid batteries require periodic replacement during the lifetime of many vehicles. Leapmotor says its CTC 3.0 system is designed for lifetime maintenance-free operation, potentially eliminating the need for owners to replace an auxiliary battery every few years. At large scale, Leapmotor believes the technology could also reduce the number of lead-acid batteries entering the waste stream. The company estimates that widespread adoption could eventually eliminate the need for tens of millions of such batteries each year. The technology also demonstrates how EV manufacturers are increasingly looking beyond range and charging speed to improve the underlying architecture of electric vehicles. Leapmotor’s Next Generation Starts in 2027 The LEAP 5.0 architecture and CTC 3.0 High-Low Fusion Battery are designed to work together as the foundation for Leapmotor’s next-generation EVs. Rather than simply increasing battery capacity or adding new software features, the technologies target the physical architecture of the vehicle itself. More compact components, greater interior space and a simplified electrical system could allow Leapmotor to develop EVs with different packaging possibilities from today’s conventional designs. The first production vehicles based on the new architecture are expected to be unveiled in 2027, marking the next major stage in Leapmotor’s EV development.

artigo.texto: Georgia governor’s race: Where Bottoms and Jackson stand on data centers Where do Georgia's candidates for governor stand on data centers? Metro Atlanta leads the nation in new data center construction, but Georgia lawmakers have yet to pass major regulations governing the industry's growth. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms supports pausing new data center development while the state studies the industry's economic, environmental and infrastructure impacts. Republican Rick Jackson says local governments, not the state, should decide whether data center projects move forward in their communities, while adding guardrails such as greater transparency and requiring facilities to cover their utility costs. For their complete positions and more in-depth analysis on data center development, growth and regulation, follow our "Where They Stand" series on AJC.com as we break down the candidates' views on the issues shaping Georgia's future. artigo.texto: Dois projetos australianos de armazenamento em baterias entram no Market Management System da AEMO Dois empreendimentos de armazenamento em baterias de escala utilitária na Austrália avançaram para uma fase decisiva de registro de mercado, conforme noticiado pelo GPE NEMLog, um rastreador de dados de projetos em todo o Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade. As instalações são o Tailem Bend BESS 3, da Vena Energy, na Austrália do Sul, e o Wooreen BESS, em Victoria, de copropriedade da EnergyAustralia e da Banpu Energy Australia. Em 15 de setembro de 2026, os dois sistemas foram admitidos no Market Management System do Operador do Mercado de Energia da Austrália sob os códigos TB3B1 e WOORB1, respectivamente. Geoff Eldridge, do GPE NEMLog, observou que ingressar no Market Management System é diferente de alcançar a plena operação comercial, mas permite que uma unidade avance para testes e comissionamento antes da participação padrão no mercado. Tailem Bend BESS 3 O Tailem Bend BESS 3 tem um máximo operacional registrado de 204MW, uma capacidade registrada de 263MW e 408MWh de armazenamento, o que corresponde a uma duração de duas horas e uma taxa de rampa de 82MW por minuto. Situado a cerca de 2,5km a sudeste do município de Tailem Bend e a aproximadamente 89km a leste-sudeste de Adelaide, o projeto se conecta ao Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade por meio da Subestação Tailem Bend adjacente, da ElectraNet. Ele fica ao lado de outros dois ativos da Vena Energy no mesmo local. A Vena Energy, divisão de desenvolvimento de renováveis do Vena Group, sediado em Singapura, iniciou a construção desse projeto autônomo em dezembro de 2025, com comissionamento previsto para 2027. Este é o terceiro projeto de baterias do desenvolvedor na Austrália, depois do Wandoan South BESS, de 100MW/150MWh, em Queensland. A iniciativa sucede a conclusão, pela Vena Energy, de uma bateria menor no mesmo local. Em janeiro de 2025, a empresa instalou uma bateria de 41,5MW ao lado de sua usina solar existente de 87MW em Tailem Bend, finalizando o que chama de Tailem Bend 2 Hybrid Project e elevando a produção combinada na rede de suas duas usinas solares co-localizadas de 182MW para 223,5MW. A Austrália do Sul obtém aproximadamente 75% de sua demanda anual de eletricidade de fontes eólicas e solares e pretende alcançar 100% de energia renovável líquida até o fim de 2027. Wooreen BESS O Wooreen BESS tem um máximo operacional registrado de 350MW, uma capacidade registrada de 491MW e 1.400MWh de armazenamento, resultando em uma duração de quatro horas e uma taxa de rampa de 140MW por minuto. Ele está em desenvolvimento em Hazelwood North, no Vale Latrobe, em Victoria, ao lado da existente Jeeralang Power Station, da EnergyAustralia, e a cerca de 138km a leste-sudeste de Melbourne, situado dentro de um aglomerado em expansão de armazenamento e infraestrutura de rede em toda a Gippsland. A EnergyAustralia, geradora e varejista de energia australiana, alcançou o fechamento financeiro do projeto em fevereiro de 2025 e iniciou a construção em poucos dias. O sistema de armazenamento em baterias deve entrar em operação antes da aposentadoria da usina termelétrica a carvão Yallourn, de 1.450MW, da EnergyAustralia, prevista para meados de 2028. Em julho de 2025, a EnergyAustralia alienou uma participação de 50% no projeto para a tailandesa Banpu Public Company, que opera na Austrália como Banpu Energy Australia, em uma transação avaliada em aproximadamente AU$700 milhões, ou US$490 milhões. O grupo finlandês de tecnologia marinha e de energia Wartsila foi contratado para fornecer o hardware das baterias, a engenharia, o comissionamento e um contrato de serviço de 15 anos, utilizando suas unidades Quantum High Energy e a GEMS Digital Energy Platform. A Wartsila concluiu a entrega e a instalação de todas as 1.038 unidades Quantum no local em julho de 2026. O sistema foi projetado para operar em modo grid-forming, a fim de fornecer inércia sintética à medida que a geração a carvão se retira da rede de Victoria. A Zenviron, joint venture do grupo de engenharia Monadelphous e da desenvolvedora de energia renovável ZEM Energy, recebeu o contrato de balance-of-plant do projeto em fevereiro de 2025, abrangendo projeto, construção, instalação e comissionamento. Tilt Renewables atua como desenvolvedora do projeto, e as operações comerciais do Wooreen têm como meta 2027. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de acumuladores elétricos de íons de lítio (exceto usados) na Austrália, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Acumuladores Elétricos de Íons de Lítio (Exceto Usados) abrange células e baterias secundárias de íons de lítio novas e não utilizadas, projetadas para armazenamento e fornecimento de energia elétrica, incluindo separadores, em formatos retangulares, quadrados, cilíndricos, prismáticos ou tipo bolsa. O escopo abrange acumuladores completos prontos para integração em equipamentos, bem como células individuais e módulos que fazem parte de um sistema de bateria maior. Acumuladores usados, gastos ou resíduos destinados à reciclagem ou descarte são excluídos. artigo.texto: Camel Group 12V Sodium-Ion Battery Selected for European OEM Pre-Development Project WUHAN, China, Aug. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Camel Group Co., Ltd. (Shanghai Stock Exchange: 601311.SH) announced that its 12V sodium-ion battery business has been selected for a pre-development project with a major European automotive manufacturer, bringing the company’s sodium-ion battery technology into the OEM’s technology development and validation process for next-generation low-voltage applications. The project builds on Camel Group’s engineering development of cylindrical sodium-ion battery samples and its small-batch production capabilities for sodium-ion battery products. It follows the adoption of Camel Group’s 12V lithium-ion batteries by major European automakers and represents another step in the company’s overseas R&D collaboration in next-generation low-voltage battery technology. Sodium-ion batteries are attracting increasing attention in automotive applications as manufacturers explore alternative technologies for evolving vehicle electrical architectures. Their resource availability, low-temperature performance and cycle-life potential make sodium-ion technology a potential option for automotive low-voltage battery systems, particularly amid evolving battery regulations and decarbonization requirements. Camel Group has more than four decades of experience in low-voltage batteries, with a product portfolio spanning conventional lead-acid, EFB, AGM, 12V lithium-ion and 12V sodium-ion batteries. In sodium-ion technology, the company has completed the engineering development of cylindrical battery samples and established small-batch production capabilities. Camel Group is also the lead proposing organization for the international standard proposal 12 V Sodium-ion Batteries for Automotive Start-Stop Applications. The proposal was unanimously approved by IEC/TC21 and has formally entered the international standardization process. The European OEM project provides an opportunity for further validation of Camel Group’s sodium-ion battery technology and product adaptability under European automotive requirements. Camel Group will continue to advance sodium-ion battery technology and deepen collaborative R&D with automotive manufacturers in China and overseas markets, developing low-voltage battery solutions focused on safety, adaptability and stable performance under diverse operating conditions. artigo.texto: COMMERCE CITY, Colo. — Commerce City leaders are deciding Monday night if the city should hit pause on data center development. At their regularly scheduled meeting, city council will consider a six-month moratorium on approving data center development plans or zoning applications. See the full story from Alex Dowd in the video below Council communications say the city’s land development code doesn’t address some of the “unique characteristics of data center facilities.” The draft ordinance says data centers can have significant impacts on city infrastructure like power and water supply, neighborhood character and surrounding land use. With growing interest in building these large scale computer system warehouses, city council officials are deciding if they should take a step back and “establish a reasonable period of time during which permit applications, site development plans and amendments, and zoning applications for new or expanded data centers will not be processed or approved.” The ordinance says that during the six-month pause, officials and city staff will take the time to research and potentially develop amendments to existing regulations that specifically address data centers. A survey from Magellan Strategies shows that Colorado residents are overwhelmingly opposed to data centers in their neighborhoods with 86% of surveyed voters opposing a data center near their neighborhood. This isn’t the first time a Colorado city has considered this type of pause. In early August, Aurora City Council voted down a similar six-month moratorium. Instead, Aurora officials opted to create regulations to address community concerns heard during that meeting. Weeks later, the council voted unanimously to ban evaporative cooling systems for new developments. That’s an option for Commerce City officials. While the staff recommendation is to pass the six month ban as written, councilmembers have the option to accept, amend, revisit or reject this ordinance. If accepted, the city won’t be able to approve any data center development plans or applications until March 2027. That timeline can be extended with another council vote. artigo.texto: Kochi: The severity of the present power crisis in Kerala is something the state has not faced in the past two decades. Adverse climatic conditions caused by El Nino, a spike in the use of air-conditioners and electric vehicle chargers, unavailability of power across the country and failure on the part of the state govt in implementing short-term solutions at a fast pace â all these have contributed to the current situation. It seems things will change for the better â at least for a few months until next summer. The state procured around 380MW from other states, especially from north India, during April-May 2026. Keralam recorded the highest power consumption in April this year â more than 6,100MW. Back then, the north Indian states had adequate power and less consumption. Keralam entered into a power swapping agreement with those states by assuring that electricity would be returned in the July-Sept period, when Keralam normally gets good rain and has surplus power. The northern states where the monsoon arrives much later will need more electricity in these months. In Sept, Keralamâs obligations to return power procured under power swapping will end. It means the stateâs power shortage will become less by 380MW. Similarly, the state govt is negotiating with other states to procure power to tide over the current crisis and is expecting a positive outcome. Given the fact that the shortage of power Keralam now faces is around 1,000 MW, the crisis may subside to a certain extent soon. But from March to May next year, it is almost certain that Keralam will stumble upon a severe power shortage unless the state govt takes immediate steps anticipating the crisis. âIn Sept 2025, our demand was around 4,000 MW. Now, it has increased by more than 1,000 MW due to soaring temperature and subsequent use of air-conditioners among other factors. Unlike in the past, there is a power shortage across India. So, we wonât get power even if we try to buy it,â KSEB chairperson and managing director M G Rajamanickam said. Of the total 5,51,994MW power generated in India as on July 31 this year, 1,64,595MW is solar energy. âThe total renewable energy produced in the country is more than 2 lakh MW. Of this, private generators produce around 60%. Apprehensions are being raised whether the private generators have any role in creating the shortage of power. The fact remains to be probed,â said KSEB Employees Association president Manoj E. Experts in the power sector say that Keralam must design both short-term and long-term plans to mitigate the crisis. âKSEB should prepare a resource adequacy plan with a clear vision on the next 10 yearsâ demand and supply. The board submitted its plan to us last Dec, but it was incomplete. There should be a meticulous plan for 8,765 hours in a year. For this purpose, the board should map the current availability. KSEB must prepare a least-cost capacity addition plan as well,â said Kerala State Electricity Regulatory Commission member B Pradeep. âKSEB and govt should ensure that the plan is being implemented as well,â he added. The total capacity of solar power plants across Keralam is around 4,500MW. The irony is that most of the solar power generated in the state is being wasted due to lack of storage facilities. KSEB has designed projects to set up a battery energy storage system (BESS) to the tune of 1,900MW. Of this, BESS facilities at Mylatti in Kasaragod (125MW) and Sreekantapuram in Kannur (40MW) may be commissioned by Jan. âWe have the potential to increase the solar energy capacity to 3,600MW-4,000MW. Several applications by consumers to set up rooftop solar plants are pending before KSEB. What we need are BESS facilities,â said energy transition consultant Sasi Kottayil. âAround 64% of solar power generated during daytime is excess. Besides KSEB setting them up, there should be community BESS facilities at panchayat level. Local bodies can set them up with the support of cooperatives. Energy can be available as cheaply as Re 1 per unit from other states during daytime. KSEB can procure that energy during daytime and store it in BESS for meeting the demand at night,â he added. According to KSEBâs projection, the gestation period (the time for setting up a facility and commissioning it) is around 18 months. But Kottayil says that a community BESS facility can be set up in a container, in three or four months. A pumped storage system is another long-term solution for which new reservoirs must be built downstream of the existing dams of hydel projects. Water flowing down from the dam after power generation could be stored in the reservoir downstream and pumped again to the dam upstream to generate power. But the gestation period of the pumped storage systems is around 8-10 years. After the mid-eighties, KSEB has not launched any major projects to generate power. âWeâve been depending on procured power to meet our needs all these years. In the absence of our own projects, power crisis may be the order of the day. Maharashtraâs demand is around 30,000MW, but it generates around 27,000MW. So, their dependency on other states is only around 10%. All south Indian states face power crises, but most of them generate a high quantity of energy on their own. But our generation is just around 25%. That means we have 75% dependency on other states. Here lies the key problem,â Rajamanickam said. âOther states have a mix of hydel, wind, solar, thermal and nuclear plants. So, if one mode of energy does not come through, they can depend on another. Setting up thermal plants in Keralam is not viable. But our potential in hydel projects is yet to be tapped fully. There should be a consensus in this regard. artigo.texto: Report finds Oregon data centers used electricity equal to over 70% of all homes in state PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - Researchers from ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia have released a new report on data centers in Oregon. According to the report, there are 111 data centers in the state, and those consumed more than 14 terawatt-hours of electricity last year. That’s equal to about 71% of all the electricity sold to Oregon homes combined. Meanwhile, consumption has nearly quadrupled since 2020. By 2030, researchers say data centers could account for roughly one-third of Oregon’s entire electricity demand. The report says 32 more data centers are already planned or under construction across the state, adding even more strain to the grid. Researchers say Oregon’s energy system will need new generation and transmission infrastructure to keep up with the growth. Copyright 2026 KPTV-KPDX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Google files request for 200+ additional emergency generators at Fort Wayne data center IDEM approved 140 backup generators for the project earlier this year FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA) - Google announced on Monday morning that it has submitted a request to the Indiana Department of Environmental Management to add more than 200 additional emergency generators to its Fort Wayne data center. The tech giant has sent in a third air permit modification application to the Indiana Department of Environmental Management to add 228 emergency generators. In April, IDEM approved a request to add more than 140 emergency diesel generators to the data center campus following public pushback. That approval also included five smaller generators classified as “insignificant” by state law. Those generators joined the 34 main diesel generators that IDEM first greenlit for the project back in 2024. A Google spokesperson said in its latest request that the additional 228 backup generators will be used only as a safety net if the local power grid goes down. They say aside from outages, the units will also run during legally required maintenance checks, and anticipate less than 10 hours of testing per generator annually. The EPA-certified emergency generators use ultra-low sulfur diesel or renewable diesel alternatives like Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO), Google says. The company says that even if the new request is approved, the site will remain below its state-mandated emissions cap. Google also says it has installed air pollution controls on several generators, which will modify units to ensure they meet or exceed EPA Tier 4 emission standards. Currently, there is no information on IDEM’s website that indicates that a public hearing will be held on the request. 21Alive News has reached out to the department for further clarification. Earlier this month, the department approved developers’ request to fill just over two acres of wetlands. In September of last year, IDEM approved a similar request to fill more than two acres of wetlands in an earlier expansion phase. artigo.texto: Mais de 1 milhão de candidatos a emprego procuraram vagas em data centers no site de recrutamento Indeed neste ano. Em agosto, o volume de buscas era oito vezes maior que no início de 2022. Pesquisas do site de empregos constataram que, entre os trabalhadores horistas responsáveis por manutenção e instalação, os data centers oferecem salários cerca de 42% maiores do que funções semelhantes em outros tipos de empresa. Segundo o Indeed, um gerente de projetos em um data center ganha por volta de US$ 115 mil por ano — cerca de R$ 591 mil pela cotação de R$ 5,14 por dólar. A Digital Realty afirmou que engenheiros iniciantes em suas instalações podem ganhar aproximadamente US$ 66 mil por ano, ou cerca de R$ 339 mil, enquanto a remuneração média pode superar US$ 120 mil, o equivalente a cerca de R$ 617 mil, para profissionais mais experientes. Profissionais com conhecimento em sistemas elétricos, engenharia de redes e sistemas de refrigeração são muito procurados, disse Brandi Galvin Morandi, diretora de recursos humanos da operadora de data centers Equinix. Grandes empresas de tecnologia, entre elas a Meta Platforms, investiram na formação de mão de obra especializada para construir essas instalações. Na Virgínia, onde há uma grande concentração de data centers, o Northern Virginia Community College lançou, com a ajuda do setor privado, um programa de capacitação para o trabalho nessas unidades. “Essas são instalações essenciais, que operam 24 horas por dia, e isso exige uma combinação específica de formação técnica, disciplina de segurança e experiência prática — algo que está em falta diante da velocidade com que o setor cresce”, disse Cindy Fiedelman, diretora de recursos humanos da Digital Realty. A empresa opera mais de 300 data centers em seis continentes. Em unidades como a de Ashburn, a Digital Realty aluga espaço para grandes empresas de tecnologia que precisam de capacidade computacional. Entre seus clientes estão Oracle, Meta e IBM. A Digital Realty também enfrenta a reação pública cada vez mais intensa contra a construção de data centers. Em Atlanta, a companhia busca uma exceção a uma proibição local de data centers perto de terminais de transporte enquanto tenta construir na cidade uma unidade de US$ 500 milhões — cerca de R$ 2,57 bilhões. Moradores se opuseram ao projeto, que atualmente se encontra num impasse. Um porta-voz da Digital Realty afirmou que o projeto criaria empregos bem remunerados e que a empresa estava “comprometida em chegar lá da maneira correta”, em parceria com a comunidade. A unidade de Ashburn reúne trabalhadores administrativos e operacionais. Entre eles estão seguranças, técnicos que cuidam da estrutura de cabos dos clientes, profissionais da cadeia de suprimentos que buscam materiais e engenheiros que monitoram possíveis problemas. As funções são semelhantes em outros data centers pelo país. A parte mais importante do trabalho é manter os centros em funcionamento. A Digital Realty estima que seus data centers ficam operacionais durante 99,999% do tempo, mas agora busca alcançar 99,9999%. A diferença parece pequena, mas equivale a reduzir o tempo de interrupção de seis minutos para 30 segundos por ano. Don Atkinson trabalha na empresa há cerca de 14 anos, depois de passar 17 anos nas Forças Armadas e exercer uma função na manutenção de sistemas de energia de reserva. Hoje, aos 53 anos, ocupa um cargo de gestão e orienta engenheiros mais jovens. Assim como muitos trabalhadores do setor, Atkinson tenta lidar com a mudança repentina na opinião pública a respeito de um ambiente de trabalho no qual construiu uma carreira estável. “Nós amamos os Estados Unidos, amamos o país, amamos o setor, e é simplesmente estranho”, disse ele sobre a reação pública. Atkinson também observou que ele próprio não usa muita inteligência artificial. “É um momento estranho.” Outro funcionário, Malcolm Mosely, disse que sua família às vezes menciona as questões políticas envolvendo os data centers, mas ele tenta não se concentrar nisso: “Eu apenas venho aqui fazer meu trabalho”. Em uma quinta-feira recente, Mosely estava dentro de uma gaiola preta repleta de fios amarelos, verificando um cabo de interconexão que liga a operação de um cliente à de outro. Waddy, que trabalha na unidade de Ashburn há três anos, tem formação superior de curta duração em administração e anteriormente trabalhava com vendas em uma empresa de aquecimento, ventilação e ar-condicionado. Ele começou no turno da noite do data center, ajudando a manter máquinas de clientes espalhados pelo mundo. Desde então, subiu na hierarquia. Suas rondas diárias incluem a inspeção da galeria de tratamento de ar da unidade, onde enormes aparelhos de ar-condicionado bombeiam ar frio para o restante do data center. No andar de cima, o salão de dados parece um vestiário, com servidores empilhados em gabinetes ou gaiolas que as empresas podem alugar. Não há logotipos nem nomes de empresas, porém, porque concorrentes mantêm operações lado a lado. O uso de protetores auriculares é recomendado no local para evitar danos provocados pelo rugido dos servidores quando se chega perto deles. No telhado, Waddy verifica centenas de condensadores dispostos em fileiras organizadas para ajudar a resfriar a instalação. Ele procura defeitos ou estragos causados por pássaros que gostam de bicar os equipamentos. Do telhado, é possível ver ao longe um guindaste usado na construção do data center de um concorrente. “É agradável aqui em cima”, disse Waddy. “Adoro esta ronda.” Traduzido do inglês por InvestNews
