artigo.texto: Gov. Josh Shapiro on Friday cited the borough of Archbald in Lackawanna County as influencing his thinking on the need for giving communities more local control over data center proposals. During an appearance in Scranton to celebrate Fidelity Bank’s move of its headquarters into the downtown, Shapiro fielded questions from the media and addressed the issue of data centers. He referenced a data-center executive order he signed Aug. 18 that requires all data center proposals applying for state permits to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Requirements, and that “blocks speculative, irresponsible data center projects from moving forward, giving local communities more power over data center development,” according to an announcement posted on the state website. “I just signed an executive order a few weeks ago that in effect puts local communities in charge of deciding what’s going to happen in their communities. The commonwealth won’t even consider a permit application unless and until the local community endorses that project and it’s been signed by their county counsel or city counsel, or what have you. And I want to tell you that the genesis of that executive order was a result of me listening to people across Pennsylvania who wanted to be able to dictate what their communities look like,” Shapiro said. “There was one community in particular that had probably the most impact on my thinking on this issue, and that was the community of Archbald. When I went up to Eddie Staback Park and I saw what one of these developers wanted to do on the left-field line where parents should be enjoying watching their kids play baseball, they wanted to put a data center right where those parents should be enjoying their kids, I said, ‘No way. We’re not going to let this happen.’ “ Shapiro continued: “When I saw, and listened to, local leaders feel as though they were getting bulldozed by developers, and they were losing power to these big powerful corporate interests, I said, ‘No way.’ And so we rebalanced that equation. We put local communities back in charge of what was going to happen in their communities. If a neighborhood decides this is something they want, then we will entertain that. But if a neighborhood decided they don’t want this in their communities, those projects are dead. And the people of Archbald, I want to say thank you for speaking up. I heard you and you impacted policy all across our commonwealth.” The crowd of about 125 people applauded. Some of the new rules in the data-center executive order would do the following: •Direct the Department of Environmental Protection to evaluate permit applications from proposed data centers “only if developers have made a legally binding commitment to meet GRID Requirements and have received local approval.” •Prohibit state agencies from entering into nondisclosure agreements regarding data center proposals. •Remove all AI data center proposals from Shapiro’s “Fast Track” permitting process established nearly two years ago under a different executive order that aimed to speed up large-scale economic development and infrastructure projects. Shapiro signed the PA Permit Fast Track Program in November 2024 at an event in Hazleton at NorthPoint Development’s Hazleton Logistics 141 Project Building off the Arthur Gardner Parkway. At that time, another NorthPoint initiative, “Project Hazlenut,” entailed creating a data center campus on the west side of Interstate 81, north of the Humboldt North Industrial Park in Hazle Twp. Other data center proposals soon started cropping up in 2025 throughout the region, including in Lackawanna County. Many data center proposals in the state are speculative in nature, such that many developers do not have tech companies on board or lined up to fill the facilities. Over the last year-and-a-half, Lackawanna County emerged as a hotbed for largely speculative data center development encompassing thousands of acres and more than a dozen proposed campus projects. Though some developers have shifted plans to fewer buildings with bigger footprints, the county has around 90 proposed data centers, previously peaking at close to 100. Multiple proposals are tied up in litigation. Archbald has became a particular focus of a large number of data center proposals and opposition. Concerns here and beyond generally have evolved since early 2025 from getting steamrolled and paved over with massive data center campuses, to anticipated huge demands for electricity and water for cooling that would strain existing systems, to noise and air pollution from large numbers of diesel generators that data centers also will require. Earlier this month, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission issued its annual Electric Power Outlook Report that projects data centers and related power plants could cause a nearly 19%-a-year jump in demand statewide for electricity over the next five years. The PUC forecasts residential and commercial electricity demand to grow modestly through 2030, but industrial use driven primarily by anticipated large-load customers to increase by a whopping average of 18.56% annually. The state describes Shapiro’s data-center executive order as laying out “strict requirements that data center developers must meet regarding energy affordability, community engagement, workforce and economic development, transparency and environmental protection.”

artigo.texto: Data center developer Quantica Infrastructure has begun construction on its massive project in Yellowstone County. Postcards mailed to area residents said that in early September the company began staging equipment on the nearly 8-square-mile property outside the town of Broadview. The project, which would be among the largest in the world as currently planned, has generated fiery public opposition, with opponents crowding into county commission meetings to boo the commission and demand action. They’ve tried a couple of legal methods to assert some control over the project, but to no avail. The latest effort to persuade commissioners to enact interim zoning and pause the project for study is running headlong into a wall of resistance from county officials. While Missoula County took this step in July, Yellowstone County Attorney Scott Twito has advised commissioners against doing the same. Twito said any action by the county government to stop the data center project would trigger a lawsuit, and possibly hefty fines for county taxpayers. The first on-site work at the Big Sky Campus is the construction of access roads and a well. Workers began earlier this month. Drilling the well could begin “as early as the end of September,” the mailer stated. Quantica spokesperson Travis Hall declined to name the company doing the well work but said it is an “experienced environmental and engineering services firm in Billings.” Quantica has agreed to use local, unionized labor when possible, under a memorandum of understanding it signed with the Southeastern Montana Building and Construction Trades Council in June. Riley McCauley, vice president of the council, said they won’t have details on job numbers or wages until Quantica has secured an “end user,” or a digital or AI company, to purchase the facility. Some project opponents fear the data center will draw down local water supplies, which are needed for both residential and agricultural uses. Quantica said that shouldn’t happen. The company plans to tap into an “underutilized” aquifer, the Madison Aquifer, that is 1,300 feet deeper beneath ground than the one used for Broadview area homes and businesses. That one is called the Eagle Aquifer. Quantica expects the project will require up to 150,000 gallons of water per day during construction and 20,000 gallons each day once operational. That’s approximately what a 100-room hotel uses each day at full occupancy, according to the California Hotel and Lodging Association. Big Sky Digital Infrastructure will use a closed-loop cooling system that continuously circulates liquid near hot computer servers to absorb heat and transfer it to cooling equipment. The system uses less water than other types but more electricity. Jon Reiten, a retired Montana Tech professor and expert on Eastern Montana hydrology, said it’s correct that drawing from the Madison Aquifer won’t impact the shallower Eagle Aquifer that Broadview uses. Reiten appeared on a panel discussion about the Broadview data center in January, organized by the Montana Environmental Information Center. “And it’s going to be completely cemented and cased off,” Reiten said of the well. “If everything is done properly, there should not be a problem. That should not affect the shallower wells that are in that area.” Reiten said the water in the Madison Aquifer is warmer, likely more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit. He said the company could build a cooling pond for the well water. But, he said, it’s also salty, and salty water tends to corrode equipment, as it does at the Signal Peak coal mine in Roundup, he said. The mine has a well drilled into the same Madison Aquifer that Quantica plans to use. artigo.texto: Grid Constraints Steer Dutch Data Centers Beyond Amsterdam Amsterdam remains a top European data center hub, but power constraints are shifting new capacity to Rotterdam and other regional Dutch markets with available grid connections. Amsterdam’s data center market continues to grow, but the very infrastructure that made it a European hub increasingly determines where new capacity can be built. As of Q1 2026, the city was Europe’s fourth-largest data center market, with inventory up 11% year over year, or 64.3 MW, according to CBRE’s 2026 market review. Its vacancy rate tightened to 9.4%, evidence that customers continue to absorb capacity even as power constraints and planning restrictions limit development. JLL’s latest EMEA report shows that in H1 2026, Amsterdam delivered 16.3 MW, while Paris added 72.5 MW over the same period. Amsterdam still offers the connectivity, customers, and operators of a top-tier hub, but faster growth is shifting toward locations that can provide large power blocks on reliable schedules. The Dutch market is therefore set to become more geographically dispersed. Amsterdam remains the commercial and network center, while Rotterdam, Groningen, Eindhoven, and other regional markets compete for projects the capital cannot accommodate. Amsterdam’s Network Advantage Holds Amsterdam’s status within the FLAP-D group – Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin – rests on an interconnection ecosystem built over decades. In 2025, the Amsterdam Internet Exchange (AMS-IX) handled 35.66 exabytes of traffic, four times its 2015 volume, and ended 2025 with 902 connected parties. That density keeps carriers, cloud providers, content companies, and enterprises close to the networks they need, conferring an advantage on established colocation operators that newer markets cannot quickly replicate. “Amsterdam is characterized by the availability of skilled labor and an established infrastructure by large colocation service providers such as Equinix and Digital Realty,” said Luis Fernandes, senior research manager for cloud, data centers, and enterprise infrastructure at IDC, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. He also noted the large number of subsea cables landing in the Netherlands from multiple regions. Geography reinforces this position. Amsterdam offers low-latency access to major European business centers, a mature enterprise customer base, and an energy market where operators can pursue renewable power purchase agreements (PPAs). “Add to this a favorable energy mix with a large component of offshore wind farms, as well as a prime market for sustainable PPAs,” Alex Mariage, head of regional operations at global data center consultancy BCS, told Data Center Knowledge. “This continues to make Amsterdam a very attractive and traditional opportunity for global investments.” These advantages support demand, but they do not guarantee a grid connection. The challenge is to preserve Amsterdam’s network ecosystem while placing workloads where power is actually available. The Equinix AM3 data center tower in Amsterdam. (Image: Getty Images) Deliverable Power Dictates the Next Build Deliverable power now outweighs land prices, incentives, and even fiber in site selection. Developers need to know when a connection will arrive, how much capacity it will provide, and whether equipment can be procured in time to use it. “Site selection in 2026 is driven primarily by deliverable power,” Assad Noori, executive director and EMEA head of data centers at JLL, told Data Center Knowledge. “If developers cannot secure megawatts on a predictable timeline, incentives, land costs, and fiber connectivity become secondary.” “If developers cannot secure megawatts on a predictable timeline, incentives, land costs, and fiber connectivity become secondary.” – Assad Noori, executive director and EMEA head of data centers at JLL AI has amplified the volume of requests reaching utilities and developers. Noori noted that single-site requirements, once in the 30-60 MW range, can now reach 300 MW, while transformer lead times can extend up to three years. Power commitments and long-lead equipment orders must therefore precede construction by years. “Cost and delivery timeline are now co-equal with availability in site decisions,” he said. Behind-the-meter generation can help when grid queues become too long. Noori advises developers to establish their queue position, connection cohort, offtake and export rights, backup service terms, exit rights, and penalties before committing to a site. Amsterdam’s limited land has encouraged taller data centers, enabling more intensive site use but complicating planning and permitting. Flood risk is addressed through national and regional defenses, with some facilities adding perimeter floodgates. Mariage said the Dutch engineering response to land and water constraints is mature, but the electricity bottleneck is now slowing projects. “Grid congestion is the key challenge here,” he said. “Every investor will confirm that this aspect is the top constraint slowing down projects and investments at the moment.” Capacity Shifts to Rotterdam and Regional Hubs Amsterdam’s constraints do not suppress demand; they widen the search radius. National policy generally restricts hyperscale facilities to designated zones in Hollands Kroon (including Middenmeer) and Het Hogeland (home to Eemshaven). Meanwhile, colocation and other developments are testing a broader field of Dutch locations. Rotterdam stands out for certain workloads, combining port infrastructure, proximity to Amsterdam, an established business base, and experience in reclaiming former harbor land. The AMS-IX added a Rotterdam point of presence in April 2026, strengthening the city’s role on the national connectivity map. artigo.texto: BALTIMORE COUNTY, Md. — Data centers have been up for debate in Baltimore County for quite some time. Currently, there's a moratorium on data center developments until January 1st. On Tuesday, Baltimore County Council will decide whether or not to extend that pause to December 2027. "The public needs much more of an opportunity to comment on data centers," said Councilman David Marks, "This is a very complex issue that involved land use, taxation, water use, and we don't want to rush judgment on any of these issues." At a council meeting last week, many neighbors agreed but urged members to take it a step further. "Extend the moratorium and change "am" to "or" and seriously consider whether they should be there at all. It's our land, our home, and we have carried enough on the east side," one resident said. However, another man asked for an amendment to allow the moratorium to end early once appropriate regulations are adopted. "Data centers can provide significant income and economic opportunities for Baltimore County including good family sustaining union jobs that means opportunities not only for experienced trades people, but also new workers," he told council members. President and CEO of the Maryland Tech Council, Kelly Schulz is also against the pause. She previously told WMAR-2 News that the county could risk missing out on opportunities for growth. "I think this is a way to look at a way to advance our innovation and our technology industries," Schulz said. The vote is scheduled for Tuesday at 6 p.m. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. Email the WMAR-2 Newsroom if you have info, photos or videos to share. artigo.texto: 'We don't know how to be proactive': Data center fight intensifying in central Wisconsin "UPFRONT' recap: Inside the proposed data center controversy in Wisconsin Rapids Wisconsin Rapids Mayor Matt Zacher said he backs a one-year moratorium on data center construction amid growing controversy in the city surrounding a proposed data center on the city's old paper mill site. "The problem I see in this situation is that we are acting reactively," Zacher said on WISN 12's "UPFRONT" which is produced in partnership with WisPolitics. "We don't know how to be proactive necessarily because nobody's really ever done; there's no playbook on this." Last week, the city's plan commission unanimously rejected a conditional use permit from New York-based PNK Group, which is proposing the 200-acre data center on the city's old paper mill site. The recommendation is now before the full city council alongside a separate proposal for a one-year data center moratorium. "They kind of throw it in our lap," Zacher said. "They know that we're unqualified. I'm not saying, you know, I'm doing pretty well, if I do say so myself, trying to juggle all of these things. But am I really qualified for this high level of a situation and negotiation and trying to figure this stuff out? And I think if the data centers were really being super real and fair about what's happening, they would back off. They would give us some time." The city's plan commission heard more than three hours of public comment last week on the proposal, a majority opposing the data center, including GOP State Rep. Scott Krug, who represents Wisconsin Rapids. "It's nothing against anybody in the trades," Krug said. "There will be other projects, and we will get a chance to use that local labor and make sure that the IBEW and the electric workers and pipefitters and the steamfitters and all the guys who lost their jobs at the mill are going to have a chance in Wisconsin Rapids again, but it's not going to be this one." GOP State Sen. Patrick Testin said four key state Senate races ahead of November are "tight" and "statistical toss-ups" in the battle for control of the chamber. "That's why we keep telling all of our staff that are up in these key races, we keep telling the candidates keep working, keep knocking doors and getting their message out there," said Testin, who leads the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate. The four key districts include the 5th between Republican Mike Roberts and Democrat Robyn Vining, the 21st featuring Republican Jim Croft and Democrat Trevor Jung, the 17th featuring GOP State Sen. Howard Marklein and Democrat Jenna Jacobson and the 31st featuring Democrat State Sen. Jeff Smith and Republican Michele Magadance Skinner. "We affectionately call them the core four," Testin said. "When you look at the odds in the math, we have to win two out of those four to come back in the majority. And I believe that we are going to, at least, not win all of them, but I feel good with where we're at." When asked if Republicans are urging candidates to distance themselves from President Donald Trump, Testin said, "Well, look, we can't control what happens in D.C. We can't control the cost of gas. What we can control is things like income taxes, property taxes and do what we can to make things more affordable." "I think despite the fact that there are some national headwinds," Testin added. "I think we are well positioned to come back in the majority." Watch: WisPolitics Editor JR Ross has the latest analysis on key state Senate races.

artigo.texto: Brasília - Após o Redata virar lei na quarta-feira, 16 de setembro, uma divergência dentro do governo sobre se o gás natural também poderá ser usado como energia (além das fontes renováveis já previstas) para abastecer os data centers que terão direito a incentivos fiscais pode adiar ainda mais a implementação do programa no País. Ao NeoFeed, o Ministério da Fazenda admitiu que a expectativa é que o decreto, que o Executivo já prepara com essa e mais uma série de regulamentações do Redata, seja publicado até o fim deste mês. O documento estava previsto para sair no mesmo dia em que o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) sancionou a lei. Isso acontece pois há posições opostas dentro do próprio governo em relação às questões energéticas relacionadas aos projetos que receberiam as isenções de PIS, Cofins e IPI. E a tendência é que a Casa Civil tenha que arbitrar a respeito, segundo uma fonte a par das negociações disse ao NeoFeed. Em uma frente, os ministérios de Minas e Energia e o de Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) vêm sinalizando positivamente para o uso do gás como uma das fontes dos data centers. Quem tem defendido essa exceção costuma argumentar nos bastidores que a fonte seria complementar, uma vez que algumas energias renováveis são intermitentes - solar e eólica. De outro lado, no entanto, o Ministério da Fazenda já defende restrições e entende que apenas as fontes de energia limpas (hidrelétrica, eólica, solar) podem ser usadas para abastecer as estruturas de data centers, apurou o NeoFeed. Na verdade, a lei aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional no início do mês e sancionada em meados de setembro por Lula já prevê o uso de energias renováveis para alimentar os data centers. Mas toda a confusão se deu por uma mudança feita já quando o projeto tramitava pelo Senado: o texto substituiu a expressão “energias renováveis ou limpas” por “energias renováveis ou de baixa emissão de carbono”. Logo, o governo terá que definir também quais as condições seriam admitidas para essa baixa emissão. E caso o gás natural seja aceito como uma das fontes aptas a participar dos projetos de data centers, ainda assim o governo deve exigir compensação de emissão de carbono para o gás. Além do decreto, também será editada uma portaria interministerial. Além da Fazenda, do MME e MDIC, também vêm participando das discussões no governo os ministérios do Meio Ambiente, das Comunicações e de Ciência e Tecnologia. Além da questão energética, a regulamentação do Redata precisa indicar a lista de quais componentes e equipamentos poderão receber os benefícios fiscais e quais documentos as empresas precisam apresentar para se cadastrar no programa. Apesar da indefinição sobre as fontes de energia, a Pasta da Fazenda, responsável pela concessão dos benefícios fiscais, avalia que haverá tempo hábil, ainda em 2026 para que as empresas interessadas se habilitem para o programa. “Com a regulamentação lançada, dependerá da iniciativa das empresas. Mas haverá condições e tempo suficiente para fazer habilitações neste ano, se houver pedidos instruídos adequadamente”, respondeu o ministério. Procurado, o MME não respondeu aos contatos da reportagem. Acertos e urgências Affonso Nina, presidente da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais (Brasscom), admite que a lei, embora restritiva para algumas fontes de energia, foi positiva em trazer ganhos ambientais para os próximos projetos de data center no País. “Esperamos que o decreto seja o menos burocrático e saia quanto antes para habilitar as empresas este ano ainda”, afirma Nina, ao NeoFeed. “Mas estamos na expectativa de quando isso vai ser fechado e entendemos que o decreto ainda depende dessa definição da energia.” O executivo lembra que o gás natural representa 6% da matriz energética e mesmo que ele seja autorizado pelo governo a ser utilizado nos data centers habilitados pelo Redata ainda assim os projetos vão demandar necessariamente outras fontes de energia. Ele pondera também que os data centers têm um consumo “ínfimo de água”. Na leitura de Nina, porém, o Redata é apenas uma das necessidades do setor para destravar investimentos da ordem de R$ 90 bilhões durante os próximos cinco anos a partir de 2027. Para viabilizar esse montante de recursos, é necessária a redução de ICMS pelo Confaz no âmbito dos Estados e também reverter uma medida da Camex de fevereiro que aumentou as alíquotas de imposto de importação para vários itens úteis para os data centers”, pontuou. “Existe o apetite do investidor, o clima é positivo e digamos que já fizemos 1 a 0, mas precisamos de 3 a 0 para nos classificar no campeonato. Faltam ainda outros dois gols. O Redata sozinho não resolve”, afirma ele. “Enquanto tudo isso não acontecer, é possível que os investimentos em datacenters no Brasil não aconteçam nesse volume esperado. E enquanto isso o Redata perde muita eficiência”, complementa. A Frente Parlamentar pelo Brasil Competitivo (FPBC), que articulou pela aprovação do projeto no Congresso, também comemorou a sanção da lei do Redata, mas advertiu que a regulamentação precisa viabilizar os investimentos necessários. “Agora começa uma nova etapa: precisamos de uma implementação que dê segurança aos investidores e preserve a competitividade necessária para transformar o potencial brasileiro em projetos concretos”, diz Tatiana Ribeiro, secretária-executiva da FPBC e diretora-executiva do Movimento pelo Brasil Competitivo (MBC). A Frente defende neutralidade tecnológica, critérios objetivos de emissões e a possibilidade de diferentes fontes e soluções energéticas, inclusive de forma combinada. E diferentes modelos de suprimento, como contratação no mercado livre, autoprodução, geração própria ou dedicada e conexão ao Sistema Interligado Nacional. artigo.texto: NESTA EDIÇÃO. Amazonas e Sergipe pressionam por espaço para gás natural na regulamentação do Redata. MPTCU pede auditoria sobre mineração de terras raras no Sul de Minas. Sua retrospectiva semanal chegou! EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: Os governadores do Amazonas e Sergipe enviaram ofícios ao presidente Lula (PT) na quinta (17/9), pedindo que a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) considere o gás natural entre as fontes elegíveis para abastecer futuras instalações que receberão o incentivo. A preocupação é que a limitação ou bloqueio da fonte pode restringir investimentos nos seus estados. Em dois ofícios separados, Roberto Cidade (União/AM) e Fábio Mitidieri (PSD/SE) defendem que o governo federal adote critérios de desempenho ambiental e energético, em vez de excluir previamente determinadas tecnologias — isto é, o gás fóssil. Enquanto o governador do Amazonas argumenta a favor do aproveitamento das reservas e infraestrutura de gás natural do estado — que ainda precisa resolver como levar eletricidade a mais de 150 mil pessoas no escuro — para viabilizar a instalação desses centros de processamento de dados ultraeletrointensivos. Fábio Mitidieri está de olho na expansão da produção de gás com o projeto Sergipe Águas Profundas (SEAP), que prevê duas plataformas com capacidade conjunta de processamento de até 22 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia. Autor da emenda de redação que abriu caminho para o gás nos data centers, o senador Laércio Oliveira (PP/SE) estima uma demanda de 6 milhões de m3 de gás por dia com a construção de um centro de processamento de dados na ZPE. O que está em jogo A lei que cria o Redata foi sancionada na terça-feira (15), junto com a Lei Complementar que viabiliza a concessão de benefícios fiscais de até R$ 7,2 bilhões ao setor de data centers Para acessar os incentivos, os empreendimentos precisam garantir que 100% da energia elétrica consumida deve vir de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. É este último termo que está em debate. A falta de consenso no governo sobre o enquadramento ou não do gás natural como fonte de baixa emissão no regime fez com que a definição ficasse fora do decreto, também previsto para ser assinado na terça. Uma portaria interministerial deve ser publicada na sequência, complementando a regulamentação. Nem o decreto saiu ainda: a discussão está em andamento na Casa Civil, apurou a eixos. E vale dizer: a atração de infraestrutura digital para o Brasil significa uma alavanca da demanda energética. O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) contabiliza 38 GW em pedidos de conexão de data centers à rede — o equivalente a quase um terço da capacidade instalada do país. No mundo todo, o consumo de energia por servidores de inteligência artificial deve dobrar até 2030. Estimativas da Kearney apontam que em 2025, os servidores de IA representaram entre 23% e 27% da eletricidade consumida pelos centros de dados. Essas previsões também estão animando a indústria nuclear. Esta semana, a Agência Internacional de Energia Atômica (AIEA) afirmou que a capacidade de energia nuclear pode mais que triplicar até 2060, em meio ao boom da IA. A expectativa é que reatores modulares se tornem uma fonte significativa e nova de energia de baixo carbono, compensando reatores que estão sendo desativados. Terras raras na mira do MPTCU Um dia após o governo federal sancionar o marco legal dos minerais críticos, o Ministério Público junto ao Tribunal de Contas da União (MPTCU) pediu ao TCU, na quinta (17/9), uma auditoria sobre os projetos de mineração de terras raras no Sul de Minas Gerais. A ideia é verificar se os órgãos federais estão preparados para acompanhar a expansão dessa atividade na região. O foco está nos impactos que podem se acumular ao longo do tempo, especialmente sobre água, solo, biodiversidade e saúde pública. O pedido também inclui um levantamento sobre o estágio dos projetos, possíveis passivos ambientais e as garantias previstas para a recuperação das áreas após o fim da mineração. A preocupação ganhou força depois de uma visita de uma comitiva interministerial a Poços de Caldas, Caldas e Andradas, em junho. O grupo recomendou que os projetos sejam analisados em conjunto, e não de forma isolada, já que estão próximos de áreas residenciais, unidades de conservação e da antiga mina de urânio da INB. O MPTCU também quer que o TCU acompanhe de perto a fiscalização da mineração na região, incluindo a arrecadação da Compensação Financeira pela Exploração de Recursos Minerais (CFEM). O órgão aponta ainda a necessidade de atenção a possíveis perdas de receitas e à fiscalização das atividades. Por trás da discussão está uma região com características ambientais bastante particulares: além do histórico ligado à mineração de urânio, o Planalto Vulcânico do Sul de Minas concentra nascentes, aquíferos e fontes de águas minerais e termais. Para o MPTCU, o avanço dos projetos de terras raras exige monitoramento contínuo desses recursos. O caso também serve de alerta para os próximos passos que serão dados na Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (PNMCE) sancionada esta semana (16/9). A nova política tem como objetivo ampliar a agregação de valor no Brasil, estimulando pesquisa, lavra, beneficiamento, transformação mineral e mineração urbana. Mas deixa aceso o alerta de organizações ambientais que temem os impactos de uma corrida desenfreada por esses recursos. O texto também cria o Conselho Nacional para Industrialização de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (Cimce), vinculado à Presidência da República, a quem caberá definir e atualizar a lista de minerais críticos e estratégicos, formular o plano nacional para o setor e selecionar projetos prioritários. O conselho também poderá participar da análise e da homologação de reorganizações e mudanças de controle societário relacionadas a ativos minerais. A expectativa é que a primeira reunião do Conselho ocorra em até dez dias. A semana na eixos Curtas Biodiese

artigo.texto: On Aug. 18, the Amherst County Board of Supervisors voted to end by-right approval of data centers. The same day, a developer filed an application. That is where Virginia is in the fall of 2026: every county south of the Occoquan has a proposal on the table, every board is writing rules at the speed of a public comment period, and the share of Virginians who would welcome a data center next door has fallen from 69 percent to 35 percent in three years. The money is real. Loudoun County took in $1.2 billion in data-center property taxes this fiscal year, 39 percent of its budget, and cut its real-estate rate ten years running. That is why the applications keep coming to Amherst, Botetourt, Pittsylvania and Halifax, and why every board that says no eventually gets asked again. What is also real is that Loudoun got the money and almost nothing else. Two hundred buildings, and not one of them warms a school, dries a crop or grows a tomato. Every one of them throws its heat into the sky through a cooling tower, at the owner’s expense, because nobody ever asked for anything different. Virginia has now asked. This spring the General Assembly passed HB 323, the first law in the United States directing a state to put data-center waste heat to use. It cleared the Senate 39 to 0. It orders Virginia Energy to find the opportunities, connect the data centers to the heat users, study what the Nordics and the Dutch already do, and hand the legislature a strategic plan. That report was due Sept. 1. The 2027 session is where it becomes law or becomes a shelf. Here is what Southside and the Valley should ask for that Loudoun never did. Every data center is a furnace. Nearly all the electricity that goes in comes out as heat, and the newest liquid-cooled halls put it out as warm water, exactly the temperature a greenhouse wants in a Virginia January. A two-and-a-half-acre greenhouse on that water can grow on the order of 695,000 pounds of fresh produce a year with no boiler and nothing burned. Write a covenant into the rezoning that at least 15 percent of it goes to the host community, and one building’s waste feeds about 400 of your neighbors, year-round, from the fence line. Add the fish house that runs on the same loop, the farm store, and the homes on radiant floors at the end of it, and the campus that was going to take the farmland has instead built the farm, and the jobs that come with it are agricultural, not just electrical. None of this requires a subsidy. It requires a question. Loudoun never asked, “Where does the heat go?” because in 2010 nobody knew it was worth asking. Every county in the commonwealth knows now. So three things, in order: To Virginia Energy and the HB 323 work group: Name a demonstration site. A plan that says waste heat is promising and should be studied further is the same plan every state has. A plan that says here is the county, here is the campus, here is the greenhouse, and here is the date the first harvest comes off the line is the one other states copy. Southside has the land, the power corridors, the research institutes and the appetite. Put the pilot where the applications are landing. To the 2027 General Assembly: Make heat reuse a condition of the site assessment, not a line in a study. The state already requires an applicant over 100 megawatts to assess impacts on farmland, water, parks and sound. Add one column: what beneficial use will be made of the heat, and what share of it goes to the host community. Developers will price it in, because they price in everything a county asks for, and the ones who plan for it will win the rezonings the ones who don’t are losing. To every board of supervisors with an application in front of it this fall: You do not have to choose between Loudoun’s money and Amherst’s no. Ask the applicant where the heat goes. If the answer is “the cooling tower,” you have learned what kind of neighbor they intend to be. If the answer is “the farm,” you have a site plan worth voting for. Virginia wrote the law. Nobody in the country has done that yet. The only question left is whether we are the first state to use it or the first state to file it. Andrew Potter is the founder and CEO of Intelligent Harvest, a Lynchburg company that develops greenhouses and community farms powered by data-center waste heat.

artigo.texto: The Eugene City Council returned Sept. 14 from their summer break to a room packed full of residents. All members of the council, barring Ward 3 councilor Alan Zelenka, were in attendance. Mayor Kaarin Knudson expressed her appreciation for those in attendance, who would later share their thoughts during public comment. Mayor Knudson’s proclamations Knudson then moved on to acknowledge the Fiesta Cultural and Cascade Chorus Barbershop Harmony Day events, which took place earlier this month. Knudson also highlighted the Society for the Legitimization of the Ubiquitous Gastropod Queen Celebration Week, which will take place Sept. 20 through 26. Following these proclamations, council members were given the opportunity to speak on items of personal interest. These comments largely regarded the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks in New York City on Sept. 11, 2001. Ward 2 councilor Matt Keating read the words of a plaque he visited this summer at the United States Capitol building, which honors United Airlines Flight 93 and said, “May we never forget.” Randy Groves, councilor representing Ward 8, highlighted the annual stair climb hosted by local firefighters, which takes place in remembrance of those lost at Autzen Stadium each year. He spoke to his personal experience on that day as a former local firefighter and fire chief of Eugene Springfield Fire. “Our first priority, of course, was always to protect this community,” Groves said. Knudson closed by encouraging community members to reflect on their personal experiences regarding that tragedy. “It is important to think about what we do when we feel afraid and how we decide to walk into the future with courage and compassion,” Knudson said. Dozens of public commentators speak to council Approximately 72 individuals were signed up to give public comments, while more spectated. The public comment period is restricted to 90 minutes or ending at 10 p.m., whichever comes first. Only 43 of those 72 were able to address the council before time expired. The majority of public comment was in response to a recent proposal to use the former Hynix site for a data center. Residents expressed everything from environmental concerns to personal beliefs as reasons for councilors to bar this land purchase or construction. Many called for a moratorium, a legally authorized period of delay, which could allow for further public discussion and regulations to be put in place. However, Knudson revealed that this action would not be necessary since the construction of a data center at this site is already not allowed under city zoning regulations. In a Sept. 8 letter, the city outlined that the site is within an E-1 or Campus Employment zone, which does not currently list data centers as a permitted use for the land. Additionally, a city council work session is currently scheduled for Dec. 14 to discuss data centers in more detail. This letter’s content and city action were acknowledged by numerous public commentators as a “step in the right direction,” however, they still advocated that there is far more work to be done. Theo Milligan, a resident of Ward 5, explained that Eugene’s nature and greenery are among its defining characteristics and appeals. Milligan expressed their belief that “a data center would be the antithesis of our entire community.” With the Willow Creek Preserve nearby the proposed site, they worry that a data center would poison the land, saying “We cannot let this happen.” Later on in the public comment, Ellen Bridges, a lifelong resident of the Pacific Northwest, sang a song for the councilors. “I am going to sing out for the love of clean water, … of clean air, (and) the freedom of silence,” Bridges said. They explained their belief that while data centers are not necessary, these things are for the health of a city. Finally, Bridges thanked the council and urged them to set a good example, ending their statement with, “The only data center that I want is a library.” Nate Rhoads, during their comments, cited National Public Radio, which said that despite political polarization both the Democratic and Republican parties can agree on two things. “One: Dolly Parton was a saint. And two: the majority of voters … opposed data centers in their communities,” Rhoads said. They went on to explain that as a constituent and a taxpayer, they are “somehow (the) boss” of council members, with Rhoads stating, “As one of your many bosses, I am telling you, just say no to large-scale data centers.” In addition to comments regarding data centers, residents also raised concerns about public safety and policing in Eugene. One resident shared the effects that losing the CAHOOTS program has caused. Jacob Trewe of Ward 1 said, “There is a clear and evident gap in public safety that needs addressing.” True went on to cite a study by the Rohlfs Lab at the University of Oregon that showed that of the 235 calls that CAHOOTS used to cover, now 126 calls per week are being unaddressed. Board President Lisa Levsen of Neighbors Feeding Neighbors in Eugene spoke out regarding the policing in Washington Jefferson Park, where meals are served. “We have people who are afraid to come for meals because they don’t want to be arrested,” Levsen said. Levsen went on to urge councilors to create further conversation and positive change to “take care of our most fragile citizens.” The next Eugene City Council meeting will be held Monday, Sept. 28.

Summary As AI workloads drive unprecedented growth in data center capacity and density, cooling infrastructure has become an increasingly critical factor in getting facilities online quickly and reliably. Traditional piping methods such as welding, brazing and grooving can introduce labor-intensive processes, sequential work dependencies and skilled labor constraints that make it difficult to keep pace with aggressive construction schedules. This webinar explores how modern press technology can help data center owners, engineers and contractors rethink the design and installation of cooling and fluid systems. Viewers will learn how eliminating hot work and reducing installation time can support parallel construction workflows, accelerate commissioning and create a more scalable approach to high-density data center development. The session will also examine opportunities to improve consistency, quality and sustainability across cooling infrastructure while maintaining the standards and performance required for mission-critical environments. Key Takeaways: - Understand the mechanical infrastructure challenges affecting AI data center speed-to-market. - Learn how press technology can significantly reduce piping installation time. - Explore how eliminating hot work enables safer, more parallel construction workflows. - Discover ways to improve consistency, commissioning efficiency and system quality at scale. - See how press systems support chilled water, cooling loops and other critical data center applications.

artigo.texto: Jørgensen urged tech companies to view EU efforts to regulate their environmental impact as an "opportunity" that could help them win over a skeptical public. | EP BRUSSELS — Brussels on Monday unveiled an environmental rating scheme for data centers that power artificial intelligence, a move the EU's energy chief described as the first step in pressuring tech giants into aligning with the continent’s climate efforts. The new rules, which will apply from August 2027, oblige big data centers to display a label grading them on their energy efficiency, water usage and clean power uptake on a scale of A to G, much like the EU's influential appliances ranking. “This will add a lot of transparency and hopefully provide the incentives for these data centers to be as sustainable as possible,” said Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen in an interview with POLITICO ahead of the label's presentation. Advertisement The new label is optional for smaller data centers, “but later we are also going to introduce minimum performance standards which, of course, will put more pressure on those who may not voluntarily wish to be as sustainable as we want them to,” he added. While Australia and Singapore already have schemes rating the energy efficiency of data centers, the Commission's new label would be the most comprehensive worldwide — asking tech companies to be transparent not only about their power use but also their impact on the local and global environment via information on how much water they consume, how clean their electricity is, whether they reuse the heat they generate and more. The EU executive's performance standards, which the Commission wants to present in spring 2027, are expected to tighten the screws by setting mandatory sustainability thresholds for newly built or retrofitted data centers. Those two initiatives are an attempt at ensuring the European Union can compete in the artificial intelligence race without sacrificing its commitment to climate neutrality in 2050, Jørgensen said. “We need to deal with this in a way that data centers in the future are not something that will hurt our energy systems, and thereby our competitiveness and capabilities of decarbonizing and making sure we have security of supply for our citizens,” he said. “If we do not make sure that these big power consumers are indeed in line with our overall objectives… then they will risk undermining our ability to live up to our own targets,” Jørgensen warned. Data centers are already hoovering up 2.5% of the bloc’s electricity use, a share expected to double in the coming years, he noted. “We’re looking at a huge change.” Advertisement Monday's announcement is a delegated regulation, meaning that it can take effect without the input of EU governments and the European Parliament. The two institutions have two months to object to the regulation, however. The label will be generated automatically each year from figures companies are already required to report under the bloc's energy efficiency rules, though an accompanying Commission report acknowledges that compliance with those rules is low: Only 36% of sites in the EU disclose required data. Go green, get popular Data center operators have lobbied against the Commission's plans. The European Data Center Association in April warned that the requirements would kill investment and in June insisted that the bloc must prioritize AI ambitions over its climate goals. Earlier this year, a Commission document seen by POLITICO indicated that around 20 percent of Europe’s data centers could land at the bottom of the new rating scheme. But Jørgensen urged tech companies to view EU efforts to regulate their environmental impact as an "opportunity" that could help them win over a skeptical public. In the United States, a backlash is mounting against AI infrastructure, in part over its voracious appetite for energy and water. Similar protests are starting to emerge in Europe. Advertisement “We do see some places where public opinion is maybe turning a little bit against these data centers, we've seen it in some places in Europe and we see it even more so in the United States of America,” said Jørgensen. “So I firmly believe that it's also in the interest of the data centers to be able to show how sustainable they are.” But he indicated that the EU would not impose bloc-wide rules requiring data center operators to provide their own clean energy, something his Commission colleague Teresa Ribera advocated for in a recent interview with POLITICO. “This will always be a national decision,” he said. Still, government efforts such as Spain’s recent move toward forcing data centers to provide a share of their own renewable power are “a part of the solution in many places, because the consumption of these data centers will be so big,” he added. Overall, Jørgensen said, the EU wants to avoid developments such as in the U.S., where data centers are increasing the demand for polluting fossil fuels. “My overall message to the Big Tech sector is: We want AI, of course, we want data centers, we want Europe to be a place for investments, but it's in the interest of them and of the European Union that we do it in a way that is sustainable,” he said. “And we will be setting demands for them.”

artigo.texto: - ABB introduces Infinitus, the industry’s first source-to-rack direct current portfolio for AI data centers designed for architecture flexibility - Breakthrough Infinitus solid-state transformers help maximize energy efficiency and reduce physical footprint, alongside DC power distribution and protection technologies to enhance overall system performance - Infinitus direct current portfolio expected to drive similar benefits across other industries including industrial buildings, manufacturing, renewables, and marine operations ABB today announced the launch of Infinitus, a portfolio of direct current (DC) solutions designed to manage the increasing power demands of AI data centers. The portfolio will accelerate the adoption of DC architectures in data centers improving energy efficiency and reducing power infrastructure footprint, while increasing available computing capacity. ABB expects other energy-intensive industries to make the same transition. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global data center electricity demand to more than double by 2030 and ABB estimates that approximately 25-40% of new capacity installed in 2030 could be using DC distribution. Next-generation AI chips are expected to draw 1 MW per rack and beyond, an increase from today's almost 200 kW, requiring a shift to DC architecture that can support performance while driving energy efficiency. With 800 VDC distribution, the footprint is more compact while eliminating redundant conversion steps and cutting heat losses of conventional alternating current (AC) systems. A recent BCG / ABB report calculated that DC distribution delivers energy efficiency gains of more than 5% and increases available space for compute racks. For a 500MW data center, a 5% efficiency gain can mean 25 MW more power for revenue-generating IT loads and more than US $300 million in potential additional revenue per year. With 5% efficiency gains for a 500 MW data center campus, the energy savings over one year would be equivalent to powering Washington D.C. for almost a full week. Giampiero Frisio, President of ABB’s Electrification business area, said: “ABB has pioneered DC technology for more than 25 years across several segments. We are working closely with chipmakers, hyperscale customers, supply partners and industry bodies to set the standards and the pace for the roll-out of high-efficiency DC architectures. Infinitus is the first portfolio providing the building blocks for any data center architecture - either DC native or hybrid AC/ DC - to power next-generation AI chips efficiently. This technology will bring similar energy efficiency gains to other energy-intensive industries such as large scale manufacturing, renewables and marine operations.” Infinitus is the industry's first integrated source-to-rack DC portfolio. At its core is ABB’s breakthrough Infinitus solid-state transformer technology, enabling sites to operate with a smaller footprint and greater energy efficiency. As the only major electrification supplier with both the world's first fully IEC-certified solid-state circuit breaker and an industry-first static medium-voltage UPS in production, ABB delivers a breadth of technology unmatched in the market. ABB’s Infinitus DC portfolio includes five key building blocks: - Medium Voltage Powertrains deliver stable resilient power from the grid or on-site generation; - DC Sources and Power Quality converts AC to DC removing conversion from white space; - DC Power Distribution delivers power safely and reliably, enabling higher power density in a smaller footprint; - DC Power Protection provides protection for operators, AI servers and hardware from DC overcurrents; - Cooling Optimization reduces energy consumption across grey and white space with DC connected variable speed drives and motors. ABB works with customers to design solutions tailored to their specific power demands, facility layout, and energy mix. This partnership approach ensures each deployment is optimized for maximum efficiency and reliability. The Infinitus portfolio complements traditional AC systems with DC flexibility that supports customers across all power architectures while also enabling unprecedented efficiency, reliability, and scalability for AI-era data centers. For next-generation data centers, this integrated architecture enables the high-density, high-efficiency power delivery that future AI chips demand. With a number of main components produced in the next twelve months, the first DC-native facilities using the complete Infinitus portfolio are expected to be installed and operational within two to three years. The portfolio launch extends support for ABB's continued collaboration with NVIDIA, first announced in October 2025, to develop 800 VDC power architectures for gigawatt-scale AI facilities. ABB brings more than 25 years of DC experience and over 700 patents spanning renewables, power generation, energy storage, motors and drives. ABB is a global technology leader in electrification and automation, enabling a more sustainable and resource-efficient future. By connecting its engineering and digitalization expertise, ABB helps industries run at high performance, while becoming more efficient, productive and sustainable so they outperform. At ABB, we call this ‘Engineered to Outrun’. The company has over 140 years of history and around 110,000 employees worldwide. ABB’s shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange (ABBN) and Nasdaq Stockholm (ABB). www.abb.com

artigo.texto: Evento no Acre adota metodologia para compensar pegada de carbono e reúne especialistas em painel A sustentabilidade e a transição para uma economia de baixo carbono deixaram de ser pautas do futuro para se tornarem compromissos do presente na Amazônia. Durante a realização do Inova Amazônia Summit, em Rio Branco, o evento não apenas debateu o assunto, mas aplicou na prática o conceito de neutralidade ao descarbonizar as suas atividades. A iniciativa é viabilizada em parceria com a climatetech de descarbonização Compensei, responsável por aplicar a metodologia MRC (Medir, Reduzir e Compensar) ao longo de toda a programação. “O Carbono Neutro é um evento onde a gente a Compensei consegue medir e reduzir as emissões e compensar o impacto ambiental e climático. É a metodologia MRC: medir e reduzir e compensar. Primeiro a gente mede o quanto de emissão o evento está gerando desde o pré-evento, da seleção de fornecedores, montagem e desmontagem, e durante o evento a gente faz algumas ações para redução dessas emissões”, explicou João Vitor, analista de Inteligência Comercial. As emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE) geradas pelo evento serão mapeadas e neutralizadas por meio de créditos. “O Sebrae está investindo em créditos de carbono dentro de um projeto da Amazônia, que é justamente esse que remove o carbono da atmosfera. O crédito de carbono equivale a uma tonelada de gás de efeito estufa removida da atmosfera. Para engajar os visitantes, o evento disponibilizou o “Carbonômetro”, uma ferramenta acessível via QR Code nos crachás, permitindo que cada participante calcule sua pegada de carbono individual. Além da medição, o evento estimulou atitudes sustentáveis como a gestão correta de resíduos, o uso de copos de papel e a substituição do plástico descartável por garrafas reutilizáveis. “Hoje a nossa missão é impactar o máximo de pessoas, máximo de empresas e o máximo de eventos pra que todo mundo consiga avançar cada vez mais na ação climática. Essa iniciativa do Sebrae representa um grande passo e uma grande visibilidade principalmente para nossa Amazônia e para tantos microempreendedores que estão aqui trazendo produtos sustentáveis e trazendo inovação”, explicou. Painel aborda oportunidades e integridade dos créditos verdes na Amazônia Conectado às ações práticas de descarbonização do evento, o painel “Mercado de carbono: oportunidades reais para a Amazônia, integridade e créditos verdes”reuniu especialistas para discutir os caminhos que transformam o potencial ambiental do bioma em resultados concretos para o território e para os pequenos negócios. A moderação do painel foi conduzida por Elaine Novetti, analista técnica do Sebrae Nacional, especialista em gestão de pequenos negócios administração marketing e gestão de pessoas. O debate reuniu referências na área ambiental e de inovação. Vilena Ribeiro, bióloga, doutora em Biodiversidade e CEO da Compensei, enfatizou o papel da ciência e o avanço institucional do Sebrae ao incorporar parâmetros de sustentabilidade nas diretrizes. “Nós somos uma startup que trabalha com inovação aplicada à sustentabilidade. Então nós temos três eixos grandes de atuação fornecendo esses serviços tanto para empresas quanto para eventos e hoje é uma grande felicidade da gente estar aqui junto ao Sebrae Nacional como uma empresa licitada, o que significa que o Sebrae incorporou em todas em toda a sua concepção de eventos”, disse. “Eu sempre falo que o impacto negativo, o que a gente tem que fazer é transformar em impacto positivo. Esse é o primeiro passo, já o segundo passo é reduzir as emissões a partir do momento que eu conheço da minha operação e do meu evento e o que eu posso fazer para reduzir ao máximo as emissões. Isso é muito importante, é mais um passo que está sendo dado para atendimento dessa agenda 2030”, continuou. Contexto histórico e o papel do Brasil Resgatando a trajetória global do mercado climáticos, Thiago Mendes lembrou que a estruturação desse mercado teve início com o Protocolo de Kyoto, em 1997. Mendes citou a participação brasileira em iniciativas históricas, como o projeto do Banco Mundial (Prototype Carbon Fund) no final dos anos 1990, que utilizou áreas degradadas e florestas plantadas para produção de carvão vegetal no setor siderúrgico. “O Brasil chegou a ser o maior produtor de créditos de carbono do mundo entre 2003 e 2004, antes de ser ultrapassado por China e Índia. No entanto, a nossa principal vantagem comparativa — a capacidade de remoção de carbono pelas florestas tropicais — ainda precisa ser plenamente contemplada e valorizada”, destacou Thiago. Tecnologia espacial e o monitoramento MRV O engenheiro aeroespacial, pesquisador com certificação NASA e CEO da DivTER Amazon SarTec, Renan Santos detalhou como a tecnologia aeroespacial resolve gargalos históricos de medição e verificação na Amazônia através de geotecnologias e inteligência artificial. “Trabalhamos com o radar de abertura sintética (SAR), capaz de mapear a biomassa e monitorar a floresta mesmo sob a cobertura de nuvens, que atinge até 70% do tempo na região. Desenvolvemos uma plataforma para viabilizar projetos de REDD+ com rapidez e transparência, cruzando dados de desmatamento, biomassa e riscos de incêndio”, explicou Renan.

artigo.texto: 91% of Florida readers fear what AI data centers could cost them Floridians are definitely worried that AI data centers could have a negative impact on our resources and environments. The centers are used to store information along with accessing and analyzing it. If we're doing something on the internet then chances are a data center is being used. The enormous structures can reach 100,000 times the size of a football field, can require as much electricity as 100,000 to 2 million homes, and also use an enormous amount of water without creating jobs. There has been so much recent pushback against the construction of these behemoths and that carried over into your responses with 91% of readers who took our poll say they are worried. Last week I asked: Are you worried about the strain on resources AI Data Centers could cause in Florida? The Results: Yes: 91% No: 9% Hey Jeff, you got a few billion dollars lying around and nothing to do with it? Yea Bill, I do. As a matter of fact, I was talking to Mark and Sergey earlier today and they are in a quandary as well about billions of dollars of “flat money” burning holes in their pants pockets. Okay Jeff, I’m going to get in touch with Jack, he’s in worse shape than all of us, and we five need to sit down and figure out how we’re going to survive this. So, Microsoft called Amazon who googled Google and Meta morphed into Alibaba and the forty thieves. Or something like that. AI Hyper-scalers, doing their best work to make a few bucks by offering up Data Centers around the world. In our best interests, or at our expense? Yes, I am worried about the strain on Florida resources in support of AI Data Centers. In fact, this topic fits well with the previous “Opinion” question about Florida being a good place to retire to. Is power rationing in our future? There’s a moral lesson at play here and greed is a big part of it. Mega-rich brainiacs can recognize an “AI eve of destruction.” Question is, can they recognize the need to prevent it, and how? --Wallace Wildenradt, Satellite Beach Our political leadership failed to fully disclose the true social and community costs of data centers. It was only after public pushback that the darker side of these projects came into view: few long-term jobs, mounting strain on the electrical grid and residential utility bills, and massive consumption of what may become the next great environmental crisis — clean water. The question our leaders owe their constituents an answer to is simple: how did this happen? And more pointedly — what caused them to fail us on a project of this magnitude? The answer, I'd argue, starts with money. Not our money, but the money that funds political campaigns and sets political agendas that too often serve donors rather than voters. It's not a complicated theory. It's the obvious one. This failure points to two necessary responses. First, Citizens United needs to be overturned. Until corrupt money is removed from politics, elected officials will keep answering to funders instead of constituents. Reversing it is a critical step toward returning power to the individual voter. Second, it's time for a moratorium on data center development — a deliberate pause to gather facts, assess real costs, and build a plan that balances two legitimate goals: protecting citizens' rights to liberty and a decent standard of living, and advancing the technology our economy needs.Neither of these reforms will originate with the political leaders currently in office. They are, after all, the direct beneficiaries of the status quo. Change will have to come from us. We the people must demand transparency and hold our leaders accountable — or we will find ourselves living subordinate to money and greed, at growing cost to our standard of living and, most consequentially, to our environment. --Larry J. Medley, Naples We are already struggling to keep the aquifer levels at a level to keep our land safe from sinkholes and salt water intrusion. Let's add a negative source of revenue that has zero benefits except for the hyper wealthy! While we're at it, let's pave over more woods for more development! Such bigly ideas! Seriously, stop building more and wasting resources. We should be building up, not out. Also, grass lawns are the worst invasive plants. —Susan Fender, Keystone Heights I'm very worried about the strain and safety of these AI Data Centers and AI in general. Florida is growing extremely too fast already; the existing aging infrastructure is rapidly failing as I write this. It's not even able to keep up with current conditions let alone adding a bigger strain with any additional building. Allowing facilities of this magnitude is unconscionable as we do not have the resources to sustain them. We cannot even sustain the rapid population/building growth happening now. And it absolutely should not fall on the locals to subsidize any of this. We as a state have already allowed our springs to be tapped and run dry, never to return, creating water shortages. The price of electricity is through the roof and is only one hurricane or fuel price increase away from leaving people unable to even pay their electric bill. Not to mention AI is only as smart as the people who program it. In my opinion, all I see is an extremely overpriced, overrated resource drain that will destroy our entire eco system. AI = GIGO (garbage in garbage out) all while destroying our entire planet including humans. I believe it is drastically reducing peoples' ability to think for themselves, but that's a whole other discussion. I honestly think everyone needs to take a giant step back from the AI being forced into everything and regain control of our own autonomy. I personally can't stand all of this AI stuff. Call me old fashioned if you will, but when people could think for themselves, the world was a better place. Just my two cents. I do not trust AI at all. —Juli Donall, Port St. John There is a lot of bad information being disseminated

artigo.texto: Iowa needs to regulate data centers at the state level | Opinion AI data centers may be an innovation revolution impossible to prevent, but they should be regulated. - Bruce Lear lives in Sioux City. He has been connected to public schools for 38 years. Growing up, organized sports consisted of Little League, or high school baseball in the spring and summer. Fall and winter meant basketball since our school was too tiny for football. There were no sports academies or traveling leagues. But we did have the town basketball court. It was a kid sanctuary where kid law prevailed. No adult supervision, no minimum or maximum age, and both genders were welcome. The rules were simple and strictly enforced. If you cried, you left. We called our own fouls loosely. If you overshot, and the ball went into the crick, you retrieved it. There were arguments, and fights, but there was urgency to end conflict, because finishing the game was more important than the fight. We needed rules or our game would be swallowed by conflict. Another view: Local control is best, even with data centers Now, like the basketball court, data centers need rules that are clear and enforceable, or Iowa small towns and rural life will be swallowed just like our basketball games. Currently, Congress seems to lack urgency and understanding on how to catch up to the data center invasion. It sounds like a bad movie, but it’s a serious threat. Even the creators of AI are warning there needs to be a slowdown. That means the urgency to govern is in the hands of local and state lawmakers. It’s time to play catch-up. History tells us this happened before during the industrial revolution. As industry grew and became more powerful, there were no laws regulating child labor, worker safety, wages and other general working conditions. Working-class people suffered while robber barons lived in gilded mansions. I fear the new crop of robber barons are tech billionaires who are quickly trying to build data centers before the laws catch-up. They promise high-paying jobs but offer no guarantees. They don’t acknowledge their huge consumption of electricity and water, and they ignore the impact these large structures will have on the community. Mark Twain was right when he reportedly said, “History may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes.” I can hear that haunting rhyme echoing across Iowa fields while politicians dither. President Donald Trump said, “Towns that reject data centers risk becoming backwards and poor.” But in a recent Emerson College poll, 60% of Iowans believe data centers will negatively impact the environment. The Iowa Legislature needs to act quickly and decisively. Here are my suggestions for regulating data centers in Iowa. In 1991, Iowa lawmakers allowed gambling but also passed strict guidelines. The Iowa Gaming Commission had to approve the location, communities had to vote to see if the majority supported the idea, and each casino was required to provide a percentage of revenue to a separate nonprofit organization for distribution to benefit the community and surrounding area. I’m on one of those boards now. I believe this model would work for data centers with these five other requirements. - Billionaire tech companies don’t need tax breaks to locate in Iowa. - The tech company must strengthen the electrical grid and pay for its use. - The tech company must in writing assure the community there is sufficient water supply and pay for upgrades to the system and water used. - The tech company must reduce the noise pollution. - The tech company must guarantee the number of permanent jobs. AI data centers may be an innovation revolution impossible to prevent, but they should be regulated. No one should ever threaten violence, but we should vote for politicians willing to seriously regulate data centers. Bruce Lear lives in Sioux City. He has been connected to public schools for 38 years. He taught for 11 years and represented educators as an Iowa State Education Association regional director for 27 years until retiring. Contact: BruceLear2419@gmail.com.

artigo.texto: Acme Solar Holdings hit a fresh all-time high of ₹455.0 on the NSE on September 21, capping a run that has taken the stock up over 100% over eight months and almost 125% from its 52-week low of ₹195.65, touched on January 27. Over just the past six months, the return stands at 76.7%. Set against that: the Nifty 50 spent most of 2026 barely above the record it had already set in September 2024, weighed down by sustained FII selling, while the Nifty Midcap 100 has managed roughly 2% year-to-date and even the more richly rewarded Nifty Smallcap 100 sits at about 13%. Acme Solar's gain isn't just ahead of the market, it is several multiples ahead of even the best-performing broad index. In doing so, it has comprehensively outperformed peers as well, That scale of outperformance has invited scepticism at times, with Acme Solar's own market history showing why: the stock actually slipped on July 30, the day it reported its strongest quarter yet, as investors weighed rich valuation multiples and rapid cash burn against an aggressive expansion plan. What has changed since is not the narrative. The BESS pivot was flagged as early as April 2025, when CEO Nikhil Dhingra called hybrid and FDRE capacity "a critical pivot in our business strategy", but the evidence that the narrative is actually being executed, quarter after quarter and, increasingly, week after week. What the Q1 numbers actually said The July 30 print, unflattering stock reaction notwithstanding, was genuinely strong. Total revenue for Q1 FY27 came in at ₹954 crore, up 63% year-on-year; EBITDA rose 56% to ₹831 crore at an 87% margin; profit after tax jumped 80% to ₹235 crore. Capacity utilisation factors (CUF) hit a record 30.9%, up from 28.5% a year earlier. None of that was BESS alone, but BESS was doing disproportionate work inside those numbers. The company commissioned 2.3 GWh of battery storage in the quarter, taking cumulative commissioned capacity to 3.62 GWh, roughly 40% of all commissioned BESS capacity in India at the time. That capacity alone generated ₹226 crore of the quarter's ₹954 crore in revenue — about a quarter of the total, from a business line that barely existed eighteen months ago. Management also used the call to upgrade full-year guidance, telling analysts the company is now on track for more than 10 GWh of BESS capacity by FY27, pulled forward by nearly three quarters from the original schedule with 70-80% of that target already contracted and locking in more than ₹1,400 crore of near-term revenue at realisations of ₹8-10 per unit through the DEEP portal and HP-TAM markets. Chairman Manoj Upadhyay told the call the company intends to keep 10-12 GWh of BESS capacity available for the short-term market annually over the next five years, even as capex increasingly shifts toward PPA-backed long-term projects. September is where the promise turned into proof If the July call supplied the guidance, September supplied the proof of delivery. On September 16, Acme Solar commissioned 66.68 MW of solar capacity alongside 300 MWh of BESS in Rajasthan. On September 17, a subsidiary commissioned Phase-II of the BESS component of its SJVN-contracted FDRE project in Bikaner — 52.32 MW/209.28 MWh of the eventual 300 MW/1,200 MWh discharge capacity, with commercial operations dated September 19 and the remainder targeted for Q3 FY27. That single subsidiary now has 105.95 MW/423.80 MWh of BESS commissioned. The stock's jump to its record high including the spike on September 18 tracked directly to this run of operational updates, not to any new guidance or analyst upgrade. The market rewarding delivery, essentially in real time. That is the more interesting read on this rally than the headline return itself. Acme Solar isn't being re-rated because the BESS story is new; it's being re-rated because each quarter narrows the gap between what management said it would build and what has actually been switched on and started earning. For a sector where announced capacity and commissioned capacity routinely diverge by years, that gap-closing is, on its own, a data point worth more than the guidance slide it came from. The obvious caveat None of this makes Acme Solar's valuation cheap. At its current price-to-earnings ratio and a market capitalisation heading of over ₹32,000 crore, the stock is pricing in a great deal of future execution alongside the execution already delivered and has outpaced even analyst price targets, which were averaging around ₹428 against a stock now trading near ₹455, suggest the sell-side broadly agrees the easy re-rating has already happened. The next leg of this stock's story depends less on hitting the 10 GWh BESS targetwhich looks very doable, and more on what realisations look like once 10-12 GWh a year is actually competing for space in India's still-developing short-term power and ancillary services markets. Competitors like Adani Green Energy, ReNew and NTPC Green will have noticed, and it remains to be seen how fast they can 'pivot' to a BESS powered strategy yet.

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) have emerged as a critical piece of the power sector ecosystem – with applications across generation (to help manage resource intermittency and provide firm clean power), and across transmission and distribution (to help improve grid stability, load management and a variety of ancillary services). As the power systems become more complex, reliable and secure industrial networks with efficient connectivity are important for seamless communication between various assets – right from renewables or other power supply source, battery containers, power conversion systems, and energy management systems, to SCADA, substations, and grid operators. The government’s plan is to deploy 80 GW of BESS over the next decade, and this would need significant upgradation and enhancement of reliable and secure industrial connectivity systems for uninterrupted operations of utility-scale and industrial BESS projects. Secure communication infrastructure is vital to leverage real-time data for remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, and operational efficiency, and also protect critical assets from cybersecurity risks. The mission of this webinar on “Connected Energy Storage: Building Reliable and Resilient BESS Infrastructure” was to highlight the critical importance of industrial networking for implementing BESS. The webinar focused on key aspects of BESS communication networks and their applications in enabling real-time monitoring, remote diagnostics, cybersecurity, and scalable integration with the power grid. The webinar brought together power producers, renewables and BESS developers, EPC contractors and system integrators, utilities and grid operators, large C&I consumers as well as energy consultants and digital transformation leaders. The webinar delved into discussions around the following topics: - What are the key challenges being faced across renewable energy projects, commercial and industrial facilities and T&D assets with respect to operation of BESS? How do you expect the challenges to evolve as power systems become smarter and more distributed? - What are the key connectivity challenges faced by BESS installations, including remote locations and network disruptions? What role can real-time connectivity play in improving asset visibility, predictive maintenance, and remote operations across distributed BESS sites? - What connectivity technologies and network architectures are already in use to build scalable and resilient BESS infrastructure in India? What are the key design priorities for organisations with respect to BESS communication networks? - With increasing connectivity comes increasing cyber risk. How should utilities, IPPs, and industrial operators approach cybersecurity for BESS infrastructure? The webinar panel included: - Durgesh Agarwal, DGM, NTPC Green Energy - Nitesh Bhutada, Founder, Newen Systems - Naresh Chandak, Senior Vice -President (New Business and Renewable Energy), IndiGrid - Udyut Goyal, Head Business Development, AmpereHour Energy - Dhaval Makhecha, Senior Solutions Account Manager, Belden India - Gaurav Shanbhag, Solution Consulting (Energy & Transportation), Belden Inc For any questions, please write to ashima.gupta@indiainfrastructure.co.in

artigo.texto: RWE has taken the final investment decision (FID) to build a 400 MW/1,100 MWh battery energy storage system at its Moerdijk power station in the Netherlands as part of the system integration solutions for the 795 MW OranjeWind offshore wind farm being developed with TotalEnergies. The battery will comprise 208 lithium-ion battery containers and will be able to deliver its full 400 MW output for almost three hours. Construction is scheduled to start in due course, with commissioning planned for the second quarter of 2028, RWE said on 21 September. OranjeWind, also known as Hollandse Kust West VII, is being built approximately 53 kilometres off the Dutch coast and will comprise 53 Vestas V236-15.0 MW turbines. Offshore construction has already started, with monopile installation currently underway. Turbine installation is planned for 2027, and the wind farm is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The new battery will be connected to the national grid through the existing substation at RWE’s Moerdijk power plant. Under capacity steering agreements with transmission system operator TenneT, it will be dispatched to relieve grid congestion in Noord-Brabant and create additional capacity for parties currently on the grid connection waiting list. The battery will also provide grid services, including instantaneous reserve. RWE already operates a 7.5 MW/11 MWh battery at Moerdijk, also developed as part of OranjeWind’s system integration package, which entered commercial operation in June 2025. OranjeWind’s system integration package also includes electrolysers, e-boilers and smart charging, as part of the tender requirements for the offshore wind farm site, which RWE secured in 2022.
