artigo.texto: Normal to consider longer moratorium on new data centers, Bloomington schedules 2 public hearings MCLEAN COUNTY (25News Now) - Leaders in Normal are considering an extension of the town’s moratorium on new data centers to allow more time for state regulations, however there is no indication whether Bloomington would also consider a longer pause. On Normal’s Town Council agenda Monday night is a proposal to extend the moratorium for six more months until May 31 of next year as the Illinois General Assembly considers the POWER Act. The bill would address concerns about price increases, electricity shortages and environmental impacts. Normal’s current moratorium, expiring Nov. 30, was enacted last spring. “Legislative priorities may have shifted since then. There is renewed interest at the state level for data-center regulation,” Normal town staffers said in a council memo. “Any state action on data centers will necessarily affect how the town handles data centers,” staffers said. Bloomington Mayor Dan Brady told 25News that the city will continue with plans to hold public hearings before the planning commission in October and November. Brady said the first hearing is scheduled for Friday, Oct. 16, and the second hearing will be Monday, Nov. 16. Both meetings start at 4 p.m. at the Bloomington Center for the Performing Arts. artigo.texto: 3 Buy-Rated REITs Collecting Rent From Warehouses, Data Centers and Shopping Centers Three landlords collecting rent from warehouses, data centers and grocery stores are all printing record leasing numbers heading into late 2026, and the common thread behind each one reveals a demand story that goes deeper than the property type. Three property types, one edition. Industrial and logistics, data centers and grocery-anchored shopping centers each run on a different demand engine, but all three landlords below are printing record leasing and raising guidance into the back half of 2026. Prologis alone signed a record 67 million square feet of leases in Q2, its fourth record in the past seven quarters. This is a cross-type edition. Future REIT Rent Check installments return to a single property type. All three names here are equity REITs that own the buildings and collect the rent. No mortgage REITs. No hidden interest-rate spread bets. Dividend safety in each case is measured against core FFO per share, not GAAP EPS. Prologis: The Industrial and Logistics Landlord Prologis (NYSE:PLD | PLD Price Prediction) owns and develops logistics real estate across roughly 20 countries, with a 14,000-acre land bank representing 240 million square feet of embedded development opportunity. Market cap sits near $129.0 billion, and the traded around $134.59 on Sept. 18, up nearly 17% over the past year. The demand backdrop is broadening. Prologis reported period-end occupancy of 95.5%, up 20 basis points sequentially, with U.S. net absorption of 66 million square feet in the second quarter, the highest since 2022. Rent change on rollover ran above 36% on a net effective basis and 22% on cash, and cash same-store NOI grew 8.5%. Management said the portfolio still carries a 17% net effective mark-to-market, roughly $800 million of embedded NOI, before any further market rent growth. Dividend read: PLD pays a $1.07 quarterly dividend, an annualized $4.28 per share. Raised 2026 Core FFO guidance of $6.22 to $6.30 per share covers that payout with meaningful cushion, and the payout has climbed every year on the recent record, from 96 cents in 2024 to $1.01 in 2025 and $1.07 in 2026. Bull case: Record leasing, accelerating cash rent spreads, a balance sheet that improved to 4.8x debt-to-Adjusted EBITDA from 5.3x, and a data-center power pipeline expanded to 5.8 GW, with 1.6 GW secured. CEO Dan Letter framed it directly: “As we look across the business, it’s clear we’re entering the next phase of growth where logistics, data centers, and energy increasingly reinforce one another.” Risk: E-commerce and trade-policy sensitivity. Softer occupancy in Asia at 90.6% and Central PA at 83.7%, plus tariff uncertainty and FX exposure across 20 countries, are the drags that could pinch same-store growth if global goods flows cool. Digital Realty Trust: The AI and Cloud Landlord Digital Realty Trust (NYSE:DLR) owns and operates global data centers, including more than 300 sites serving approximately 6,000 cloud, network, enterprise, and service provider customers. Market cap sits near $66.5 billion. Shares traded around $183.88 on Sept. 18, up nearly 19% this year. This is where the AI CapEx story lands on physical real estate. Every gigawatt of accelerated compute needs a building, a substation, and fiber. DLR is that landlord. Q2 zero-to-one-megawatt-plus interconnection bookings hit a record $108 million. Total backlog reached a record $1.9 billion at 100% share and $1.4 billion at DLR share, roughly 30% of in-place data center rent. Cash renewal spreads were above 25% in the quarter, and the greater-than-one-megawatt bucket delivered a 66.7% mark-to-market. The development pipeline stands at 1.4 gigawatts under construction at a total cost of $20 billion, 63% pre-leased, with an expected stabilized yield of 11.5%. Dividend read: DLR pays $1.22 quarterly, an annualized $4.88 per share. Raised 2026 Core FFO guidance of $8 to $8.10 per share covers the dividend with room to fund development. Management now expects double-digit Core FFO per share growth in 2027 and beyond. Bull case: An AI demand cycle that CEO Andy Power says his company is positioned to absorb without a boom-bust break. Per CNBC coverage from Tuesday, a potential AI slowdown is not the “end of the world” for data center real estate, according to the Digital Realty CEO. Backlog visibility, record interconnection, and the 600-megawatt Kansas City expansion with a runway of up to 2 gigawatts of utility power extend the growth algorithm well past 2027. Risk: Power constraints and capital intensity. Development CapEx guidance ran to $4.25 billion to $4.75 billion net of partner contributions, and any softening in hyperscale demand, permitting delays, or supply chain disruption on transformers and switchgear would slow the delivery cadence supporting that pre-leased backlog. That same power-and-equipment bottleneck is why we mapped the suppliers behind the buildout, from cooling to switchgear, in a free report on the AI infrastructure names that aren’t chipmakers. artigo.texto: OPINION: Public outrage takes center stage at PUCN meeting over data center's power play It would be easy to underestimate those who attended the special agenda meeting of the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada in Carson City last week. The hearing room on the second floor of the Legislature was filled with a mostly older crowd. Many wore green T-shirts that reflected their support for the environment and niceties such as clean air and water and preventing the planet from turning into a piece of crisp bacon. Such crowds often make members of officialdom groan and struggle to keep that "here we go again" look off their faces. On Sept. 17, the folks in the T-shirts had plenty to say about the potential environmental and health risks of Fleet Data Centers' proposed use of large natural gas-fueled generators to power the company's behemoth hyperscale facilities in Storey County. The data centers are designed to accommodate the voracious energy appetite of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the race is on to facilitate the giga-giants. With NV Energy overwhelmed by data center electricity requests and unable to service Fleet, Fleet has responded with a so-called temporary plan that would generate 362 megawatts of power. That's enough power to light up as many as 362,000 regular homes — several times more than the total residences in nearby Reno, speakers noted. Those speakers also noted the obvious — that the rush to develop without first securing a mainstream power source appears to put Fleet, a subsidiary of Tract Capital Management, at odds with state law and Nevada's mandated renewable energy standards. The fact that Thursday's special agenda meeting of the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada had to be moved to a larger space to accommodate interest from the actual public says a lot about the subject. The crowd didn't surprise Reno resident Mitchell Brown Silveira, who has been following data center developments for more than a year at various city council and county commission meetings out of a sense of growing urgency. Not that he was overly confident about winning this fight. Perhaps he's seen other good causes go under the steamroller of Nevada's growth-is-always-good philosophy. "I feel like everything we do is like a stay of execution," he says. "It's like when we succeed, it just pops again somewhere else. It's never a true victory. It's never a true win. It's a stop measure. I wish that the Nevada Legislature would just ban this." Most Nevada elected officials — and those seeking to replace them — now regularly drop their changing views on data center development into campaign speeches and press interviews. That's a considerable change in just a few months. Facing the increasing probability of becoming a one-term governor, even Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) appears to have begun to hear the music. That's due in part to election year politics, but is also in response to growing concerns about the developments' health and environmental impacts across the nation. That makes those folks at the meeting more canaries in the coal mine than people with a little time on their hands. To that end, I watched a number of physicians and former respiratory therapists and technicians add their experienced and informed comments during the meeting. They talked about the health risks of methane-producing natural gas in a rapidly heating region. Carson City physician Sandra Koch called the health risks associated with natural gas power plants "too large to ignore." She was the first of several physicians and medical technicians to warn about the heart, lung and other maladies exacerbated by the noxious emissions. "Every rule we place on electricity generation in this state — emissions limits, safety inspections, testing schedules — exists because unregulated combustion hurts people. It raises the rates of heart attacks, strokes, asthma, mental health, lung disease. Any money we bring in will pale in comparison with the increase in healthcare costs from the disease created. "The request for the behind-the-meter energy generation is troubling because it isn't about a new kind of power plant. It's about whether Nevada intends to enforce its own laws evenly, or whether any sufficiently large or well-connected business can get an exemption." Something the physician Koch said during her three minutes should have rung in the commissioners' ears. "No business should be able to opt out of regulation because compliance is inconvenient or slow," Koch said. "Once that door opens for a few companies, it will be open for all of them." With the public watching this issue more closely, those mandated to protect the best interests of Nevadans would have been wise to follow the doctor's advice. Instead, and to little surprise given the players involved, the commission approved the construction of two private power plants that, while officially temporary, are likely to be operating for years to come. artigo.texto: Umicore Major supplier of premix anode slurries for EV batteries According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Anode Slurry Premix market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global anode slurry premix market is positioned for robust expansion over the 2026-2035 forecast period, with demand projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 6-9%. This growth is underpinned by the rapid scale-up of lithium-ion battery electrode production, particularly for electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. Anode slurry premix, a ready-to-coat blend of active anode material, conductive carbon, binder polymers, and solvent or water, has become a critical intermediate in battery manufacturing, enabling consistent viscosity, dispersion stability, and higher coating speeds. artigo.texto: A US battery storage pilot sponsored by tech giant Google has demonstrated how batteries can capture surplus renewable energy and deliver it during hours with greater fossil generation. Announced 17 September, the demonstration created what the project partners describe as the first environmental revenue stream for battery energy storage system (BESS) assets. The three-month pilot, conducted by Quintrace, part of global sustainable energy infrastructure investor Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners, developer esVolta and renewable energy procurement advisor LevelTen Energy, used hourly, time-stamped Granular Certificates (GCs) to allocate solar energy to grid-connected BESS and shift it to hours when Google’s energy consumption exceeded its renewable supply. esVolta contributed its 240MW/480MWh Anole project and 100MW/200MWh Burksol project to the pilot. Quintrace provided the software platform used to implement verification, whilst LevelTen managed the registry accounts to prevent double-counting and provided the transaction framework for the storage-shift agreements. However, the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), a corporate climate action organisation, is beginning to require hourly reporting for large energy users, and the GHG (greenhouse gases) Protocol is currently evaluating how to address this issue. The pilot was designed to demonstrate both a commercial pathway that gives BESS operators a carbon-based revenue stream and a tracking pathway that accurately accounts for and retires the hourly certificates behind it. Google contracted for defined daily charging and discharging windows based on forecasted gaps in carbon-free energy generation, and the operators dispatched their batteries in line with those guidelines. Contract structure maintains operator control The agreements had a distinctive structure: Google contracted with the battery operators to time-shift environmental attributes it already owned, without tolling the batteries or assuming any merchant or dispatch risk. This structure left the operator in full control of their assets, including pre-defined flexibility to pursue energy price signals and to respond to grid emergencies. Over the pilot period, the batteries charged with renewable energy during the defined mid-day charging window and discharged during the defined evening window, with each hour verified by Quintrace against the EnergyTag standard. Across the three-month pilot, the batteries charged and discharged a total of 9.2GWh during the respective windows. Quintrace’s software follows renewable energy from the moment it charges a battery to the moment it is sent back to the grid. The company claimed its dynamic loss calculations ensure the clean energy claimed is only the clean energy actually delivered. The software can also apply different accounting approaches to fit each agreement structure between battery operator and buyer. Earlier this month, Google announced with renewables developer-operator MN8 Energy, zinc hybrid cathode battery and storage system maker Eos Energy Enterprises, that the companies would be backing the Mammoth Solar project in Kanawha County, West Virginia. The project combines 86MW of solar, 10MW/100MWh of Eos’ Z3 zinc-based long-duration energy storage (LDES) solution, and a 70MW/280MWh lithium-ion (Li-ion) BESS. The latest announcement adds to a growing number of Google-backed pilots and investments into BESS and LDES. If you put it behind the meter and you are using it solely for a specific customer, you’re losing some of the functionality of the asset.” NeoVolta secures $53 million capacity reservation for Ontario AI data centre projects In other news, San Diego-based home battery storage company NeoVolta has announced that its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power, has entered into a binding capacity reservation agreement with Infinite Grid Capital (IGC) to provide BESS equipment for Northern Ontario Edge artificial intelligence data centre projects for calendar year 2027. Announced 17 September, the approximately US$53 million binding commitment represents the first major commercial commitment under NeoVolta Power’s previously announced utility-scale framework with IGC, which contemplates approximately 1.1GWh of potential BESS deployments and approximately US$200 million of potential supply across multiple markets. The capacity reservation agreement is intended to support the Northern Ontario Edge AI data centre project and represents an initial commercial step within NeoVolta’s broader relationship with IGC. NeoVolta hosted a grand-opening ceremony for its NeoVolta Power facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, on 17 September. The 210,600-square-foot facility is a purpose-built domestic BESS manufacturing platform designed to assemble commercial, industrial and utility-scale energy storage products. The company’s initial Pendergrass production line is advancing through commissioning and site acceptance testing, with the production ramp remaining on track for Q4 of 2026. artigo.texto: Schaeffler and CATL deepen collaboration on Battery Management Systems and Integrated PowerBox Solutions - Schaeffler is shaping the rail freight transport of the future - The autonomous axlebox generator, modular power system and electromechanical actuators are accelerating the automation of rail freight wagons - First projects are undergoing field tests At InnoTrans 2026 in Berlin, Schaeffler is showcasing the axlebox generator, modular power system ITRS (Innovative Technology for Railway Systems) and electromechanical linear actuators – innovative system components that are already readying freight wagons for automated and interconnected rail logistics. Frank Steinmetz, who heads rail freight transport activities within the rail sector at Schaeffler, says: Our innovations form the basis for automated processes in rail freight transport, whether for digital automated couplers or automated opening and closing systems. ”They enable loading and unloading processes to be accelerated while substantially reducing downtimes. A reliable and operationally safe power supply is a key prerequisite for the ongoing development of such solutions – and that’s precisely what we are facilitating in collaboration with our partners in the rail industry.” As a key component of the ITRS system architecture, axlebox generators offer an autonomous power supply for rail freight wagons and provide the technical basis for digitalization, connectivity and automation in rail freight transport. Electromechanical linear actuators replace pneumatic or hydraulic systems and offer significant advantages in operation: they support the digital monitoring of positions and speeds, are robust and durable – even under harsh operating conditions – and work according to the “power-on-demand” principle, where energy is only consumed if the actuators are actively engaged. Axlebox generator for autonomous electricity production Thanks to their autonomous energy supply, Schaeffler axlebox generators are enabling key functions in the next generation of rail freight cars. They generate energy within the power system as the basis for automation solutions, to reduce or completely replace manual activities. These include the automatic triggering of actuators for the automatic opening and closing of tarpaulins, doors and hatches on bulk cargo wagons. Axlebox generators represent a permanent and reliable energy source for other electronic components used for communication, for sensors to capture load status, for GPS trackers, or for automated brake testing. Schaeffler axlebox generators are designed for standardized European bogie configurations and axles in rail freight transport (Y25 and UIC standard) and can therefore be used in new vehicles or retrofitted to existing freight wagons. First automation projects undergoing field tests Schaeffler is working with its Slovenian partner Realtronik on solutions for automating rail freight wagons based on the modular, integrated system ITRS. ITRS is a power system consisting of a Schaeffler axlebox generator and coordinated battery management system from Realtronik, which provides a high-performance onboard power supply for the corresponding applications. The first successful pilot projects in the market using the power system are receiving positive feedback from customers and highlight the need to push technologies for the automation of freight wagons to be able to increase the share of rail freight in the overall market. Linear actuators for electrified freight cars With its EWELLIX electromechanical linear actuator series CAHB-2xE and CAHB-2xS (smart variants with integrated controller) and the powerful EMA series of high-performance linear actuators (EMA50 to EMA100, 10kN to 50kN), Schaeffler is replacing pneumatic or hydraulic systems with a highly efficient alternative. In harsh railway operations, the electromechanical linear actuators offer significant advantages: they support the digital monitoring of positions and speeds and are largely unaffected by temperature fluctuations over a large range. In addition, they work according to the “power-on-demand” principle, using energy only if directly activated. In the event of an unforeseen power failure, they are self-locking, which keeps the flaps in a secure position. To overcome the pressing challenges in rail freight transport, the associated logistics have to be digitalized, interconnected, and automated. By presenting the axlebox generator, ITRS power system, and electromechanical linear actuators at InnoTrans, Schaeffler is showing how automation solutions for rail freight transport can already be technically supported and implemented. The bottom-up approach with incremental extensibility, depending on requirements and degree of automation, enables fast and cost-efficient solutions for automation and digitalization. artigo.texto: Why Should Delaware Care? A proposed data center near Newark drew criticism from local residents about the facility’s potential to raise electric bills and damage the environment. It now appears that part of the site will instead host the Christina School District’s Networks Schools for Employable Skills. For months, Newark-area residents have voiced concerns about a proposed data center near the town border, saying it would use too much water and energy and be too noisy. Two months after New Castle County Councilman Tim Sheldon brokered a handshake deal to pause the project, it appears the property’s management company may be moving forward with different plans for at least some of the site. Earlier this month, New York-based developer Shelbourne submitted plans to the county to convert half of an existing building in the White Clay Center, a Newark-area industrial and office park, into a 10-classroom vocational technical school. If the application is approved, the building would be part of Christina School District’s Networks Schools for Employable Skills, according to letters submitted to the county as part of the application. The Networks School focuses on teaching students with individualized education plans (IEPs) “real-world job skills.” Norma Brister, the principal of the Networks School for Employable Skills, told Spotlight Delaware the space would not mark an expansion of the school. Instead, it would allow the school to be housed at one location. Brister said the school is currently located at 30 Blue Hen Drive and also has four “enterprise areas” roughly 4 miles away at the Shue-Medill Middle School. During an August board meeting, Christina school board members approved an agenda item to relocate the school as soon as January 2027. Although an exploratory site plan was submitted on behalf of the school earlier this month, that does not mean the deal has been finalized. What happened to the data center plans? Shelbourne originally planned to demolish the existing White Clay Center office and industrial buildings and construct a three-building data center campus totaling 850,000 square feet. Those plans were previously wrapped into a larger community backlash in Delaware against the growth of the data center industry, which is booming across the country because of the promises of artificial intelligence technology. According to an email exchange between Sheldon and land use attorney Shawn Tucker, the deal depended on the county’s all-but-guaranteed approval of an exploratory plan application from the developer, which would grandfather the land into zoning rules that existed prior to this year. That means the developer would not have to follow the county’s recently-passed data center regulations if the developer ultimately decides to build a data center there. But the data center plan has not yet been approved by the county. The county’s planning department submitted additional comments about the plan last month, including asking the developer to confirm there is enough energy supply to serve the site. Sheldon said the developer is still trying to get the data center plan approved while also seeking out other tenants for the vacant buildings in the business park. “They’re not pushing it, but they’ve gotta keep their options open,” he said.

About us Enerdata is an independent research company that specialises in the analysis and forecasting of energy and climate issues. artigo.texto: The Evolution of Data Center Design: Meeting the Demands of AI AI acceleration is redefining first principles AI training and inference have raised the stakes for how fast we can build and how reliably we can operate. The result is a step‑change in expectations for thermal performance, electrical architectures, deployment velocity, and resiliency. Our industry’s response will shape the next wave of capacity and the sustainability and community impact of facilities located near where people live and work. At ebm‑papst, we see three themes converging: hybrid cooling as the operating norm, HVDC readiness in new builds, and resilient, local‑for‑local supply chains that keep projects on schedule despite global volatility. No matter the theme, the mandate is the same: upfront design for efficiency, acoustics, interoperability, and redundancy. Hybrid cooling is here to stay Rack-level liquid cooling is becoming unavoidable for modern chip thermal loads; air alone cannot remove that heat density. Yet liquid does not eliminate the need for air movement in the data center. Airflow management around enclosures, corridors, and supporting systems remains critical to equipment reliability and serviceability. Facilities maintain cool temperatures inside the data center by rejecting heat outdoors, commonly through air cooled chillers, cooling towers, or dry coolers. What that means for design teams: - Plan for coexistence: Expect rack-level liquid cooling and air throughout the room, coordinated by controls that understand both domains. - Engineer for acoustics: As campuses move closer to communities, noise abatement for outdoor equipment will become a siting and permitting issue. - Target every watt: Efficiency is capacity. Watts saved in cooling translate into watts available for computing, especially in power‑constrained markets. Power density keeps rising without bigger footprints Computing density continues to rise, while real estate and retrofit constraints remain tight. Operators are asking for more airflow and higher static pressure in the same mechanical footprint. That challenges the entire system, from fan and motor selection to controls and mechanical integration. The winning designs will deliver higher power density without sacrificing efficiency or acoustics. Practical implications: - Specify equipment that can scale output within fixed geometry while maintaining high wire‑to‑air efficiency. - Use model‑based design and digital twins to simulate thermal interactions across the room and on the roof line before steel is cut. - Treat controls as a first‑order lever: smarter modulation beats brute force. Aligning electrical and thermal strategies for HVDC While retrofits to high‑voltage DC (HVDC) are often impractical for existing sites, new builds increasingly evaluate HVDC‑ready architectures (frequently discussed around ~800 VDC). Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, which can reduce copper in bus bars and conductors and lower the cost. HVDC distribution can also simplify power quality, reducing harmonic mitigation hardware on sensitive circuits. For thermal systems, this shift is more than an electrical detail. It affects drive selection, controls, and EMI/EMC considerations across fans, pumps, and outdoor equipment. Designing cooling assets to be compatible with HVDC ecosystems helps future‑proof facilities as the powertrain evolves. Interoperability first: BMS and protocol pluralism No two owners standardize their operational technology stacks in the same way. To stay deployable, cooling equipment should be BMS‑agnostic, supporting a wide set of protocols, including Modbus, BACnet, PROFINET, and others. This “interoperability-by-default” mindset reduces integration friction and shortens commissioning timelines, especially on fast‑tracked AI builds. Couple that with on‑premises digital twins that mirror plant behavior, and operators can test control strategies in software, apply AI‑guided optimization, and roll successful tactics into production with confidence. We’ve consistently seen strong alignment between simulated and realized efficiency gains when these models are calibrated and maintained. Supply‑chain resilience is a design decision Localization is more than a procurement strategy; it’s a project‑schedule strategy. A local‑for‑local manufacturing model (Americas, Europe, Asia) lowers tariff exposure, reduces transit time, and provides redundant regional capacity when disruptions strike. In a market where schedules are measured in weeks, not quarters, the difference between six weeks of ocean freight and a domestic lead time can define a project’s critical path. The most effective operators share multi‑year demand signals. Two‑to‑three‑year forecast corridors, supplemented by longer‑range directional views, enable upstream suppliers to secure critical components and expand capacity ahead of demand. That collaboration is how the industry turns macro uncertainty into dependable delivery. The grid constraint is a catalyst for better designs Many U.S. metros face power availability constraints that will shape site selection, phasing, and even micro‑siting. Some operators are assessing on‑site generation (including low‑ or zero‑carbon options) while advocating for utility‑led capacity expansions. Regardless of which path wins in each market, the mechanical plant must be ultra‑efficient, acoustically responsible, and ready to ramp in step with staged electrical availability. What we’re working toward as an industry - Hybrid cooling that’s quiet, efficient, and serviceable at scale. - HVDC‑ready cooling assets that integrate cleanly into evolving powertrains. - Interoperable controls that plug into any owner’s BMS ecosystem. - Digital‑twin‑driven operations that turn models into measurable savings. - Local‑for‑local resiliency with redundant regional manufacturing and long‑range planning. - Community‑minded design that respects neighbors while unlocking compute growth.

artigo.texto: Trending WILLIAMSPORT -- A draft of a curative amendment for data centers was introduced at the Lycoming County Planning Commission meeting this week, the next step in trying to get ahead of the growing expansion of data centers in the state. Although a copy of the document was only available for the members of the commission, John LaVelle, of Entech Engineering Inc.,the company that had been hired to work on the amendment, offered some general comments on the issues that are addressed in the amendment. In June, at the request of the Lycoming County Planning and Community Development Department, the county commissioners approved the drafting of the amendment to the county's land development ordinance which triggered an 180-day period in which to get that accomplished and approved. Jason Bogle, chair of the Planning Commission stressed that what they were looking at was only a draft and that nothing was set in stone. In Pennsylvania if there are not specific areas designated for a use, a developer can come into a municipality and pick wherever they would like to build their facility. Because data centers were not specifically addressed in the county's zoning ordinance, LaVelle pointed out that the county had been vulnerable before they voted to draft the curative amendment. "We don't have a data center use in the local county building ordinance, so right there, you have a situation where…until you do the curative amendment, you had exposure there where somebody could have come in and asked for locations," he said. The state's fair share doctrine does not allow refusal of a legitimate business within a municipality or in the case of those entities covered by the county's zoning ordinance, somewhere within those areas. Currently there are 19 municipalities that are governed by the county's zoning ordinance. "Within the fair share considerations, you have to recognize the use. You need to explain what the use is and you need to give the use a place where it can be developed," LaVelle said. "And then you need to apply safeguards, special exception regulations, review standards that need to be met in order to have the use play well with surrounding uses and community," he added. Topics that were mentioned at the meeting which are included in the amendment were power sources for the centers, water supply, zones permitted, setbacks and noise generated by the facilities and de-commissioning. "Within the development review standards, the ordinance basically asks to report a land development plan that lays out the campus itself," he said. "Is it a campus or just the building itself…what's the backup power generation plan? Where's the infrastructure going to go," he said. In terms of noise and vibration, the amendment can include pre-and post-construction noise sections. "We also ask what are the methods of supply for water and electricity and cooling," he said. He cautioned that although the amendment can state a preference for a specific type of system, such as a closed loop system, it cannot design the data center. Before the commission's next meeting, Bogle asked the members to discuss any questions they have with the planning department in order for any revisions or adjustments to the amendment can be made so that a recommendation to the county commissioners. Public comment would go out 30 days before the commissioners hold public comment hearings, with the first, he said, possibly taking place in mid-November.

artigo.texto: What are the real effects of data centers? (Voice of the people) What are the real effects of data centers? Data centers store and process digital data. They are used by medical facilities, financial institutions, government agencies and everyone else that processes data in a remote location or “cloud,” including Internet and cell phone users. Some data centers have the capability to process data for artificial intelligence. What makes data centers so controversial that some areas, including entire states, have placed a moratorium on their construction? Is it the fear of AI, operational and contractual complexity, lack of concrete information or unacceptable experiences with existing data centers? All can be true and reason for concern. Do data centers provide enough benefit to mitigate these concerns? This question must be publicly addressed by local government leaders before data centers are permitted. It is an easy question to ask, but it is very hard to answer. How do you monetize harm to the environment, use of limited resources, risk of unfulfilled promises or changes to the quality of life and to the character of an area? How do you value public input? Knowledge and transparency are the keys to the answer. An unbiased, expert consultant needs to generate an area-specific, detailed report that addresses these concerns and lists the pros and cons. Edward McDonald, Auburndale Nation needs a well-education populace Professor Bruce Anderson's column, "Is college worth the cost?" [8-30-2026] concluded that it is. I would like to add another reason: Our nation needs to have a well-educated population that can think critically. The first failure in being able to think critically is believing to be true that which we want to be true. It's called confirmation bias. Our higher education system is broken, as is our tax system: We are permitting billionaires and large corporations to skim trillions of dollars out of the economy while giving little or nothing back. There are now 40 million Americans with federal student debt totaling $1.6 trillion. College was at one time affordable. I spent 12 years in college, grad school and law school, with a four-year hiatus in the U.S. Army. My total tuition was less than $17,000. The schools? Whittier College, USC, Harvard Grad School, Harvard Law School. The total for tuition today? $689,000. What we need to do is to educate our students so that they know how to take back our country from the oligarchs. College should be geared to do that. In fact, critical thinking skills should be taught in our public schools, starting in the sixth grade. Richard Sutherland, Winter Haven Do your homework on candidates. Who do they owe? I am a native Floridian living my 100th year of life in my home in Lakeland and I want to encourage voters to please do your due diligence on the candidates for statewide offices before the November election. It is imperative that all of the immense political power that will be exercised by the election winners will be vested in the hands of the best possible candidates. For instance, we all need to be concerned about the motives and qualifications of those aspiring candidates given huge amounts of money by large campaign contributors, as well as those candidates who might have a personal financial interest in the future outcome of artificial intelligence technology and its required data centers. My beloved state of Florida has managed an amazing recovery and progressed a long way from the Great Depression of the 1930s and World War II in the 1940s thanks to the leadership of some outstanding Florida officials. We now have a statewide population of about 24-million and we are one of the fastest-growing states in the nation. We cannot afford to squander any of that hard-earned success at the hands of the wrong winners of the upcoming election. John A. Causey, Lakeland Want to contribute? artigo.texto: Vishal Mittal, founder and CEO of Delectrik makes the case for flow batteries to meet India’s long-duration needs in an exclusive ESN Premium interview. Vishal Mittal founded Delectrik in 2016, drawing on a background in chemical engineering and 25 years of experience in fuel cells and flow batteries to pursue the goal of creating an effective vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) for renewable energy storage. The startup found it hard to do business in the price-conscious Indian market. So, the flow battery manufacturer went further afield and instead made its first customer deployments overseas, in Australia. Delectrik—the name is a portmanteau of “decentralised electric network”—began with kilowatt-hour scale batteries. Repeat customer orders saw the systems scale up to 20-foot, then 40-foot and into the megawatt-hours. Yet the company, completely self-funded, was still bootstrapped: “surviving based on margins on the products we were selling,” Mittal says. The answer was, again, about scale: this time, to pursue opportunities that brought the company’s focus back to India. Having built a low-cost battery technology, the next logical step was to close a first utility-scale contract. “That’s when we started focusing on the Indian market, because as an Indian company, directly going from small megawatt-hour to utility-scale contracts overseas is very difficult,” Mittal says. India also has an energy sector in which state-owned or partially state-owned companies supply about half of the grid’s electricity. It was a subsidiary of one of these, NTPC, that awarded Delectrik an initial 600kW/3,000kWh flow battery pilot in June 2024. NTPC had always sought alternative technologies to lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries and was “quite excited” to see Delectrik as an Indian company exporting advanced energy storage technology overseas, Mittal claims. The 3MWh, 5-hour duration system has now been in successful operation for close to a year at NTPC’s R&D centre, NTPC Energy Technology Research Alliance (NETRA) in Uttar Pradesh. “NTPC were quite excited in terms of what we were doing as an Indian company with all these exports,” leading to that initial contract, Mittal says. NTPC’s 100MWh project This paved the way for the later award of a milestone project for India’s non-lithium energy storage sector. In February 2026, NTPC subsidiary NTPC Renewable Energy invited bids to deploy a 100MWh VRFB long-duration energy storage (LDES) system at Khavda renewable energy park in Gujarat. Delectrik was selected to provide the system in July, after making a joint bid with infrastructure solutions provider Bondada Engineering. The project must be designed as a 16.7MW VRFB with 100MWh capacity (~5.9-hour duration) and will be built at the 30GW Khavda complex, which features a mix of renewable energy and storage technologies. Due to the size of the projects up for tender, Delectrik did not satisfy some of the commercial requirements for bidders, such as minimum company turnover in the tens of millions of dollars. So, the company paired with EPC Bondada, which carried out the bidding, but the project will effectively then be handed back to Delectrik as the OEM-plus-EPC. The flow battery player is now bidding on several projects overseas, and Mittal hints at interest in tenders in Australia, Japan, South Africa and the ASEAN region. The CEO won’t share details about the flow battery’s costs but argues that the NTPC tender win is evidence that Delectrik has developed a competitive technology. “You could argue ‘these are the benefits of the technology,’ but at the end of the day, when you actually talk to utilities, they can pay some premium, but they’ll not pay a very significant premium over where lithium is today, so I think that’s where our advantage comes in, in terms of where we are with respect to our cost points,” the CEO says. “India is a fairly price-sensitive market, and if we have been able to close such large projects with actual utilities—these are not Amazon or Google’s data centres—these are power utilities, which look at every cent and penny.” This is why, Mittal says, Delectrik is “very bullish” that the company could “get to a gigawatt-hour-scale order book in the next 12 months.” Why would the market choose flow batteries? Nonetheless, utilities are not trialling flow batteries for purely economic reasons. The drivers are manifold: decoupling from China-dominated lithium battery supply chains, the thermal safety advantage and perhaps most of all, the potential for low-cost, long-duration energy storage (LDES) at scale are among them. “The market is now demanding longer duration storage. Even in India, where it started with 2-hour, 4-hour, now that the penetration of renewable energy is increasing, the market really needs these 6-hours+ of storage,” Mittal says, and the utilities and power generators are typically the ones willing to take the forward bet on technology. India is pursuing goals of 500GW new non-fossil fuel energy generation by 2030 and net zero emissions by 2070. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has modelled a need for ~74GW/411GWh of energy storage in India by 2031-2032. Crucially, this includes two technology types: 47GW/236GWh of battery storage and 27GW/175GWh of pumped hydro energy storage (PHES). artigo.texto: Sacramento is joining the nationwide debate over data centers after news surfaced this week of a proposal that could be in the works in South Sacramento. Following the news, Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty asked city staff to look into impacts of data centers within city limits at Tuesday’s city council meeting. “There’s growing interest and curiosity and somewhat concerns about the issue across our country and locally about data centers,” McCarty said. “... I want Sacramento to be prepared if and when a project comes our way.” The mayor’s direction comes after an Abridged by PBS KVIE report found a New York-based company has requested power from Sacramento Municipality Utilities District for a large-scale data center, with eyes on a property in Southeastern Sacramento. City and state leaders are skeptical about the benefits of data centers.. Constituents both in Sacramento and across the country worry their presence would cause noise pollution, raise public utility rates, strain local power grids and monopolize water sources. All the while some developers in town worry Sacramento could get left behind if it doesn’t start building soon. Data center advocates say they bring jobs and contribute tangible benefits to surrounding communities. As it stands, the city of Sacramento does not have a policy for the high-powered data centers that are required for the advancement of AI technology and use. Local leaders aren’t sold The project generating news buzz would be located in Councilmember Eric Guerra’s District 6. Guerra, who also sits on the California Air Resource Board, told CapRadio this week that he is opposed to the projects. “I met with these folks. I let them know that data centers aren't allowed in the city,” Guerra said of the New York-based company Link Logistics. “The issue of air quality, the concerns about cost of water and utility, those are problems. Until those questions are answered I'm opposed to anything moving forward.” The hypothetical project would also reside in Sacramento County’s District 1, where Guerra is running for an open seat on the Board of Supervisors. His opponent in the county race and 2024 mayoral runner-up Flo Cofer shares his skepticism. “I think that it is important that we don't put the cart seven miles before the horse. I would urge that our elected leaders in the region don't make decisions without consulting experts,” Cofer said. “Don't use pressures from industry to decide and help to push the speed along with which we make a really important decision for our region.” Could Sacramento fall behind? Some in the local business community see the concern around AI as overblown. They also say they don’t want the region to be left behind. John Vignocchi, urban developer and CEO of Sacramento Region Business Leaders Council, said the AI boom is similar to the advent of the railroad system. “If you think back to the 1800s, railroads were unsightly. They went through farms and hunting grounds and other beautiful landscapes. They obstructed views. They were loud and noisy,” Vignocchi said. “But Sacramento back then made a decision to go all in on the railroad, and that made our town relevant. Other towns that didn't stagnated.” Vignocchi said some of the concerns, such as noise pollution, are legitimate, but some are unfounded. “The illegitimate issues, the water consumption, the electricity consumption, AI is going to kill us all, that doomerism is unfounded,” Vignocchi said. Khara Boender, director of Government Affairs for the Data Center Coalition, told CapRadio in a statement that data centers benefit communities and provide essential infrastructure to improve quality of life. “The industry often creates permanent, high-wage jobs (many of which do not require a college degree), provides significant economic investment, and generates substantial local and state tax revenue that helps fund schools,” she said. Environmental advocates raise equity and concerns for the future How data centers impact the environments they’re built in is one of the central debates communities across the country are facing. Herman Barahona is the executive director of Sacramento’s Environmental Justice Coalition. He said his group is deeply concerned with data center impacts on the local environment. “This valley tends to store all kinds of pollution because of its geographic setup,” Barahona said. “We know that this cannot have any good impacts in the long run for the environment.” Barahona also noted his group is disappointed with the lack of transparency from SMUD. “It’s obvious that all these decisions at some point were introduced to SMUD, which handles all our electricity needs for the community,” he said. “There was no process for the community to know about these. How they purchase energy, if there were any NDAs (nondisclosure agreements) signed, we don’t know anything about that.” In reference to the South Sacramento proposal, SMUD told CapRadio earlier in the week it’s not able to share any information with the public due to customer privacy. “We’ve supported data centers here for decades, and with interest from larger-scale projects, we’re developing a fair and equitable large load policy to guide how we plan and connect these customers,” SMUD said in a statement. “SMUD does not make land-use decisions; once projects are approved at the city or county level, we have an obligation to provide power.” Activists say they are also worried about the human cost of data centers. Laurie Litman with Third Act Sacramento, a climate and democracy advocacy group, said the thought of putting a data center in South Sacramento comes from an opportunistic place. “They're taking advantage of places where people are less organized, are less wealthy, are ignored.” Litman said. “Besides all the environmental costs, just the fact that they would consider siting it in South Sacramento where the air quality is worse, it, on every level, checks the boxes of continuing corporate and, and wealth

artigo.texto: The annual fall symphony of carnival music, deep fryer sizzles and laughter at the fairgrounds near Lake Perris could one day be joined by wooshing helicopters and — to many residents’ dismay — the hum of data center machinery. A data center — a building housing computer servers and supporting technology — is part of a project envisioned for 5 acres of the Southern California Fair and Events Center, also known as the Lake Perris fairgrounds. Last month, the fairgrounds board approved a nonbinding agreement with Global Stack USA, which wants to build what it calls a statewide “resilience network” of data centers, heliports and parking that turn fairgrounds into emergency response hubs when disaster strikes. Plans for the Perris fairgrounds could include a helicopter landing pad, parking structure and a shipping container-sized data center that would efficiently use water and power, according to Global Stack. “California’s repeated natural disasters underscore the need for continued investment in emergency preparedness and the public infrastructure communities rely on,” Global Stack CEO Dan Kang said via email. “By bringing together public assets and private investment, we are proposing a new model designed to strengthen that infrastructure while creating sustainable revenue to support fairgrounds for the long term.” The type of data center proposed by Global Stack has been described as an “edge” data center. Those centers place computing capacity “closer to users or devices to reduce latency and network traffic,” Shaolei Ren, a UC Riverside professor of electrical and computer engineering, said in an email. “It is typically smaller and more distributed than hyperscale facilities used for very large-scale cloud computing or (artificial intelligence) training,” Ren said. “Some applications like AI inference and video streaming benefit from nearby computing.” Nationwide, data centers are widely assailed for hoarding water and electricity — driving up utility bills in the process — and are seen as helping AI evolve to the point where it might threaten human existence. The Perris proposal already faces pushback. Residents shared concerns about the project Wednesday, Sept. 16, with the Perris Planning Commission, which during that meeting recommended a data center ban in the city. Such a ban would not apply to the state-owned fairgrounds, which is part of California’s 46th District Agricultural Association and overseen by a board appointed by the governor. The city has no jurisdiction over what gets built at the fairgrounds, Perris spokesperson Stephen Hale said via email. The company defends its proposed projects in the frequently-asked-questions portion of its website. “Because emergency resilience is the whole point, a system meant to keep a community connected during an outage cannot itself be a heavy burden on the grid,” the FAQ reads. “So it isn’t.” Located southwest of the Lake Perris State Recreation Area, the fairgrounds host the Southern California Fair every October. The property also is home to the Perris Auto Speedway and the Toro Wapo Arena Event Center. Southern California Fair CEO Russell Vandenberg said the fair receives no state money and relies on income from property leases. “A lot of fairgrounds are struggling financially,” Vandenberg said. “There’s a lot of maintenance that is deferred through the years just because of the lack of adequate funding to take care of major projects.” On Global Stack’s website, Kang is quoted as saying he was concerned about California’s emergency systems being able to reach every community. “Later, while producing events at California’s fairgrounds, I saw something others had overlooked,” he said. “These public assets represented hundreds of acres of strategically located land throughout the state. They needed sustainable revenue, and California needed stronger emergency resilience. That realization became the foundation of Global Stack.” Vandenberg said Global Stack approached the Perris fairgrounds about the project during a regularly scheduled Sacramento gathering of fair executives. Besides Perris, Global Stack pursued similar projects at fairgrounds in Ventura County and Calistoga, but both projects faltered following local pushback. Global Stack also is seeking a project at the Cow Palace events venue near San Francisco. In all, Global Stack said it’s looking at projects at more than 50 potential sites that could lead to more than $20 million in infrastructure investment and create more than 70,000 jobs. Vandenberg said his board “was interested in discovering additional information” about the project and directed him to sign a nonbinding agreement so Global Stack could flesh out its plans for the fairgrounds. According to Vandenberg, Global Stack wants to develop 5 acres of the 110-acre fairgrounds property. Global Stack’s website describes the heliport as “supporting the everyday activity of a fairground and its surrounding community” and shifting to first-responder and medivac use in an emergency. The parking structure would be a moneymaker for the fairgrounds, Vandenberg said. “I can’t think of any fairgrounds in the state that couldn’t use a parking structure,” he said. “That would be a huge benefit if that was part of the project.” The data center would be about the size of a shipping container, according to Global Stack. “It’s not (one of) the mega type facilities that you might have heard of,” Vandenberg added. On its website, Global Stack said the data center would “process critical information locally, right where it is needed” and that data would be processed locally “rather than routed to facilities owned by out-of-state or international corporations.” Computer servers like those in data centers can generate heat. artigo.texto: After the entry of several renewable energy companies into the Indian stock market, more renewable Independent Power Producers (IPPs) are now looking to jump onto the bandwagon. The latest entrant is Singapore-based Sembcorp’s Indian renewable energy arm, Sembcorp Green Infra. The company has proposed a ₹3,750-crore IPO at a time when it is expanding beyond conventional wind and solar projects into battery energy storage systems (BESS), round-the-clock (RTC) power, and firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) projects. Sembcorp Green Infra is preparing to tap the public markets with a ₹3,750-crore initial public offering, but the company's proposed use of the proceeds suggests that the issue is as much about strengthening its balance sheet as it is about supporting its next phase of growth. The proposed issue is entirely a fresh issue of equity shares. There is no offer-for-sale component. Of the proceeds, ₹3,000 crore is proposed to be used for repayment or prepayment of certain borrowings of the company and its subsidiaries, with the balance earmarked for general corporate purposes. The draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) was filed with SEBI in September. In the latest move, SEBI has now asked the company to furnish more details towards the issue, a procedural issue. Hybrid, RTC & FDRE Gain Ground The timing is significant. Sembcorp Green Infra is building a portfolio in which battery energy storage systems (BESS), hybrid projects, round-the-clock (RTC) power and firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) are becoming increasingly important. From wind and solar to dispatchable power Sembcorp Green Infra's India business had more than 7.6 GW/GWh of total capacity as of March 31, 2026, according to the company's website. Its portfolio spans 105 projects across 13 states and Union Territories, with more than 3.4 GW of solar capacity, more than 2.8 GW of wind capacity and more than 1.4 GWh of energy storage. The company describes itself as one of India's top 10 renewable independent power producers by operational capacity as of March 31, 2026. It also says it was among the country's top three wind operators among IPPs by operational capacity at that point. But the more important change is in the nature of the projects Sembcorp is pursuing. Instead of relying only on standalone solar and wind generation, the company is integrating storage with renewable generation to provide power in a more predictable manner. Sembcorp says its hybrid solutions are designed to provide round-the-clock clean energy. That puts BESS at the centre of the company's next growth phase. BESS becomes a bigger part of the portfolio Sembcorp's India portfolio already includes more than 1.4 GWh of energy storage. The company has been building its capabilities around projects where storage is combined with renewable generation rather than treated as a standalone asset. This matters because the emerging renewable market is increasingly moving towards projects that can deliver power when it is required, rather than simply generate electricity when the sun is shining or the wind is blowing. For Sembcorp, this creates an opportunity to combine its existing wind and solar portfolio with storage and build more complex power supply structures. The company's own description of its Indian business highlights the integration of energy storage with renewable generation as a means of providing round-the-clock clean energy. RTC and FDRE could drive the next project pipeline. The company's move towards RTC and FDRE projects is part of the same shift. RTC projects require renewable generation to be structured around a contracted supply profile, while FDRE projects go a step further by combining renewable generation and enabling technologies such as storage to provide power in a more firm and dispatchable manner. For an IPP such as Sembcorp, these projects can require significantly more complex project design than a conventional solar or wind farm. They can involve multiple generation technologies, storage and sophisticated scheduling and dispatch arrangements. The proposed IPO therefore comes at an important point for the company. The ₹3,000 crore debt repayment is not earmarked directly for building new BESS or renewable projects. Instead, reducing borrowings can strengthen the company's balance sheet as it continues to develop and finance a portfolio that is becoming more capital intensive. That distinction is important. The IPO itself is not a ₹3,750-crore project-funding programme. It is primarily a fresh-equity raise with a large debt-repayment component. IPO as a balance-sheet reset For Sembcorp Green Infra, therefore, the ₹3,750-crore IPO is best viewed in two parts. The first is straightforward: ₹3,000 crore is intended for debt repayment or prepayment. The second is strategic. Sembcorp is increasingly positioning its Indian business around a combination of solar, wind and storage, with hybrid, RTC and FDRE projects forming a more important part of its portfolio. The company already has more than 7.6 GW/GWh of capacity across its Indian platform and more than 1.4 GWh of energy storage. Its stated strategy of integrating storage with renewable generation points towards a business model where the ability to deliver power reliably could become as important as adding renewable megawatts. That makes the proposed IPO less about directly funding another tranche of solar or wind capacity and more about strengthening the financial platform from which Sembcorp can pursue a more complex renewable portfolio. For India's renewable market, that shift is worth watching. As the sector moves from simply adding generation capacity towards providing firm and dispatchable clean power, the companies that can combine renewable generation, storage and long-term contracted supply will increasingly operate in a different segment of the market. Sembcorp's IPO is coming at precisely that transition point.

artigo.texto: The data center backlash is reshaping American politics — one community at a time With striking speed, the widespread debate around data centers has become a fault line in American communities, cutting across political parties, splitting constituencies and forging unexpected alliances. In city halls and county commission chambers, east to west and north to south, people are squaring off against their local representatives. It starts with distrust Data centers have "upended politics as we know it," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. It's more than a not-in-my-backyard issue, he says — it also reflects existential fears that artificial intelligence will take jobs or eliminate humanity entirely. "People just feel like they no longer have control over the technology, [and] that worries them," West says. "This is a real grassroots movement. It's ordinary people all across the country, both Republicans and Democrats." For this story, NPR traveled to data center hot spots and spoke to dozens of activists, politicians, developers and everyday Americans. The picture that emerges is complicated. Data centers have been an economic boon for some communities, helping to lower land taxes and providing jobs. At the same time, the proliferation of secretive deals that often involve elected officials signing nondisclosure agreements has exacerbated suspicions. A recent poll by The Economist and YouGov of nearly 1,600 adults found that about two-thirds of Americans oppose new data center construction in their communities. A rare cocktail of concerns has fueled the opposition, according to Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University. "It's aligning interests in ways that aren't traditional," he says. "If you're in power right now and you are dealing with this issue, you have a target on your back." Elected officials have had to scramble to recalibrate. "It's a recognition that the ground shifted under their feet and they were not ready for that to happen," Borick says. Parties are divided In Loudoun County, Va., data centers are driving a wedge between fellow Democrats. On one side is Juli Briskman, a member of Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors, who has led efforts to slow further data center development. On the other is Phyllis Randall, also a Democrat and the board's chair, who has argued in favor of data centers for the tax revenue they bring into the county, even while acknowledging they are "a double-edged sword" for nearby residents. Briskman is running to unseat Randall in next year's primary. She says her opposition to data centers dates back to 2020, when the board was seeing land-use cases seeking to convert residential and flex-industrial properties into the centers. "I feel like I have been singing this song for a while, and now all of a sudden everyone's grabbing my music and singing along with me," Briskman says. Randall did not respond to NPR's request for comment. Briskman is tapping into a sentiment in her area. Kasey Hatch lives near Loudoun County's Vantage VA2 data center, which is powered by eight natural-gas-fired turbines. Residents say the turbines produce a constant low-pitched rumble along with a high-frequency whine that has become a major source of noise complaints in the surrounding neighborhoods. Hatch, an IT infrastructure engineer for a bank who uses AI in her job, says she and her staunchly Republican cousin "never saw eye to eye on politics." But to her surprise, the last time they met, they were "on the same page about everything" when it came to data centers. At the grassroots level, that translates into Democrats and Republicans working together on an issue of mutual interest. Nusheen Farahani also lives near VA2 and is part of a group of women organized against the facility who regularly show up at public hearings. "I'm a liberal and I'm a Democrat, and the people that are in our little team … not all of them are liberals or Democrats," Farahani says. A similar story is playing out in Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Indiana, to name just a few, where locally organized groups are uniting against data centers — and elected officials. According to the Data Center Opposition Report, which tracks grassroots nonprofits on the issue, some 640,000 people are active in the anti-data center movement and 220 new groups sprang up in just the three months from June through August. They are driven by a feeling that government is part of the problem, according to Ben Green, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan's School of Information. With that comes a real sense of abandonment, he says. "If the policymakers, if my city council or zoning board or township board and governor, if they're on the side of the companies, who's standing up for me?" The economic impact Data centers have been around for a lot longer than the recent AI hype, quietly humming along in the background of the modern internet, powering cloud computing and storing vast amounts of data. AOL set up in Loudoun County, for example, back in the 1990s, giving the tech industry an early beachhead in the county that has only grown due to demand from government agencies in nearby Washington, D.C. To be sure, these facilities have brought economic benefits to the counties where they are located by creating billions of dollars in private investment, construction jobs and a limited number of well-paying positions at the data centers themselves, all the while providing an infusion of tax dollars that have stabilized and even lowered the tax burden for ordinary property owners. And among the many people NPR spoke to for this story who oppose data centers, nearly all acknowledge using AI in their daily life. Farahani, for example, says she "begrudgingly" uses chatbots for certain tasks "to make things easier." artigo.texto: RWE has taken the final investment decision (FID) to build a 400 MW/1,100 MWh battery energy storage system at its Moerdijk power station in the Netherlands as part of the system integration solutions for the 795 MW OranjeWind offshore wind farm being developed with TotalEnergies. The battery will comprise 208 lithium-ion battery containers and will be able to deliver its full 400 MW output for almost three hours. Construction is scheduled to start in due course, with commissioning planned for the second quarter of 2028, RWE said on 21 September. OranjeWind, also known as Hollandse Kust West VII, is being built approximately 53 kilometres off the Dutch coast and will comprise 53 Vestas V236-15.0 MW turbines. Offshore construction has already started, with monopile installation currently underway. Turbine installation is planned for 2027, and the wind farm is scheduled to become operational in 2028. The new battery will be connected to the national grid through the existing substation at RWE’s Moerdijk power plant. Under capacity steering agreements with transmission system operator TenneT, it will be dispatched to relieve grid congestion in Noord-Brabant and create additional capacity for parties currently on the grid connection waiting list. The battery will also provide grid services, including instantaneous reserve. RWE already operates a 7.5 MW/11 MWh battery at Moerdijk, also developed as part of OranjeWind’s system integration package, which entered commercial operation in June 2025. OranjeWind’s system integration package also includes electrolysers, e-boilers and smart charging, as part of the tender requirements for the offshore wind farm site, which RWE secured in 2022.

artigo.texto: O olhar único que há 50 anos acompanha o que é notícia no Brasil e no mundo Data centers: nova lei abre caminho para investimentos, mas regulamentação é desafio O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sancionou na quinta-feira a lei do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), que concede incentivos tributários para empresas que instalarem ou ampliarem data centers no país. O projeto foi aprovado no Congresso durante a semana do esforço concentrado, no início de setembro. Na avaliação do Instituto Brasileiro de Telecomunicações e Soluções Digitais (IBTD), o Redata resolve uma parcela importante do custo de entrada ao suspender tributos federais incidentes sobre equipamentos. A competitividade brasileira, no entanto, dependerá também de outras condições, como regulamentação rápida e previsível, disponibilidade de energia, capacidade de transmissão, expansão de backbones, conectividade internacional, licenciamento e segurança regulatória. — Agora abre-se uma nova etapa voltada à regulamentação e à criação das condições necessárias para transformar o incentivo tributário em investimentos efetivos — salienta André Martins, presidente do Instituto Brasileiro de Telecomunicações e Soluções Digitais (IBTD). Com a publicação oficial da lei no Diário Oficial, deverão ser regulamentados os dispositivos operacionais e os requisitos de habilitação ao regime, além dos procedimentos a serem adotados pela Receita Federal e pelos órgãos competentes para a fruição dos benefícios, explica o IBTD. Com essas regras definidas, poderão ser anunciados os primeiros projetos de investimento por empresas interessadas. Um dos pontos de maior impacto do texto sancionado está na mudança da regra energética. Na versão aprovada pela Câmara, os empreendimentos deveriam atender à sua demanda por meio de fontes "limpas ou renováveis". No Senado, a redação passou a considerar fontes "renováveis ou de baixa emissão", alteração que abre espaço para a participação de fontes como gás natural e energia nuclear, além das hidrelétricas, salienta Alexei Vivan, sócio e head de Energia do CGM Advogados. A definição dos critérios para enquadramento será detalhada na regulamentação do Redata. O desafio agora é o regulamento, que precisa definir com clareza o que é baixa emissão para que a segurança jurídica prometida pela lei chegue, de fato, aos projetos, salienta Bruna Correia, sócia da área de Energia do BMA Advogados, que defende a inclusão das fontes de baixa emissão na nova lei. — É uma decisão acertada, porque o sistema elétrico é equilíbrio: solar e eólica são centrais para a transição, mas a segurança do suprimento depende de fontes despacháveis, que podem ser acionadas de imediato e não variam com o sol e o vento, e o gás natural cumpre esse papel. Para a advogada, o Redata acerta ao condicionar o benefício fiscal a contrapartidas que chegam à vida das pessoas. Segundo ela, a exigência de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão e o limite de consumo de água de 0,05 litro por kWh fazem com que o data center cresça sem disputar com as cidades vizinhas a água e o ar de que elas dependem. — Os aportes de 2% em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação financiam ciência feita aqui e ajudam a formar pesquisadores e engenheiros capazes de desenvolver tecnologia no Brasil, e não apenas operar a que vem de fora. E a oferta de ao menos 10% da capacidade ao mercado doméstico abre essa infraestrutura a startups, universidades e empresas brasileiras, que ganham acesso a processamento de dados no próprio país — esclarece.

artigo.texto: Redata abre caminho para atrair data centers ao Brasil Novo regime reduz desvantagens do país, mas avanço depende de regulamentação, ação dos Estados e energia competitiva O Brasil tem diante de si uma oportunidade importante para ampliar sua participação na economia digital. Os investimentos globais em data centers, inteligência artificial e capacidade computacional estão crescendo rapidamente e a disputa pela atração desses recursos já está em curso há algum tempo. Nesse cenário, a recente aprovação do Redata pelo Congresso e sua sanção presidencial representam um passo importante para que o país ganhe competitividade em relação a outros mercados. A relevância desse avanço está no papel estratégico que os data centers desempenham na economia atual e futura. Essa infraestrutura é essencial para o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e de outras atividades intensivas em capacidade computacional. Por isso, a discussão sobre o novo regime vai além da instalação de novos empreendimentos. Trata-se de criar condições para que o Brasil amplie sua capacidade computacional e, a partir dela, desenvolva e atraia atividades de maior valor agregado, além de estimular investimentos associados em energia, equipamentos e serviços. A dimensão dessa oportunidade é expressiva. Os anúncios de investimentos internacionais em infraestrutura digital alcançaram US$ 270 bilhões em 2025, segundo relatório da UNCTAD, colocando o setor à frente até mesmo das energias renováveis. O Brasil já está no radar de grandes empresas globais de tecnologia, mas participa dessa disputa com uma desvantagem relevante. Sem os efeitos do Redata e uma resposta tributária também dos Estados, o custo para construir um data center no Brasil pode ser cerca de 34% superior ao observado nos Estados Unidos e em países vizinhos da América do Sul, segundo análises da Brasscom. O Redata é, portanto, um passo relevante. Mas sua efetividade dependerá agora da implementação. A regulamentação federal precisa assegurar critérios objetivos, procedimentos céleres e previsibilidade para os investidores, preservando o espírito do texto aprovado pelo Congresso. Será igualmente importante avançar em convênio do Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária para reduzir substancialmente a carga tributária estadual. Essa combinação aproximaria custos brasileiros dos concorrentes e destravaria projetos concretos. Entre as vantagens do Brasil, a energia é central. Data centers são intensivos em consumo energético e precisam operar 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Demandam, portanto, energia contínua, confiável e a preços competitivos. O Brasil parte de uma posição privilegiada por ter uma matriz predominantemente renovável e potencial para combinar diferentes fontes. Os próprios data centers podem estimular novos investimentos em energia limpa e contribuir para a expansão da oferta. Há também uma dimensão estratégica para a relação entre Brasil e Estados Unidos. Os 2 países têm integração relevante em serviços digitais, computação em nuvem, tecnologia e equipamentos, justamente os segmentos em que o Brasil busca atrair investimentos para agregar valor. O Redata pode favorecer essa cooperação e, embora as discussões tarifárias sigam uma agenda própria, investimentos em infraestrutura digital ajudam também a construir uma agenda bilateral positiva, baseada em tecnologia e inovação de longo prazo e estratégica. O Redata, portanto, não é um ponto de chegada, mas um 1º passo. Se vier acompanhado de regulamentação eficiente, ação dos Estados e maior cooperação internacional, o Brasil terá condições de disputar uma parcela maior dos investimentos globais em infraestrutura digital. Mais do que atrair data centers, a oportunidade é ampliar nossa capacidade computacional, desenvolver tecnologia interna e criar empregos qualificados e de alta remuneração.
