artigo.texto: Infra em 1 Minuto: uso de gás em data centers divide governo Pedro Rodrigues defende critérios de emissão no Redata e liberdade para investidores escolherem a matriz energética O Poder360, em parceria com o CBIE (Centro Brasileiro de Infraestrutura), lança neste sábado (19.set.2026) o 180º episódio do programa “Infra em 1 Minuto”. No vídeo, o especialista em energia Pedro Rodrigues, sócio do CBIE, analisa a divergência no governo sobre a inclusão do gás natural entre as fontes que poderão abastecer data centers beneficiados pelo Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter). O programa é publicado semanalmente no canal do Poder360 no YouTube. Assista ao vídeo (2min6s): O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sancionou na 3ª feira (15.set.2026) a lei que institui o Redata. O regime suspende a cobrança de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, modernização e ampliação de data centers no país. Para receber os benefícios, os empreendimentos deverão comprovar que toda a demanda de energia elétrica será atendida por contratos de fornecimento ou autoprodução de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A lei não especificou quais tecnologias poderão ser classificadas como de baixa emissão. A definição será feita por uma portaria interministerial. GÁS NATURAL NO REDATA A versão aprovada pela Câmara exigia que os data centers usassem energia 100% renovável. O Senado acrescentou as fontes consideradas de baixa emissão. A mudança abriu espaço para a inclusão do gás natural, a depender da regulamentação. O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) defende que o combustível seja contemplado. Segundo o ministério, o gás pode assegurar o fornecimento firme exigido pelos centros de processamento de dados, que funcionam continuamente e consomem grande quantidade de eletricidade. O Ministério da Fazenda ainda não definiu uma posição. O secretário-executivo, Rogério Ceron, afirmou que o governo discute o alcance da expressão “baixa emissão”. Entre as alternativas estão exigências de compensação para fontes emissoras, como a compra de créditos de carbono. Rodrigues afirma que condições adicionais podem reduzir a competitividade do gás na geração de energia para os empreendimentos. “Não faz sentido dar incentivo fiscal para baratear o equipamento e, ao mesmo tempo, encarecer a energia, que é a base de tudo”, declarou. ENERGIA FIRME Segundo Rodrigues, os data centers precisam de fornecimento ininterrupto de eletricidade. Falhas podem comprometer serviços de armazenamento, processamento de dados e inteligência artificial. As fontes solar e eólica variam conforme as condições climáticas. As usinas termelétricas a gás, por sua vez, podem ser acionadas seguindo a necessidade do sistema. Para o especialista, a regulamentação deveria estabelecer critérios objetivos de emissão, sem determinar antecipadamente as tecnologias que poderão ser usadas. “Data center não pode piscar. Precisa de energia firme, 24 horas por dia”, afirmou. Rodrigues defende que os investidores escolham a combinação de fontes considerando custos, segurança do fornecimento e parâmetros ambientais estabelecidos pelo governo. “Quem escolhe a fonte é o investidor, não o regulador”, disse. artigo.texto: The annual fall symphony of carnival music, deep fryer sizzles and laughter at the fairgrounds near Lake Perris could one day be joined by wooshing helicopters and — to many residents’ dismay — the hum of data center machinery. A data center — a building housing computer servers and supporting technology — is part of a project envisioned for 5 acres of the Southern California Fair and Events Center, also known as the Lake Perris fairgrounds. Last month, the fairgrounds board approved a nonbinding agreement with Global Stack USA, which wants to build what it calls a statewide “resilience network” of data centers, heliports and parking that turn fairgrounds into emergency response hubs when disaster strikes. Plans for the Perris fairgrounds could include a helicopter landing pad, parking structure and a shipping container-sized data center that would efficiently use water and power, according to Global Stack. “California’s repeated natural disasters underscore the need for continued investment in emergency preparedness and the public infrastructure communities rely on,” Global Stack CEO Dan Kang said via email. “By bringing together public assets and private investment, we are proposing a new model designed to strengthen that infrastructure while creating sustainable revenue to support fairgrounds for the long term.” The type of data center proposed by Global Stack has been described as an “edge” data center. Those centers place computing capacity “closer to users or devices to reduce latency and network traffic,” Shaolei Ren, a UC Riverside professor of electrical and computer engineering, said in an email. “It is typically smaller and more distributed than hyperscale facilities used for very large-scale cloud computing or (artificial intelligence) training,” Ren said. “Some applications like AI inference and video streaming benefit from nearby computing.” Nationwide, data centers are widely assailed for hoarding water and electricity — driving up utility bills in the process — and are seen as helping AI evolve to the point where it might threaten human existence. The Perris proposal already faces pushback. Residents shared concerns about the project Wednesday, Sept. 16, with the Perris Planning Commission, which during that meeting recommended a data center ban in the city. Such a ban would not apply to the state-owned fairgrounds, which is part of California’s 46th District Agricultural Association and overseen by a board appointed by the governor. The city has no jurisdiction over what gets built at the fairgrounds, Perris spokesperson Stephen Hale said via email. The company defends its proposed projects in the frequently-asked-questions portion of its website. “Because emergency resilience is the whole point, a system meant to keep a community connected during an outage cannot itself be a heavy burden on the grid,” the FAQ reads. “So it isn’t.” Located southwest of the Lake Perris State Recreation Area, the fairgrounds host the Southern California Fair every October. The property also is home to the Perris Auto Speedway and the Toro Wapo Arena Event Center. Southern California Fair CEO Russell Vandenberg said the fair receives no state money and relies on income from property leases. “A lot of fairgrounds are struggling financially,” Vandenberg said. “There’s a lot of maintenance that is deferred through the years just because of the lack of adequate funding to take care of major projects.” On Global Stack’s website, Kang is quoted as saying he was concerned about California’s emergency systems being able to reach every community. “Later, while producing events at California’s fairgrounds, I saw something others had overlooked,” he said. “These public assets represented hundreds of acres of strategically located land throughout the state. They needed sustainable revenue, and California needed stronger emergency resilience. That realization became the foundation of Global Stack.” Vandenberg said Global Stack approached the Perris fairgrounds about the project during a regularly scheduled Sacramento gathering of fair executives. Besides Perris, Global Stack pursued similar projects at fairgrounds in Ventura County and Calistoga, but both projects faltered following local pushback. Global Stack also is seeking a project at the Cow Palace events venue near San Francisco. In all, Global Stack said it’s looking at projects at more than 50 potential sites that could lead to more than $20 million in infrastructure investment and create more than 70,000 jobs. Vandenberg said his board “was interested in discovering additional information” about the project and directed him to sign a nonbinding agreement so Global Stack could flesh out its plans for the fairgrounds. According to Vandenberg, Global Stack wants to develop 5 acres of the 110-acre fairgrounds property. Global Stack’s website describes the heliport as “supporting the everyday activity of a fairground and its surrounding community” and shifting to first-responder and medivac use in an emergency. The parking structure would be a moneymaker for the fairgrounds, Vandenberg said. “I can’t think of any fairgrounds in the state that couldn’t use a parking structure,” he said. “That would be a huge benefit if that was part of the project.” The data center would be about the size of a shipping container, according to Global Stack. “It’s not (one of) the mega type facilities that you might have heard of,” Vandenberg added. On its website, Global Stack said the data center would “process critical information locally, right where it is needed” and that data would be processed locally “rather than routed to facilities owned by out-of-state or international corporations.” Computer servers like those in data centers can generate heat. artigo.texto: Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled a package of legislative proposals to rein in the data center industry in Virginia, with goals to tighten environmental regulations, increase cost allocation for the industry, and make the proposal process more transparent by barring non-disclosure agreements between localities and data center developers. The plan does not include a moratorium on data center development while the details of the plan are refined, a step several environmental and advocacy groups and citizens have demanded in recent weeks. Dubbed the “Data Center Accountability Framework,” Spanberger’s plan outlines five pillars as key priorities: transparency, environmental protections, lowering energy costs, promoting clean energy, and focusing on local workers. “The Framework is a thorough plan to end data center secrecy, protect our environment, lower energy costs for families, bolster our clean energy economy, and make sure Virginia workers have the protections and assurances they deserve,” Spanberger said in a press conference to announce the plan at the Virginia State Capitol. Spanberger also signed Executive Order 22, which will kick-start her plans for clamping down on the industry ahead of the next legislative session that will begin in January 2027. Transparency Perhaps the most concrete of the directives is a measure to ban nondisclosure agreements between data centers and executive branch agencies, departments, state boards and commissions. It also bars these agencies from requiring such agreements for data center projects. The order does not impact the use of nondisclosure agreements by localities, but the governor said she plans to work with the General Assembly to pass a law banning the agreements at the local level. In the framework package, the governor also proposes eliminating by-right local approvals of data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power. Many counties statewide have taken steps towards requiring conditional use permits, which require public hearings and a vote of approval from local leaders. Additionally, the governor wants to remove data centers from Virginia’s fast-track permitting process that allows permit approvals for the projects to speed up when they are proposed in “business ready” locations. The fast-track process is a remnant of Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration, which encouraged and supported the rapid build out of the state’s data center industry as a means to boost Virginia’s business reputation. Environmental protections The framework directs lawmakers to develop policies to create standards for energy efficiency, water use and land impacts. Budget language that passed the General Assembly in June directed the Department of Environmental Quality to identify “water scarcity areas,” data centers’ water use for cooling could put drinking water availability at risk. Data centers located in those areas, mainly east of Interstate 95, will have to reduce their water use. The framework also outlines a plan to expedite noise regulations that were also in the budget language, but does not state when those regulations will be put into place. Currently, DEQ has until 2029 to research the lowest possible sound levels data centers could operate on and make that the standard across the board. Lower energy costs Spanberger’s new data center plan requires utilities to allocate more of the energy infrastructure costs largely spurred by data centers onto the industry. Dominion Energy has already taken action on this front, after the utility created a new rate class, GS5, which mostly includes data centers and large manufacturers. The State Corporation Commission approved the new rate class last November. Like the recommendations in the framework from the governor, the G5 rate class includes 14-year contracts, as well as specific cost allocations for energy generation, distribution, and transmission costs. The SCC also recently directed Dominion to create a new tariff to directly assign the cost of high-voltage transmission lines that are only necessary due to data centers to those customers. Spanberger supported the tariff, which is reflected in her framework. Tech giant Microsoft has already put the State Supreme Court on notice that it could appeal that order. Microsoft representatives said in an email last week that the company hopes “any rates ultimately put in place are transparent, fair and reflect the costs each customer creates.” But filing notice of appeal, they continued, “Microsoft preserves its ability to challenge any implementation that does not meet these expectations.” Elevating clean energy, hiring Virginia workers Another component of Spanberger’s plan looks to limit the amount of power data centers can produce on-site through natural gas generators and other “behind the meter” methods that don’t draw from the electric grid. The plan also proposes making it easier for data centers to bring clean energy options on-site by reforming utility charges for clean energy investments. PJM, the regional grid operator for 13 states including Virginia, recently proposed a new rule to direct data centers to pay for their power generation or cover their energy needs by backstop power purchases. This would help bring more power on the grid when it’s strained on very hot and cold days. Several recent proposals by data centers in the commonwealth show the industry’s growing interest in building its own gas turbines to power data facilities. That method skirts around the Virginia Clean Economy Act, which requires the retirement of carbon emitting power sources by utility companies by 2050. The framework prioritizes hiring local workers to build data centers and using local businesses for procurement and contractors. How to Achieve Sustainable Power Without Changing Your Existing Backup System
SCHWABMÜNCHEN, Germany, Sept. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CNTE has deployed a 700kW/1,624kWh battery energy storage system at an industrial facility in Schwabmünchen, Germany, integrating the site's existing 440kWp solar PV system, 500kW diesel generator and grid connection into a coordinated hybrid energy system.
The project was designed to address several practical challenges at the factory, including limited utilization of surplus solar generation, inefficient low-load diesel operation, high fuel and maintenance costs, and the need to maintain power continuity for production.
CNTE installed 7 STAR-H (100kW/232kWh) liquid-cooled energy storage units, managed through its Energy Management System (EMS). The EMS coordinates PV generation, battery storage, grid power and diesel generation according to site demand, enabling the factory to make more efficient use of its existing energy assets.
One of the key benefits is improved solar self-consumption. Instead of allowing surplus PV generation to go underutilized, the battery stores energy for use when demand rises, helping reduce electricity purchased from the grid. Based on project assumptions, the system could generate approximately €27,000 in potential additional energy-cost savings, alongside approximately 449MWh of annual solar generation.
The battery system also reduces reliance on diesel generation during power interruptions. In a representative two-hour outage scenario, the project estimates that storage could save approximately 254 liters of diesel, equivalent to around €570 in fuel costs. Beyond direct cost savings, the project supports the factory's broader sustainability objectives by increasing renewable-energy utilization and reducing unnecessary diesel consumption.
The Schwabmünchen project also demonstrates a practical model for industrial facilities that already operate solar and backup-generation assets. By adding battery storage and intelligent energy management, existing infrastructure can deliver greater economic value, improved energy resilience and lower fossil-fuel dependence without requiring a complete redesign of the site's power system.
About CNTE
CNTE is a global energy storage solution provider invested by CATL, serving utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential applications worldwide. The company combines R&D, intelligent manufacturing and localized service to support more efficient, resilient and lower-carbon energy use.

By adding battery storage and intelligent energy management, existing infrastructure can deliver greater economic value, improved energy resilience and lower fossil-fuel dependence without requiring a complete redesign of the site's power system.
About CNTE
CNTE is a global energy storage solution provider invested by CATL, serving utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential applications worldwide. The company combines R&D, intelligent manufacturing and localized service to support more efficient, resilient and lower-carbon energy use.

It is co-published here with permission. In January, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wisconsin) called data centers “exciting new technology” and voted for a federal bill to speed their construction. But by May, as he was running for governor of Wisconsin, he was promising to repeal the state tax breaks that lure them. And within a week of the Aug. 11 Democratic primary in the Badger State, Tiffany’s campaign was on the air branding his opponent “Data Center David Crowley”—a Republican attacking a Democrat for being too cozy with Big Tech. The ad focused on a statement Crowley gave at a candidate forum in November 2025 that Wisconsin had the opportunity to become a major artificial intelligence and data center hub “not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe and really sets us apart in making sure that we continue to invest in businesses and companies here.” But early this summer, Crowley began insisting that local communities should have absolute veto power to reject any such project and that data center developers should pay for all grid and infrastructure upgrades. Voters in the battleground state’s most important race could be forgiven for experiencing whiplash. Data centers are now what the Wisconsin Examiner called the biggest issue in the governor’s race, and the public has turned on them faster than on anything the state’s leading pollster has measured in 15 years. And Tiffany has navigated that turn to outflank Crowley with tougher rhetoric, his own reversal notwithstanding. A longtime fossil fuel supporter, Tiffany is also using the unpopularity of data centers in service of a much older fight against renewable sources of energy such as wind and solar. He recently called for the state to not close coal-fired plants, arguing that they “are a backbone of baseload power, and cannot simply be replaced with intermittent generation provided by wind and solar.” Nothing Has Moved This Fast “It’s been one of the fastest changes in public opinion that we’ve seen in Wisconsin,” Charles Franklin, director of the Marquette Law School Poll, told Capital & Main. “We’ve been doing the Marquette poll for 15 years, and in that time nothing else has moved this fast.” When Marquette first asked about data centers last October, 55% of registered voters said the costs of data centers outweighed the benefits. By February it was 70%, and by August 78%. What struck Franklin more was the absence of a partisan split: 54% of Republicans, 55% of independents and 56% of Democrats were all opposed last fall. “Almost nothing we see in Wisconsin shows that small a partisan gap,” Franklin said. That backlash reshaped the Democratic gubernatorial primary. At a Milwaukee town hall the week before the vote, five candidates competed to out-tough one another on the developers dubbed “Big Tech oligarchs” by Francesca Hong, a Democratic state representative who is also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America party and a gubernatorial candidate. Hong made a one-year moratorium on data centers the centerpiece of her campaign, but she lost the primary to Crowley. “Data Center David” Tiffany, who had reportedly hoped to run on economic issues, moved fast to claim the voters Hong had galvanized. He pledged to end the sales tax exemption the state legislature adopted for data centers—a break the Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimated could cost the state more than $2 billion. Crowley countered with accountability framing. “They have to pay their own way,” he said. “They need to pay for their own infrastructure, and they need to bring their own new clean energy.” Behind the ad copy, the two men actually agree on a lot. Neither supports Hong’s proposed moratorium. Both back the same guardrails: a ban on nondisclosure agreements between data center companies and local governments, a local veto over whether a project gets built and protection for residential rates. The general election is a contest over credibility and degree, not direction. What Crowley won’t do is promise to claw back the existing tax breaks, and that is the detail that Tiffany has zeroed in on. Tiffany’s central claim—that Crowley is “funded by the people building” data centers—is easy to misinterpret. The more than $350,000 in campaign contributions that an unnamed Tiffany spokeswoman cited to the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel came largely from building trades unions whose members would pour the concrete for data centers, not the tech companies that own the buildings. “David Crowley is honored to have the support of thousands of hard-working union members who are suffering from the affordability crisis MAGA extremist Tom Tiffany and Donald Trump created,” an unnamed Crowley spokesperson said in an email to Capital & Main. Campaign finance reports also showed donations to him from lobbyists for OpenAI and Oracle and a donation from Amazon, which is actively building data centers across the country. artigo.texto: Trump-Xi summit underscores risk of outright data center bans Former senators urge Congress to avoid ‘misguided panic’ in order to allow America to win AI race As President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet later this month, much of the attention will center on trade, tariffs and security. Behind those issues lies a larger competition that will determine the economic and military balance of power for decades to come: leadership in artificial intelligence (AI). While Beijing remains the top threat to American leadership in AI, an equally concerning wave of state and local data center bans is undercutting the infrastructure American AI and our digital lives require. These measures, while well-intentioned and based on real concerns that require a serious response, threaten our national security. In fact, more than 300 communities across 44 states have adopted moratoriums or bans on data centers, including one in five counties in Georgia. In July, New York became the first state to halt permits for large facilities. Texas has paused new grid connections while regulators audit the backlog. State legislatures have filed nearly 2,000 bills regulating AI. Meanwhile, China has made its intentions clear. Beijing’s new five-year plan sets a $1.4 trillion target for its AI industry and is preparing to double its national data center capacity by 2030. From our experiences on the Senate Intelligence and Budget Committees, we saw firsthand how our adversaries use technology to plot against us and how innovation drives our economy. Between us, we spent four decades in the Senate, a Georgia Republican and a North Dakota Democrat, and we disagreed on plenty. But we agree on this: outright bans on data centers pose an existential threat to American competitiveness and national security. A ban here does not stop AI from being built. It just means that communities will forfeit thousands of construction jobs, millions in tax revenue, and the economic growth a data center brings. To be sure, the communities enacting these restrictions have honest concerns about water usage, electricity consumption and siting issues associated with new data centers. Those anxieties are understandable and deserve straight answers and assurances from developers. But the good news is that the facilities being built today are increasingly environmentally efficient and effective job creators. For example, newer data centers employ closed-loop recycled water systems, which cut freshwater use by up to 70 percent. Microsoft’s latest data centers use the same amount of water annually as a single restaurant. The same principle applies to power. Initiatives like the Ratepayer Protection Pledge ensure that tech and data center developers, not residents, bear the burden of extra energy costs from data center infrastructure. The fears that AI will destroy employment opportunities overlook the massive blue-collar boom these facilities generate. Don Slaiman from the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) wrote in the New York Times that data center work will double union hours, and The Economist found that data center construction has helped create hundreds of thousands of new jobs since 2023, with many installation and maintenance positions paying roughly 40 percent more than comparable work elsewhere. Additionally, Meta’s $115 million investment in its Workforce Academy is helping train the workforce of the future. In Indianapolis, Baton Rouge, Houston and Columbus, alumni who entered the program with no previous experience are now working on critical job sites. Now, Lowe’s, Nvidia, Bank of America and more are teaming up to train 1 million plumbers, electricians and other skilled trade workers over the next decade. These investments are revitalizing the American workforce in communities that haven’t seen this kind of investment in decades. But private companies cannot overcome public policy barriers. Training workers can only create jobs if there are projects to put those skills to use. It’s time for all levels of government to work with the private sector instead of proposing bans on data centers. - To start, Congress should codify a unified national AI framework into law to prevent a patchwork of 50 conflicting state rules. - Next, federal and state agencies must fast-track the grid upgrades and data center permits that allow our new workforce to build the digital backbone of the future. - Finally, all levels of government must prioritize grid modernization. This includes onshoring turbine and transformer production, securing the grid from physical and cyber threats, streamlining permitting and expanding transmission capacity to build the AI infrastructure necessary to maintain American leadership. Winning the AI race will strengthen America’s economy, national security and technological independence for decades. We cannot let misguided anti-data center panic surrender our advantage. Kent Conrad represented North Dakota in the Senate from 1987 to 2013 as a Democrat. Saxby Chambliss represented Georgia in the Senate from 2003 to 2015 as a Republican. Both serve as advisers to the American Edge Project, which is supported by Meta and other domestic tech organizations.

artigo.texto: GK Energy Secures 150 MW Battery Storage Project From MSEDCL With ₹42.84 Crore Annual Revenue GK Energy has bagged a long-term domestic contract from MSEDCL to establish a 150 MW / 300 MWh battery storage project in Maharashtra. The utility contract features a fixed tariff of ₹2.38 lakh per MW per month, locking in predictable annual revenues of ₹42.84 crore (excluding GST) for a period of 15 years. Market snapshot: GK Energy Limited has secured a Letter of Award (LoA) from the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (MSEDCL) to develop a 150 MW / 300 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Maharashtra. Backed by Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support, the project is scheduled for commissioning within 18 months from the signing of the Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). Data Snapshot - Awarded a letter of award for setting up a 150 MW / 300 MWh Battery Energy Storage System in Maharashtra under Viability Gap Funding. - Fixed tariff rate of ₹2.38 lakh per MW per month, providing stable annual revenue of ₹42.84 crore excluding GST over 15 years. - Reported Q1 FY27 standalone revenue growth of 71% year-on-year to ₹505.19 crore, alongside a standalone net profit increase of 61.55% year-on-year to ₹59.67 crore. What's Changed - Order Book Diversification: GK Energy is expanding its portfolio into large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems, moving beyond its traditional core of decentralized solar pumps and rooftop solar solutions. - Extended Revenue Visibility: The 15-year contractual agreement locks in an annual recurring cash flow stream of ₹42.84 crore, enhancing long-term operational predictability. Key Takeaways - Structural Shift in Portfolio: Entering the high-growth utility-scale storage sector opens up new, larger addressable markets as India accelerates its renewable grid integration. - Predictable Long-Term Cash Flows: The monthly fixed-tariff payment model mitigates standard merchant power risk, ensuring predictable annuity-style revenues. - Robust Order Book Inflows: Coupled with the recent rooftop solar empanelment, GK Energy continues to scale up its outstanding order pipeline significantly in FY27. SAHI Perspective The award of this 150 MW / 300 MWh BESS project marks a strategic evolution for GK Energy. Historically focused on retail and agricultural solar execution, the transition to utility-scale grid infrastructure validates the company's scalability. Additionally, the project is structured with Viability Gap Funding support, which substantially de-risks the capital outlay required for high-capacity battery installations, ensuring healthy project IRRs. Market Implications The project underscores the accelerating momentum in India's battery energy storage segment. Large discoms like MSEDCL are aggressively building storage capacity to balance high-penetration renewable grids, creating multi-gigawatt opportunities for specialized clean energy EPC players like GK Energy. Trading Signals Market Bias: Bullish The BESS award establishes a high-margin, long-term annuity revenue stream of ₹42.84 crore annually for 15 years, complementing GK Energy's record-high Q1 FY27 standalone revenue growth of 71% year-on-year to ₹505.19 crore. Overweight: Renewable Energy, Power Infrastructure, Energy Storage Trigger Factors: - Timely signing of the formal BESPA agreement with MSEDCL within prescribed timelines. - Successful grid integration and commissioning of the BESS system within the 18-month execution window. - Working capital efficiency as the company handles multiple large-scale solar and storage projects simultaneously. Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months) Industry Context As India scales up its non-fossil fuel capacity toward the 500 GW target by 2030, battery storage infrastructure is turning critical for grid stability. Standard discom frameworks are rapidly incorporating BESS bids under regulatory guidelines to bridge solar-generation peaks and evening consumption surges. Key Risks to Watch - Execution timeline pressure, as the contract mandates completion within 18 months from the date of the BESPA signing. - Fluctuations in global battery cell chemistry prices, which could impact technology procurement margins during construction. - Risk of counterparty payment delays from state distribution utilities, although MSEDCL has historically managed disciplined payment cycles. Recent Developments In August 2026, GK Energy secured a ₹454.5 crore letter of empanelment to deploy 100 MW of rooftop solar systems across 1 lakh households. Earlier in July 2026, the company also bagged a ₹235.92 crore order from MSEDCL for 10,000 off-grid solar-powered water pumping systems. Closing Insight GK Energy's pivot to battery energy storage with the 150 MW MSEDCL win establishes a critical base of long-term recurring cash flows, indicating a successful diversification that pairs well with its massive solar pump and rooftop order book. artigo.texto: Acme Solar Holdings hit a fresh all-time high of ₹455.0 on the NSE on September 21, capping a run that has taken the stock up over 100% over eight months and almost 125% from its 52-week low of ₹195.65, touched on January 27. Over just the past six months, the return stands at 76.7%. Set against that: the Nifty 50 spent most of 2026 barely above the record it had already set in September 2024, weighed down by sustained FII selling, while the Nifty Midcap 100 has managed roughly 2% year-to-date and even the more richly rewarded Nifty Smallcap 100 sits at about 13%. Acme Solar's gain isn't just ahead of the market, it is several multiples ahead of even the best-performing broad index. In doing so, it has comprehensively outperformed peers as well, That scale of outperformance has invited scepticism at times, with Acme Solar's own market history showing why: the stock actually slipped on July 30, the day it reported its strongest quarter yet, as investors weighed rich valuation multiples and rapid cash burn against an aggressive expansion plan. What has changed since is not the narrative. The BESS pivot was flagged as early as April 2025, when CEO Nikhil Dhingra called hybrid and FDRE capacity "a critical pivot in our business strategy", but the evidence that the narrative is actually being executed, quarter after quarter and, increasingly, week after week. What the Q1 numbers actually said The July 30 print, unflattering stock reaction notwithstanding, was genuinely strong. Total revenue for Q1 FY27 came in at ₹954 crore, up 63% year-on-year; EBITDA rose 56% to ₹831 crore at an 87% margin; profit after tax jumped 80% to ₹235 crore. Capacity utilisation factors (CUF) hit a record 30.9%, up from 28.5% a year earlier. None of that was BESS alone, but BESS was doing disproportionate work inside those numbers. The company commissioned 2.3 GWh of battery storage in the quarter, taking cumulative commissioned capacity to 3.62 GWh, roughly 40% of all commissioned BESS capacity in India at the time. That capacity alone generated ₹226 crore of the quarter's ₹954 crore in revenue — about a quarter of the total, from a business line that barely existed eighteen months ago. Management also used the call to upgrade full-year guidance, telling analysts the company is now on track for more than 10 GWh of BESS capacity by FY27, pulled forward by nearly three quarters from the original schedule with 70-80% of that target already contracted and locking in more than ₹1,400 crore of near-term revenue at realisations of ₹8-10 per unit through the DEEP portal and HP-TAM markets. Chairman Manoj Upadhyay told the call the company intends to keep 10-12 GWh of BESS capacity available for the short-term market annually over the next five years, even as capex increasingly shifts toward PPA-backed long-term projects. September is where the promise turned into proof If the July call supplied the guidance, September supplied the proof of delivery. On September 16, Acme Solar commissioned 66.68 MW of solar capacity alongside 300 MWh of BESS in Rajasthan. On September 17, a subsidiary commissioned Phase-II of the BESS component of its SJVN-contracted FDRE project in Bikaner — 52.32 MW/209.28 MWh of the eventual 300 MW/1,200 MWh discharge capacity, with commercial operations dated September 19 and the remainder targeted for Q3 FY27. That single subsidiary now has 105.95 MW/423.80 MWh of BESS commissioned. The stock's jump to its record high including the spike on September 18 tracked directly to this run of operational updates, not to any new guidance or analyst upgrade. The market rewarding delivery, essentially in real time. That is the more interesting read on this rally than the headline return itself. Acme Solar isn't being re-rated because the BESS story is new; it's being re-rated because each quarter narrows the gap between what management said it would build and what has actually been switched on and started earning. For a sector where announced capacity and commissioned capacity routinely diverge by years, that gap-closing is, on its own, a data point worth more than the guidance slide it came from. The obvious caveat None of this makes Acme Solar's valuation cheap. At its current price-to-earnings ratio and a market capitalisation heading of over ₹32,000 crore, the stock is pricing in a great deal of future execution alongside the execution already delivered and has outpaced even analyst price targets, which were averaging around ₹428 against a stock now trading near ₹455, suggest the sell-side broadly agrees the easy re-rating has already happened. The next leg of this stock's story depends less on hitting the 10 GWh BESS targetwhich looks very doable, and more on what realisations look like once 10-12 GWh a year is actually competing for space in India's still-developing short-term power and ancillary services markets. Competitors like Adani Green Energy, ReNew and NTPC Green will have noticed, and it remains to be seen how fast they can 'pivot' to a BESS powered strategy yet.

artigo.texto: After the entry of several renewable energy companies into the Indian stock market, more renewable Independent Power Producers (IPPs) are now looking to jump onto the bandwagon. The latest entrant is Singapore-based Sembcorp’s Indian renewable energy arm, Sembcorp Green Infra. The company has proposed a ₹3,750-crore IPO at a time when it is expanding beyond conventional wind and solar projects into battery energy storage systems (BESS), round-the-clock (RTC) power, and firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) projects. Sembcorp Green Infra is preparing to tap the public markets with a ₹3,750-crore initial public offering, but the company's proposed use of the proceeds suggests that the issue is as much about strengthening its balance sheet as it is about supporting its next phase of growth. The proposed issue is entirely a fresh issue of equity shares. There is no offer-for-sale component. Of the proceeds, ₹3,000 crore is proposed to be used for repayment or prepayment of certain borrowings of the company and its subsidiaries, with the balance earmarked for general corporate purposes. The draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) was filed with SEBI in September. In the latest move, SEBI has now asked the company to furnish more details towards the issue, a procedural issue. Hybrid, RTC & FDRE Gain Ground The timing is significant. Sembcorp Green Infra is building a portfolio in which battery energy storage systems (BESS), hybrid projects, round-the-clock (RTC) power and firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) are becoming increasingly important. From wind and solar to dispatchable power Sembcorp Green Infra's India business had more than 7.6 GW/GWh of total capacity as of March 31, 2026, according to the company's website. Its portfolio spans 105 projects across 13 states and Union Territories, with more than 3.4 GW of solar capacity, more than 2.8 GW of wind capacity and more than 1.4 GWh of energy storage. The company describes itself as one of India's top 10 renewable independent power producers by operational capacity as of March 31, 2026. It also says it was among the country's top three wind operators among IPPs by operational capacity at that point. But the more important change is in the nature of the projects Sembcorp is pursuing. Instead of relying only on standalone solar and wind generation, the company is integrating storage with renewable generation to provide power in a more predictable manner. Sembcorp says its hybrid solutions are designed to provide round-the-clock clean energy. That puts BESS at the centre of the company's next growth phase. BESS becomes a bigger part of the portfolio Sembcorp's India portfolio already includes more than 1.4 GWh of energy storage. The company has been building its capabilities around projects where storage is combined with renewable generation rather than treated as a standalone asset. This matters because the emerging renewable market is increasingly moving towards projects that can deliver power when it is required, rather than simply generate electricity when the sun is shining or the wind is blowing. For Sembcorp, this creates an opportunity to combine its existing wind and solar portfolio with storage and build more complex power supply structures. The company's own description of its Indian business highlights the integration of energy storage with renewable generation as a means of providing round-the-clock clean energy. RTC and FDRE could drive the next project pipeline. The company's move towards RTC and FDRE projects is part of the same shift. RTC projects require renewable generation to be structured around a contracted supply profile, while FDRE projects go a step further by combining renewable generation and enabling technologies such as storage to provide power in a more firm and dispatchable manner. For an IPP such as Sembcorp, these projects can require significantly more complex project design than a conventional solar or wind farm. They can involve multiple generation technologies, storage and sophisticated scheduling and dispatch arrangements. The proposed IPO therefore comes at an important point for the company. The ₹3,000 crore debt repayment is not earmarked directly for building new BESS or renewable projects. Instead, reducing borrowings can strengthen the company's balance sheet as it continues to develop and finance a portfolio that is becoming more capital intensive. That distinction is important. The IPO itself is not a ₹3,750-crore project-funding programme. It is primarily a fresh-equity raise with a large debt-repayment component. IPO as a balance-sheet reset For Sembcorp Green Infra, therefore, the ₹3,750-crore IPO is best viewed in two parts. The first is straightforward: ₹3,000 crore is intended for debt repayment or prepayment. The second is strategic. Sembcorp is increasingly positioning its Indian business around a combination of solar, wind and storage, with hybrid, RTC and FDRE projects forming a more important part of its portfolio. The company already has more than 7.6 GW/GWh of capacity across its Indian platform and more than 1.4 GWh of energy storage. Its stated strategy of integrating storage with renewable generation points towards a business model where the ability to deliver power reliably could become as important as adding renewable megawatts. That makes the proposed IPO less about directly funding another tranche of solar or wind capacity and more about strengthening the financial platform from which Sembcorp can pursue a more complex renewable portfolio. For India's renewable market, that shift is worth watching. As the sector moves from simply adding generation capacity towards providing firm and dispatchable clean power, the companies that can combine renewable generation, storage and long-term contracted supply will increasingly operate in a different segment of the market. Sembcorp's IPO is coming at precisely that transition point.

artigo.texto: Envision Energy has energised Morocco’s first large-scale lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery energy storage system, but the 25 MW/125 MWh project at OCP Green Energy’s Benguerir mining site is designed for a role that goes beyond conventional grid-scale storage. The five-hour BESS is being deployed as an industrial energy-management system, integrating with the mining site's solar generation, grid conditions and electricity consumption profile. The system will store surplus solar power generated during the day and discharge it during peak consumption hours, with Envision expecting it to reduce OCP's peak-hour electricity bill by approximately 25%. The project, supplied and commissioned by Envision under a contract signed in late 2025, is currently undergoing testing before commercial operation. Five hours of storage changes the use case At 125 MWh, the system has five hours of storage duration at its 25 MW power rating. This allows the battery to shift a significant amount of daytime solar generation into periods when the industrial facility's electricity demand is higher. That makes the economic proposition different from a short-duration BESS primarily deployed for grid balancing or ancillary services. For OCP, the value of the battery is tied directly to how much renewable electricity can be shifted and how much peak-hour power costs can be avoided. Envision said the system is designed for a 25-year lifetime with daily charge-discharge cycles. The project has received $20 million from the Clean Technology Fund, managed through the African Development Bank Group. “The successful energisation of Morocco's first large-scale battery storage project demonstrates the reliability, flexibility and cost-effectiveness of integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions in industrial applications,” said John Lee, General Manager of Envision Energy for the Middle East and Africa. Storage becomes an extension of OCP's renewable strategy For OCP Green Energy, the battery is intended to address one of the central challenges of renewable power: solar generation does not necessarily coincide with industrial electricity demand. Omar Kadir, CEO of OCP Green Energy, described storage as the “natural extension” of the company's energy strategy, saying it allows the company to reconcile variable renewable generation with the continuous electricity requirements of its industrial operations. The project is therefore less about simply adding 125 MWh of battery capacity and more about connecting renewable generation with an industrial load that requires power beyond daylight hours. The company also sees storage as having implications beyond its own operations, with Kadir saying the technology could support greater integration of renewable energy into Morocco's national power system by adding flexibility and resilience. A potential model for industrial decarbonisation The Benguerir project could serve as a reference point for the use of long-duration storage at energy-intensive industrial facilities, particularly where companies are increasing their reliance on renewable electricity but still face a mismatch between generation and consumption. Morocco is targeting 52% of installed electricity capacity from renewable sources by 2030, making the ability to manage variable renewable generation increasingly important. For Envision, the project also provides an opportunity to demonstrate its storage technology in an industrial environment in the Middle East and Africa. The immediate commercial objective, however, remains specific: use solar power when it is generated, store the surplus and deploy it when the mine needs it most. That makes the Benguerir BESS not just a grid battery, but a tool for managing the economics and reliability of renewable power at one of Morocco's major industrial sites.

artigo.texto: The Scoop The data center buildout is driving a rush of venture capital investment in clean tech, breathing new life into startups that were at risk of being steamrolled by the Trump administrationâs pullback on climate policy. Global climate tech venture investment hit $26 billion in the first half of this year, 55% above the previous year, according to climate tech finance tracker Currence.ai. Data centers and the products and services that help them operate are in particularly high demand, with startups in the sector seeing their fundraising and valuations jump. Itâs an opportunity to push some new carbon-cutting tech across the âvalley of deathâ between pilot and commercial scale, to the benefit of the global energy transition at large â but also links clean techâs fortunes to a digital infrastructure buildout whose ultimate scale remains uncertain. âVenture capital sees the data center opportunity, and is focused on it,â Frank OâSullivan, managing director for energy at VC firm S2G Investments, told Semafor. âThereâs an opportunity over the next little while to see a lot more clean tech success stories emerge. The risk is that the driver of all of this â the data center bubble â might pop.â In this article: Timâs view This week, climate tech investors will descend en masse on New York for Climate Week, a forum for a vast range of cutting-edge firms to show off and find money. As political support for decarbonizing the existing energy system has dried up, data centers have emerged as a new center of financial gravity, drawing in unprecedented billions from the biggest tech and Wall Street firms. Much, perhaps most, of that investment is going into conventional energy assets that are not necessarily climate-friendly. But with AI companies under intense pressure to reduce their resource consumption â for reasons of cost, if nothing else â a lot is trickling down to tech originally conceived for the energy transition. âWeâre experiencing a very hot time for a bunch of the stuff we were already in,â said Tom Chi, founding partner of clean tech investor At One Ventures, which focuses on deep tech innovations with environmental benefits. Thatâs setting up potential new windfalls for shops like his: One company in Chiâs portfolio, Blue Energy, a startup building low-cost modular components for advanced nuclear plants aimed at drastically cutting the amount of time needed to build them for data centers, has seen its pre-IPO valuation shoot up by orders of magnitude. That type of growth acts like a beacon to other non-energy investors, and suddenly Chi has found his companiesâ funding rounds increasingly crowded. âItâs a really weird moment because weâre having a bunch of tourists come in,â he said. âWeâre investing alongside firms that have spent their entire history doing enterprise SaaS, and now theyâre sitting here trying to understand desiccants for cooling systems.â Conversely, the focus on AI-relevant technologies is pushing climate tech VCs to look in unusual directions: S2G recently invested in Alliance North America, which makes high-end, low-emissions diesel generators. A technology that facilitates fossil fuel consumption âdoesnât seem like it would be in our bailiwick,â OâSullivan said. But because of its use for powering data centers more efficiently, âthat has mushroomed into an enormous opportunity, and suddenly youâre decarbonizing by stealthâ relative to conventional generators. Room for Disagreement More capital is usually welcome, Chi said. But firms with less experience, and less in-house engineering expertise, can have unrealistic expectations about the time, capital, and skill required to bring a novel hard tech to scale and profitability compared to software â which could ultimately lead to disappointment and cutbacks. Itâs also likely that as the space becomes more crowded, more mistakes will be made, inflating the valuations of companies that donât really have a strong business model when you get down to the nuts and bolts, and creating conditions for spectacular failures. And if clean tech startups are only valuable when they have data centers as primary customers, some technologies that are important for emissions reduction will fall through the cracks: VC investment in carbon management tech and low-carbon fuels both plummeted this year, according to Currence.ai. Notable - Republican regulators in North Carolina moved to block a gas-fired power plant for an Amazon data center. The project would run contrary to Trumpâs Ratepayer Protection Pledge, they said.

artigo.texto: Data centers – Em menos de uma década, o consumo de gás natural pelos data centers dos Estados Unidos poderá ultrapassar a demanda registrada pela Alemanha e pelo Japão somados. A previsão consta de um levantamento publicado pela Bloomberg na última segunda-feira (14). De acordo com a estimativa, a estrutura necessária para manter em funcionamento os data centers voltados à inteligência artificial deverá consumir 18 bilhões de pés cúbicos de gás natural por dia nos EUA até 2035. O volume é quase duas vezes maior que a previsão feita no começo de 2026, indicando uma expansão significativa do número de instalações no país ao longo deste ano. LEIA: OpenAI revela 6 casos de comportamentos inesperados de suas IAs Preços em alta nos próximos anos Empresas como Google, Meta, Microsoft e Amazon já utilizam o gás natural como uma opção para gerar eletricidade continuamente e reduzir os riscos de interrupções associados à geração eólica e solar. A fonte também é utilizada para abastecer as próprias estruturas de geração. • Como algumas dessas companhias estão aplicando recursos na construção de usinas termelétricas dentro dos próprios data centers, o relatório calcula que entre 2,9 e 3,4 bilhões de pés cúbicos por dia sejam consumidos exclusivamente nessas instalações; • O volume corresponde a quase toda a demanda atual de gás da infraestrutura de data centers dos EUA; • Com isso, a expansão da demanda poderá produzir efeitos sobre o mercado em geral, pressionando os preços do gás natural nos próximos anos; • O impacto não ficaria restrito ao setor de tecnologia: empresas que utilizam essa fonte de energia e até os consumidores deverão ser afetados. A questão ambiental também é apontada pela publicação. A partir das projeções de consumo, o levantamento estima 1 milhão de toneladas métricas adicionais de gases de efeito estufa emitidas por dia em razão da demanda dos data centers, o equivalente a aproximadamente 12% das emissões registradas atualmente no país. A BloombergNEF, responsável pelo estudo, destaca que as projeções apresentam margens de erro “grandes”, devido à imprevisibilidade e às demais variáveis envolvidas. Dessa maneira, o resultado real pode ser ainda maior do que o calculado ou ficar abaixo do projetado. artigo.texto: Elevated Materials receives $50 million from DOE for battery manufacturing The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has selected battery component developer Elevated Materials for federal funding, granting the Californian firm $50 million to support the development of a new facility on American shores. Elevated Materials representatives say the new facility will have an annual manufacturing capacity of about 3.5 GW, with the firm producing ultra-thin lithium films for next-generation battery products. With a total price tag of $100 million, the funding will fund about half of the facility’s total construction and early operations. The new facility is expected to accelerate Elevated Materials’ path to achieving gigawatt-hour-scale for both production and commercialization of its products. The firm aims to create a new domestic source of ultra-thin lithium-metal films and prelithiated materials, in turn enabling higher energy batteries that charge faster than ever. “The United States has made advanced battery manufacturing a national priority, and securing a domestic supply of critical materials that significantly increases energy density is central to that effort,” says Elevated Materials CEO Jim Cushing. “We developed this technology in California with support from DOE R&D programs and are proud to have been selected by the Department of Energy to now ramp it up to giga-watt scale.” Bringing the next generation to the U.S. market Elevated Materials was among a group of seven companies that the DOE chose for a combined $500 million in funding. As the federal agency aims to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing and reduce reliance on international supply chains, the department’s Battery Materials Processing and Battery Manufacturing Grants program has become a high priority. The new facility will be a core part of the U.S.’s battery production supply chain going forward, according to officials from Elevated Materials officials. The firm’s roll-to-roll vacuum deposition platforms will manufacture its ELi brand of ultra-thin lithium metal films. From there, the ELi products will enable “next-generation anode architectures” across a number of markets, including grid-scale energy storage, EVs, consumer electronics, and defense applications. “Demand has been particularly strong for lithium metal anodes, where ELi significantly improves both safety and performance,” the company says in a recent news release. “Over the past year, Elevated has achieved record output of ultra-thin lithium metal films, shipping over 250,000 meters of material to more than 30 customers worldwide.”

artigo.texto: ST. LOUIS — Mayor Cara Spencer Thursday signed a bill that tightens regulations on major data center developments as St. Louis faces a $3 billion proposal for the former Famous-Barr building. Spencer said Bill 49 provides neighborhood safeguards such as setback requirements for homes, schools, parks and transit hubs. It also includes comprehensive environmental standards, including a renewable energy scaling model, limits on noise and water usage, and prohibitions on evaporating cooling systems. “This bill sets forward a transparent, standardized framework with upfront exact application requirements, ensuring that projects are evaluated against the same benchmark from day one,” Spencer said. Major developers also will need to hold early public community meetings and sign public impact agreements with the city for infrastructure upgrades, safety and neighborhood welfare improvements. “We’ve made it clear that St. Louis not only expects new data centers to run on renewable energy, but also that developers invest their resources to expand clean energy infrastructure and to innovate in ways that protect the air that we breathe and the water that we drink,” Aldermanic President Megan Green said. Bill 55 also passed, Green said, which states that the city will not incentivize data center projects with local tax breaks. A regulation that was important to AFT St. Louis, Local 420. She added that this “gives a clear message that we expect them to pay their fair share of taxes from day one.” City officials thanked everyone who worked on the data center regulations. Spencer also acknowledged the thousands of emails and phone calls from residents regarding the bill. “We thank you for your continued participation, your continued advocacy, your continued questions, your continued concerns as we lean in this together,” Spencer said. Officials say the large-scale data center proposed for the former Famous-Barr would create jobs and draw tens of millions of dollars to the city and school district annually. Spencer said she did not have a timeline or an update on the project.

artigo.texto: Why Should Delaware Care? A proposed data center near Newark drew criticism from local residents about the facility’s potential to raise electric bills and damage the environment. It now appears that part of the site will instead host the Christina School District’s Networks Schools for Employable Skills. For months, Newark-area residents have voiced concerns about a proposed data center near the town border, saying it would use too much water and energy and be too noisy. Two months after New Castle County Councilman Tim Sheldon brokered a handshake deal to pause the project, it appears the property’s management company may be moving forward with different plans for at least some of the site. Earlier this month, New York-based developer Shelbourne submitted plans to the county to convert half of an existing building in the White Clay Center, a Newark-area industrial and office park, into a 10-classroom vocational technical school. If the application is approved, the building would be part of Christina School District’s Networks Schools for Employable Skills, according to letters submitted to the county as part of the application. The Networks School focuses on teaching students with individualized education plans (IEPs) “real-world job skills.” Norma Brister, the principal of the Networks School for Employable Skills, told Spotlight Delaware the space would not mark an expansion of the school. Instead, it would allow the school to be housed at one location. Brister said the school is currently located at 30 Blue Hen Drive and also has four “enterprise areas” roughly 4 miles away at the Shue-Medill Middle School. During an August board meeting, Christina school board members approved an agenda item to relocate the school as soon as January 2027. Although an exploratory site plan was submitted on behalf of the school earlier this month, that does not mean the deal has been finalized. What happened to the data center plans? Shelbourne originally planned to demolish the existing White Clay Center office and industrial buildings and construct a three-building data center campus totaling 850,000 square feet. Those plans were previously wrapped into a larger community backlash in Delaware against the growth of the data center industry, which is booming across the country because of the promises of artificial intelligence technology. According to an email exchange between Sheldon and land use attorney Shawn Tucker, the deal depended on the county’s all-but-guaranteed approval of an exploratory plan application from the developer, which would grandfather the land into zoning rules that existed prior to this year. That means the developer would not have to follow the county’s recently-passed data center regulations if the developer ultimately decides to build a data center there. But the data center plan has not yet been approved by the county. The county’s planning department submitted additional comments about the plan last month, including asking the developer to confirm there is enough energy supply to serve the site. Sheldon said the developer is still trying to get the data center plan approved while also seeking out other tenants for the vacant buildings in the business park. “They’re not pushing it, but they’ve gotta keep their options open,” he said.

artigo.texto: A Fraunhofer IEE study, commissioned by BSW-Solar, identifies 150 GW of additional PV potential in Germany with the addition of BESS across 1,313 substations Batteries can shift solar output away from periods when transformers reach their operating limits, according to the study The modeled 150 GW potential would require around 60 GW/240 GWh of battery storage under the study’s reference scenario Germany could potentially accommodate 150 GW of additional solar PV through the use of smart battery storage at existing substations, according to a Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Economics and Energy System Technology (IEE) study, commissioned by the German Solar Association (BSW-Solar). Currently, the country targets to achieve 215 GW of solar PV capacity by 2030. It exceeded 129 GW at the end of August 2026 (see Germany’s August 2026 Solar Installations Exceed 1.6 GW). The study identifies this technical potential across 1,313 rural substations with high renewable generation. It estimates that around 60 GW/240 GWh of battery storage would be needed under its reference scenario. The analysis starts from the observation that transformers do not operate at their rated capacity throughout the year. Moreover, electricity demand, wind generation and solar output vary by time, leaving transmission capacity unused during many periods. Intelligently controlled large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) located directly at a substation could then charge when local solar generation pushes power flows toward the transformer limit. It could then release the stored electricity later. This, according to the analysts, would allow more efficient use of existing transformer capacity, relieving the load on the substations. As a result, on an annual average, only about one percent of the additionally generated solar power would need to be curtailed due to transformer capacity limits, according to the study. The analysts offer this conclusion after analyzing data from 20 transformers at 13 substations operating in the networks of Pfalzwerke Netz and Westnetz. The transformers had capacities ranging from 15 to 80 MVA, with simulations based on hourly data for 2025. “If storage systems charge where and when peaks in solar power generation occur, they can specifically alleviate grid bottlenecks and enable the integration of additional solar power. This could lead to savings of billions in grid expansion costs, among other benefits,” said Carsten Körnig, CEO of BSW-Solar. The association says the findings are relevant to the Bundestag’s proposed Grid Package which aims to better coordinate renewable energy, storage and grid expansion. BSW-Solar argues that the government must ensure that existing grid capacity is used more efficiently alongside further grid expansion. It also wants the administration to designate grid bottleneck areas only after grid operators have implemented digitalization of medium- and high-voltage networks and conducted feasible storage tenders.

artigo.texto: By Mitch Perry, The Florida Phoenix David Jolly has already made it clear he’s a critic of large-scale data centers, for which Floridians continue to express disapproval up and down the state. The Democratic gubernatorial candidate had already said that if elected in November, he’d issue a one-year moratorium on construction of these facilities. But after visiting a region of Northern Virginia this week with the highest density of data centers in the country, he says he’s seen first-hand the economic and public health disruption they inflict on communities and that it’s not what he wants to see in the Sunshine State. “I visited a family with a home, you open the door and you’re hit with the noise pollution,” he said Friday after attending an event with Habitat for Humanity in Pinellas County. “You walk outside, you see the turbines that are fueling the energy. Down the street, there were four kids who developed respiratory conditions who had to seek medical help.” Data centers also are deflating real estate prices in their communities, Jolly said. He learned of a home near a massive data center that sat on the market for nearly a year and ended up selling for $80,000 below list price. “Let’s be honest about what’s happening in Florida,” he said. “Big tech, big data, the utilities are rushing into a relatively unregulated environment, or at least a favorably regulated environment. And that’s why you’re seeing voters who feel like they don’t have the economic or political power to push back, stand up, and say, ‘Please don’t do this.’ Local communities in Florida continue to say they don’t want data centers. This week, the Orange County Commission advanced a plan to temporarily ban data center development. Commissioners reached a consensus for a 6-to-18 month moratorium, depending on how long county staff need to research the potential harms, according to Orlando Weekly. Three local governments in Florida have permanently banned construction of data centers, and 19 are pausing such development, according to FloridaDataCenters.org. Already operating However, 12 data centers are already operating in Florida and another eight are planned, according to Cleanview, a marketing intelligence company. The Florida Legislature approved and Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation earlier this year that bans public utilities from passing the electricity costs of data centers onto residential and small business customers. It also preserved local authority over zoning, permitting, and land use for such centers, and gives local governments authority to set strict standards or deny projects. Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has expressed support for letting local governments decide whether they want to construct data centers. He has dismissed Jolly’s one-year moratorium as “politics.” And Donalds said in Tampa earlier this month that construction of data centers would not resemble what Jolly visited this week. “In Northern Virginia, they built them next to apartment complexes and residential neighborhoods,” he said. “We’re not going to allow that in Florida. … If you’re going to do it, just do it a couple of miles down the road. Don’t do it in residential neighborhoods.” Advocates for data centers say they are needed in the United States, lest this country lose the race for AI superiority to China. The strongest advocate for that position is President Donald Trump. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing data center-related proposals covering at least 17,600 acres of public land across six states — Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming, the Washington Sun reported Friday. Jolly says he’s perfectly fine if the other 49 states build data centers — just not Florida. “There is no long-term economic impact from the data centers. There is the upfront construction jobs, but that there’s not the legacy economic impact that actually justifies the disruption of a community,” he said. “Look I do think that our national policymakers do need to work through some things to the extent that it’s a national security strategy. Let the White House and the Congress figure it out. But as Florida and Florida voters, we’re saying don’t build them here, let the other 49 states build them. It doesn’t hurt our national security strategy to say no to data centers in Florida.” The Donalds campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

artigo.texto: Entidades pressionam Confaz por redução de ICMS para data centers após sanção do Redata Manifesto reúne CNI, Brasscom, Conexis, TelComp e outras associações em defesa de convênio nacional para equipamentos destinados ao setor Um grupo de entidades empresariais e setoriais pediu aos Estados e ao Distrito Federal que aprovem, no âmbito do Confaz, um convênio para reduzir o ICMS incidente sobre bens e equipamentos destinados à implantação, expansão e modernização de data centers. A reivindicação foi apresentada em manifesto divulgado após a sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), que reduziu a tributação federal sobre investimentos no setor. O regime foi instituído pela Lei nº 15.504, sancionada em 15 de setembro. Assinam o documento entidades como CNI, Brasscom, Conexis, TelComp, ABDC, ABES, Assespro, Fecomercio SP, Firjan, NEO e Associação Brasil Digital, além de outras organizações ligadas a tecnologia, telecomunicações e infraestrutura digital. O argumento central é que, sem uma medida coordenada sobre o ICMS, a redução dos tributos federais promovida pelo Redata não seria suficiente para colocar o Brasil em condições mais competitivas na disputa internacional por investimentos em data centers. “O Redata é uma realidade, e o Convênio do Confaz é uma necessidade”, afirma o manifesto. Entidades dizem que ICMS pesa sobre investimento Segundo as signatárias, o ICMS responderia por 64% da carga tributária incidente sobre o investimento inicial, ou CAPEX, de um data center. O percentual é apresentado pelas próprias entidades no manifesto. Com base nessa avaliação, o grupo defende que os Estados adotem uma política coordenada para reduzir a tributação estadual sobre os equipamentos empregados nos empreendimentos. Para as entidades, um convênio nacional teria ainda a função de reduzir diferenças tributárias entre Estados e dar maior previsibilidade às empresas sobre a carga incidente nos investimentos. O texto sustenta que uma solução negociada dentro do Confaz seria preferível a iniciativas estaduais isoladas, por evitar uma disputa de incentivos fiscais entre unidades da Federação. “O Brasil deu um passo decisivo. Agora, é essencial que os Estados completem esse avanço”, dizem as entidades. Redata concentrou benefício nos tributos federais O Redata instituiu benefícios sobre tributos federais incidentes na aquisição doméstica e na importação de determinados componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados ao ativo imobilizado dos data centers. A legislação prevê, entre outros instrumentos, suspensão de PIS/Pasep e Cofins e dos respectivos tributos incidentes na importação, além de IPI e, nas condições previstas em lei, Imposto de Importação. A adesão ao regime depende do cumprimento de contrapartidas. Entre elas está a obrigação de disponibilizar ao mercado interno ao menos 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados instalada com os benefícios do programa. O desenho federal, entretanto, não elimina por si só a incidência do ICMS, tributo estadual. É justamente essa parcela que as entidades querem incorporar à política de estímulo por meio de um acordo no Confaz. Manifesto relaciona medida à competição internacional As entidades argumentam que a decisão precisa ser tomada enquanto cresce a disputa internacional por novos projetos de infraestrutura computacional. No manifesto, afirmam que investimentos globais estão sendo direcionados a países que ofereçam condições tributárias, regulatórias e energéticas competitivas e previsíveis. Também relacionam a expansão dos data centers a atividades como computação em nuvem, telecomunicações, serviços financeiros, saúde, pesquisa, governo digital e processamento de alta capacidade. A avaliação das signatárias é que a construção desses empreendimentos também mobiliza investimentos em energia, redes de telecomunicações, equipamentos, construção civil e serviços especializados. Com isso, o grupo pede que o Confaz autorize uma redução de ICMS aplicável aos equipamentos utilizados em novos projetos, ampliações e modernizações de data centers. Frente pela redução reúne telecom e tecnologia Entre as signatárias estão a Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES), Brasscom, Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), Conexis, TelComp, Associação NEO, Fecomercio SP, Firjan, Fenainfo, Assespro, ABEP-TIC, Associação Brasil Digital e dig.ia. O movimento ocorre poucos dias depois da sanção do Redata e desloca a discussão tributária para os Estados. A decisão sobre eventual benefício de ICMS, contudo, depende de negociação no Confaz. Até que um convênio seja aprovado, os incentivos assegurados pelo novo regime permanecem concentrados na esfera federal. *Com assessoria de imprensa

artigo.texto: EVEO amplia operação no Nordeste com data center em Recife Nova região amplia presença iniciada em Fortaleza; empresa recebeu aporte de R$ 100 milhões e mira R$ 500 milhões em receita até 2030. A EVEO vai ampliar sua presença no Nordeste com a ocupação do novo data center Tier III em Recife, construído pela Atlantic Data Centers (V.tal). A operação se soma à infraestrutura mantida pela empresa em Fortaleza desde 2024 e faz parte do plano de expansão regional da companhia. A base de clientes da EVEO no Nordeste cresceu 62% no último ano e acumula alta de 272% desde o início da operação regional, em 2024. Em 2026, o volume de novos negócios na região supera o registrado no mesmo período de 2025, segundo a empresa. A demanda está concentrada em servidores dedicados, private cloud e capacidade computacional com GPUs para aplicações de IA. A intenção da companhia é aproximar a infraestrutura dos clientes e reduzir a dependência de atendimento a partir de outras regiões. Recife será nova região de operação A entrada em Recife já vinha sendo preparada pela EVEO. Em março, a companhia informou que a capital pernambucana faria parte da próxima etapa de expansão geográfica, após a abertura de Fortaleza e o avanço da operação internacional em Miami. Com a nova unidade, a empresa passa a contar com presença em dois polos do Nordeste. Recife está a cerca de 800 quilômetros de Fortaleza, distância que pesa em aplicações mais sensíveis à latência e na oferta de infraestrutura local para empresas da região. Expansão também avança fora do Nordeste O movimento em Recife ocorre em paralelo à ampliação da capacidade da companhia em outras regiões. Em julho, a EVEO anunciou a contratação de 100 novos racks na unidade SPO02 da Ascenty, em Osasco, destinados principalmente a cargas de IA, private cloud e servidores dedicados. A expansão é apoiada por um aporte de R$ 100 milhões recebido da XP Asset em 2026. Segundo a empresa, os recursos estão sendo direcionados à compra de equipamentos, aumento de capacidade e expansão das operações no Brasil e no exterior. Ao fim de 2025, a EVEO informou ter alcançado R$ 100 milhões em receita recorrente anualizada, o ARR. A companhia mantém a meta de chegar a R$ 500 milhões em receita até 2030. Escritório regional também cresce A presença no Nordeste inclui ainda um escritório em João Pessoa, inaugurado em 2025 como a primeira unidade regional da empresa fora de São Paulo. Em julho deste ano, a operação foi transferida para um espaço maior na capital paraibana, acompanhando o crescimento da equipe local e da base de clientes na região. A chegada a Recife amplia a estratégia de descentralização da EVEO, que hoje mantém operações de data center em São Paulo, Curitiba, Fortaleza e Miami e vem expandindo capacidade para atender cargas de processamento, nuvem privada e aplicações de IA. (Com assessoria de imprensa)
